She touches the mark only before an opening --- not at a bank, not at the reading on Account-day --- and moves her lips along the loaves so the days to Kindling are a shape no collector can take up. She stands a half-pace from every open slate in the yard and at the Cross, refuses a neighbour a number with \emph{the house} and \emph{ask the pot}, and carries the basket down and back saying nothing about where they have been or what was read over him. On Stone 19 she moves the basket out of a draught without looking at his face and calls it nothing; she measures the Ash by thumb and leaves both ridges for the Last Day. The crust in the fold goes cold and stays where it was put. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour with the slate, the clerk’s soft sentence, the figure at the moot and the number her son will not speak, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 15 through 24 the keeping takes the measure of a tend and a year. The rule of the mark holds before each opening and at no bank or reading; the household’s number lives in loaves moved along a shelf, in the space at the end of the kindling and in a fist shut on a door-latch, and she will not say it even when the district gives out three and then two. She sends Tarn for a collector and carries the boy to the neighbour’s room, setting him where he can see and not join, with a half-pace kept from the open slate. At the Last Day’s sweeping she measures the ridge against the death-house’s with a thumb laid flat first, and lets the woman at the tubs say the grey will be left and burned and called dealt with. On Stone 30 she carries him down to the year’s last market for a reading and not an opening, stands a half-pace off with her burn shut, and brings him back under the roof to his bed, banked coals and two crusts in the fold she has neither named nor removed. The wall has acquired no door in ten days: it keeps out the neighbour with the fist, the clerk’s soft sentence, the figure read over the basket and the number Tarn will not speak, and keeps the boy warm without entering the warmth.

On Days 25 through 30 the keeping takes the measure of the Five and crosses the turn of the year. The year’s fire comes into the house in a clay dish from hands along the yard, and she touches the mark once before the opening and at no other hour --- a rule that holds as exactly on Ilmen 1, where there is no opening, as it held inside Y.H. 812. She says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, gives every instruction to the fire and the wool, and enters neither the flame nor its payer. At the Weighing she keeps her half-pace from the slates and does not repeat the name the clean voice reads; at the Long Night she banks the fire and keeps the dark with stories; at the Remembering she goes around Garl’s name as around Ash left in a corner; on the Last Day she measures both ridges with one thumb and will not let the grey be swept early. On Ilmen 1 a neighbour calls the burned Ash dealt with, and she does not; the coals stay banked, the mark stays untouched, the two crusts stay in the fold, and she carries the keeping into 813 without explaining any of it. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the payer of the warmth, the name read at the Weighing, the reading in the next room and the year the district has already entered on its slates, and keeps the boy warm without entering the warmth.

On Days 31 through 37 the keeping takes the measure of the first warm days of the new year and adds no explanation. She says \emph{the house} and gives every instruction to the fire, the bucket and the wool; the half-pace from Alda and the turned slate stand in for the arrangement again; the widow’s mark is touched before the opening on Ilmen 6 and at no other hour, not at the bank, not for a date, not for a nearly full sound. She feeds him from the house’s own dish, puts the fold right without looking at his face, neither takes out nor names either crust, and carries him three doors down to the shade of the nineteen steps and back up the yard at dusk. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the payer of the warmth, the fourth note under a floorboard, the number in a fist at the well and the cough three doors down that everybody calls weather.

On Days 38 through 44 the keeping takes the measure of a death the Court does not enter and adds no explanation. She holds the basket on the bank with her feet apart in the wet clay while the yard lifts Dessa Silt out with their hands, and turns the boy’s face toward what is being done rather than away. She does not send for a collector and nobody remarks on it; the household goes to the fire and to its buckets instead, and warmth left where it fell and the morning came. On Ilmen 11 she measures the clean dark line where the Vail Ash turned its corner against the ridge two doors down, lays one thumb in each and carries the knowledge back without saying which was which; she does not fetch a broom. On Ilmen 13 she fetches a clay jar from House Silt, sets the basket just inside a door standing a finger’s width open, opens no slate and turns no errand into a visit to a bank, then sets the jar on the shelf by the wall at home. On Ilmen 14 and 15 she carries the boy upriver and leaves him in shade where no slate lies, stands a half-pace off a woman with a slate under her arm on the way home, and sets him on his bed at dusk with the fold put right and no look at his face. The private roll stays unshown, the wall acquires no door, and she has said nothing about the payer of any warmth or the woman in the water.

On Days 45 through 47 the keeping takes the measure of three days after the blessing and adds no explanation. She carries him under the north bridge and back at a half-pace from every open slate and sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without a look at his face. The mark is touched once before the opening on Day 45 and at no other hour --- not at a dusk bank, not for a date, not for a nearly full sound, not for the carrying of a basket. The month’s days go around in loaves moved along a shelf, a glance at the clay jar on the wall shelf and the space where a loaf should stand; at the well she goes around an open slate as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it over, and tells a neighbour the house sent the number up the road. She feeds him from the house’s own dish and does not say who paid for the milk. She does not touch the mark when the smoky crust goes out of the fold on Day 46, does not say that it is gone, and does not go around it with a broom. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the payer of the coal that went up with a bird, the hand that took the crust, the number that passed from fist to mouth to shoulder, and a woman dead nine mornings with no collector called.

On Days 48 through 54 the keeping takes the measure of seven more days of thaw and adds no explanation. She tells the fire it is the thaw, gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and says the house where another woman would say I; at the well and at the racks she goes at a half-pace from every open slate, goes around a slate propped at the rack end as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, and does not touch the widow’s mark, because a well is not an opening. On Account-day she sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade and carries him home saying nothing about what was read over him. Each dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft and puts the fold right without looking at his face. She stands a half-pace off while Alda writes and does not ask what was written, and says nothing about the payer of any warmth or about the woman dead sixteen mornings with no collector called. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the slack frame, the silence where an argument stood, the fifth note under a floorboard, the number that went from fist to mouth to shoulder, and the omission nobody will name.

On Days 55 through 60 the keeping takes the measure of the approach to Silt and the month named for what the river does, and adds no explanation. She tells the fire it is the thaw when a stranger at the well speaks of a sealed counting room and men dead of the breath, and she does not join the story to the kiln under her own roof; whatever she would put away she puts in the private roll nobody is shown, and there is nothing to put away. On Ilmen 27 she carries the basket three doors down into House Silt, sets it just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light and away from any open slate, straightens a chipped cup and does nothing else; she stands a half-pace from Alda and the birth-slates and asks nothing. Her instruction goes to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and she says the house where another woman would say I. The stores go around in loaves and glances and a space at the row’s end that she does not call a number; the days to Silt are three, two, whatever the moot will say, and she gives the boy no figure. On Ilmen 29 she lays one thumb flat in the clean dark line where the Ash ridge turned and the same thumb in the ridge two doors down, a finger’s width wider, and fetches no broom for either, while the yard prepares a sweeping done a month ago. At the last market she keeps the half-pace, sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade and carries him home at dusk. On Silt 1 she stands over a fresh hairline of grey beside the clean dark line with a broom in her hand and does not sweep, saying it is the thaw; the mark is touched before the kiln is opened and not for the grey, a basket or a bank, and the carried fire keeps four, four and a gap under blind ash. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the Greybank story, the new grey, the withheld number, the sixth note that was not written and the woman dead twenty-two mornings with no collector called.

On Days 61 through 67 the keeping takes the measure of a week in which the river rises and the district calls it weather, and adds no explanation. She gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and keeps the half-pace from every open slate at the racks, the Fishstairs, three doors down in House Silt and at the well. She tells the fire it is the thaw when the brook comes up clay-heavy and when the ice is honeyed all through, and the new hairline of grey in the Vail corner lies finer than the old clean dark line and is not swept because the house says it is the thaw. There is no opening in any of the seven days, so the widow’s mark is not touched once, not at a rack, a well, a door or a basket. In House Silt she stands a half-pace off while Alda lays the slates writing-down and writes what she will not leave lying, and asks nothing; the arrangement between the two women holds without a word, a wall with a door neither opens. Each dusk she carries him up at a half-pace, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and puts the fold right without looking at his face. The private roll stays unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and the higher water has given her nobody to answer. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the sixth page, the gone stone, the second cord, the clerk’s slate and the rising river, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 68 through 74 the keeping takes the measure of a flood that comes up around everything the house has left where it lies and then goes down again, and adds no explanation. She carries him to the edge of the thin brown sheet and back at the half-pace, says \emph{the house}, gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and tells the fire it is the thaw when a neighbour says the house was saved. The Ilm comes up over the Fishstairs, stands on the second step at the Cross on Account-day, and goes around both the clean dark line at the Vail corner and the burned line two doors down; she stands over the standing line and the new finer grey with a broom and sweeps neither, and gives the broom its instruction before anybody. No opening comes in seven days and the widow’s mark is not touched once. On Silt 13 she carries him three doors down and back with the door a finger’s width open and no slate opened, and asks nothing about the sixth page or the tin; the arrangement with Alda holds without a word. She does not go down to the child in the yard whose foot stays cold, though it is told of her that she once sat three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everyone was kind, and the boy does not lay the two together. At dusk of the last day she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face, and leaves the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the flood, the cold foot, the two lines and the empty place beside the one crust, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 75 through 77 the keeping takes the measure of a recovery that is another kind of avoidance. The yard sweeps around what the water left and calls the new grey thaw, and she stands over both lines with a broom and sweeps neither; a figure goes from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrives nowhere, and she answers a woman who wants it by sending her to the pot. A warm loaf passes from a man from Slate Row into a foundling’s pocket with no slate between them, and she neither looks nor connects the two. The half-pace, the unentered basket, the untouched mark and the private roll all hold exactly as they held before the flood; the wall has acquired no door, and the boy is still not written as Vail.

On Days 78 through 84 the keeping takes the measure of a lean week that changes nothing and adds no explanation. The flood has gone into mud that sets into a brown skin over the ruts, and she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody: go around what the water left, the clean dark line at the Vail corner, the new finer grey beside it and the space under the lowest rack, because it cost enough to come in and will cost more to take out. She sweeps none of them. The house keeps its number in loaves moved along a shelf, glances at the clay jar and a space at the row’s end nobody calls a figure, while she says \emph{the house}, sends every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom, and never to the basket. Three doors down she sets the basket at the edge of the light away from any open slate and stands a half-pace from Alda’s writing; at the well she goes wide around a slate set out to dry and does not touch the mark. When a second man come downriver from Greybank tells the bucket-round of a counting room shut in the war with the men inside dead of the breath, she tells the fire it is the thaw and lets it lie, joining nothing to her roof. No opening comes in seven days and the mark hangs where it hangs. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the second telling, the thinner crowd, the gone board, the cold foot and the empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 85 through 90 the keeping takes the measure of a month turning on the same mud it came in on, and adds no explanation. The boy is eighty-five through ninety days old, three months at the close, and she carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the yard, the well, the racks, House Silt, the Fishstairs, the Cross and the moot-post’s shade, setting him on his bed under the roof each dusk and never in the Debt Loft. On Silt 26 and Seed 1 she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody --- go around what the water left, it cost enough to come in, it will cost more to take out --- stands over the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack, and sweeps none of them; when a woman asks what the month will cost she moves her lips along the loaf shelf, glances at the clay jar and tells her to ask the pot. Every instruction goes to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket; she says the house where another woman would say I. When the second telling of the shut counting room goes over the bucket she tells the fire it is the thaw and joins nothing to her roof, though she lost a husband to that danger and has never once described it that way herself. Three doors down she sets the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from every open slate, stands a half-pace off while Alda presses the fold too long and writes what she will not show, and asks nothing. On Silt 30 she sets him in the moot-post’s thin shade with cold iron at his cheek while Berr reads one in twelve over fewer bodies and takes himself out of his own sentence, and carries him home saying nothing about what was read over him. No opening came in six days and a month’s turning is not an opening, so the widow’s mark hung where it hung; the private roll stayed unshown and she has not said whose child he is. At the turn into Seed the first work is sweeping and the work after it lies east of Low Kiln in strips she has not gone to see. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the second telling, the thinner crowd, the out-of-line landing, the foundling’s half-beat, the turned slate, the cold foot and the unnamed empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

Through Days 91–93 the keeping takes the measure of the first planting week and adds no explanation. The house’s work moves east of Low Kiln into strips she goes around with a broom and a look, and her rule holds exactly: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate at the well, the strips, House Silt and the Fishstairs. On Seed 2 she gives the broom its instruction before anybody, goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack, sweeps none of them, and at the well sends a woman asking the planting cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}, leaving the empty place at the row’s end with no figure. She tells the fire it is the thaw each day and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot; its payer has gone unnamed for ninety-three days. No opening came in three days --- not a strip, a broom, a basket, a well, a market, a door or a bed --- so the widow’s mark hung where it hangs; she has lost a husband to that danger and has never described it that way herself. Three doors down she sets the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, away from every open slate, opens none and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row, standing a half-pace off while Alda presses the fold too long and writes what she will not show. Jorra’s dust and the damper ahead of her sentence, Tarn’s six counted and seventh held, Mira’s cords, Berr’s box and Alda’s tin all stay as they were. At dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread frozen; the private roll stays unshown and she has not said whose child he is. The wall has acquired no door.

Through Days 94 through 100 the keeping takes the measure of a planting month that has become waiting and adds no explanation. The house’s arithmetic is now two empty places on the loaf shelf --- the old space at the row’s end nobody calls a number and a new gap that came in the night of Seed 5 --- and she moves her lips along the row, glances at the clay jar, gives the instruction to the pot, the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, and says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}. To a woman at the well she says ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there, because \emph{the house has said it}, and leaves the space at the row’s end with no figure. She goes around the brown skin holding a boot-print, the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack with a broom and a glance and sweeps none of them, telling the fire it is the thaw each day and turning the coals with the back of a broken pot. The carried fire’s payer has gone unnamed for a hundred days and the coal the gull took is entered in no slate. No opening came in seven days --- a strip, a shelf, a basket, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings --- so the widow’s mark stayed where it hung; she lost a husband to that danger and has never described it that way herself. Three doors down she set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, away from every open slate, opened none and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long. At the going of the light on Day 100 she set the boy on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face and left the thread frozen and unwiped; the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the fire’s four, four and a gap through the floor, in two separate places as for a hundred days. The private roll stayed unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and nothing was joined, paid, explained or ended. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

Through Days 101 through 103 the keeping takes the measure of a planting month that has become three ordinary days of two absences nobody joins. A neighbour at the loaf shelf reaches past the bare board, names the row’s old space as a thing the planting brought in and the empty place at the boy’s ear as a child’s appetite in one breath, takes her loaf and goes with her pot; Sella moves her lips along the row, glances at the clay jar and leaves both gaps with no figure, and does not hear the two places as one. On Seed 13 she agrees with the early thaw and the late and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying; Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence and the household straightens around his silence, and a neighbour at the bucket-round only mentions a room shut in the war with men dead of the breath, which she answers by telling the fire it is the thaw and joining nothing to her roof. On Seed 14 she sets the basket at the end of the fish-trade shade where no slate lies and then three doors down just inside a finger’s-width-open door, opens no slate and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row, and asks nothing about the writing, the tin or the fold pressed too long. Every instruction goes to the fire, the wool, the water, the pot and the broom and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, tells the fire the thaw each day and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot. No opening came in three days, so the widow’s mark hung where it hung; the carried fire’s payer has gone unnamed for a hundred and three days and the two lines in the corner stayed unswept. At dusk each day she set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen, carrying one crust and its unnamed empty place and two shelf gaps in another room that does not touch it. The private roll stayed unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and the wall has acquired no door.

On Days 104 through 106 the keeping takes the measure of the hands going into the strips and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and four, then one hundred and five, then one hundred and six days old and nobody under the roof says so. She gives the instruction to the broom and the bucket before anybody and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, keeps the half-pace from every open slate at the strips, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the well, the Fishstairs and three doors down in House Silt, and goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. At the loaf shelf she hears a neighbour name the old gap and the boy’s empty place in one breath and leaves both gaps unfigured, hearing two sayings and not one absence; the T097 witness is advanced, not paid. She hears the yard want the thaw early and late, agrees with both and wants the late because it puts off the paying. Jorra’s dust and the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence and Tarn’s knife and seventh year go unremarked: the household still straightens around a silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted. She tells the fire it is the thaw through all three days and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and six days; the fire keeps its four low pulls and the missing fifth, and the carried fire stays under blind ash and the back of a broken pot. No opening comes in three days --- a strip, a shelf, a rack, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings --- so the widow’s mark hangs where it hangs. Each dusk she sets the boy on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour’s one-breath joining, the near-spoken number of hands, the men in the back room, the seventh year at the edge of the sill and the two empty places in rooms that do not touch, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 107 through 109 the keeping takes the measure of the planting month entering its last tend and an Account-day read over the worked strips, and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and seven, then one hundred and eight, then one hundred and nine days old and nobody under the roof says so. Every instruction goes to the broom, the bucket, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, keeps the half-pace from every open slate at the well, the wheel-shed, the loaf shelf, the Fishstairs, the Cross, the moot-post’s shade and three doors down, and goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. At the loaf shelf she hears a neighbour name the row’s old gap as a thing the planting brought in and go off with her pot without seeing the empty place at his ear, and hears a second say it two days later; she leaves both gaps unfigured, hearing two sayings and not one absence, and the T097 witness advances toward the far-off finger without being paid. She gives the instruction to the broom before she gives it to anybody, and Tarn takes it only then and sweeps the collector’s road without turning along it while his seventh year lies at the very edge of the sill and his breath stays unspent. On Seed 19 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gives the end of it to the pot and the household straightens around his silence, and she gives the house no name for the men. She tells the fire it is the thaw on all three days and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nine days; at the fire she counts something under her breath and pushes a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, and the grey streak at her temple shows pale. No opening comes in three days — a strip, a shelf, a rack, a wheel-shed, a market, a reading, a door and a bed are not openings — so the widow’s mark hangs where it hangs and the private roll stays unshown. Each dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread frozen; one brown-edged crust lies stiff in the fold with its empty place unnamed and the shelf keeps two gaps in a room that does not touch it. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour’s one-breath joinings, the men in the back room, the seventh year at the edge of the sill and the two empty places in rooms that do not touch.

On Days 110 through 112 the keeping takes the measure of the planting month’s last tend and adds no explanation. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the worked strips, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs and three doors down, setting him on his bed under the roof each dusk and never in the Debt Loft. Every instruction goes to the bucket, the broom, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house}, moves her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glances at the clay jar and gives nobody a figure, and leaves a neighbour’s one-breath joining unjoined and the widow’s mark untouched, because a shelf, a strip, a rack, a well, a market, a post, a road, a door, a basket and a bed are not openings. At the well she sends a woman asking the planting’s cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}; at the fire she tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot and feeds them, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and stands a moment counting under her breath toward no opening with the grey streak pale at her temple, pushing a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist and not looking toward the bed. On Seed 22 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, the household straightening around his silence; the debt’s broom checks half a beat behind the wheel-keeper’s finger and goes on, and she asks nothing about either. Three doors down she stands a half-pace off while Alda writes what she will not show and asks nothing about the writing, the tin or the date over a dead woman’s sign. No opening came in three days, the private roll stayed unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and the wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the third shaping of the shelf’s absence, the first small change in the two silences under the roof, the fist that would not give its number and the two empty places in rooms that do not touch, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

Through Days 113 through 115 the keeping takes the measure of the planting’s last tend and adds no explanation. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the loaf shelf, the worked strips, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs, the Cross and three doors down in House Silt, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft at the going of the light and leaving the thread frozen and unwiped. Every instruction goes to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the wool, the water and the fire and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house}, moves her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glances at the clay jar cold under its glaze and gives nobody a figure, and sends a woman with wet sleeves to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}. She hears a neighbour lay the shelf’s old space and the empty place at his ear under one cause in a single breath and does not make the joining either, and the witness advances unpaid. At the fire she tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, feeds them and says \emph{The house will keep it}, standing a moment with the back of the pot in her hand counting under her breath toward no opening, her grey streak pale in the dying light, and not looking toward the bed. On Seed 25 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; the household straightens around his silence and the debt’s broom goes on over the flagstones without the check it made the day before, the stones keeping the stopped place, and she asks nothing about either. No opening comes in three days, the widow’s mark hangs untouched, the private roll stays unshown, and she has not said whose child he is. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour’s one-breath joining, the fist that would not give its figure, the moved equality under the roof, the two shelf gaps and the empty place in the fold, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Did not enter the birth room and said nothing. Woodsmoke and wet wool came ahead of her, then the cold off the yard, then the hand with the little-door burn across its back --- lintel, threshold, two straight sides. It felt for heat at the child’s belly, found none, opened and shut once above the covered bundle and withdrew. She stepped back out into the Clay Yard without looking at child or women. The crust and the warmed stone had already come from her hearth, neither entered against anybody; the kiln breathed through the wall afterward. She still intends to take him on the third day.

\item Ch 2: Kept the fire and the house through Days 2 and 3. At first light touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln and at no other time, gave instruction to the pot and the fire, would not let anyone fill Garl’s seat or take his coat down, and said the house kept a roll of its own. Announced that the boy would come under the roof and was answered \emph{he’s not Vail}; got quieter and did not reply. On the third morning came for him, crossed to the bench first, lifted him with the little-door hand, said \emph{the boy} and \emph{the house}, carried him up the Clay Yard and laid him on fresh straw. Gave the bed to the foundling and the loft to Tarn without explaining either, told the pot it would pay for itself in the thaw, and left the charred slate in the kiln ash untouched.

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. Carried the boy out of the kiln-house in a basket under a fold of wool --- he left the house and its heat went out behind him --- and held him like a pot filled that must not be slopped. Did not touch the widow’s mark, since the coals were only being banked. Counted off the question of the mother with \emph{Account-day} and the question of the house with \emph{the house}; put the fold back over his face and ears without looking and spoke the instruction to the wool and the wind. Kept a half-pace from the slate on the block and did not set the basket where it lay open. At the Slate Row end refused to answer Berr about the confirmed widow’s mark, pulled the wool over the boy’s ear, and let the uncalled debt lie. Lifted the basket off the post in the late afternoon and turned back up the Clay Yard without a word about where they had been or what had been read over the top of him; the wool smelled of woodsmoke and the door did not quite shut.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 4: Days 5 and 6. On Stone 11 touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln and at no other time, fed the household from her own dish, put the fold right without looking and gave the instruction about the draught to the fire. On Stone 12 carried the boy two doors down to a neighbour’s house for the Drawing, turned the basket with her knee and set it at the edge of the light, not where the slate lay open, and said \emph{a pot filled is a pot carried} to the girl at the hearth. Stood a half-pace from bench and bed with her burn shut on nothing and did not look toward the basket when the man gave. At dusk banked the coals under ash with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{that’ll hold} to the fire, put the fold right without looking at his face, and said nothing about where they had been, what had been taken or from whom. Did not touch the mark at the bank. Did not answer Jorra’s \emph{the back room’s cold}; shifted the damper instead. Fed the boy gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish and entered neither the spoon nor the boy.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 5: Days 7--9. Touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln on Stone 13 and at no other time, held it a moment longer than the touch required, and gave the instruction to the fire. Fed the boy barley gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish, spoon wiped on her sleeve, and said \emph{the house}, never \emph{I}; put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face and did not wipe the drool. At dusk banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark. Carried him down to the Fishstairs on Stone 8 and to the market’s edge on Stone 9, kept the half-pace from open slates and the shade where no slate lay, laid marks for two pair of eels and counted them with her eyes, and said nothing about the cuff, the cord, the crust or where they had been. On Stone 15 counted her loaves and bits with her lips twice and returned to the same place, keeping the days to Kindling as a shape and not a number; neither thanked nor refused the crust and did not take it out.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Days 10--14. On Stone 16 touched the widow’s mark before lifting the kiln lid and at no other hour, moved her lips along the loaf shelf so the days to Kindling stood as a shape, and did not touch the mark when Alda came or at the dusk bank. Kept a half-pace from the neighbour’s slate at the threshold and told her to ask the pot; let Garl’s uncalled debt lie in the space where the sentence ended. On Stone 18 said \emph{the house} and gave the neighbour the pot instead of a number; at the yard well kept the half-pace and drew water; at dusk did not touch the mark. On Stone 19 turned the coals with the back of a broken cup, called the crack in the ice weather, slid the basket a hand’s breadth out of the draught without looking at his face, measured the ridge with her thumb --- near two thumbs here, a finger more two doors down --- and said leave it, it’ll be swept on the Last Day. On Stone 20, Account-day, did not touch the mark because a reading is not an opening, carried him down in the basket and set it in the moot-post’s shade, kept a half-pace from every open slate, did not look into the basket, and carried him home through the doors going shut. Put the fold right without looking at his face, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{that’ll hold}. Neither took out nor named the cold crust Mira had put in the fold.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Days 15--24. Touched the widow’s mark before each opening (Stone 21, 25, 27, 29, 30) and at no other hour, including the bank and the reading at the last market. Counted fuel and bread into the last tend with her lips and loaves, moving three here, two there and one set apart with its brown edge turned up, and came back to it twice; answered the man who brought a number from the ice in a shut fist with \emph{It’s a cold} and fed the fire. Sent Tarn for a collector for a neighbour two doors down, carried the basket there and set it at the edge of the light away from any open slate, standing a half-pace off with her burn shut on nothing. Kept the boy’s ears out of the draught off the brook by speaking to the wool, fed him from the house’s own dish with the spoon wiped on her sleeve, and entered neither. On Stone 29 laid her thumb in the Vail ridge and then the death-house ridge and came back without saying which was which; let the debt against the tiles be circled and not named, and said Garl’s sayings to the pot and the fire. On Stone 30 carried him down for the reading with the mark untouched because a reading is not an opening, set him in the moot-post’s shade, kept her half-pace, and at dusk set the fold right without looking at his face, put him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and banked the coals with the back of a broken pot. Neither took out nor named either crust, and said nothing about where they had been.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 8: Days 25--30. On Kindling took the year’s fire in a clay dish from hands along the yard and tipped it into the kiln, touching the widow’s mark for one breath before the opening and at no other hour; nobody said where the flame came from or what it cost and she did not enter either. Fed him gruel from the house’s own dish and gave the instruction to the fire and the wool, saying \emph{the house}. Through the Five touched the mark before openings only, never at a bank; at the Weighing kept her half-pace from every open slate and did not repeat the name the clean voice read; on the Long Night let the fire go out at dusk and told the Return in the dark; at the Remembering went around Garl’s name as around Ash and let Alda lay dates where it should have stood; on the Last Day would not let anyone sweep early, measured the Vail ridge with her thumb and the neighbour’s a finger’s width thicker two doors down, and left both where they lay. On Ilmen 1 let a neighbour call the burned grey dealt while she said nothing, kept the coals banked so there was no opening and the mark stayed untouched, put the fold right without looking at his face, fed him from the house’s own dish and said nothing about where any warmth came from or who had paid.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 9: Days 31–37. At the yard well on Ilmen 2 drew her bucket with the little-door burn closing first on the rope and then on nothing, said \emph{That’ll do} to the bucket and \emph{Keep it off him; it’s the river wind} to the wool, said \emph{the house} and did not say who paid for the warmth in the household dish. On Ilmen 3 fed him gruel from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear, did not wipe his mouth, and at the bank turned the coals with a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a dusk is not an opening. On Ilmen 5 stood a half-pace off while Alda reached for the slate first, laid dates where a name should stand and turned a fourth note writing-down into her shawl, and asked nothing. On Ilmen 6 touched the widow’s mark before the opening, held it one breath, let go, and did not touch it again for a pot, a note or a nearly-full sound; moved the damper after Jorra. On Ilmen 7 answered the man with the figure in his fist by speaking to the fire --- \emph{It’s a cold. That’s all it is. Feed the fire} --- and did not ask what was in the fist. On Ilmen 8 carried him three doors down and set the basket in the shade at the end of nineteen steps without looking into it, then carried him up the yard at dusk; turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a bank was not an opening. Neither took out nor named either crust and no third came; said nothing about the payer of any warmth.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 10: Days 38–44. On Ilmen 9 held the basket on the bank at the Slip Brook with the little-door burn shut on the wicker, turned the boy’s face toward the bank and did not set him down while the yard lifted Dessa from the clay; went to the fire afterward and sent nobody toward the road for a collector, and did not name the omission. Gave the instruction to the wool and the pot, said \emph{the house}, did not touch the widow’s mark because there had been no opening. On Ilmen 11 laid her thumb in the clean dark line where the Ash had turned and then in the ridge two doors down, brought it back without saying which was which and fetched no broom; fed him from the house’s own dish and left both crusts where they lay. On Ilmen 12 kept a half-pace from the eel-board and the writing at the gate. On Ilmen 13 carried a clay jar from House Silt, held the basket level inside the door a finger’s width open, opened no slate and set the jar on the shelf by the wall at home. On Ilmen 14 and 15 carried him upriver to the Weir, left him in the shade out of the draught, stood a half-pace from a slate under a woman’s arm on the way back, and at dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face. Still had not said who paid for the warmth or that the woman in the brook was the mother of the child under her roof.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 11: Days 45–47. Carried him below the north bridge at dawn and up the Clay Yard at dusk, setting him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face; every instruction to the fire, the pot and the wool, and the house where another woman would say I. Touched the widow’s mark once before opening the kiln on Day 45 and at no other hour, not at any bank. Went around the month in loaves and glances, moved a loaf along the shelf and came back to the same place, glanced at the clay jar on the wall shelf, and let nobody say the stores were thinner. Fed him gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear, wiped the spoon on her sleeve and did not wipe his mouth. At the well kept a half-pace from every open slate, went wide around a slate at the rack end and gave the instruction to the bucket; told a neighbour the house had sent the number up the road. Did not touch the mark at the dusk banks and did not name either the payer of the warmth or the crust that went out of the fold. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 12: Days 48–54. At the well she told the fire it was the thaw and gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket, never to the basket, saying the house; she went at a half-pace from every open slate and around a slate propped at the rack end, and did not touch the widow’s mark because a well is not an opening. On Account-day she set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and carried him home without a word about the figure read over him. Each dusk she set him on his bed under the roof, not in the Debt Loft, and put the fold right without looking at his face. She stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote a fifth note and did not ask what was written, and said nothing about the payer of the milk, the payer of any warmth, or the crust that went out of the fold on Day 46. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 13: Days 55--60. On Ilmen 26 at the yard well told the fire it was the thaw when a man come downriver from Greybank spoke of a counting room shut in the last war with the damper closed and men dead of the breath, and did not connect it to the Vail kiln (T065); touched no mark, because a well and a story over a bucket are not openings. On Ilmen 27 carried the basket three doors down into House Silt, set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from every open slate, opened no slate, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row, stood a half-pace off while Alda laid the slates writing-down and pressed the fold too long, and asked nothing (T058, T084). Through the days gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket, never to the basket, said the house, and kept the days to Silt in loaves, glances and an uncalled space at the shelf’s end. On Ilmen 29 laid one thumb in the clean dark line where the Ash ridge turned and the same thumb in the ridge two doors down, a finger’s width wider, and brought the knowledge back without saying which was which and without fetching a broom (T013, T009). At the last market kept the half-pace and carried him home at dusk with one crust and an empty place in the fold. On Silt 1 stood over the new hairline of grey in the corner with a broom in her hand and did not sweep, telling the fire it was the thaw and would go when it goes; touched the widow’s mark before the opening and at no other hour; kept the carried fire under blind ash and broken pot at four, four and a gap; set him on his bed under the roof, not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, and said nothing about the river beginning to move under the ice.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 14: Days 61–67. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, and kept her half-pace from every open slate at the racks, the Fishstairs, House Silt and the well. Told the fire it was the thaw when the brook came up clay-heavy and when the ice was honeyed all through; left the new finer grey beside the clean dark line unswept. No opening came in seven days and she did not touch the widow’s mark once. On Silt 5 carried the basket three doors down, set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote and asked nothing. Each dusk set him on his bed under the roof, not in the Debt Loft, and put the fold right without looking at his face, carrying one crust and an empty place through seven days unnamed. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 15: Days 68–74, Silt 9–15. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, and kept the half-pace from every open slate at the Fishstairs, the Cross, the racks and three doors down. Carried him to the edge of the thin brown sheet and back; told the fire it was the thaw when a neighbour said the house had been saved and did not say it herself. Stood over the clean dark line and the new finer grey with a broom and swept neither, and gave the broom its instruction before anybody (\emph{Go around}); went wide around the space under the lowest rack. Touched the widow’s mark at no hour in seven days, because no opening came at a rack, a shore, a step, a door or a bed. On Silt 13 carried him three doors down and back with the door a finger’s width open and opened no slate, asking nothing about the sixth page or the tin. Did not go down to the child in the yard whose foot stayed cold, and the boy did not lay it beside the child of hers who cooled while everybody was kind. At dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped; one crust stiff in the fold with the empty place unnamed. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 16: Days 75–77, Silt 16–18. Kept the house through the mud the flood left: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and the half-pace from every open slate at the racks, the well, the Fishstairs and House Silt. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the finer grey and the space under the lowest rack with neither line swept; told the fire it was the thaw. Told a woman who wanted a figure to ask the pot what a wet thing costs, and did not say the house was saved. At the well went wide around a slate set out to dry, did not touch the widow’s mark, and did not look at the foundling in cast-offs, his green sliver or the warm loaf in his pocket, and did not connect the man from Slate Row with either. No opening came in three days and the mark was not touched. Carried him up at dusk each day, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped; one stiff crust and its unnamed empty place. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 17: Days 78–84, Silt 19–25. Kept the house through the lean week: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate at the well, the Cross, House Silt and the racks. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack, sweeping none of them and telling the fire it was the thaw. At the yard well on Silt 25 heard the second man from Greybank tell the bucket-round of the counting room shut in the war with the damper closed and the men dead of the breath; told the fire it was the thaw, made nothing of it and did not join it to her roof. Carried the boy three doors down on Silt 21, set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from any open slate, opened none and turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row, and stood a half-pace off while Alda laid the slates down before the fold and wrote what she would not show. Let Jorra’s dust and his finger at the damper pass unasked, let Tarn’s six counted and seventh held stand as the house’s one unchecked entry. No opening came in seven days and the widow’s mark was not touched; the private roll stayed unshown. At dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped, one brown-edged crust with the empty place beside it still unnamed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 18: Days 85–90, Silt 26–30 and Seed 1. Kept the house through the turning of the month: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate at the yard, the well, the racks, House Silt, the Fishstairs, the Cross and the moot-post’s shade. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody on Silt 26 and Seed 1 and went around the boot-print in the brown skin, the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack, sweeping none of them and telling the fire it was the thaw. To the woman who asked what the month would cost moved her lips along the loaf shelf, glanced at the clay jar and said to ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there; put no figure to the space at the row’s end and let a man say the strips east of town would want hands by the morrow without giving the hands or the strips a number. When the shut-room story went over the bucket again told the fire it was the thaw and joined nothing to her roof. Three doors down set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long and wrote what she would not show. On Silt 30 set him in the moot-post’s thin shade with cold iron at his cheek while Berr read one in twelve over fewer bodies, carried him home at dusk and said nothing about what had been read over him. Jorra’s dust and his damper ahead of her sentence, Tarn’s six counted and seventh held, Alda’s tin and Berr’s box all stayed as they were; no opening came in six days and a month’s turning was not one, so the widow’s mark was not touched. The private roll stayed unshown and the empty place at the row’s end stayed unnamed. At dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped, one crust and its unnamed empty place carried into Seed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 19: Days 91–93. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the strips east of Low Kiln, the Clay Yard, the yard well, the Fishstairs and House Silt, and set him on his bed under the roof each dusk and not in the Debt Loft. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket; gave the broom its instruction before anybody --- \emph{Round it. The month’s for planting and there’s nothing planted here. It cost enough to come in; it’ll cost more to take out} --- and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack, sweeping none of them. On Seed 2 told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and, to a woman who asked what the planting would cost, moved her lips along the loaf shelf, glanced at the clay jar, left the empty place at the row’s end with no figure and said \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there} and \emph{the house has said it}. Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days; its payer had gone unnamed for ninety-three days and the coal the gull took was entered in no slate. Did not touch the widow’s mark at a strip, a broom, a well, a market, a door or a bed, because none was an opening. Three doors down set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long. At the close put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; one brown-edged crust lay stiff in the fold with the empty place unnamed and no third.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 20: Days 94–100, Seed 5–11, the planting become waiting. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate in the strips, the Clay Yard, the yard well, House Silt, the Fishstairs, the Cross and under the roof, setting him on his bed each dusk and not in the Debt Loft. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket, the broom and the pot and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 5 told a woman at the well to ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there because \emph{the house has said it}; on Seed 6 moved her lips along a loaf row that now stood with two empty places and said nothing about either, while a neighbour’s hand passed over the new gap and went on with her pot. Told the fire it was the thaw on all seven days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and kept its payer unnamed for a hundred days. Did not go down to the child below the sill whose foot stayed cold, though it is told of her in the yard that she once sat three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everybody was kind; she has never told that story herself and would not describe it that way. At the close put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread frozen and unwiped, and did not touch the widow’s mark because no opening came. The two shelf gaps and the empty place in the fold stayed in rooms that do not touch and were not named, joined or solved; the private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 21: Days 101–103, Seed 12–14, the third week of the planting become waiting. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate in the Clay Yard, at the loaf shelf, at the Fishstairs and three doors down in House Silt, setting him on his bed under the roof each dusk and not in the Debt Loft. Gave every instruction to the pot, the fire, the broom, the wool and the water and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, told the fire it was the thaw on all three days and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and three days. On Seed 12 moved her lips along a loaf row that stood with two empty places, glanced at the clay jar and left both gaps unfigured while a neighbour named them in one breath as a planting and an appetite; she did not join them. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 13 said \emph{Yes, house} to an early thaw and a late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying; stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote three doors down, and did not ask about the writing or the tin. On Seed 14 carried him down to the eels, set the basket where no slate lay, and midday set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door three doors down, away from every open slate, opening none. At dusk put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; touched the widow’s mark at no hour, because a shelf, a strip, a basket, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings. The private roll stayed unshown and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s gap stayed apart and unnamed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 22: Days 104–106, Seed 15–17, the hands at last going into the strips. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the worked strips east of Low Kiln, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs and three doors down in House Silt, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft at dusk each day. Gave the instruction to the broom, the bucket, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, gave the broom its instruction before anybody (\emph{Go around. It cost enough to come in. It’ll cost more to take out}) and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 15 moved her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glanced at the clay jar and gave nobody a figure while a neighbour said the old space at the end came in with the planting and went off with her pot; she did not join the two tellings. Told the fire it was the thaw and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and four days; the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. On Seed 16 said \emph{Yes, house} to the early and late thaw and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, stood a half-pace off while men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, and gave the house no name for the men. On Seed 17 set the basket at the very end of the fish-trade shade, told the wool and the water and never the basket, and midday set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door three doors down away from every open slate, opening none and turning no errand into a walk to Slate Row; said nothing about the writing, the tin or the fold pressed too long. At dusk put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; touched the widow’s mark at no hour, because a strip, a shelf, a rack, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings. The private roll stayed unshown, the two shelf gaps and the fold’s one crust stayed apart and unnamed with no third, and no bond changed hands, no tin or box opened and no new scar or possession.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 23: Days 107–109, Seed 18–20, the planting month entering its last tend. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the yard well, the wheel-shed, the loaf shelf, the Fishstairs, the Cross and the moot-post’s shade, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft at dusk each day. Gave the instruction to the broom, the bucket, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, gave the broom its instruction before she gave it to anybody (\emph{Over the road first, then the Clay Yard, and let the line lie where it lies}), and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 18 three doors down set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long; said nothing of the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. At the loaf shelf that afternoon moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced at the clay jar and gave nobody a figure while a neighbour called the old gap a thing the planting brought in and went off with her pot without seeing the empty place at his ear; did not join the two tellings. Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and fed it, the fire answering four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nine days; stood a moment at the fire with the back of the broken pot in her hand counting something under her breath, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the wrist that carries the burn, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 18 said \emph{Yes, house} to those who wanted the thaw early and those who wanted it late, and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying. On Seed 19 stood a half-pace off while men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, giving the house no name for them; told the fire it was the thaw and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a wheel-shed, a rack, a yard and a basket are not openings. On Seed 20 set the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade before the crowd thickened, gave the instruction to the wool and the wind and never to the basket, kept her half-pace from every open slate and carried him home at dusk saying nothing about the figure read over the strips. Touched the widow’s mark at no hour and kept her private roll unshown; put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; one stiff crust and its unnamed empty place, the shelf’s two gaps in the other room, no third. No new scar or possession; the grey streak at her temple is more marked.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 24: Days 110–112, Seed 21–23, the last tend of the planting. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the worked strips, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs and three doors down, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each dusk. Gave the instruction to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the wool, the water and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, went around a slate set out to dry and the space under the lowest rack, and gave nobody a figure. At the loaf shelf moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced at the clay jar cold under its glaze and let a neighbour reach past the bare board and go off naming the old gap a planting and the new one the price of a wet thing without joining the two sayings or touching the widow’s mark. At the well on Seed 22 sent a woman who asked what the planting cost to the pot: \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it.} Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}; stood a moment with the back of the pot in her hand counting something under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the wrist that carries the burn, the grey streak pale at her temple, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 22 gave the broom its instruction before anybody and Tarn took it up; men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, the household straightening around his silence, and she gave the end of it to the pot. His broom checked half a beat behind the standing finger and went on, and she asked nothing about either. At the Fishstairs and three doors down set the basket where no slate lay and opened none, standing a half-pace off; said nothing about the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. The carried fire kept four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and twelve days. No opening came in three days, the widow’s mark hung where it hung and the private roll stayed unshown; one crust in the fold and two shelf gaps in another room were not named, joined or solved.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 25: Days 113–115, Seed 24–26, the last tend of the planting held with the seed up. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the loaf shelf, the worked strips, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs, the Cross and three doors down, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each going of the light, putting the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and leaving the thread frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting needed before it went away. Gave the instruction to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the wool, the water and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, moved her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and gave nobody a figure. At the shelf on Seed 24 sent a woman with wet sleeves to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and heard a neighbour call the old gap a planting and the child’s empty place an appetite in one breath without joining the two or touching the widow’s mark. Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 25 stood a half-pace off while men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gave the end of it to the pot and the household straightened around his silence. Tarn took the broom only after its instruction and his stroke went on without the half-check of the day before, the flagstones keeping the stopped place; she asked nothing about either. Three doors down at midday set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long; said nothing of the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. At the Fishstairs and the Cross on Seed 26 set the basket where no slate lay and opened none. No opening came in three days and the widow’s mark stayed untouched; the private roll stayed unshown and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s gap stayed apart and unnamed. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter{Fenna Clay}{the girl in High Kiln who mixed the glaze and knew the note}{build/portraits/fenna-clay.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Fenna, Fenna Clay, Fenna of the Glaze Room, the green girl}\CRfield{Role}{love-interest}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 800, High Kiln, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic)}\CRfield{Origin}{High Kiln, Sill, Grath; House Clay, glaze-mixers for four generations}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Glaze Room, High Kiln; the kiln-masters’ household; a widow’s mark held in trust}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 40}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Twelve when she first appears and in the years after a woman of moderate height with the pale-green staining of lead glaze at the corners of her mouth that the district calls \emph{the green} and that she has never tried to hide, because a glaze-mixer without the green is a glaze-mixer who does not taste her work. Her hands are stained blue-green to the second knuckle and the stain is in the creases permanently, so that when she holds a cup at the Cross people look at the cup and not at her. She has a single lock of hair that never takes the dye of the kiln smoke and stays the colour of dry straw, which the High Kiln children say means she will marry someone from the lowlands, which she has spent years trying to disprove. She smells of lead glaze, crushed galena, vinegar and the sweetish heat of the Glaze Room in Ember, which is a beautiful smell and a poisonous one, and she is the only person in Sill who will tell you so in the same breath. The thing people notice first is the green at her mouth; the thing they notice last is that she taps everything — cups, tables, the wheel-shed frame when she visits — with a knuckle, and listens, and has never been able to stop.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Practical, dry, with the glaze-mixer’s habit of naming a thing by what it is made of rather than what it is: not \emph{a cup} but \emph{a lead cup}, not \emph{a lie} but \emph{a glaze over a crack}. She has a way of saying the dangerous thing in the vocabulary of the workshop, so that it can be taken as instruction if the listener prefers, which is the same defence Dessa Silt uses with different materials. She does not giggle and does not lower her eyes, which in High Kiln marks her as odd and in Low Kiln marks her as strange in a way that draws the boy from the yard across the river. When she is frightened she becomes technical, giving proportions and temperatures, because a recipe is a thing that holds still. She will not say \emph{please}, because her mother taught her that a glaze-mixer who begs gets the lead order wrong.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “It’s lead. The pale line at your gum is lead. I can tell you when it started, and you won’t thank me for it.”

\item “You tapped that before I did. Why did you tap it before I did? Nobody taps before the glaze-mixer.”

\item “A good glaze hides the crack. That’s its whole purpose and its whole defect. Ask a potter which he wants and he’ll lie to you.”

\item “I’m from High Kiln. You’re from the yard. If anybody writes it down it becomes a thing with a number on it, and I don’t want a number.”

\item “Don’t set it near the fire. I know you know. I want to hear you say it in our house’s words, not theirs.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was born in High Kiln to a family of glaze-mixers who have supplied the Vail kiln-house and half the tables of Sill for four generations, which means her household is comfortable and quietly hated. She learned the trade at nine by tasting the mix the way her mother did and by tapping a fired pot with a knuckle to hear whether the glaze had filled the flaw or only covered it. She is good at it — better than her mother, which nobody in High Kiln will say aloud — and has a habit the masters call \emph{the ear}, which she has inherited from a grandmother nobody remembers and which she considers a recipe like any other: a thing that can be learned by doing it wrongly often enough.

She met Corin at the market when she was twelve and he was nine, when he turned his head toward a cup on her family’s table before she tapped it, and said, in the flat way of the yard, that it would crack at the handle in a season. She tapped it. It answered flat. She has never forgotten the exact sound, or the fact that he did not wait to be asked. They have spoken at the Cross, at the Fishstairs, at the edge of the Clay Yard which she is not supposed to cross, for years, in the intervals when a child from High Kiln and a foundling from Low Kiln can be seen together without anybody making a number of it. She has never called him Corin in front of anyone; she calls him \emph{the one who taps early}, and he has never corrected her.

When they are both older she will be the person who can tell him what a glaze does to a crack and why the Court’s fine ware is beautiful, which is the physical answer to the question of why the rich are beautiful and repeated. She will also be the person who refuses to be his if it means being entered on a slate, which is the first time he will meet a love that will not be booked. She is, in her own account, a woman who has spent her life covering flaws and has never once mistaken the covering for the repair.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
The green at her mouth is the beginning of sweet-sickness, which she knows, and she has told no one in her house, because a glaze-mixer who admits the sickness loses the wheel and her mother’s table. She fears that the boy from the yard will one day be entered in a Court roll and become a person with a number, and that she will be unable to look at him in the same way. She fears her own talent: she is better at hiding cracks than anyone in Sill, which is a useful trade and a way of life built on a lie that kills slowly. Her contradiction: the girl who insists that a glaze hides nothing has spent every day of her life hiding the pale line at her own gum, and calls it \emph{the green}, which is what everyone calls it, which is how Sarn makes a sickness into a trade-mark.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants to mix a glaze that does not poison the mixer, which is an impossibility in Sill and the reason she will eventually leave for Vhalen, where the glass men use different fluxes and do not taste their work. She thinks she wants the boy from the yard to say the thing he never says. What she needs is to understand that she cannot be kept whole by someone who is himself cracked, and that loving a mender is not the same as being mended, and that the crack that is visible is the only honest part of either of them. Their romance can only begin in adulthood, when both have survived their first firings and the green at her mouth has become a thing they can speak of plainly.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Corin} — the boy who tapped early. The bond is a shared ear and a river between two districts; she has the note by inheritance, he has it by a life he cannot explain, and neither has ever asked the other where it came from, which is how they have kept it safe. The tension is class and the slate: she has a house-name and he does not, and a marriage between them would be an entry in a roll, which is the last thing either of them can afford.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — buys her family’s glaze and has never once paid the full price, which Fenna has decided is a kindness from a woman who cannot afford to be kind, which makes it worse. Sella has also never once asked why the girl comes to the edge of the yard, which Fenna has decided is the same kindness from the opposite direction.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — whom she has known all her life and who would sooner burn a slate than let a High Kiln girl into the wheel-shed. Jorra has never said why, and Fenna has decided it is because he is afraid she will hear the wheel too, which is true and not the whole of it.
