No bond was paid or repaired this chapter: the box stayed locked and the good reason intact.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
He enters at the Account-day moot of Stone 10, Y.H. 812, wiping his thumb on his apron before touching the slate, and says \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} in a low voice that makes the shouting stop because the crowd has to lean in. He never says \emph{I}; he says the district, the account and the notice, and apologises in the form of an instruction. He sets the slate down twice and twice it answers flat, and he does not hear what the boy hears. Later, at the Slate Row end of the Cross, he confirms Sella’s widow’s mark as a kindness that is entered, leaves Garl’s debt against the tiles uncalled, and goes back to the moot with the red cord folded square. The locked box in his house has not been shown or named. He has been on the page for one chapter and is already the local face of the Court: reasonable, clean-handed, with a good reason for every cruelty and no idea that he has given any.

On Stone 14 the Thane comes down to the eel trade and is the same man in a market that he was at the Cross: the clean thumb, the passive grammar that takes the speaker out of his own sentence, the hand that counts a figure before he lets it go. He calls the levy for the feast and says it is not called by him, and takes four eels where six should go and does not seem to notice, which is how a man can be short and kind and reasonable in the same breath. The number of days to the Five is let out into the market air and is still nothing anybody can spend.

On Stone 20 he is the same man at the Cross that he was at the eel trade: the thumb wiped clean before the slate, the passive grammar that takes the speaker out of his own sentence, the figure passed over with a finger to make sure it is still where he put it. Two hundred people lean in because they have to; he reads one in twelve as the notice says, calls the levy for the feast and says it is not called by him, and goes around the uncalled debt against the tiles as carefully as Sella goes around Ash in a corner. He confirms the mark and the fire and sets the printed figure down where everyone can see it. The boy lies in the post’s thin shade with cold iron at his cheek and hears a number he cannot spend, and Berr never once looks into the basket or enters what he has left lying where it lay. He goes home by dusk believing he has done the district a kindness.

On Days 15 through 24 the same arithmetic is done at a remove. He is not on the page until Stone 30, when he reads the figure again at the last market of the year and says the levy was called for the feast and not by him, the grammar that takes the speaker out of his own sentence now ordinary market speech in every mouth around him. He goes around Garl’s uncalled debt without naming it, sets the printed figure where everyone can see it, and gives out that the Five are three days off while the district gives out three and then two and then whatever it has already decided to pay. The boy lies in the moot-post’s shade with cold iron at his cheek, and Berr never looks into the basket or enters what he has left lying where it lay. He goes home believing his own sentences and the box stays locked.

On Days 25 through 30 the same arithmetic is done at a remove and then begins a new year. He is glimpsed once, at the Weighing, with the red cord folded under his coat and the green at one corner of his mouth, wiping his thumb before he touches his slate and passing a finger over the figure; he reads a name the household will not repeat and goes off explaining nothing, the box still locked. The officer’s clean voice wears his grammar in a temple’s clothes, and a whole return is announced for somebody absent --- the district’s ordinary kindness, now in an institution’s mouth. At the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1 one in twelve is still printed and unchallenged, the true deduction is spoken by nobody, and Garl’s uncalled debt is left where it lay through the turn of the year. He goes on believing his own sentences and the box stays locked.

On Days 31 through 37 the same arithmetic is done at a remove and the withholding becomes a district habit. On Ilmen 7 Berr comes back from the river with the red cord folded under his coat, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, keeps a number he does not care to give and tells a neighbour there will be a slate at the watch; one in twelve stays printed and unchallenged and the true subtraction is spoken by nobody. He never looks into the basket. The boy files the twice-wiped thumb beside the other record-first hands without joining it to any of them, and watches the green at the corner of the mouth. The box stays locked and the true deduction stays in it.

On Days 38 through 44 the same arithmetic goes on over a body entered nowhere, and the withholding becomes ordinary market speech. On Ilmen 10 he came to the Cross with the red wool cord folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} into the top of the leaning crowd, passed a finger over the figure and put himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}. The true subtraction went over the basket unspoken, the number for the thaw went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and was never given, and Garl’s uncalled debt lay in the space where a name might have stood. He looked nowhere near the basket in the moot-post’s shade and went home believing his own sentences. He was not at the Weir on Ilmen 14 or 15. The clerk he keeps at the Court’s table and the clerk set at the Fishstairs for a measure nobody called both reached for the slate before the person; the boy kept the three record-first orders on separate trays and did not join them. The box in his house stayed locked and the true deduction stayed in it.

On Days 45 through 47 the same arithmetic is done at the remove of a yard and the withholding becomes the district’s ordinary speech. On Day 47 he comes up from the road with the red cord folded under his coat and the green at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a slate he will not open and says a number goes into a slate and not into a well. He takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}, never looks into the basket and goes off with the box still locked; the number for the thaw passes from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrives nowhere. The clerk at the Fishstairs still sits for a measure nobody called and the woman in the brook is still uncollected, and Berr’s twice-wiped thumb stays on the boy’s tray of record-first hands, not joined to the midwife’s, the neighbour’s at this well, the clerk’s behind the Court table or the man who priced the basket. He goes on believing his own sentences and the true deduction stays in the box.

On Days 48 through 54 the same arithmetic is done once more over a body the Court has not entered and the withholding stays the district’s ordinary speech. On Account-day at the Cross he comes to the block with the red wool cord folded under his coat and green glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing and reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket; the true subtraction goes over it unspoken and the crowd goes back to the pigs. To a neighbour who begins to ask he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well; there’ll be a slate at the watch}, taking himself out of his own sentence; the number for the thaw goes from fist to mouth to shoulder and is given to nobody. The bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself. He goes off toward High Kiln believing his own sentences, never looking into the basket, with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside.

On Days 55 through 60 the same arithmetic is done once more over a body the Court has not entered and the withholding stays the district’s ordinary speech. On Ilmen 30, the last Account-day and market before Silt, he comes to the block with the red wool cord folded under his coat and green glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing and reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket. He calls the levy for Silt and takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}; the true subtraction goes over the basket unspoken and the number for the thaw goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and is given to nobody. The bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself. Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles goes around the space where a name might have stood and is not called. The soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs is glimpsed hand-to-slate-before-eyes and silent, filed apart from Marra, the Drawing collector and the Court-table clerk; Berr does not look into the basket and goes off toward High Kiln believing his own sentences. The box in his house stays locked and the true deduction stays in it.

On Days 61 through 67 the same arithmetic is done at the remove of a market edge and the withholding stays the district’s ordinary speech. On Silt 2 Berr comes up short below the north bridge with the red cord folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened and passes a finger over what is written. He says a number goes into a slate and not into a well and that there will be a slate at the watch, taking himself out of his own sentence and never saying \emph{I}; the green at his mouth and the twice-wiped thumb are the same tells the boy has kept for years. He does not look into the basket, and goes off toward High Kiln with the box still locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness. The soft-cuffed clerk sits silent at the landing with his hand to his slate before his eyes to the stalls, and the boy keeps the two orders of reaching apart. Nothing is called, paid or explained, and the figure the buyer gave for the pair goes into the noise of the stalls and is gone.

On Days 68 through 74 the same arithmetic is done over a district under water and the withholding stays the district’s ordinary speech. On Silt 10, Account-day, he comes up short at the dry step with the water sitting on the one below, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened, passes a finger over the figure, reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the water and the basket and takes himself out of his own sentence, never saying \emph{I} and never looking into the basket. The true subtraction goes over it unspoken, the number for the flood’s cost goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrives nowhere, and the bell goes four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself. He goes off toward High Kiln with the box still locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness; the soft-cuffed clerk stays set at the Fishstairs and the boy keeps Berr’s twice-wiped thumb on its own tray, not joined to that hand or to any other record-first hand. Nothing is called, paid or explained, and the figure over the basket goes into the noise of the stalls and is gone.

On Days 78 through 84 the same arithmetic is done over a thinner district and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. On Silt 20 he comes to the block with the red cord folded under his coat, green glaze at one corner of his mouth and hot clay over the smell of nothing at all, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing and reads one in twelve over fewer bodies than stood at the flood’s Account-day. The true subtraction goes over the basket unspoken and the printed figure stands unchallenged; a figure read aloud is not the figure paid. He takes himself out of his own sentence and goes off believing he has done a kindness, with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside. Garl’s debt against the tiles is left where it lay, neither paid nor settled, never done with. The bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself; the clerk at the Fishstairs still sits for an uncalled measure. The boy files the twice-wiped thumb on a tray of its own and does not join it to any other hand. Nothing is called, paid or explained.

On Days 85 through 90 the same arithmetic is done over the last market of Silt and goes over the turn of the month unchanged. On Silt 30, the tenth day of the tend and the last market of Silt, he comes up to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and nothing under it, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before he touches nothing, reads one in twelve twice over the basket, passes a finger over the figure and says \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}. To a man who brings a number in a fist and asks what the thaw will cost he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. If the house wants it, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} --- and the number goes from the fist to his mouth to the shoulder of a man going up toward High Kiln and arrives nowhere. The true subtraction goes over the basket unspoken and the printed figure stands unchallenged; a man can stand under it all morning and go home with the number still in his fist and never have entered it. He takes himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on and goes off toward High Kiln with the box in his house locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness. The bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself; across the market a woman stands with green at one corner of her mouth and the boy files it in silence without a name for the mouth or the woman. The soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs is still set for a measure nobody called. On Seed 1 a month turns over the arithmetic without noticing and he is not on the page; Garl’s debt against the tiles is neither paid nor settled and the box stays locked. The boy keeps the twice-wiped thumb on a tray of its own and does not join it to any other hand, and no figure read aloud is the figure paid.

On Day 91 the same arithmetic is done over worked ground instead of a market, and the withholding stays the district’s ordinary speech. He comes down from the north road to look at the strips east of Low Kiln, short, with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it, the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth and hot clay over the smell of nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing and holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm. To the man who brings a number up out of a fist and asks what the planting will cost now that seed has gone into the ground he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip. If the house wants it, there’ll be a slate at the watch}, and to the yard says \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}. He never says \emph{I}; he takes himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, and the true subtraction goes over the strips unspoken. A figure read aloud is not the figure paid and nothing in the strip changes its figure because a man has looked at it. He does not look into the basket, files his twice-wiped thumb on its own tray beside the other record-first hands, and goes off toward High Kiln with the box in his house locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness. The uncalled debt against the firing of tiles stays neither paid nor settled.

On Days 94 through 100 the same arithmetic is done over the worked strips and then over a planting month that has become waiting, and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. On Seed 10, Tenthday and the second Account-day of Seed, he comes to the reading block at the Cross with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and nothing under it; his hands are large and clean and he wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing. He reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, passes a finger over the figure, calls the levy for Seed and says \emph{It is not called by me}, and says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if the house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch}. The true subtraction goes over the basket unspoken and the number for what the planting will cost goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrives nowhere; a figure read aloud is not the figure paid. The bell goes four, four and a gap over the market and nobody crosses himself; he keeps the heard bell beside the told bell in two places. At the Slate Row fringe a man whose name is on no roll, with soft hands and a patient face, hands a figure to a slate and holds it at the edge where nobody else can see; the boy files the soft hands apart from Marra, the Drawing collector with grey fingertips, the Court-table clerk and the Fishstairs clerk, apart from the child and the loaf, and does not call it a sale. Berr goes off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box in his house locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness. He has not looked into the basket, has never said \emph{I}, and no new scar, possession or change of voice is recorded.

On Days 101 through 103 the same arithmetic is done from the clay road rather than the block and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. He comes up the clay road on Seed 13 from the Cross with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and nothing under it, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, calls the levy and takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{There’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. The true subtraction goes over the basket unspoken and the number for the planting goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrives nowhere, a figure read aloud that is not the figure paid; nothing in the strip changes its figure because a man has looked at it. He does not look into the basket, files his twice-wiped thumb on a tray of its own beside the other record-first hands, and goes off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box in his house locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done a kindness. The uncalled debt against the firing of tiles stays neither paid nor settled and the soft-cuffed clerk stays set at the Fishstairs for a measure nobody called.

On Days 104 through 106 the same arithmetic is done over worked ground with hands in it and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. On Seed 15 he comes down off the north road at midday with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest a breath longer than the writing required. He reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the work, calls the levy and says it is not called by him. To a man who brings a number up out of a fist and asks what the planting will cost now that hands have gone into it he says a number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if the house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch --- \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. The figure read aloud is not the figure paid and the true subtraction sits in the locked box in his house up the road; nothing in the strip changes its figure because a man has looked at it. He never looks into the basket and goes off toward High Kiln believing he has done the district a kindness. Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles stays neither paid nor settled and the boy files his twice-wiped thumb on its own tray beside the other record-first hands, not joined to any of them. Offstage on Seed 16 and 17.

On Days 107 through 109 the same arithmetic is done over the planting month’s last tend and its Account-day, and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. On Seed 20, Tenthday and Account-day, he comes up to the reading block at the Cross short, with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and, under it, nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before he touches nothing and holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest a breath longer than the writing required, the way a man checks a dish he has already set down to be sure it will not slop. He reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd over the worked ground where the hands went in on Seed 15, calls the levy and says \emph{It is not called by me}. To a man who brings a number up out of a fist and asks what the planting cost now that hands have been in it, he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if the house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. The sentence passes around the square like a bucket passed from hand to hand and nobody thinks to ask who is carrying it. The figure read aloud is not the figure paid; the true subtraction goes over the strips unspoken and sits in the locked box in his house up the road, and nothing in the ground changes its figure because a man has looked at it. The bell at the Cross goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself; word comes up that the soft-cuffed clerk is still set at the Fishstairs for a measure nobody called. Garl’s uncalled debt against the firing of tiles goes around the space where a name might have stood and is not called. He never looks into the basket and goes off toward High Kiln with the box still locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness.

On Days 110 through 112 the same arithmetic is done over the planting month’s last tend and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. He appears once, on Seed 22 in the afternoon at the outer edge of the yard well, and is offstage for the other two days. He comes up short off the north road with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath; his hands are large and clean and he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, holding a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required. He reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the leaning yard and says \emph{A number goes into a slate and not into a strip; if your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. A man brings a number up out of a fist toward the well, looks at it, thinks better of giving it, puts the fist back in his sleeve and goes off, so the figure arrives nowhere; the district’s whole arithmetic is done in the open air, from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and nowhere, and a figure let fall is still a figure carried. The boy files Berr’s twice-wiped thumb and his finger over the figure on a tray of their own, not joined to the neighbour’s reaching hand at the shelf or to any other record-first hand. Berr does not look into the basket and goes off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box in his house locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness; Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles goes around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with, and a thing kept is a thing that will one day be asked for.

On Days 113 through 115 the same arithmetic is done offstage and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. He does not appear; on Seed 26 the boy sets the twice-wiped thumb and the finger over a figure on a place of its own among the record-first hands, beside the midwife’s reaching hand, the neighbour’s at the well, the Court-table clerk’s, the man who priced him, the wheel-keeper’s, the woman who keeps the fire’s and the midwife’s again — all kept apart and none joined. At the Cross a man whose name is on no roll holds a figure to a slate at the edge with a thumb resting on the corner afterward, without wiping twice and passing a finger over the number as Berr would have done, and the boy files the soft hands apart from him and from every other tray: no wiped thumb, no sentence with the speaker taken out of it, no sale. A number brought up out of a fist toward the well on Seed 24 is looked at and put back in the sleeve, arriving nowhere, the district’s arithmetic done in the open air without him. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles stays neither paid nor settled, never done with; Sella’s mark is untouched, Jorra’s dust unspoken, Alda’s notes where they belonged. He is off up the clay road with the box locked in his house and the true deduction inside, and nobody under the Vail roof has called him or thanked him or asked him for the figure.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. At the Cross, before two hundred people and eight pigs, wiped his thumb on his apron before touching the clean slate and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} in the voice that stops the roar; added that a household which has heard otherwise has heard wrong, that the account stands as read, and that there will be a slate at the watch for any household that wants the figure again. Read it a second time in the afternoon for the households that came late. Set the slate down twice; both times it gave its small flat answer, unremarked. Wore the red wool cord of his office folded square and tasted his own glaze without appearing to. At the Slate Row end confirmed Sella’s widow’s mark as a kindness entered by the factor at Greybank, spoke around the uncalled debt against the firing of tiles, did not ask to see the mark, and left the debt as he found it. Did not look into the basket and never addressed the boy.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 5: Day 8, at the Fishstairs. Came down the steps with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat, hands large and clean, thumb wiped on his apron before he touched his slate, lead-glaze green at one corner of his mouth and hot clay over the smell of nothing. Said \emph{the levy is called for the feast; it is not called by me} to the eels, accepted four eels where six should go, and gave out \emph{three days to the Five} from the top of the steps with a finger passed over the figure. Did not acknowledge the two eels short against his two marks short of six years and did not look into the basket.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Day 14, Stone 20, Account-day, at the Cross. Came to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat, hands large and clean and lead-glaze green at one corner of his mouth; wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching the slate. Read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of a crowd of two hundred, added that a household which has heard otherwise has heard wrong, passed a finger over the figure and said \emph{The figure stands as read. There’ll be a slate at the watch if the house wants it again.} Said \emph{the levy is called for the feast; it is not called by me.} Spoke of the kiln-house, the mark confirmed by the factor at Greybank and the fire kept under the roof, and went around a consignment of tiles where a debt might have stood, never naming it. Did not look into the basket and went home by dusk believing his own sentences. The box in his house stayed locked.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Day 24, Stone 30, Account-day and the year’s last market. Came to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and lead-glaze green at one corner of his mouth; wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching the slate and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd, passed a finger over the figure, and said the levy was called for the feast and was not called by him. Went around the uncalled debt against the firing of tiles without naming it, set the printed figure where everyone could see it, and did not look into the basket. The household’s stores went into the last tend and the Five were spoken of as three days off; the district argued three, two and whatever the moot had already decided to give out. Went back to the pigs by dusk believing he had done the district a kindness. The box in his house stayed locked and the true deduction stayed in it.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 8: Day 26, Weighing. Glimpsed at the edge of the reading with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and green glaze at one corner of his mouth; wiped his thumb before touching his slate and passed a finger over the figure. An officer in a clean voice wearing a temple’s clothes read the measures --- his Cross grammar in an institution’s mouth --- announced a whole return for a person not in the room and read a name the household would not afterward repeat; he explained nothing, looked nowhere near the basket and went off with the box in his house still locked. On Ilmen 1 one in twelve stayed printed and unchallenged at the Opening of the Slates and the true deduction was spoken by nobody. The box stayed locked and the uncalled debt against the tiles stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 9: Day 36, Ilmen 7, came back from looking at the ice with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth; wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, passed a finger across the figure on a narrow slate he held, and had a number he did not care to give. To a neighbour at the well who started to ask said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. If your house wants it, there’ll be a slate at the watch}, saying \emph{your house} and not \emph{my account}, and took himself out of his own sentence. Went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and looked nowhere near the basket. One in twelve stood printed and unchallenged and the true subtraction was spoken by nobody.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 10: Day 39, Ilmen 10, Account-day. Came to the Cross with the red wool cord folded under his coat and green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} into the crowd, called the levy for the thaw and took himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}. To a neighbour who started to ask said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well}; the true subtraction went over the basket and the number for the thaw went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and was never given. Went around Garl’s uncalled debt without naming it, did not look into the basket and went off with the box in his house still locked. Not at the Weir on Ilmen 14 or 15.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 11: Day 47, Ilmen 18. Came up the yard from the road below with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat, green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth and hot clay under the smell of nothing at all; the women at the tubs made room for him as for a slate left out in the rain. Wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened, passing a finger over it and letting his eyes rest longer than the writing required. Said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. The house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch}, taking himself out of his own sentence; never said I. Did not look into the basket and went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside. The figure that had gone from fist to mouth to shoulder went with him into a slate and stayed there.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 12: Day 49, Account-day, Ilmen 20. Came to the Cross with the red wool cord folded under his coat and green glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket; the true subtraction went unspoken. To a neighbour who began to ask he said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well; there’ll be a slate at the watch}, taking himself out of his own sentence; the number for the thaw went from fist to mouth to shoulder and was given to nobody. The bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself. He went off toward High Kiln with the box still locked and never looked into the basket.

\end{itemize}

Read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the leaning yard, said \emph{A number goes into a slate and not into a strip. If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a hand goes out of a field before the dressing goes on. A man brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it, thought better of giving it, put the fist in his sleeve and went off, so the figure arrived nowhere; nothing in the strip’s account changed its figure because a man had looked at it. Never said \emph{I} and did not look into the basket; the boy put his twice-wiped thumb and his finger over the figure on a tray of their own, not joined to the neighbour’s reaching hand at the shelf or to any other record-first hand. Tarn said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying. Went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the narrow slate under his coat and the box locked in his house behind him and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness; Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles went around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with. At the Cross a man from Slate Row whose name was on no roll held a figure to a slate at the edge where nobody else could see it and rested his thumb on the corner afterward without wiping twice and passing a finger over the number as Berr would have done; the boy filed the soft hands apart from him and from Marra, the Drawing collector, the Court-table clerk and the Fishstairs clerk, a sixth shape on no tray, with no sixth sighting of the neat dark hand and no sale. A man brought a number up out of a fist toward the well on Seed 24, looked at it, thought better of giving it and put the fist back in his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles went around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with; Sella’s widow’s mark stayed untouched, Jorra’s dust and the back room unspoken, Alda’s second notes where they belonged. Never said \emph{I} and never looked into the basket; the box stayed locked in his house up the clay road and the true deduction inside, and he believed he had done the district a kindness. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\CRcharacter*{Marra}{the woman at the edge of the flare light}{build/art/characters/marra.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Collector Marra, Marra of the Grey Coat, the woman with the slate, the hand that writes}\CRfield{Role}{antagonist}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 768, the Hearthseat, on the Keel}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; officer of the Keeping)}\CRfield{Origin}{the Hearthseat; no house, no kin; entered on the rolls in Ledgerhand}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Warm Court, collector’s office; secretly the Unbanked}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 1}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
In the death scene she is a grey shape at the edge of the flare light in a coat the colour of wet ash, holding a slate, writing; the writing does not stop when the van takes him. In Sarn she is a woman in her forties with the neat, unremarkable face of an officer who has spent her life at tables rather than in rooms. Her fingertips are the colour of wet ash and have been since Y.H. 803, which she attributes to cold rooms in a voice that invites no question. She wears her hair pinned tight and her cuffs buttoned to the wrist, partly from the trade and partly because she does not want the hand seen. She has the collector’s habit of touching the slate before she touches the person, and a smaller habit — noticed only by people who have watched her for years — of touching her own wrist afterwards, where the iron clip would go, as if checking that it is not there. She smells of cold iron, slate dust and nothing else, which is the most expensive smell in Sarn.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
She apologises in clauses she does not finish. She is precise about other people’s warmth and vague about her own, and the vagueness is not evasion but a genuine absence: she has entered so many measures that she has lost the habit of entering herself. She speaks the Ledgerhand passive as naturally as breathing — \emph{the measure is banked, the return is recorded, the account stands} — and then, rarely, a plain sentence breaks through, usually about a child, and is immediately corrected into the grammar again. When she lies she becomes even more exact, giving dates and figures that nobody asked for.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The measure was drawn at the fourth beat. I’m sorry, I — the account stands. That’s all that’s required.”

\item “I don’t remember my fingers. I mean, I remember that they were — they were warm once. That isn’t in the report.”

\item “You were written before you were seen. That’s an irregularity. It isn’t a cruelty. There’s a difference, and I’ve entered it.”

\item “Forty measures. One return. If you add it and it doesn’t balance, you’re adding it wrong. I’ve added it. I know what it balances to.”

\item “I’ve been paying since. Don’t ask me with what. It isn’t in the report.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She entered the Keeping as a collector’s assistant in Greybank in Y.H. 790, arriving from the Hearthseat with a slate and an unusual care for the measurement of other people’s warmth. Her early reports were models of the craft: exact, unembellished, quiet about her own deductions. Within four years she was collecting in the Sill district; within twenty her fingertips had begun to go grey; within twenty-five she was the collector of the Low Kiln levy and the woman the district crosses the street to avoid. She has never been reprimanded and has never been promoted, which is a distinction she has thought about more carefully than either.

In the winter of Y.H. 812 she was standing at the edge of a flare light on an expressway in a country she could not have named, writing because the trace in front of her would not cool. She did not cause the crash and did not touch the child. She wrote the measure of a man who gave at the moment of breaking and whose promise was too heavy to bank. She wrote a name — Corin — before she had seen the infant’s face. Then she went home to Sarn and forged the assessment: a whole return with memory intact, booked at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures, with the deduction entered as zero. The money came from forty children of Low Kiln. The collector’s clerk who carried the slate has never been able to spell the buyer’s name.

She has been paying for the return ever since with her own fingers, a little warmth at a time, drawn without a slate and booked nowhere. In Y.H. 803 a slate in Greybank was found with a line that did not balance; it was corrected in a second hand and filed without comment. The first hand was hers. The second was also hers, written with the other hand so that the file would show two officers.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
Her fingers. And underneath them, the forty. She can add and she has added, and the difference between what a whole return costs and what the Hearth was told it cost is a number she carries the way Dan carries Tasha’s chart — as a small, hard, private knowledge of the shape of her own conduct. She fears the Weighing, where the year’s measures are read aloud in a clean voice, because one of them is hers and it is not on any roll. She fears that the boy will one day look at her with that clinical attention and add her up the way she has added up everyone else. Her contradiction: the woman who invented an officer’s exactness to hide a forgery has made the forgery the most exact thing in her life, and calls it \emph{the account standing}.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants the sealed world too — the Unbanked’s paradise, where nothing leaks and nothing is owed — and she wants the instrument they sent for to be whole enough to do the sealing. She thinks she wants the boy to live. What she needs is to understand that she has already spent him: forty children bought one man, and no amount of careful handwriting makes that a balance. When she finally confesses it, it will be in a clause she does not finish, and the boy will finish it for her, in the plainest words, and the world will not end.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Corin} — the return she paid for and has never watched grow. She knows his name before she knows his face, and when she meets him in Slate Row she will look at him the way a surgeon looks at a chart: to check whether her own work held. He will be the first person to ask her about the fingers, and the first to hear her say \emph{I don’t remember} and understand that she means \emph{I do}. \emph{Ch 1:} she is a coat the colour of wet ash at the edge of a flare, a hand moving on a slate, and the same pause in a dark hand on a birth-slate in Low Kiln. He has filed the hand without a name and has not put the two together.

\textbf{Rusk} — the other half of the purchase. He taught the boy; she bought him. They have not spoken plainly in twelve years and have arranged their lives so that they never have to. She has begun to be afraid that he is gentler with the boy than the work permits, which in her vocabulary is the same as saying he has begun to love him.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — she took his signature on the levy of forty and let him forget the purchaser’s name, which he did deliberately and with relief. She has never thanked him and never will; a debt acknowledged is a debt entered.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — Alda crossed herself at a birth-flower and wrote nothing in the Court’s book. Marra has read the Court’s book. She has never asked Alda what else she wrote, because a hearth-maid’s second note is the one thing even a collector cannot lawfully want.

\textbf{Haldre} — whose paper named the ending she has been paying for. She has never read it. She has heard it described once, by Rusk, and has spent the years since doing the work without the theory, which is a more Sarnish arrangement than either of them will admit.

\textbf{Steward Derren} — her head of office, whom she has never contradicted and never trusted. He has praised her exactness twice. She has decided that his praise is the most dangerous thing in the Hearthseat.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
Chapter 1 gives the first of her two entrances before she enters. She is a grey shape at the edge of the flare light: a coat, a head, a hand, writing without stopping while the van burns. She is not named, not to Dan and not to the reader, who is allowed to think she caused the fire. The writing has the same rhythm of short strokes and a decided pause as the strange dark hand on the birth-slate in House Silt, and Dan sets the two side by side without putting them together. The fingers, the forged assessment, the forty and the unfinished apology are all still buried.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Appears only as the image at the edge of the flare light --- coat the colour of wet ash, hand on a slate, short strokes, a pause, more strokes, the writing not stopping when the fire takes the van. Unnamed in the Sarn narration and unremembered by name. She wrote a name before anyone saw the child’s face; by morning that pause is sitting on a slab of grey stone within reach of a midwife’s hand.

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter*{Ulda}{the friend who knew exactly what to say}{build/art/characters/ulda.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Ulda, Ulda of the Fishstairs, the foundling with the ready laugh, the boy who sold the mark}\CRfield{Role}{antagonist}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 809, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath (foundling; one name only)}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; foundling, one name only)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; no house, no kin, no slate until the Court entered him}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Fishstairs; the Waiting Room clerk; quietly, the keeping of small secrets for people who pay}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 16}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Three years older than Corin and twice as easy in the world, with a narrow face that is always slightly amused and a set of clothes that are somebody else’s cast-offs worn as if they were a uniform. He has a gap where a front tooth was knocked out at the Fishstairs and he grins through it, which makes people forgive the things he says before they have decided whether to be offended. He keeps a sliver of green lead-glaze in a string around his neck, picked up in High Kiln, and rubs it with his thumb while he decides what a person wants to hear, which is almost always the thing they have already said they want and a little more. He smells of river silt, small ale and the warm stone of other people’s hearths, because he is always in somebody’s kitchen and never in his own. The thing people notice first is the grin; the thing they notice last is that when Corin turns his head toward a pot, Ulda turns it too, a half-beat late, and has never once been able to explain why.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Fast, warm, fluent in the proverb-form of Low Kiln and quicker than the adults at it. He is the only child in the yard who can make the kiln-hands laugh, and he does it by saying the thing the adults are thinking in a voice that makes it harmless. He never says \emph{I want}; he says \emph{they say}, \emph{everyone knows}, \emph{your house wouldn’t mind}, which is a way of wanting without owning the want. When he is lying he gets affectionate, which is the tell that Mira Silt has learned to read and that Corin, for years, took for kindness. He has a habit of finishing another person’s sentence for them, correctly, and then looking surprised that it was not what they meant.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “—and a good deal,” said at the well in Ch 16, finishing a kiln-hand’s sentence in a quick, warm, affectionate voice. “That’s the whole of the account. Everyone knows it. I’m only saying.” This is his first plain sound in the book: a borrowed sentence, harmless on the surface, that makes the yard laugh before anybody has decided whether to be offended.

\item “Everyone knows the Vail boy isn’t Vail. I’m not saying it. I’m saying everyone knows it. There’s a difference.”

\item “You heard it before I tapped it, didn’t you? That’s not a trick. That’s a thing you should be careful with, Corin. I’m only saying.”

\item “I didn’t tell the clerk. I told him a thing and he wrote it down. That’s not the same, is it? You tell me, because I can never tell which part’s mine.”

\item “The mark. Under your sleeve. I saw it at the Weir and I didn’t say. I didn’t say for three years, Corin. That’s what I’m asking you to remember.”

\item “Sella’s kind to you. She’s kind to me too, when she’s thinking of something else. Don’t make it more than it is.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was born in Low Kiln to a mother entered in the name-pot and returned thin, and he has never known which of the several dead in him is his mother, which he describes as \emph{a family, in a manner of speaking}. He was entered on a slate at three because the Court began counting foundlings in Y.H. 782, and has had a name on a roll ever since, which makes him, in his own account, a man of property compared with Corin, who for his first years had none. He attached himself to the Vail yard at five because there was alwaysbread there and because the boy with the flower was interesting in a way Ulda could not name. He became the foundling’s friend in the way poor children become friends: by sharing a crust, by knowing which boards at the Fishstairs are safe, and by being the person who says the thing aloud that the other one is thinking.

He has sold small secrets at the Fishstairs since he was nine — which household has paid the levy, which collector takes his ale before a draw, which hearth-maid has begun to keep a second set of notes — and has never thought of it as betrayal, because a secret in Low Kiln is a thing that belongs to whoever can use it. In Y.H. 811 he told a Waiting Room clerk that a foundling under the Vail roof could hear the full note of a pot before it was tapped. The clerk wrote it down. Ulda was eleven and was paid in a loaf, and has entered the loaf in no account, which is the only thing about the whole business he has never been able to explain to himself.

Three years later he will tell the same clerk about the branching red mark under the boy’s sleeve, which he saw at the Weir and has kept for exactly the right moment, and the clerk will write that down too. He will do it because he has begun to be afraid that Corin will one day be taken by the Court and Ulda will not be there to be useful, which in his vocabulary is the same as being abandoned. He will say afterwards that he did it to protect him. He will believe it for a while.

\textbf{On his age in these chapters.} In Y.H. 813, when he first comes plainly into the yard in Chapter 16, he is a small foundling of three or four in somebody else’s cast-offs, not the eleven-year-old of the dialogue above. The sentences about the Waiting Room clerk, the paid loaf, the mark under the sleeve and the sale at eleven belong to years hence and are written here as the shape of the man he will become, not as words this child speaks now. In Chapter 16 he is given one borrowed sentence and nothing of his own; his sheet was reconciled to this on his first appearance. If he is given a second speaking appearance while the boy is still an infant, treat the later dialogue as years ahead of him and give him no secret to sell yet.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He has no house and has made a career of being the person who fits into other people’s. His wound is that he cannot want anything in his own voice: every desire comes out as \emph{they say} or \emph{everyone knows}, so that he can deny it if it is refused. He fears the name-pot, because a foundling entered on a slate can be entered again, and fears more than that the day Corin looks at him with that clinical, quiet attention and sees the thing he did at eleven. His contradiction: the boy who tells everyone’s secrets has kept one of his own for three years — the mark — and calls the keeping of it loyalty, when it is a thing he has been saving to spend.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants a place in a household, any household, where the door closes on him and somebody says his name without a slate in front of them. He thinks he wants Corin to stay in Low Kiln and be his friend forever, which is the same as wanting the boy not to become what he is becoming. What he needs is to understand that a person cannot be kept by being useful, and that the loaf he was paid at eleven has gathered interest for three years in an account he cannot read. When he finally says the thing he did, it will be in the affectionate voice, and it will be the first honest sentence he has ever spoken, and Corin will not believe him at first, which is the correct response.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Corin} — his friend, the only person he has never tried to manage, which is why the betrayal will work. Ulda knows the boy hears things and has spent years pretending not to notice so that the boy will keep being ordinary beside him. The tension is a love that expresses itself as a careful inventory of the beloved’s weaknesses, held in reserve. \emph{Ch 16:} the boy in the basket is still an infant and Ulda does not know him yet; he turns his own head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy turns his, is as surprised as anybody and cannot say why, and rubs the green sliver at his neck. The half-beat is the physical tell of what he will one day do, filed in the boy’s private file without a cause written across it. \emph{Ch 18:} the delay came a second time at the market’s edge on Silt 30, half a beat after the boy’s turning and after the knuckle, and he stopped, rubbed the sliver and could not say why; no loaf, no slate, no sentence. The boy keeps the second delay on its own tray beside the first and still writes no cause across either.

\textbf{Mira Silt} — she reads his affection as the tell it is and has told him once, at the Fishstairs, that a boy who sells a secret has no way of buying it back. He answered with the weather and has never forgotten that she did not laugh.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — he carries messages for her and has never once told her that the boy she thinks is dead is three doors away, because a secret that big would make him important, and a boy who is important gets entered on a slate.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — he is always in her kitchen and she has never once said he may not be, which he has decided is the same as being wanted and is not.

\textbf{The Waiting Room clerk} — a man whose name is not on any roll, who pays in loaves and ale and has taught Ulda that a secret is worth exactly what somebody will give for it. This is the man who will buy the mark.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — who would throw him out of the yard if he knew half of it, and whom Ulda watches carefully, because Jorra has broken three birth-slates and is therefore a person who could be useful or a person who could be dangerous.

\textbf{Ch 17.} On Silt 19 he is glimpsed once, silently, at the yard well — a small foundling in cast-off clothes worn like a uniform, a gap in his grin, the green sliver of lead-glaze at his neck. He turns his head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy’s and rubs the sliver, and is as surprised as anyone; no sentence is finished for a kiln-hand this time, no loaf passes, no slate is seen. The boy files the delay as an object on a place of its own and keeps his own turning beside it without letting the two touch. He is not seen again that week; nothing has changed hands that a slate could read and the sale stays a shape, not a betrayal paid. The half-beat and the loaf from Silt 16 gather interest in an account the child cannot read.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} He is still a shape and not a friend in the boy’s file: the Silt 16 loaf and the half-beat have gathered another seven days of interest, and nothing has crossed that any slate could read. Corin does not know him yet and he has no line of his own; Mira still reads the affection he has not learned to hide, and Sella’s kitchen door is still open without anybody saying he may not come in. Jorra would throw him out if he knew half of it, and the Waiting Room clerk still waits for a better price than a loaf. No bond changed hands on Seed 9: no loaf, no slate, no sentence finished, no secret sold.

\textbf{Ch 23 (bonds).} He is still a shape and not a friend in the boy’s file: the Silt 16 loaf and the half-beat have gathered another three days of interest and nothing has crossed that any slate could read. Corin does not know him yet and he has no line of his own; Mira still reads the affection he has not learned to hide, and Sella’s kitchen door is still open without anybody saying he may not come in. Jorra would throw him out if he knew half of it, and the Waiting Room clerk still waits for a better price than a loaf. On Seed 19 he was glimpsed once at the market’s edge, unnamed and silent, cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap in his grin and the green sliver at his throat; when a pot was set down his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped, and he rubbed the sliver and opened his mouth on the tail of a kiln-hand’s sentence without finishing it. No loaf passed, no slate was seen and no secret sold; the delay stays a thing that comes after the knock, not a hearing and not a seventh, and the sale stays a shape.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
He enters in Chapter 16 as the grin at the well, finishing a kiln-hand’s sentence in the affectionate voice that makes the yard laugh, a small foundling of three or four in a coat with a man’s shoulders and breeches cut off at the knee, worn like a uniform he was never measured for. The gap where a front tooth had been goes into every circle of the yard ahead of him and comes back with permission to say anything; the sliver of green lead-glaze on a string at his neck is rubbed with his thumb while he decides what a person wants to hear, which is usually what the person has already said and a little more. He says what everybody is thinking in a tone that makes it harmless, and he never says \emph{I want} --- he says \emph{they say}, \emph{everyone knows}, \emph{your house wouldn’t mind}. When a woman sets a pot down his head goes toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stops and comes back; he rubs the green sliver and cannot say why he turned, and is as surprised as anybody. When a man from Slate Row whose name is on no roll holds out a warm loaf, his mouth opens on a sentence with the shape of \emph{everyone} or \emph{your house} and stops where a want would have stood, because he has no form of words for a want that is his own and is too quick a child to say a thing that could be refused to him by name. The loaf goes into the pocket of the cast-off coat, which holds a bit of string and nothing any clerk could read, with no slate between them; the man says something low that does not carry and the child nods as though he had understood it. He is named on the sheet but not in the narration. He stays a shape in the boy’s file --- a delay, a sliver, a loaf, an unfinished sentence --- and no secret has changed hands that any slate could read, no betrayal has been paid. The loaf has begun to gather interest in an account he cannot read, and the half-beat is held for the day it lands as the physical tell of what he did.

On Days 78 through 84 he is a shape at the edge of the recovery, not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. He appears once, at the yard well on Silt 19, in cast-offs worn like a uniform with a green sliver at his throat; when a pot is set down his head goes toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, and he stops, rubs the sliver and cannot say why he turned. The boy files the delay beside his own turning without letting the two touch, because a thing that comes after the knock is a different thing from one that comes before it and this was neither a hearing nor a seventh. No acceleration of a kiln-hand’s sentence, no warm loaf, no slate, no secret; he is gone for the rest of the week and nothing has been sold that any clerk could read. The half-beat stays the physical tell held for the day the small sales land as betrayal, and the loaf from the man from Slate Row goes on gathering interest in an account he cannot read.

On Days 85 through 90 he is a shape at the edge of the last market of Silt, still not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. He is glimpsed a second time on Silt 30 at the market’s edge, unnamed in the narration: a small foundling in cast-offs worn like a uniform, a gap where a front tooth had been and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat. When a pot is set down his head goes toward it a half-beat after the boy’s --- after the knuckle and after the note --- and then stops; he rubs the sliver with his thumb and cannot say why he turned. No sentence is finished for a kiln-hand, no loaf passes, no slate is seen and no secret sold. The boy files the delay on a place of its own beside his own turning and does not let the two touch, because a thing that comes after the knock is a different object from one that comes before it. He is not Marra, not the Fishstairs clerk and not the Court-table clerk and is joined to none of them; the sale stays a shape and the betrayal stays years ahead. The half-beat and the warm loaf from the man from Slate Row go on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read, and the month turns into Seed with nothing changed hands that any slate could read.

On Days 94 through 100 he is a shape at the edge of the planting month, still not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. He is glimpsed a third time on Seed 9 at the edge of the Fishstairs market, unnamed in the narration: a small foundling in cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap where a front tooth had been and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat. When a pot is set down his head goes toward it a half-beat after the boy’s --- after the knuckle and after the note --- then stops; he rubs the sliver with his thumb and cannot say why he turned, opens his mouth on the tail of a kiln-hand’s sentence and lets nothing out that a slate could take down. No new loaf passes, no slate is opened within reach of the basket, no secret changes hands that a slate could read and no loan or sale is paid. He is not Marra, not the Fishstairs clerk and not the Court-table clerk, and is joined to none of them. The boy files the delay on a place of its own, after the knock and not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh, and keeps his own turning beside it without letting the two touch. The half-beat and the warm loaf from the man from Slate Row go on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read, and any dialogue on his sheet remains years ahead of the child in the basket.

On Days 107 through 109 he is a shape at the edge of the planting month’s last tend, still not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. He is glimpsed once on Seed 19 at the dawn market below the north bridge, unnamed in the narration, at the edge of the fish-trade shade where a whole market walks carefully over the out-of-line landing and a soft-cuffed clerk sits for a measure nobody called. He is in cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap where a front tooth had been and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat. When a kiln-hand sets a pot down near the eel shade the boy hears its full note and his head goes toward it; the foundling’s head goes a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stops in the middle of the turn. He rubs the sliver twice with his thumb and could not have said why he turned, and there is no word in the market’s language for the thing that made him turn, which was not the note and came after it. A kiln-hand at the edge says the tail of a sentence and leaves it hanging, and the foundling’s mouth opens on the end of it the way a child’s mouth opens to finish a thing heard a hundred times, and nothing comes out that any clerk could have taken down. No loaf passes, no slate is opened within reach of the basket and no secret changes hands that a slate could read. The boy files the delay on a place of its own, after the knock and not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh, keeps his own turning beside it without letting the two touch, and sets the watcher’s turning beside the two tellings of the shelf as a third shape, joining none of them. Somewhere a long way off a hand will lay them together and call the joining an account; it is not his hand and it is not today. The half-beat and the Silt 16 loaf go on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read, and any dialogue on his sheet remains years ahead of the child in the basket.

He rubbed the sliver again and went back to watching the grown faces. No secret spoken, no slate seen, no betrayal paid; the half-beat and the loaf filed as separate objects in the boy’s private account.
