\CRcharacter{Steward Derren}{the reasonable man at the head of the account}{build/portraits/steward-derren.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Steward Derren, Derren, the head of the Keeping, the voice that never rises}\CRfield{Role}{villain}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 749, the Hearthseat, on the Keel}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; officer of the Keeping)}\CRfield{Origin}{the Hearthseat; slate-name entered on the rolls, no house and no kin}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Warm Court — Steward of the Hearth; keeper of the sealed files}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 640}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Sixty-three and spare, with the dry, maintained look of a vessel that has been carefully tempered and has never been allowed to run cold. He dresses in the Hearthseat’s plain dark wool with a strip of lead-grey at the collar that denotes the office and nothing else; he has no rings, no house-mark and no ornament, because an officer who wears a thing gives the rolls something to read. His hands are clean to the point of aggression — the hands of a man who has not carried fuel in forty years and does not need to. His voice is low, level and slightly warm, which is the most frightening thing about him, because his listeners must lean in and therefore agree to the sentence before it is finished. He has a trick of resting his fingertips on a slate while he speaks, not to consult it but to keep it flat, the way another man might keep a cup from sliding. He smells of warm stone, clean paper and the faintest trace of the Hearth-fire, which follows him from the Weighing Hall and which he has never tried to hide.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Ledgerhand grammar made flesh: every sentence passive, every verb removed, every cruelty in the third person. He never raises his voice, never says \emph{I} where he can say \emph{the Keeping}, and never says \emph{you} where he can say \emph{the account}. He has eleven words for a deduction and will use the exact one, which is his way of being honest within the only vocabulary he considers real. When he is contradicted he becomes interested, which is worse than anger. He has one habit that his officers have learned to fear: he writes the thing down while the person is still speaking.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The measure is banked. The account stands. Nothing is lost that we have kept. That is the whole of it, and it is not a threat.”

\item “You have said a thing that cannot be entered. I have entered it anyway. That is my kindness.”

\item “The world cannot be saved. The counting can be continued. Those are different propositions, and only one of them is my work.”

\item “One in twelve is printed on the notice. What a household believes is not in the notice, and is therefore not in the Keeping.”

\item “I have read the sealed file. You have not. Shall I tell you what it says, or shall we go on as we were?”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was entered on the rolls at twenty-two and has never held another name. He rose not by cleverness but by an unbroken capacity to be present when a difficult slate had to be signed: the Ash Rising of Y.H. 668, the suppression of Haldre’s paper in 710, the sealing of the First Seam survey in 806, the Long Cold of 811. In each case he was the officer who wrote the final line in a hand that did not vary, and in each case the line was a kindness in the grammar of the Keeping — the district was quieted, the paper was suppressed, the survey was sealed, the levy was raised for the Hearth. He has never been accused of cruelty and has never understood an accusation when one was made, because he cannot see the person inside the account, and has spent forty years perfecting the not-seeing.

He has read the sealed file. He knows the Hearth is a wound and the Keeping is salvage from a failing repair. He knows the deduction in Low Kiln is one in three and that the printed notice is a founding invoice dressed as mercy. He knows the oldest repairs under the world are neither clay nor stone, and he knows what the Keldish translation and the Court translation of them were: both guesses, both near. He has read Haldre’s paper and has not burned his copy. He keeps it because it is the only honest document in the Hearthseat and because he has decided that honesty, left where it is, does no harm. He is not a believer. He is a continuance.

In the first weeks of Stone, Y.H. 812, he authorised a private whole return of forty unspent measures without recording the purchaser. He did this personally and with perfect composure, and has entered nothing about it anywhere except in the sealed file, where the entry reads: \emph{The instrument is in place. The account is carried.}

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He has no wound he will admit to, which is itself the wound: a man who has trained himself not to feel the cold has become unable to feel anyone else’s. He fears the Waste growing inward, because it is the only thing in his ledger that does not balance and cannot be written down as a kindness. He fears a hot trace that will not cool, because it is the only measure that will not enter an account. He fears, most of all, a man who looks at a dying body and says plainly \emph{leave it}, because that sentence has no passive form and therefore cannot be entered, and a thing that cannot be entered is a thing the Keeping cannot survive. His contradiction is not hidden and not a secret: he knows the world cannot be saved by the Keeping, and he continues the Keeping anyway, and calls the continuation mercy.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants the account to continue. He thinks he wants the world kept. What he needs is to understand the difference — which he already knows and has chosen to forget — and that a man who continues a failing repair is not keeping the world but spending it, one district at a time. He will never understand this in any way that changes him. He will understand it perfectly in the way that lets him write it down.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Marra} — his collector, the most exact hand in his service, whose fingers are going grey and whose reports have never once mentioned her own deductions. He has praised her twice and once asked her, gently, whether she believed the printed figure. She said the account stood. He has not asked again, because the answer confirmed what he needed: she is one of his own, in the sense that she has learned not to see the person.

\textbf{Derren the Younger} — an officer’s son with access to the sealed file and a different last name in his heart. The younger man has begun to ask about the oldest repairs in language that is almost the Deep Hand. Steward Derren has not stopped him, which is the most dangerous permission in the Hearthseat.

\textbf{Pell Varr} — the Assessor-Marshal who put down the Ash Rising by list. They are the two men who understand what a district costs, and they have never once discussed it, because a discussion would require the word \emph{I}.

\textbf{Haldre} — the keeper who vanished in Y.H. 704. Steward Derren keeps Haldre’s paper in a drawer beside the sealed file and reads it on the Last Day, when the ash in the corners is not swept. He has decided that Haldre was right and that being right changes nothing.

\textbf{Rusk} — a name in a sealed file, a person of the sealed opinion, whom the Steward has never met and has caused to be watched for thirty years without ever ordering an arrest. He likes the man’s questions and has said so in a report, which is the closest thing to affection in the Hearthseat.

\textbf{Corin} — not yet a name in his account, only an irregularity in a slate from Greybank: a whole return whose deduction is zero. He has read that slate twice and has written nothing in the margin, which for him is an act of extraordinary restraint and the beginning of an interest.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
No chapters are written yet. He enters in a room gone cold — a single scene away from Dan, in the Weighing Hall or a counting room — where a slate is read aloud and a man is quietly entered. The reader will feel the shift in the prose before they know why.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No chapters written yet; first appearance planned for Ch 640 (a Court scene away from Dan).

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter*{Tarn Vail}{the debt with hands}{build/art/characters/tarn.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Tarn, the Vail’s Tarn, Tarn of the Yard}\CRfield{Role}{other}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 790, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; returned thin)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; no house of his own}\CRfield{Allegiance}{House Vail, clay-bound for seven years from Y.H. 806}\CRfield{Status}{alive — clay-bound, with the seventh year at the very edge of the sill and still held at the close of Day 115}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 2}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Twenty-two and bent at the shoulders from six years in the slip pit, which makes him look older than his term. He has grey Ash in the creases of his knuckles that no amount of scrubbing lifts, and a pale ring round his left wrist where an iron clip sat in Y.H. 806, when he was bound. He is a narrow man with a narrow face and the habit of putting the smallest tool on the bench into his pocket when he thinks nobody is looking, because a man who owns nothing should know where the small things are. He sleeps in the Debt Loft above the wheel-shed and keeps his few possessions in a clay pot with no mark on it. He smells of wet wool, tallow and the sour tang of a corner that has not been swept. The thing people notice first is how quickly he moves; the thing they notice last is that he stops moving altogether when he is told he is doing well.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Deferential with a nail in it. He calls everyone \emph{house}, including Sella, and says \emph{I owe} where another man would say \emph{I am}. He never argues; he agrees so thoroughly that the argument has nowhere to go. When he is frightened he becomes helpful, which in a kiln-house means doing three things at once and quietly putting the fourth right. His jokes are not jokes; they are statements of fact made in a tone that invites someone else to laugh so that he does not have to.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Yes, house. I’ll sweep it. I swept it this morning. I’ll sweep it again.”

\item “Six years. One to go. I’ve counted every one, and I won’t count the next.”

\item “He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.”

\item “I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check.”

\item “You can’t return a man to himself. They tried with my mother. She came back with somebody else’s hands.”

\item “I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check.” --- said of his own accord, to nobody, in the tone of a man stating the weather.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
His mother was banked in Y.H. 792 and came back thin to the district’s name-pot, with fragments of a life she could not name and hands that frightened him because they were not her hands. He was born of that return, which means he carries a little of somebody else’s interest in a life he cannot place, and has been told all his life that this makes him useful. In Y.H. 806, at sixteen, his mother’s account was entered against him and he was bound to House Vail for seven years, a term he did not choose and has counted every day of. He has worked the slip pits, swept the yard, banked the fire and carried the household’s small accounts in his head for six years.

He was sent to fetch a collector for Garl Vail in the Long Cold and turned back at the frozen ford. Sella never asked whether he had gone. Jorra, who was thirteen, never asked either, which Tarn has decided is worse. He was in the house when Corin arrived and watched the boy be given a bed while he slept in the loft, and he has never said the thing he thinks about it, because a clay-bound hand who complains about beds is a clay-bound hand who can be returned to the slate.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He is a debt with a body, and one year of a seven-year term left. He fears that when the term ends there will be no house to take him and he will be entered again for vagrancy, which is how the district keeps people. He fears the Second Want in himself — the shape that comes over him some nights and leaves him reaching for a tool he has never used. He fears Sella’s kindness more than Jorra’s command, because the kindness is the thing he cannot enter in any account and therefore cannot pay back. His contradiction: the man who owns nothing is the one who notices when a tool is missing and the one who keeps the house’s accounts most exactly.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants a slate with his own name on it and no mark against it. He wants to be called by something that is not a house’s possession. He thinks he wants freedom; what he needs is to learn that freedom in Sarn is another category of account, and that a man can be unowned and still be cold, and that the thing to want is not an empty column but a way to keep warm without being spent.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Sella Vail} — she holds his debt and once, in the winter Garl died, gave him a warm stone for the loft which he has kept in his clay pot for two years. He cannot reconcile the stone with the debt, and has stopped trying, which is not the same as forgiving it. \emph{Ch 2:} he calls her \emph{house}, says \emph{I owe} where another man says \emph{I am}, and agreed with everything so thoroughly that there was nowhere for an argument to go. She gave the foundling a bed and him the loft, and he put the one sentence into the room that nobody had asked for.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — son of the house, who treats him as a brother when the wheel needs him and as a servant when it does not. Tarn has decided to hate him for it and keeps failing, because Jorra once sat up all night with him through a fever and has never mentioned it. \emph{Ch 2:} Jorra noticed a rasp left out of its place and Tarn answered him; the kindness and the command arrived in the same voice and Tarn did not separate them.

\textbf{Corin} — the foundling who arrived and was given a bed in the house. Tarn was the first to notice that the boy turns his head toward a pot before anyone taps it, and has told nobody, because a clay-bound hand who can hear the full note is worth more than his debt and he does not want to be bought. \emph{Ch 2:} he said \emph{He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.} His resentment is not envy of the bed; it is a man keeping the one thing he owns, which is the exact account of what he is owed and what he owes.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — he has carried messages between her and the house, and barley from her to Sella, and has hated being the thin part of that chain. He knows her cough is not the pits and has never said so.

\textbf{Mira Silt} — she has suspected for a year that he is more than he says, and has not asked. He has noticed her noticing, and has answered her with the weather every time.

\textbf{Garl Vail} — he was sent for a collector and turned back. The dead man’s coat still hangs behind the door and Tarn has never once touched it.

\textbf{Ch 4.} He called Sella \emph{house} and put the knife back twice where it could be checked; his broom stopped two strokes at the Vail pot’s note without a turn of the head, and the boy watched and kept the silence as carefully as he did. Six of seven years counted, the seventh not. Jorra came in from the back room with slate dust and said the back room was cold; Tarn said nothing about that either. Dessa’s cough went by him as weather, as it always did. The one thing he owns stays kept.

\textbf{Ch 5.} On Stone 13 he came up the yard with the knife already back on its sill, went through the motion of checking it with his eyes, and saw the boy turn his head toward a pot \emph{before} it was set down. His broom stopped half a stroke at the soft set-down that gave nothing, and he said nothing about either thing, as he has said nothing about the pot’s note through the wall. He counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back; when Sella told him he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths, then began again. At dusk he set the knife back where it could be checked and told the yard he had done so, unasked. He wants his exact account and grudges the house the loan of a bed; a loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and he has said neither sentence.

\textbf{Ch 6.} On Stone 16 he measured the kindling stack with his eyes --- four, four, a space where the fifth should be --- and told the stack six were counted and the seventh held back. On Stone 17 the knife went back on the sill and was announced to the empty yard, and when Sella said \emph{you’ve done well} the broom stopped altogether for two breaths before he said \emph{Yes, house} and went on; he scraped Ash from his knuckles, held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist up to the light, and put the knife back, this time without announcing it. He named the kiln’s breath as the thing that takes a man in his sleep and told of the man in Mud End the district called merciful; he wanted the late thaw because it put off the paying. His broom stopped half a stroke at the bench where no note came. On Stone 20 he told the yard again that the knife was back where it could be checked; six of seven years counted, the seventh held back, and he offered to check the ridge. He said nothing about the boy’s ear and the boy said nothing about his.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 22 his head turned a degree when a vessel carried past the door gave its flat note, and he went back to the broom without looking at the basket or calling the sound a sound; he had been sent for the collector who came with grey fingertips, and the boy put that grey on a tray of its own. On Stone 25 his broom checked half a stroke at the place in the yard where a pot cracked all the way through, and again at the place on the bench where no note had come, and he said nothing about either. He set the small knife on its sill and told the empty yard where it was on Stone 22, Stone 23 and Stone 30; counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back every day; held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist to the light; and wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Stone 29 he offered to check the width of the ridge with his thumb and took his eyes off it as a man takes his eyes off a woman who has been crying. The two silences under one roof kept their usual shape, and the loan that could hear went on being worth more than the debt that held him.

\textbf{Ch 8.} Through the Five the knife went back to its sill and the seventh year was held back every day; he announced the knife to the empty yard and said to the kindling that six were counted and the next he did not count. The Ash in the creases of his knuckles was the colour of the ridge no scrubbing lifted, and he kept the silence about the flat note all five days, as he kept the silence about the boy’s ear. On the Long Night he said in the dark that six years were counted and the next he did not, and set the knife where it could be checked; Garl’s coat held a broader man’s shape in the dark and he let the proverb go to the pot. He wanted the late thaw still, because a late thaw puts off the paying, and on Ilmen 1 he swept toward the thaw and the slip pits with the knife on its sill and the seventh year held back again.

\textbf{Ch 9.} Through Days 31–37 the knife went back to its sill and he announced it to the empty yard, six years counted and the seventh held back, Ash worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifted. He agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late, and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Ilmen 6 his head went a degree toward the pot that answered nearly full and he went back to his broom without naming the sound or looking at the basket; the boy kept the turning beside his own hearing and did not join them. On Ilmen 7 he was with the yard at the well when the Singing Sill gave its note early and did not say what it was. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled and the sentence was not said under the roof.

\textbf{Ch 10.} The small knife goes back to its sill before light and is announced to the empty yard --- \emph{It’s back. You can check} --- with six years of the seven counted and the seventh held where he always holds it; Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring catches what light there is. He sweeps around the place where the clay-heavy water came up behind the racks and sweeps the road down toward the Fishstairs over and over without once looking along it, which is the road a man goes down when a house wants a collector. No collector comes for the woman in the brook and he does not go for one, and he does not say the omission has a name. He still wants the thaw late because a late thaw puts off the paying; he agrees with the early and the late without taking either side. The loan that can hear is still uncalled and the sentence is still unsaid under the roof.

\textbf{Ch 11.} The small knife went back to its sill before the light was gone on Days 45 and 46 and he told the empty yard where it was, unasked; on Day 47 he put it back and told nobody, because the yard had already been told and a man does not say the same thing twice to a house that does not answer. Six years of the seven were counted and the seventh held back on all three mornings, the one entry in this house the house cannot check. His broom went over the road a man takes when a house wants a collector, over and over, without once turning to look along it, and no collector went down it for the woman the brook took nine mornings ago; he did not say the thing which had not happened had a name. Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring caught the light. He agreed with the ones who wanted the thaw early and the ones who wanted it late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying. When Sella said he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths before saying \emph{Yes, house}.

\textbf{Ch 12.} He kept Sella’s house in its exact account and kept his own seventh year out of it; he said house to the yard and counted six where the house could check and the seventh where it could not. With the boy he kept the older equality: a vessel gave its note past the door on Day 50 and a pot answered nearly full on Day 52, and his head did not turn at either and he said nothing about either. Jorra’s returned dust went unremarked and Mira passed without a question. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled, and he still wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying.

\textbf{Ch 13.} He agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late, saying \emph{Yes, house} to both, and went on wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. The small knife was back on its sill with six years counted and the seventh held back, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held the light and gave it back. His broom went over the road a man takes when a house wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector went down it for the woman in the brook. A vessel gave its note past the yard door on Ilmen 28 and his head did not turn; he did not name the sound or supply a Grathic word for it, and the boy did not call it a seventh hearing. Sella told him he had done well and he stopped altogether for two breaths, then set the knife where it could be checked and went back to the broom.

\textbf{Ch 14.} Before light on Silt 3 the small knife went back to its sill and was announced to the empty yard — \emph{It’s back. You can check} — and he told the kindling six were counted and the next he did not count; six years stood, and the seventh was nearly gone and still held, the one entry in this house the house could not check. Ash was worked into his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held the little light and gave it back. He said \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who wanted the thaw early and to the ones who wanted it late, agreed so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and went on wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying, though the water came with the paying. His broom checked half a stroke at the place where a pot cracked on Stone 25 and went on without a turn of the head or a name for the sound. When a vessel gave its note past the yard door he did not turn. On Silt 6 his head went a degree toward a pot that answered nearly full under nobody’s knuckle, and then went back to the broom; he said nothing and did not look toward the basket. The boy kept his turning beside his own hearing and did not join them, and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\textbf{Ch 15.} Through Silt 9–15 the seventh year presses against the rising water and is still held back. The small knife went back to its sill before light and was announced to the empty yard, six years standing in a mark worn almost flat by his thumb and the seventh nearly gone and never named, the one entry in this house the house could not check; Ash was worked into his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was and gave it back. He said \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who wanted the thaw early and to the ones who wanted it late, agreed so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying, though the paying came with the water. His broom checked at the cracked-pot place and went over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, and when a vessel gave its note past the yard door in the afternoon of Silt 15 his head did not turn and he did not name the sound or look toward the basket. He does not say that an ear which can hear is worth more than the debt that holds him, and the sentence that would call the loan lies under the roof as it has for six years.

\textbf{Ch 16.} Through Days 75–77 the seventh year presses against the mud the flood left and is still held back. The small knife goes to its sill before the light on Day 77 and he tells the empty yard where it is, six years standing in a mark worn almost flat by his thumb and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; he tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. He says \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who want the thaw early and to the ones who want it late, agrees so entirely that no argument can find a foot, and keeps wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying, though the paying has come up the road and stands in the ruts. His broom goes over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it. A vessel gives its note past the door and his head does not turn and he does not name the sound, and the boy does not call it a seventh hearing; a whole vessel’s note goes past on Day 77 and he does not turn then either. The two ears keep their equality under the roof and the two silences are of one shape with nobody putting a word between them. The loan that can hear stays uncalled. Something must give at the end of the seventh year, but the end was not written here.

\textbf{Ch 17.} The seventh year presses toward its end through all seven days and is still held. The small knife lies on its sill with six years standing in a mark worn almost flat by his thumb and the seventh nearly gone and unnamed, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; he tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. He says \emph{Yes, house} to those who want the thaw early and to those who want it late, agrees so entirely that no argument can find a foot, and keeps wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts all week. His broom goes over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, and when a vessel gives its note past the door on Silt 23 his head does not turn and he does not name the sound. Sella’s instruction still goes to the fire and the wool and never to him by name; he calls her house and keeps the exact account of what he owes that the house cannot check. The loan that can hear stays uncalled.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} He calls Sella \emph{house} and takes the broom only after she has given it its instruction; she has never asked about his seventh year or his ear, and he has never entered either. With Jorra the household keeps its old shape --- the wheel-keeper’s dust and damper and the debt’s silence under one roof, with no word between them and no question asked about the back room. With Corin the equality holds: two ears, two silences, a loan that can hear and has never been called, and the foundling’s half-beat at the market’s edge not joined to his own turning. Garl’s unforged collector sentence stays where he keeps the seventh year, neither entered; Mira’s noticing and his answered weather are unchanged. No bond has been paid, sold or spoken this chapter.

\textbf{Ch 21 (bonds).} With Sella nothing changed: he takes the broom only after she has given it its instruction, calls her \emph{house}, and she has not asked about his seventh year or his ear. With Corin the equality held through three more days: two ears, two silences, a loan that can hear and has never been called, and the foundling’s half-beat at the market’s edge never joined to his own turning. With Jorra the wheel-keeper’s dust and damper and the debt’s silence kept their old shape under one roof, neither asking about the back room. Garl’s unforged collector sentence stayed where he keeps the seventh year, and neither was entered; Mira’s noticing and his answered weather were unchanged. No bond was paid, sold or spoken this chapter and no new scar or possession came.

\textbf{Ch 22 (bonds).} With Sella nothing changed: he takes the broom only after she has given it its instruction, calls her \emph{house}, and she has not asked about his seventh year or his ear. With Corin the equality held through three more days: two ears, two silences, a loan that can hear and has never been called, and the foundling’s half-beat at the market’s edge never joined to his own turning. With Jorra the wheel-keeper’s dust and damper and the debt’s silence kept their old shape under one roof, neither asking about the back room or the ear. Garl’s unforged collector sentence stayed where he keeps the seventh year, and neither was entered; Mira’s noticing and his answered weather were unchanged. No bond was paid, sold or spoken this chapter and no new scar or possession came.

\textbf{Ch 23 (bonds).} With Sella nothing changed: he takes the broom only after she has given it its instruction, calls her \emph{house}, and she has still not asked about his seventh year or his ear. With Corin the equality held through Seed 18–20 — two ears, two silences, a loan that can hear and has never been called, and the foundling’s half-beat at the market never joined to his own turning. With Jorra the wheel-keeper’s dust and damper and the debt’s silence kept their old shape under one roof, neither asking about the back room or the ear; on Seed 19 he did not turn or speak while Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of Sella’s sentence. Garl’s unforged collector sentence stayed where he keeps the seventh year, and neither was entered; Mira’s noticing and his answered weather were unchanged. No bond was paid, sold or spoken this chapter and no new scar or possession came.

\textbf{Ch 24 (bonds).} Sella gave the broom its instruction before she gave it to him and he took it up as a man takes up a tool already named, saying \emph{Yes, house} to those who wanted the thaw early and those who wanted it late, agreeing so entirely that no argument could find a foot while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went. His chest had been tight since the dark and the breath from Seed 16 was still unspent, a small interval at the top of each reach showing where it should have gone in; the small knife lay at the very edge of its sill with six years in a worn mark and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry the house cannot check, the unforged collector sentence kept beside it. \textbf{New on Seed 22:} while Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, his stroke checked for half a beat on the flagstones and then went on toward the road without a word or a turn of the head; the place where the stroke stopped was kept as a thing nobody would enter, and neither man named the other’s silence. The boy set the half-check beside the wheel-keeper’s finger on one tray and laid no finger across them. Two ears kept their equality under the roof, the ear worth more than the debt and unsafe; the sentence that would call the loan that can hear has still never been said. Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held the little light and gave it back. No bond changed hands, no new scar, possession or change of voice; something must give at the end of the seventh year and it did not give here.

\textbf{Ch 25 (bonds).} With Sella nothing changed: he takes the broom only after she has given it its instruction, calls her \emph{house}, and she has not asked about his seventh year or his ear. With Corin the equality held through Seed 24–26 — two ears, two silences, a loan that can hear and has never been called — and on Seed 25 the change made the day before was \textbf{held and not repeated}: his stroke went on over the flagstones without the half-check behind Jorra’s standing finger, the stones still keeping the place where it had stopped, neither man naming the other’s silence. With Jorra the wheel-keeper’s dust and damper and the debt’s silence kept their old shape under one roof, neither asking about the back room or the ear; Jorra gave the men who came before first grey no name. Garl’s unforged collector sentence stayed where he keeps the seventh year, and neither was entered; Mira’s noticing and his answered weather were unchanged. No bond was paid, sold or spoken this chapter and no new scar or possession came; the breath from Seed 16 stayed unspent and something must still give at the end of the seventh year.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
He enters already sweeping, before anyone wakes, a bent man of twenty-two with grey Ash in the creases of his knuckles and a pale ring round his left wrist where the clip sat in Y.H. 806. Six years of a seven-year term lie behind him and he has counted every one and will not count the next. In Chapter 2 he pockets the small bench knife and then says of his own accord that he took it and put it back and they can check; he stops his broom for two strokes when a pot is set down and gives its flat note, turns his head a degree and says nothing; he banks the coals without looking at the fire. When the foundling is given a bed and he is given the loft he makes one short sentence of it and goes back to sweeping. His deference has a nail in it, and the nail is the one possession the house cannot check.

On Days 5 and 6 he sweeps twice and says nothing. The small knife goes into his pocket and back onto the sill where it can be checked, announced unasked both times; the broom stops for two strokes when a Vail pot gives its flat note through the wall, and he does not turn his head or name the sound. The reader sees the second ear in the house; nobody under the roof does. Six years of seven are behind him and he will not count the seventh, which is the one entry in the house the house cannot check. He keeps his head down over the broom and the one thing he owns out of the house’s reach.

On Days 7, 8 and 9 the ear is no longer only the reader’s. He sees the boy expect a note from a pot that has not yet been set down, and stops his own broom at the set-down that gives nothing, and the two of them go on under one roof without a word between them --- a loan that can hear now knowing he is not the only one, which makes the thing he owns both more valuable and more dangerous. The small knife goes back to its sill and is announced unasked; six of seven years are counted and the seventh is held back, the one entry in the house the house cannot check. He stops for two breaths when Sella says he has done well and then goes on sweeping, because an argument has nowhere to put its foot when a man agrees with everything.

On Days 10 through 14 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. He measures the kindling as a debt and finds a fifth place empty; the knife goes to its sill and is announced twice more; when Sella tells him he has done well the broom stops for two breaths, the nearest thing this house allows to being struck by a kindness he cannot enter. A pot turned toward on the bench gives nothing and his broom checks half a stroke at the empty set-down, a second silent keeping beside the boy’s. He holds the pale clip-ring to the light and says the breath takes a man in his sleep and that Mud End called such a death merciful, and wants the thaw late because a late thaw puts off what is payable. The ear is worth more than the debt that holds him, which makes it dangerous, and he has said nothing of it to anyone.

On Days 15 through 24 the seventh year stays held back and the ear is exercised twice without being spoken. He goes for a collector for a neighbour and brings back a man with grey fingertips, and on the way a carried vessel gives its flat note past the door; his head turns a degree, his hand goes back to the broom, and only the boy under the roof sees the turn. A pot cracks in the yard two paces from the basket and his broom checks at the place where it stood and goes on. The knife goes to its sill and is announced to the empty yard on Stone 22, 23 and 30; on Stone 29 he offers to check the Ash ridge by thumb, the nearest a clay-bound hand comes to touching what the house keeps out of its accounts. He still wants his exact account and grudges the house the loan of a bed; a loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 25 through 30 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The knife goes to its sill and is announced unasked to the empty yard, six of seven years are counted every day and the seventh is never named; the Ash in his knuckles is the colour of the ridge nobody will sweep and no scrubbing lifts it. In the Long Night he says the six and holds the seventh back in the dark, and sets the knife where it can be checked; the boy hears the told bell beside the heard bell and he says nothing about either. He still wants the thaw late because it puts off the paying, and on Ilmen 1, with the Ash burned and called dealt with and the district’s slates opened elsewhere, he sweeps toward the slip pits with the count unchanged. The loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 31 through 37 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The small knife goes to its sill and is announced unasked; six of seven years are counted every day and the seventh is never named; the Ash in his knuckles is the colour of the burned ridge’s old place, which is now a clean dark line. He wants the thaw late because a late thaw puts off the paying, and the thaw is coming on anyway. On Ilmen 6 his head turns a degree at the nearly-full note in open light and he says nothing, and the boy hears it and says nothing, so two not-sayings stand in the same place. The loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 38 through 44 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The small knife is on its sill before light on the first morning and back on it at dusk, announced to the empty yard, six years counted and the seventh held back; Ash is worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifts. He swept the place by the bench where no note had come, swept around the corner where the clay-heavy water had come up behind the racks, and swept the road toward the Fishstairs over and over without turning, the road a man goes down when a house wants a collector; no collector came for the woman in the brook and he did not go for one. On Ilmen 11 he set the knife on its sill, told the yard \emph{It’s back. You can check}, held the seventh year back and wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying. He agreed with both sides about the water and said nothing about the omission or the sound the yard had not heard. On Ilmen 15 the knife was back on its sill and the count unchanged, and he did not look toward the bed where the boy lay with both crusts in the fold.

On Days 45 through 47 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The small knife is on its sill before the light goes, announced to the empty yard on the first two mornings and to nobody on the third, because the yard has already been told; Ash is worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring holds the light and gives it back. His broom goes over the road to the Fishstairs without once looking along it, and no collector comes down it for the woman the brook took nine mornings ago, and he does not say that the thing which has not happened has a name. He agrees with the early thaw and the late and keeps wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. When Sella tells him he has done well he stops for two breaths and then goes on. The boy keeps Tarn’s silence beside his own and does not let the two touch; a loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 48 through 54 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The small knife lies on its sill with six counted and the seventh never named; Ash is worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring holds the light and gives it back. His eye goes a degree toward the slack oiled paper before the light does and he says nothing. A vessel gives its note past the yard door on Day 50 and another pot answers nearly full on Day 52, and his head does not turn at either and he does not call either a seventh hearing or name the sound in Grathic. He agrees with the ones who want the thaw early and the ones who want it late and keeps wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying; his broom goes over the collector’s road on Days 50 and 53 without once turning along it and no collector goes down it for the woman the brook took. He does not look toward the bed or the basket. A loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 55 through 60 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The small knife is on its sill the whole time with six counted and the seventh never named, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; Ash is worked into the knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring holds the light and gives it back. At the well and in the yard he agrees with the early thaw and the late, saying \emph{Yes, house} to each, and keeps wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. His broom goes over the road to the Fishstairs over and over without once turning along it, and no collector comes down it for the woman the brook took; the omission has no word and has not made a doctrine of itself. On Ilmen 28 a vessel gives its flat note past the yard door and his head does not turn and he does not name the sound; two ears keep their equality under one roof and the loan that can hear stays uncalled. When Sella tells him he has done well he stops altogether for two breaths, then sets the knife where it can be checked and goes back to the broom. On Silt 1 he keeps sweeping toward the thaw while the month turns and the brook runs higher; the count is unchanged. A loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 61 through 67 the seventh year presses against the rising water and is still held back. The small knife lies on its sill and is announced to the empty yard, six counted and the seventh nearly gone but never named; Ash is worked into the knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring holds the light and gives it back. He agrees with the early thaw and the late so thoroughly that there is nowhere for an argument to put its foot, and keeps wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the brook is higher and the paying comes with the water. His broom checks half a stroke at the cracked-pot place and goes on, and his head does not turn at a vessel’s note past the door; on Silt 6 it goes a degree toward a nearly-full pot and back to the broom. He does not name either sound or look toward the basket. Jorra’s dust out of the back room goes unremarked by him, and he does not look at the dusty forearms. Two ears keep their equality under one roof and the loan that can hear stays uncalled; the sentence that would call it lies under the days as it has lain for six years. A loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and it has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 68 through 74 the seventh year presses against the flood and is still held back. The knife goes to its sill and is announced to the empty yard, six counted and the seventh nearly gone and never named; Ash is worked into the knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring holds what light there is and gives it back. He agrees with the early thaw and the late so entirely that no argument can find a foot and keeps wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the paying has come up the road and stands in the hollows of the bank. His broom goes over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, and when a vessel gives its note past the door in the afternoon of Silt 15 his head does not turn and he does not name the sound. Two ears keep their equality under one roof and the loan that can hear stays uncalled; the sentence that would call it lies under the days as it has for six years. A loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and it has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 75 through 77 the seventh year stands at the edge of the sill and is held. The knife is where it can be checked and the seventh is where it cannot; the broom goes over the collector’s road without turning and a whole vessel gives its note past the door without a turn of the head. The boy has brought a new shape into the yard --- a head that turns a half-beat after the knock, a loaf that passes without a slate --- and Tarn does not turn toward that either, and the boy does not put the two turnings together. The equality under the roof is unchanged: two ears, two silences, an ear worth more than a debt, and a loan that can hear and has never been called. Something must give at the end of the seventh year, and the end was not written here.

On Days 78 through 84 the seventh year stands at the edge of the sill and is held. The lean week goes around the mud the flood left and Tarn goes around it with the same broom and the same account: six years standing in a mark his thumb has worn almost flat, the seventh nearly gone and still held back, announced to the empty yard before the light and not named to the kindling except as the one he does not count. Ash in his knuckles is the colour of the clean dark line the yard will not sweep and no scrubbing lifts it; the clip-ring at his wrist holds the little light. He agrees so completely with the early thaw and the late that an argument has nowhere to put its foot, and wants the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying stands in the ruts. His broom goes over the collector’s road over and over without a turn. When a vessel gives its note past the door he does not turn and does not name it, and the boy does not call it a seventh hearing; two ears and two silences keep their equality under one roof. The head that turns half a beat late at the well is not his and he does not join it to anything. Something must give at the end of the seventh year, and the end was not written here; the loan that can hear stays uncalled.

On Days 85 through 90 the seventh year stands at the edge of the sill through the turn of Silt into Seed and is still held. The small bench knife is on its sill before the light on Silt 26, 27 and Seed 1; he tells the sill first and the yard after where it is, six years standing in a mark his thumb has worn almost flat and the seventh never cut, nearly gone and still held, the one entry in this house the house cannot check. To the kindling he says \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. He says \emph{Yes, house} to both sides of the thaw argument, agrees so entirely that no argument can find a foot, and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts all week and goes over the boundary into Seed unchanged. His broom goes over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector comes. He has been sent for one once, in the Long Cold, and come back at the frozen ford and told the house it had been done; he keeps that sentence where he keeps the seventh year and neither is entered. A vessel gives its note past the door on Silt 27 and again on Seed 1 and his head does not turn and he does not name the sound; the boy does not call either a seventh hearing. He takes the broom from Sella’s hands on Seed 1 only after she has given it its instruction, and the first work of the planting month is sweeping. Two ears and two silences keep their equality under one roof; the loan that can hear stays uncalled. Something must give at the end of the seventh year; it did not give here, and the count crosses into Seed with the seventh still held.

On Days 91 through 93 the seventh year stands at the edge of the first planting week and is still held. He says \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late, agrees so entirely no argument can find a foot, and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. A vessel gives its note past the door on Days 91 and 92 and his head does not turn and he does not name the sound; the boy does not call it a seventh hearing. No collector comes. Two ears and two silences keep their equality under one roof, the ear worth more than the debt and therefore unsafe, and the loan that can hear stays uncalled. Something must give at the end of the seventh year; it did not give here.

On Days 107 through 109 the seventh year lies at the very edge of the sill and is still held, and the breath he decided not to spend on Seed 16 is still unspent. The next I don’t count} and to the yard \emph{I owe six}, shutting his mouth on the seventh as a man shuts a fist on seed. Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. His chest has been tight since the dark and there is a small interval at the top of each reach where the breath should have gone in; he agrees with those who want the thaw early and those who want it late so entirely that no argument can find a foot, and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. He takes the broom only after Sella has given it its instruction and goes over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it; he was sent once in the Long Cold, came back at the frozen ford and told the house it had been done, and keeps that sentence where he keeps the seventh year, entering neither. On Days 110 through 112 the seventh year stands at the very edge of the sill and is still held, and the breath he decided not to spend on Seed 16 is still unspent. The small knife lies on its sill with six years in a mark worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone, the one entry in this house the house cannot check, and he takes the broom only after Sella has given it its instruction, saying \emph{Yes, house} to both sides of the thaw argument while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. His chest is tight and there is a small interval at the top of each reach where the breath should have gone in. \textbf{On Seed 22, for the first time, the equality under the roof moves:} while Jorra’s bent finger stands in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, Tarn’s stroke checks for half a beat on the flagstones and then goes on toward the road without a word or a turn of the head, the flagstones keeping the place where the stroke stopped as a thing nobody would enter. Neither man names the other’s silence and the loan that can hear is not called; the boy sets the half-check beside the bent finger on one tray and lays no finger across them. Two ears and two silences still keep their equality under one roof, the ear worth more than the debt and therefore unsafe. He keeps the sentence from the frozen ford where he keeps the seventh year and enters neither. Something must give at the end of the seventh year; it did not give here, and the breath presses to its edge into Chapter 25.

On Days 113 through 115 the seventh year stands at the very edge of the sill and is still held, and the breath he decided not to spend on Seed 16 is still unspent. The small knife lies at the very edge of its sill with six years in a mark his thumb has worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone, the one entry in this house the house cannot check, and the unforged collector sentence is kept beside it. Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. He takes the broom only after Sella has given it its instruction and goes over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it; no collector comes. His chest is tight and there is a small interval at the top of each reach where the breath should have gone in. \textbf{On Seed 25 the first fraction of change made on Seed 22 is held and not repeated:} while Jorra’s bent finger stands in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, his stroke goes on over the flagstones without the check, the stones still keeping the place where it stopped the day before, and neither man turns or speaks. The boy sets the unchecking stroke beside the earlier half-beat on one tray and lays no cause across them. Two ears and two silences keep their equality under the roof, the ear worth more than the debt and therefore unsafe; the sentence that would call the loan that can hear has still never been said. Something must give at the end of the seventh year; it did not give here, and the held breath presses to its edge into Chapter 26.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Does not appear; the broom, the knife and the loft are held for Chapter 2.

\item Ch 2: Swept the kiln-house before anyone woke and stopped for two strokes at a pot’s flat note without turning his head or naming the sound. Put the small bench knife in his pocket, then took it out and put it back where it could be checked and said so unasked. Told Sella \emph{Six years. One to go. I’ve counted every one, and I won’t count the next.} Carried up from the Debt Loft with a broom on the third day, banked the coals, and said \emph{He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.} when the boy was given a bed. Heard the second flat note of the three days from a pot set down on the bench and did not say what it was.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 4: Days 5 and 6. Swept before light on Stone 11 and again at dusk on Stone 12, with Ash in his knuckles and the pale ring at his left wrist. Took the small bench knife out and put it back where it could be checked, saying so unasked both times. His broom stopped for two strokes at the flat note of a pot through the shed wall and he did not turn his head, name the sound or say that it was a sound at all --- the second ear in the house, witnessed only by the reader. Said \emph{yes, house; I’ll sweep it; I swept it this morning; I’ll sweep it again} to the ground and kept his head down over the broom. Six of seven years counted, the seventh not counted. He said nothing about the note all day, and nobody asked him to.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 5: Days 7--9. On Stone 13 came up the yard with the small knife already back on its sill, checked it with his eyes only, and saw the boy turn his head toward a pot before Jorra set it down; his broom stopped half a stroke at the set-down that gave nothing and he said nothing about either. Counted six years of seven and held the seventh back, and stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said he had done well, then swept again. At dusk put the knife back where it could be checked and announced it unasked, and kept his head down over the broom while Sella counted loaves and bits. Said nothing all three days about the note that did not come, and nobody asked him to.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Days 10--14. On Stone 16 measured the kindling stack with his eyes, four, four and a space at the end, and said to the stack \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} On Stone 17 set the small knife on its sill and told the yard to check, stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said \emph{you’ve done well} and said \emph{Yes, house} before going on; his broom checked half a stroke when a pot turned toward on the bench gave nothing. Scraped Ash from his knuckles with the knife, held the pale ring at his left wrist up to the light and put the knife back without announcing it this time. Named the kiln’s breath as the danger and said a man in Mud End who slept before a kiln with the damper shut was called a merciful death; said he would take the late thaw, a longer week before the paying. On Stone 18 said he had swept and would sweep again; on Stone 19 agreed a late thaw was a longer week before the paying and offered to check the ridge; on Stone 20, Account-day, told the yard again the knife was back on its sill and let his broom stop half a stroke at the place where no note had come. Six of seven years counted all five days, the seventh held back and never named.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Days 15--24. On Stone 22 set the small bench knife on its sill, told the empty yard \emph{I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check}, and said to the kindling \emph{Six counted; the next I don’t count}; was sent for a collector for a neighbour two doors down and returned with a man whose cuff was soft from washing and fingertips the colour of skimmed milk gone off, who said \emph{the measure is taken and the account stands as entered} to a slate. On the way back his head turned a degree at a vessel’s flat note carried past the door and he did not name it or look at the basket. On Stone 23 swept around the place where a pot had given nothing and said \emph{I swept it this morning; I’ll sweep it again}; Jorra’s returned dust went unremarked by him. On Stone 25 and 26 his broom checked half a stroke at the place where a pot cracked in the yard with the flat knock and he said nothing about either; he wanted the late thaw because it put off the paying. On Stone 29 held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist to the light, said \emph{I can check the width, house. I’ve a thumb as good as any}, and took his eyes off the ridge. On Stone 30 the knife was back on its sill and announced once more, unasked. Six of the seven years counted every day, the seventh held back and never named; the ear kept silent and the loan uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 8: Days 25--30. Through the Five set the small bench knife on its sill and told the empty yard where it was, and said to the kindling that six were counted and the next he did not count; the seventh year was held back on every day. Scrubbed at the Ash in his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts, and kept the silence about the flat note all five days and about the boy’s ear as before. On the Long Night said in the dark that six years were counted and the next he did not, and set the knife where it could be checked; Garl’s coat held a broader man’s shape in the dark. Wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying; on Ilmen 1 swept toward the thaw and the slip pits with the knife back on its sill and the seventh still held back, and did not touch the ridge or the mark.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

On Ilmen 2 noticed the oiled paper had stopped lifting hard before he noticed the light, and swept toward the slip pits with Ash in his knuckles that no scrubbing lifted; six years of the seven counted, the seventh held back and not said to the paper or the boards or anybody. Agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Ilmen 3 set the small bench knife on its sill and announced it to the empty yard --- \emph{I put it back. You can check} --- and scraped at the Ash in his knuckles. On Ilmen 5 swept near the bench and did not say what the pot gave or look toward the basket. On Ilmen 6 his head went a degree toward the pot that answered nearly full and he went back to his broom without naming the sound. On Ilmen 7 stood with the yard as the Singing Sill gave its low note early and the argument ended in weather, and said nothing about either. Through the seven days kept the silence about the flat note and about the boy’s ear, and carried the count into Ilmen 8 with the knife back on its sill and the seventh year held back.

\end{itemize}

Swept around the place where the clay-heavy water had come up behind the drying racks and swept the road toward the Fishstairs over and over without looking along it, the road a man goes down to fetch a collector; no collector came for the woman in the brook and he did not go for one. Agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. Said nothing about the sixth hearing the boy had heard out of a person on the bank, and did not look at the basket on the way back up the yard.

\item Ch 13: Days 55--60. The small knife stayed on its sill with six years counted and the seventh held back, the one entry in the house the house cannot check; Ash worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at his left wrist catching what light there was. At the well and in the yard he said \emph{Yes, house} to the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and to the one who wanted it late, and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying (T036). His broom went over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector went down it for the woman in the brook (T009, T090). On Ilmen 28 a vessel gave its note past the yard door and his head did not turn; he did not name the sound or supply the Grathic word for it and did not call it a seventh hearing (T061, T076). When Sella told him he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths, then set the knife where it could be checked and went back to the broom. On Silt 1 he kept sweeping toward the thaw with the count unchanged; the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

You can check}, with six years counted and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry the house cannot check; held the pale clip-ring to the light and kept Ash in his knuckles the colour of the clean dark line. His broom checked half a stroke at the cracked-pot place and went on without turning or naming the sound; a vessel gave its note past the yard door and he did not turn. \CRcharacter{Veno Brine}{the factor who can turn a damp document into a fortune}{build/portraits/veno-brine.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Veno Brine, the factor, Veno of Greybank, the man who never signs anything}\CRfield{Role}{other}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 766, Vhal, the Sallow coast}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Vhaleni)}\CRfield{Origin}{Vhal, the Sallow coast; a house with no boat-share and an excellent memory for wet paper}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Greybank counting house; agent of Sere interests in the north; Council of Tides by correspondence}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 130}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Forty-six and carefully dressed in a lowland cut that he has never quite got right, which he does not care about because the clothes are for the people he deals with and not for himself. He is a narrow Vhaleni man with a client’s smile that he can hold for an entire negotiation and drop the instant the door closes, which the clerks of Greybank have learned to read as the true end of the meeting. His hands are soft, with salt-paper stains at the fingertips, and he never carries a pen, because a factor who is seen writing is a factor whose word can be checked. He has a gold crown mounted in a ring which he wears on his little finger and which he has never earned in Grath, a detail he considers the only beautiful thing about the place. He smells of tar, wet rope, expensive soap and — when a Sere matter is in hand — myrrh, which is the smell of the empire and of a room where a person has been entered. The thing people notice first is the smile; the thing they notice last is that he never touches a slate, not even to move it, which in a counting house is a form of armour.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Vhaleni sibilance flattened for lowland ears, with long pauses and questions that contain their own answers. He says \emph{the document}, \emph{the weather}, \emph{the understanding}, and never \emph{the contract}, because a contract is a thing that can be read and he has built his life on things that cannot. He speaks of people as positions — \emph{the widow, thane, the collector} — and has a way of offering kindness with a figure attached, so that the recipient must decide which part was the gift, which is the whole art of his trade. When he is genuinely angered he becomes courteous to a degree that makes the room cold, because everyone has seen what precedes it. He has two laughs: one for clients, warm and brief, and one for himself, which is a single breath through the nose and means he has just been found out and does not intend to admit it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The paper is damp. It’s a bad season for documents. In Vhalen we consider that a virtue. A law that lasts too long stops earning, doesn’t it?”

\item “I have not paid you. I have advanced you. You’ll see the difference when the grain comes.”

\item “Forty measures for one return. Ask me why forty and I’ll tell you the figure is the figure. Ask me again in private and I’ll still tell you the figure is the figure.”

\item “I don’t buy people. I buy the shape of them. A beautiful return must remember enough to be exhibited. There’s a difference, and the Council calls it civility.”

\item “You want the girl. I want the share. We’ll write it down in the rain and see which of us has a document in the morning.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was born in Vhal to a family with no boat-share and an unusual talent for reading documents that had been left in the rain, which in the salt republic is the most marketable gift a man can have. He worked the counting house, learned that a contract on salt-paper in damp weather is no contract at all, and spent twelve years turning that fact into a fortune and two enemies, one of whom he later bought out with a damp document and a warm smile. He came up the Salt Road to Greybank in Y.H. 796 as a factor for Vhaleni glass and stayed, because the north buys measures and a factor who can buy a debt before it is due is a factor who never needs to buy the person. He has represented Sere interests in the north since Y.H. 803 without ever admitting to the Sun-Emperor’s Council that he works for them, and has sold grain, glass, quiet ash and whole returns to people who believe they are dealing with a Vhaleni and not an empire.

In the first weeks of Stone, Y.H. 812, he carried the slate for a private whole return from the Greybank factor to the collector in Sill, and could not spell the purchaser’s name, which he has never told anyone and has never forgotten. He has spent the years since trying to work out who bought forty children’s warmth for a foundling with a flower, because a man who cannot identify a buyer is a man who cannot charge him again, which in his profession is a form of insult. He has begun to suspect the Unbanked, then the Court, then a third thing that looks like both, and has kept each suspicion in a different document, all of them damp.

He has kept Solene Ember in a room with good light since Y.H. 810, which he describes to visitors as protection and to himself as an investment that has not yet matured. He has twice offered to buy Pia of the Quay’s mother’s boat-share and been refused twice, which he has entered as a debt owed to him by a girl who does not know she owes it.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He has no house and no share, which in Vhalen makes him a man whose account is always current and never his own. His wound is that he can turn any document into nothing and therefore cannot make anything that lasts, which is a strange hunger in a man who deals in permanent arrangements. He fears wet paper in the wrong hands, which is the only thing that can undo him, and fears more than that a person who reads a contract as a person rather than a shape, which is what the foundling from Low Kiln does when he looks at a vessel. His contradiction: the man whose whole trade is the convenient disappearance of evidence has kept three damp documents dry in a private drawer for ten years, because a factor who keeps nothing can never be blackmailed and a factor who keeps everything can, and he has chosen to be the second kind in secret and the first kind in public.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants a boat-share, which would make him a Vhaleni instead of a man who deals with them, and he wants to know who bought the whole return in Y.H. 812, because an unspelled name is the only account in his life he cannot close. He thinks he wants the north to remain a place where a damp document is a fortune. What he needs is to understand that a person with no account is cheaper than a person with one, which is the Council’s doctrine and his own, and that he has spent his life making people cheaper in order to call himself civility. When he finally learns the purchaser’s name, he will not say it aloud; he will write it on salt-paper in the rain and watch it disappear, which is the only honest thing he has ever done with a document.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Solene Ember} — the beautiful return he keeps in a room with good light. He is kind to her in the exact way a creditor is kind, and she has never mistaken it, which is why he keeps her and why he distrusts her. He has begun to fear that she will refuse a fourth return, which would be a loss and a precedent, in that order.

\textbf{Pia of the Quay} — the salt girl who refused his offer for her mother’s share twice. He has entered the refusal as a debt and has never collected, which in his vocabulary is the beginning of an interest he cannot name.

\textbf{Marra} — the collector whose slate passed through his hands in Y.H. 812 and whose name appeared on a document he was not supposed to read. He has not told anyone and has used the knowledge once, gently, in a negotiation, which is how he tests what a thing is worth.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — who signed the levy he carried and forgot the purchaser’s name deliberately. Veno has never pressed him, because a Thane who has forgotten a thing on purpose is a Thane who can be made to remember it at the right moment, which is a kind of leverage he has kept warm for ten years like a coal under ash.

\textbf{Corin} — the foundling whose name was written before a face. Veno has tried three times to buy his ear for the College or the Sere factors and has been refused three times, and has begun to suspect that the boy is not an account at all but a creditor, which is a category he has no word for.

\textbf{Avis Wake} — a Council member who votes against taxing the glass boats and whom Veno pays to do so, which is an arrangement the Council calls representation and Veno calls the cheapest insurance in Vhalen.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
No chapters are written yet. He enters in the Greybank counting house, smiling at a widow while declining to touch a slate, and the reader will take him for a merchant until the first damp document turns a household’s debt into nothing.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No chapters written yet; first appearance planned for Ch 130 (the Greybank counting house, the offer for the boat-share).

\end{itemize}
}

\chapter*{The Atlas}
\markboth{The Atlas}{The Atlas}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Atlas}
\CRmap{Greybank, the Court’s gate}{build/atlas/greybank.jpg}{The Court’s granary town eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, drawn as its own surveyors would draw it: the Ilm and its quay, the factor’s house where the tally for Sill is kept, the Vhaleni Counting House with Veno Brine’s private drawer of dry documents, the Court’s granaries and banking hall, the winter ford, the burial grounds, and the ends of the Clay Road and the beginnings of the Salt and Hearth Roads. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{Sill and the Lower Ilm — the country of the birth-town}{build/atlas/home-region.jpg}{The clay country about Sill, drawn out a few days’ walking: the Ilm from Nine Pots and the Ferr to Greybank, the weir, the Old Kiln, Cold Acre, Mud End and the Reedholt marsh. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap{Sill and the Two Kilns — the birth-town}{build/atlas/home-settlement.jpg}{A detailed plan of Sill on the Ilm, drawn to the ground a child can walk: the four-foot fall and the Singing Sill, the two bridges, the Fishstairs and the Cross, Slate Row, Low Kiln with the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house, High Kiln and the Glaze Room, the family houses, the smithy, the meal mill, the wells and fields, the Bone Orchard and the edge of the reedbeds. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap{Keld Keep and the First Seam}{build/atlas/keld.jpg}{The Warden’s fortress city against the Rim and the deep survey cut into the stone beneath it, drawn cold and mineral as the Keep’s own survey-clerks would draw it: the walled Keep with the Warden’s hall and the mine-reeve’s room; the Rim Road coming up from Sill and going on ten leagues to the Cold Pass and its survey post; the Listening Stones five leagues higher in the Rim; and below, the timbered shaft of the First Seam with its galleries, the Descent, the Duelling Floor cut into the stone with nine clamps to the floor and the tenth behind the board, the survey room holding the crossed-out entry of Y.H. 588 and its branching red mark, the Ninth Gallery with the tin lined with warm-stone, a seam-serpent’s passing entered only as a change in the numbers, and the hot-lead warning of the Sweating. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with a compass, a league scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the measure before the name, the Warden’s claim, the once-a-year reading of the paper, and the insistence that no map is honest past the last pass.}

\CRmap{The Hearthseat on the Keel}{build/atlas/the-hearthseat.jpg}{The Court’s city, built over the Hearth a hundred and fifty leagues south-east of Sill, drawn cool and clean as its own surveyors would file it: the Weighing Hall with the grating of cold iron over the never-out fire and the Hearth shown in cut beneath the floor; Slate Row with the College of Assessors and its second file; the Steward’s room, the sealed files, the bank where measures are pressed into newborn vessels, the rooms of fewer than twenty Kept, the back rooms, the printed notice, the Hearth Road from Greybank and the way out to the Nine Wells. Surveyed and filed in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Old Kiln and the Ash Throat — one league south of Sill}{build/atlas/the-old-kiln.jpg}{The collapsed kiln in the grey clay a league south of Sill, drawn as its surveyor would draw it: the fallen crown and its broken brickwork, the fire mouth on the south-east flank, the flue broken at the top, the concentric throat where the ash runs deeper than a man, the hollow in its wall from which a slate was carried north to Low Kiln, the grey banks that will not take a glaze, the surveyor’s stakes and his cord, the track from Sill and the marsh way to Reedholt.
