\begin{quote}\itshape the way slip takes the mould and keeps the thumbprint.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The name is written into it before it can refuse one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape On the third day it will grow worse before it grows better.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep it. Keep it anyway.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the hearth-maid warms a stone in her hand and tries it on her own wrist. This is not part of the litany. It is the part before.}

\textbf{The house answers:} Your return is recorded.

\subsection*{VII. Of the Kept}

\begin{quote}\itshape Blessed are they that are Kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape No want can reach them. They no longer feel the cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is nothing left in them for the Hearth to take,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and so they are past the need of any return.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There are fewer than twenty in the world.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Speak of them with pity. Do not ask one whether he is warm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he will say no, and you will have no other question.\end{quote}

\emph{Here I close the leaf. The dead are already in Slate Row and the new vessel is under a roof I shall not enter.}

\textbf{The house answers:} Nothing is lost that we have kept. The account stands.

\subsection*{The four sayings}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item \emph{The measure is banked} — written at the draw, in the officer’s hand, before I set the figure down.

\item \emph{The account stands} — read at the Cross, twice, over the pigs.

\item \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept} — printed on the Weighing notices and at the foot of every slate.

\item \emph{Your return is recorded} — said in the Remembering, in a clean voice, to the room and not to the person.

\end{itemize}

There is no fifth saying. The house keeps a place where a fifth would stand, and I have left the place the length of it.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the College came down on an Account-day with a cuff gone soft from washing, and ink in two fingers that would not come out. He borrowed the leaf and gave it back with my verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the wall was not malicious, it was old}, he wrote, \emph{The vessel failed, having reached its term.} Mine stands beneath.

\item At \emph{take what is owed and leave the shape}, he set \emph{the measure is drawn and the residue entered}, and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{one in twelve, printed, unchallenged}, he put a small stop in the figure and wrote the figure again above it, larger. It is the figure they like to see.

\item At \emph{they come back as they can}, he wrote \emph{a thin return is entered}, which is a true thing in a language nobody in this room speaks.

\item In the space where the fifth saying would stand he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a man at the draw does not know he is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to hold out.

\subsection*{What the other hand put back}

The house has written in the margins at the bedsides. The charcoal is thicker than mine and it leans. I have copied it as it stands.

At I: \emph{It was a good pot. It split at the lip. We set it by the door and went around it.}

At II: \emph{Take it and go. It is not ours to watch.}

At VI: \emph{She was warm when I wrote it. She was cold by the fourth day. Both are in the house roll and only one is read.}

At the four sayings, against \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept}, the same hand has written: \emph{The grey in the corner is not dirt.} Then, struck through and written again underneath, very small: \emph{We leave it. We burn it in the morning. The clean line where it stood is not the same as gone.}

At the foot, where the answer should be, a line is struck through twice. Under it:

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back warm. Come back as you were.\end{quote}

And under that, in letters pressed hard into the bark:

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

I have left the struck line standing. A thing said over a child is a thing a house has to use.

\subsection*{In Ilmen}

In Ilmen a woman was taken by the brook below the nineteen steps and no officer was called. There is a space on the leaf where her measure should stand. The clerk has not put a nought in it. I have not filled it, and nobody from Slate Row has asked why it is empty. The house says she was gone before anybody could reach her. That is true, and it is not the whole of it, and I have written both sentences down because the space is the right length for both.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lamp-black thumb is mine; I held the leaf with the same hand I write with and did not know I had marked it. The barley is from a crust laid down on the leaf and not eaten. The ring is small ale. A hair is caught in the fold and I have left it, because the fold is where the leaf opens and somebody was always leaning over to see what was written. The tallow is the woman’s, and the grey is the officer’s, and neither of them will own either mark.

\subsection*{At the foot}

\begin{quote}\itshape The measure is banked. The account stands. Nothing is lost that we have kept. Your return is recorded.\end{quote}

That is the clean voice, which is the Hearthseat’s own. Under it, in a hand that is nobody’s, struck once and written again:

\begin{quote}\itshape Four sayings and a place where the fifth would stand. We say the four. We keep the place.\end{quote}

The leaf goes back under the slate on the collector’s table. A slate is a thing that gets carried into the square and read in a clean voice; this is a thing that gets read by the light of one lamp after the house is in bed. If an officer ever finds it, let him take the verbs out. The next hand will put them back, as I did, and will warm the stone first.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Measure for Measure, Being the Sayings of the Bowls, Gathered at the Ember House and Glossed for a Boy from the North}
\CRsheetheading{Measure for Measure, Being the Sayings of the Bowls, Gathered at the Ember House and Glossed for a Boy from the North}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An under-steward’s gathering of the proverbs, courtesy-maxims, press-songs and curses of Sere, written in thin gold on prepared paper in the open courtesy hand; the sayings in the long-vowelled southern speech with the ends thrown into the fire, the glosses in the same hand with less gold in it, with the leaning corrections of a bowl-house tally-clerk, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk at Greybank, and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Gathered in Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 811 at the Ember bowl-house in the Bowl of Sere by Dalia Ember, an under-steward who keeps the fourth bowl, for a boy come down from Greybank who sat at the lower table and did not know when to applaud; written on seven leaves of prepared paper in gold ink, the sayings in the thick gold and the glosses in the thin; carried north in a glass consignment in Ash of Y.H. 812 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where a factor’s clerk corrected it and put a nought in the margin; carried on to Sill and copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813. It survives with gold worked into the grain of the first leaf, the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a small wine-ring at the third hour, a thumb of olive oil at the head, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, a green-glazed shard from a northern bowl pressed into the fold, one corner scorched where the leaf lay too near a court fire, a gold crown pressed flat between the fifth and sixth leaves, the leaning corrections of the house clerk standing above the glosses, the narrow upright correction added at Greybank above both, and a line at the back in a hand that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the fourth bowl at the Ember house. That is my whole office: to set a bowl down full at the third hour, and carry it away full when the feasting is done, and answer no questions about it. A boy come down from Greybank sits at the lower table and watches my hands to learn when to applaud. Last Grain he clapped at the new slate and the man beside him told him to clap at the old one too, which he did, and he has not been right since. I have set these sayings down for him in the thinner gold. The thick gold is kept for contracts, and a contract is a thing said to a man who is not in the room. A saying is said to the bowl. If the bowl answers, that is between them.

The manner of them first, because a saying said wrongly is a different saying. Say them with the vowels open and the ends thrown into the fire, so that the listener supplies the last of the thought. Said looking at a man, a saying becomes a lawsuit; said to the bowl, or to the fire under the bowl, it stays a saying. There are words here that are only spoken at the third hour, when the wine is up and an act of state is being announced. Write them at another hour and they look like anything. A northern clerk copied one into a slate once and was polite about it for a week, which is the longest politeness I have ever seen a northern man sustain.

\subsection*{Of the bowl and the pouring}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The pot was made to pour. The cup that keeps is the cup that sours.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Valen Openhand says it at the third hour, and the priests who say it after him are among the fullest vessels in the empire. A visitor notices this; a child of the house is taught not to. A vessel was made to be emptied gloriously and a life hoarded is a life wasted. Say it over the wine, never over the accounts, where it would be a very different sentence and might cost somebody a province.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A debt carried gracefully is an ornament of a house.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What is carried gracefully is still carried. At sixteen a girl emptied the bowl at her feast and named a debt she intended to carry, and the applause was for the debt and not for her. Three houses asked for her in the same hour. They were not asking for the debt. I have put that in because the boy will see the applause and want to know who is being honoured, and the answer is not the person.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Burn the slate by lot. Write it again before the wine is cold.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At the end of a feast one household’s debt-slates go into the fire and new ones are made. A woman whose slate burned wept, and the crowd was kind to her, and then applauded the new slate. I have set both sentences here. The boy will want one of them to be the true one; both of them are true, and the second one is the one that is copied.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A year’s grain under the dead is a warm send-off. Buy the ash back at the price they ask.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The warmest funerals in the world are ours. The Court taxes the ash and the house buys it back as quiet ash, and a great funeral can empty a province, which is then bought cheap. We call the house generous. I have not written what I think of this, because an under-steward who writes what he thinks is an under-steward looking for another house.}

\subsection*{Of courtesy and the face}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “There is no rudeness in Sere. There is only a person who has not yet been told.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Our courtesy is long and open, and a man who does not know it is never refused; he is confirmed in being a stranger. The boy has one name and is ashamed of it. A child here has seven by adolescence and keeps whichever the household prefers. He asked me why one name is not enough. I told him a bowl holds one pouring and a house holds seven, and let him make what he could of it, which is how courtesy is taught.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Say yes. If they ask which, say measure for measure.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At the third hour a public bowl of wine is emptied and an act of the Sun-Emperor is announced. A potter from the north stood beside me and asked whether a debt had been forgiven or a province ruined. The man beside him said yes. When the potter asked which, he said measure for measure and went back to his wine. I have learned that the phrase means just what the speaker decided before he opened his mouth. It is a fine phrase for an empire. It is not a fine phrase for a contract, which is why it is never written in gold.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A woman may own the bowls and the slaves and a husband’s debt. She may not enter the room where her numbers are read.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Inheritance goes to the eldest surviving child regardless of sex, and a woman of a great house may hold a great deal. The room where her measure is counted has a door in it, and her numbers are read to her by a man. This is a courtesy with a door in it. The boy asked why a woman who owns a house may not count it. I told him a door is not an argument and will not fight him, and he let it go, which is a courtesy he has learned from us already.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Concubinage is a public measure. Do not call it a kindness.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Returned slaves are kept openly and are counted as part of a household’s standing, the way a good fire or a row of bowls is counted. A kindness that can be seen and admired is not a kindness but a receipt. This is said in the court and not in the counting room. The slaves know it before the boy does; he will learn it from them, which is the ordinary order of learning in this country.}

\subsection*{Of dust and the open court}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The courts have no walls. The dust settles in the hair and nobody brushes it off.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Men sit in the heat of the court fires with their coats on the ground beside them and let the dust lie where it falls. A northern man brushes himself and is noticed. We say a man who brushes the dust off has decided he is only passing through, and a man only passing through may be charged for the hour.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The south is warm the way a kiln is warm, with the door open. A man goes thirstier here than in a northern winter.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The potter who asked about the bowl said it first and got it right. I have kept his words because our own say the warmth and leave out the thirst, which is the whole art of a southern saying. He had been told the south was warm and found it no comfort.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The burning winds take the skin off a man’s lips and leave the grain standing.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The winds come yellow off the east and a traveller’s lips go first. The grain stands through them, which is why the empire has grain and the traveller has a skin he does not recognise. We say the wind takes what is loose. It is a saying about lips and about households, and neither of them is safe in it.}

\subsection*{Of the fourth bowl}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Three go round and are poured. One stands and is carried away full.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At every feast a fourth bowl is set down full and not emptied. It stands through the feasting and is carried away still full. Nobody pours it and nobody says whose debt it holds. I asked three times and got three silences, the last of which was the kindest. The boy asked once and I told him to ask the bowl. He did. The bowl did not answer, which is the answer they gave me in finer words.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “There is a place in every account where a bowl should be emptied and is not. Go around it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The clerks go around that place the way our yard goes around a thing set down where a child might knock it. I have set the bowl in the margin where a figure should stand, because the bowl will not lie in a column. The tally-clerk has tried twice to give it a figure. Both times the figure has stood and the bowl has stood beside it, and the two have not touched.}

Bowl — Poured for — What is said over it\par

The first — the house — the debt named at the Bowl feast\par

The second — the fire — the act announced from the third hour\par

The third — the slate — the burning by lot and the new writing\par

The fourth — nobody — nothing\par

\subsection*{What they sing at the wine-presses}

\emph{Sung at the tread, not at the feast. The third verse is said to the bowl and not to the company. He has learned to keep his hands off the fourth bowl, which is more than I managed at his age.}

\begin{quote}\itshape At the press we tread and the wine comes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a neck for the house and a neck for the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the third goes down on a slate burned by lot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fourth goes back to the shelf.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We clap for the debt and we clap for the slate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we buy back the ash at the price of the grain;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the year that we burned under one we loved\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape was the year we had meant to spend anyway.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven names on a girl and the house keeps one;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the others go into the fire with the slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three go round and they all go dry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fourth stands full and is carried away.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the tally-clerk did}

A clerk of the house borrowed the leaves after the third hour, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the leaning counting-hand, with the gold gone thin and the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could spill out of a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the cup that keeps is the cup that sours}, he wrote \emph{vessels are made for use}, and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{a debt carried gracefully}, he set \emph{obligation acknowledged, current}, which leaves the ornament out and the obligation in.

\item At \emph{measure for measure} he wrote \emph{equivalence recorded}, and underlined the equivalence.

\item At \emph{buy the ash back at the price they ask}, he set \emph{quiet ash, market rate}, and put a figure in the margin where I had put the price.

\item Against the fourth bowl he wrote \emph{a reserve retained, no charge against it}, which is a true thing in the language of a counting room and has the bowl standing in it still.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing above my words. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because the boy wants to know whose hand poured, and there is always a hand.

\subsection*{What the northern hand did}

A factor’s clerk at Greybank corrected the copy on the back of the voided warrant in the narrow upright hand. He has never been south and has strong views about dust.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the courts have no walls}, he wrote \emph{the premises are unenclosed}.

\item At \emph{the dust settles in the hair}, he wrote \emph{atmospheric deposit, not entered}, which is a description of a room after everybody has left it.

\item In the margin beside the fourth bowl he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} underneath.

\end{itemize}

I have left his hand standing over mine, the way a new slate is laid over the burned one. A nought is a number. The bowl was not a number, and nobody has poured it to find out.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The gold at the head has worked into the grain and will not come out, which is why we write contracts in it and sayings in the thinner mixture: a contract is meant to last and a saying is meant to be carried. The dust in the fold came off the court bench and I have not shaken it, because the boy will one day ask what the yellow is and I should rather he asked than knew. The wine-ring is small and belongs to the third hour. The olive thumb is mine; I turn the leaves with the hand I carry the bowl with. The husk of grain stuck in the gutter came from a loaf sent north and returned uneaten, which is a journey I could enter if I chose and have not. The green shard in the fold came off a bowl the house bought from a northern potter and cracked in the first frost; the tally-clerk has asked for it twice and has not had it. The scorched corner is where the leaf lay too close to a court fire. The crown pressed flat between the fifth and sixth leaves is one the boy was paid in and cannot spend here, which makes it the only coin in the house nobody has tried to enter. In Sere the ash is bought back and burnt in a bowl; that is another way of saying nothing is left where it lay.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three are poured and the fourth stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The house does not know whose debt it holds\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and would pour it if it knew.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It is the only thing in Sere nobody has spent.\end{quote}

I asked the bowl-keeper, the tally-clerk and a factor come down from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the oiled wrap under the fourth bowl; tomorrow the third hour will come, and I shall set the bowl down full and carry it away full, and the boy will watch my hands to learn when to clap.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Nine to the Floor, Being a Drinking Song of the Duelling Floor in Keld Keep}
\CRsheetheading{Nine to the Floor, Being a Drinking Song of the Duelling Floor in Keld Keep}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A Keldish floor-song in three parts, taken down by the clerk who keeps the numbers at the Duelling Floor; the verses in the hard Rim speech, the corrections in the verbless hand of a Court survey-clerk, one answer from the Listening Stones, and a lowlander’s verse at the foot · Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the room off the Duelling Floor beneath Keld Keep, on the back of a survey sheet spoiled by wet slate, the figures on the face of it gone soft; carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road with a survey party in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank. Kept in the floor-clerk’s board box among the spoil slips. It survives with coal dust at the head, a press of wet reed across the first leaf, a smear of hot lead at the fold, an ale ring, a tallow thumb, a grey Ash print along the gutter, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the Court, one line in a hand that writes very large and very slowly, and a verse added in Grathic by a clay-man who had been levied to the Cold Pass.\par}\medskip
I keep the numbers at the floor. A man comes down from the shift or off the stone and states his measure before he states his name, and I set the two down in that order, because that is the order the Keep uses and I have never known a man to complain of it until he has had a clamp across his arm. What follows is not part of the account. It is what they sing after, in the room off the floor, with the cups out and the irons put away. No one sings it on the stone. A man with a clamp in his hand has no breath to spare for a refrain, and a man who has just opened a way in his forearm is not in a singing mood.

I have put the words down as they came. The coal dust at the head came off the sleeve of the man who dictated the third part to me; he would not wash before he had finished, and said a song that had never been in a mine was not worth the paper. The lead at the fold is not mine. I have left it where it lies, and I have not swept the grey out of the gutter either. There is no Last Day in a board box.

\subsection*{The song, as it is sung}

\emph{Sung standing. The cup in the right hand, the left palm flat on the table stone: the hand that has held a clamp does not hold a cup at the same time. The room says the refrain together. A man who has just come off the floor says the lines of his own part, and nobody says his name.}

\subsection*{The first part: the floor}

Nine to the floor and one to the stone, state your measure, then your name; the cup goes round and the cold goes round, and the number is not the same.

The iron bites and does not let go, the arm below goes the colour of rope; a man says his measure, a man says his name, and the third thing he says is a hope.

They put hot iron to the palm and ask if you owe, and the honest come back with a hand gone dead; I have known eleven honest men and not one of them lied, and nine cannot lift a cup.

Nine to the floor and one to the stone, state your measure, then your name; the cup goes round and the cold goes round, and the number is not the same.

\subsection*{The second part: the Descent}

At thirteen he goes down for a single day and comes up with a number changed; his mother asks what he saw in the dark and he tells her the dark, and his hands tell her the rest.

There is a mark on the inside of the arm where the way was cut and kept open while it scarred; it aches before the thaw and aches after, and he answers to whichever number the room has given him.

Some come up with the same number and some do not, and the clerk writes the second down without a mark beside it, which is the only honest thing a clerk can do.

Nine to the floor and one to the stone, state your measure, then your name; the cup goes round and the cold goes round, and the number is not the same.

\subsection*{The third part: what comes up through the stone}

When the lead smells hot in the lower drift, stop singing. The warm comes up through the stone like a river loosed in a room; the grub in the warm-stone knew it a tend before any man did, eating from the inside and leaving the stone standing hollow.

We go down in pairs and come up in pairs, and where there were two at the mouth there is sometimes one. The number stands. The number stands. That is what we say, and we do not say it twice.

Five leagues up where the bare stones sit, a Vorr sits still and comes down with a figure; ask him what it means and he will tell you once, \emph{the numbers are correct}, and he will tell you twice.

Karric shut the Pass in seven hundred forty-one, and the border was fixed in forty-seven by men who had never walked it; we drink to the Warden and we drink to the road, and the road has no name and the Warden has two.

\subsection*{The cup at the end}

There is a cup set at the end of the floor that nobody takes. It stands for the one whose number was changed twice. We set it out. We do not drink from it. The clerk leaves the place the length of a name.

The last cup goes to the man just off the stone, not to the one that won but to the one still standing; he drinks with the left hand, for the right has gone cold, and he states his measure, and after that his name.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaf when the survey table sat at the Keep in Ilmen. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He struck out \emph{the cup goes round and the cold goes round} in both places and set above it, \emph{the measure is circulated and the chill is entered}. Against \emph{the number is not the same} he wrote \emph{the vessel was re-entered}, which is a true thing said in a language nobody at this floor speaks. At the end, where the cup stands that nobody takes, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it.

I have put the words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a man who has just come off the stone does not know he is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to drink with. A nought is a number and a place is not. He has put a number where a place should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

\subsection*{From the Listening Stones}

The leaf went up to the stones with a surveyor who had a question to ask and was in no hurry to hear the answer. It came back with one line in a hand that writes very large and very slowly, a hand like a man learning to use a tool he has no use for:

\begin{quote}\itshape The numbers are correct.\end{quote}

I asked the surveyor whether that was an answer to the song. He said it was an answer to the numbers, which is not the same thing, and that a man who wanted a Vorr to translate a thing had chosen the wrong sort of man. I have set the line where it was written and have not glossed it. In this country a sentence that can be carried away and still mean nothing is not a small thing; it is the only kind of sentence that survives the winter.

\subsection*{The verse at the foot, in Grathic}

A clay-man from the low road was at the Pass in the year the snow lay long, and he wrote this in the bottom margin in a small careful hand, with the \emph{th} hard and the vowels short as they speak them down the Ilm. He had been levied and had not chosen to come.

\begin{quote}\itshape I do not state my measure. It was stated for me\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape by a man with a clean cuff and a number already written.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Where I come from a pot split lip to foot is a pot gone wrong\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the yard goes around the place where it stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Here they clamp it and call it a repair,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the repair gets carried all the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the corners and four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth should be --- even up here.\end{quote}

I have not struck it out. He asked me what the fifth was, and I told him I had never known a man who could say, and he said that was the answer his mother would have given and went back to the wall.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal dust is the Shift-man’s, who dictated the third part standing and would not sit. The press of wet reed came from the board walk at the Weir, where the survey party put the leaf down while a barge unloaded and it took the weather. The ale ring is not a mark anybody owns; three men put a cup in it over one evening and no man will say which. The tallow thumb is mine: I held the sheet down in the draught that comes up the shaft and did not know I had marked it. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff I had no business putting into a corner in the room where the cups were, and I have not washed it off and have no wish to.

The board box goes back under the survey table with the spoil slips. The figures on the face of the sheet are gone soft on the wet side, and the song on the dry side is plain enough to read. A man will state his measure and then his name tomorrow as he did today, and the number of some of them will be changed by the end of the tend, and the clerk will set the second down without a mark beside it, which is the only thing he is allowed to do honestly.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Nineteen Out, Nineteen Back}
\CRsheetheading{Nineteen Out, Nineteen Back}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A work song of the slip pits and the drying racks, Low Kiln · Taken down on a market morning in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, from the mouths of women treading slip in the Clay Yard of Sill, by a clerk in the factor’s house at Greybank whose name has been rubbed from the corner of the sheet; the copy stands on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice, folded into an apron pocket, and survives with slip-stains, a green bead of lead glaze, a thumb in tallow, and the clerk’s own square hand striking out one line. The song is held to be older than the Clay Road.\par}\medskip
I set this down because I was told to copy what the women sang and not what I thought they ought to have sung, which is a harder thing than it sounds. I am a clerk. My hand wants a verb where there is no verb, and a line where the line breaks off and goes around the pot instead of through it. What is written below is as near as I could come, with the knocked-out parts left standing so that a man reading it in Greybank may know what he is looking at. The slip at the top right is not mine. Nor the green. The tallow thumb is the woman’s who sang it loudest; she put her hand on the sheet to keep it from the draught and did not know she had marked it.

\subsection*{The song, as it goes round the yard}

The pit is cold before the sun, the slip is old bone under the heel; tread it, girl, and tread it again, it will mind your weight and keep it.

Tread, tread, the clay says more than the potter will say before company; a fist in the belly, a thumb at the rim, and the crack shows where you left it.

Nineteen out and nineteen back, a pot on the hip and the broom at the track; four and four and a want in the Count, and the rack keeps the dry and the pit keeps the wet.

The wheel does not care whose hands, only that they come steady and come soon; bone-pale slip to the bend of the finger, and the hollow seat keeps the shape of a man.

Set it down. Let the pot speak first. A whole one answers full under the knuckle; a cracked one gives a little flat knock and will not be told what it should have said.

Leave the crack showing. Let the glaze go over the good part and the bad part alike; a repair is a scar with a pot around it, and the pot is the one that gets carried.

Nineteen out and nineteen back, and a place at the end of the rack where nothing stands; the yard goes around it, the broom goes around it, and nobody puts a pot there, and nobody says why.

Up the terrace the glaze room breathes sweet, sweet enough to make a body careless; a pale line at the gum is the first of it, and a woman with green at her mouth still sings.

One in twelve as the notice says, three loaves to the levy and one to the dish; the bell at the Cross goes longer than a church bell, and nobody crosses himself at it, and the pigs go over the boards.

When the river comes up and takes the low steps, the steps come back a hand’s breadth out of line; the yard calls it weather and goes on using them, as a woman calls a cough weather and goes on.

Nineteen out and nineteen back, the fire keeps the breath it will not give; bank it with the back of a broken pot, and leave the grey where it lies till the Last Day.

\subsection*{The fourth line, and what I did to it}

The women sang, \emph{the pit is cold before the sun}. I struck this out, being used to a verb in its place, and wrote above it, \emph{the cold is in the pit before the sun is}. Missy Clay, who sang loudest and keeps her hand on my sheet, looked at what I had written and asked me which of us had been standing in the pit, because the cold was not in it before the sun and never had been; it came up out of it when you trod, which is a different thing and not the thing on my notice. I have left my line standing above hers so that the correction can be seen. It is the only place in this copy where the Court’s grammar has got the better of me, and I am not proud of it.

\subsection*{A note on the counting, in the same hand}

The nineteen is not a number I have ever been able to make agree with anything. It is the steps from the slip pit to the drying rack, out and back, and a woman of House Silt has walked it every day since Y.H. 806, which is six years, and will not vary it by one. I asked her why nineteen and she asked me why a tend has ten days in it, and when I told her the Court had not made the tend and could not unmake it, she said that was the answer, and went back to her tread. There is a twentieth place at the rack’s end where a pot once stood. I put it in the song because they put it in the song. I cannot tell you what pot it was, and no one I asked would tell me either, so I have entered it as a place and not as a loss.

The \emph{four and four and a want in the Count} is the kiln’s breathing, or the stack’s, or the bell’s; they use the same count for all three and keep the three counts in separate places in their heads. I put down what I heard. I would not join them for a crown.

\subsection*{The verse they would not sing before a man from Slate Row}

There is one more verse. The women broke off at it when a collector crossed the north bridge with his satchel under his arm, and took it up again when he was past the Fishstairs, and would not let me write it while he was in the square. I have it now from Missy Clay after the market, and set it here with the proper space left before it, which is the space they left in the singing:

\begin{quote}\itshape The iron comes cold and the slate comes clean,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that writes is not the hand that’s seen;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes in the pot is not what comes out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the account stands, and the bowl’s about.\end{quote}

I asked her what the last line meant. She said it was a song, and a song was not obliged to mean a thing just because a clerk had written it down. Then she put her tallow thumb on the corner of the sheet again.

\subsection*{At the foot of the leaf}

A grey ridge runs along the skirting in the room where they sang, near two thumbs wide, turning the corner without a break. It is not swept until the Last Day and is burnt the morning after, and called dealt with. I touched it with the edge of my notice and it came off on the paper, which is how the grey at the bottom of this leaf got there. If the sheet is ever read in the Hearthseat, let that be entered against me and not against the women: I moved it, and they would have left it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Salt, Current, and the Ebb, Being the Proverbs of the Vhaleni Set Down at the Pans and Glossed for a Landman}
\CRsheetheading{Salt, Current, and the Ebb, Being the Proverbs of the Vhaleni Set Down at the Pans and Glossed for a Landman}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pan-clerk’s gathering of the proverbs, counting-maxims, tide-sayings and curses of Vhalen, written in the leaning counting-hand on salt-paper the writer kept dry against the rule; the sayings in the sibilant low speech with the ends of words let fall, the glosses in the writer’s own hand, with a Council clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in Seed and Frost of Y.H. 811 by Tavi Hull, a copyist of the dippers’ tide-tallies who learned his letters in a counting house and has never held a share; written on salt-paper leaves he kept dry in a tin lined with nothing, sewn with tarred net-twine, and carried up the Salt Road with a glass consignment in Stone of Y.H. 812, where the leaves were copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled weigh-slip and corrected by a clerk of the Council of Tides. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with the wet corner left wet. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, a thumb of tar at the fold, a peck-hole where a brine-gull took the leaf for a crust, a fish-hook nick, a corner softened by rain where two sayings have gone, a rope-burn along the outer edge, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and a loop of tarred twine through the first leaf which the writer will not undo.\par}\medskip
I copy the dippers’ tide-counts at the pans outside Vhal: I write down what the water did and leave out what it meant, because the Council pays for the first and has never asked for the second. A man from the hill country asked me once what we say when there is nothing to say. I told him we say it to the water. He paid me two bits and went away believing he had learned something, which in Vhalen is the usual end of a conversation with a man from away.

These are our sayings, set in the Grathic letters because our own hand is kept for contracts, and a contract is made to be read by a man who is not in the room. Say them with the ends of the words let fall, so that the listener supplies the last of the thought. Said looking at a man, a saying becomes an argument; said to a rope, a pan, a tide, it stays a saying. A landman will hear half of what is here and call it rudeness. He would be nearer the mark if he called it a contract with the half left out.

I have written these on salt-paper and keep the leaves dry, contrary to the practice of the country, and I know it. A contract left in the rain is no contract, which we call a virtue; a saying left in the rain is no saying either, and I have met no man who sees the virtue in that.

\subsection*{Of the current man}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “There is no guest in Vhal. There is a man whose account is current.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — We have no word for guest or friend, only for a man whose account is current: one who has paid for what he took and may remain in the room. A landman calls this hard; it is only exact. A guest is a person you cannot enter, and one you cannot enter may cost you anything.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Don’t say \emph{kindly}. Kindly is the coin we don’t take.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said to one who has done something for nothing and wants to be let off it. Say so at once, that the other knows it was no favour. A favour in Vhalen is a debt with no date, and a debt with no date is the kind that keeps a man awake.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Count it by touch. The fingers don’t care what the face is saying.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A counting-house trick, and an eel-woman’s trick upriver, and the same trick. You learn a coin with the hand and let the face lie over it. I have watched a factor smile at a widow while his thumb told him the figure was short. Both were true; only one could be entered.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A stranger’s coin warms before his face.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Of a man who has come a long way in cold weather. The coin has been against his skin all the road and the face has not; you can tell where a man has been by what he carried. It is a saying about warmth, whatever a priest may make of it.}

\subsection*{Of paper and weather}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Write it in the rain and see what’s there in the morning.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Half the port’s fortunes have turned on this, and the other half on somebody forgetting to do it. A contract on salt-paper in wet weather is no contract at all. That is not a loophole in our law; it is our law. Ask a Grath man why he trusts a slate: it is stone. Ask us why we trust wet paper: it does not last.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A law that lasts too long has stopped earning.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — My mother said it before the Council made a virtue of it. A decree is repealed when it stops paying, which is honest if you consider a decree a tool and not a promise. The assessors cannot bear it. Their slates are stone, their sentences have no verbs, and both outlive the man who wrote them.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “What the rain takes, nobody can enter.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A clerk can only enter what he can still read. That is our theology of paper and most of our law. It is why we keep tide-names in the mouth and not on the leaf; a name said at the Salt Walk is written in salt, the sun takes it by noon, and no Council has found a way to tax noon.}

\subsection*{Of the draw and the tide}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The tide runs against the wind and doesn’t ask the moon.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The Sallow does as it pleases with the weather, and the dippers read what it did rather than what it ought to have done. A Grath man tells the time by a bell; we tell it by the turn of the water under the quay, which is never where the bell says. The moon is not consulted in Vhalen and would not be answered if it were.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Name the tide you haven’t seen. Salt’s teacher enough.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At fourteen the young walk the pans barefoot at low tide and name a tide nobody has seen. The dippers write the name in salt and the sun takes it. When a Vhaleni would say what he cannot write, he names a tide not yet come. It is the nearest thing to a promise we have and is not one, which is why we can say it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Trail the net at dawn. Read what comes up.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The dippers bless the nets by dragging them at first light and reading the draw. We say the Sallow has a Hearth of its own beneath the salt and the Court’s is only its chimney. I have said it all my life; no dipper has taken me down to see the one under the salt, and I have learned not to ask.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The draw takes what isn’t kept, and the Court taxes what’s taken.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The Warm goes out seaward and the assessors arrive with deductions on the salt works, as punctual as gulls. We bless the draw and pay for it, and never thought the two inconsistent. A cold country makes a man careful where his heat went.}

\subsection*{Of gulls, salt and the dead}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The gull takes the warm thing and leaves you colder than you were.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The brine-gull lifts a coal from a brazier, or a loaf, or a warmed stone, and flies off with it under its crop. No malice in it. A bird that steals warmth is no worse than one that steals bread. Say this of a man who has taken something and calls it borrowing.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Carry a barrel of rain. It’s the only thing the salt-thing won’t cross.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The salt-thing follows boats at night and taps the hull where the store is; fresh water stops it as a wall stops a man. Every captain I have sailed with carries rain in a barrel against it and would deny being afraid. The dippers bless the nets against it, which is reasonable and costs the Council nothing.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Don’t lick the Cliffs. They’re sweet and they’re lead.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The Glaze Cliffs are blue-green with old lead workings and smell faintly sweet in the heat. Children are told not to lick them and some do, for a child believes a warning about a taste before one about a poison. The sweetness stays with the man; the lead stays with the Glaze room across the water.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Seal him in a boat, push him on the ebb, watch till he’s out of sight. That’s enough.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — We do not break a pot at the door as they do across the water; we seal the dead in a salted boat, let the ebb carry them, and stand until there is nothing left to look at. The watching is held to be enough. Nobody says why; I have never seen a Vhaleni who wanted a longer ceremony.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A man who dies at sea has already returned. The sea keeps its own account.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A kindness we allow the sea. On land the collector comes with his cold tube and the Return is entered; at sea there is no slate, the warmth goes out with the tide, and we call it done. Women say it of a husband who never came back and mean they are released from entering him, which is a mercy and is not one.}

\subsection*{Of boats and shares}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The share goes through the mother. A husband’s come aboard and his word’s half a word.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Shares pass through mothers; a man who marries into a boat-owning family is come aboard, his opinion counted at half. He knows it; everyone knows it; nobody says it before company. Captains are mostly women, because the sea does not care and the Council has learned not to.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Thirty marks and a curse every hour. That’s a boat.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What our shipwrights ask to build a boat and what they say while building it. The curse is in the price, and a man who pays less gets more of it. It does not sink the boat; that would be a gift, and no shipwright in Vhal has ever given anything away.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Two marks a month and keep. One mark and a binding promise. Know which you’re being paid in.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A sailor’s share and a salt-worker’s are not the same, and a promise is not a mark however binding the man who offers it says it is. I have taken the promise myself; it was binding and worth what I could get for it, which was nothing. A man should hear both sayings before he signs either.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Seven years at the pulled bench, or till your hands give out, whichever comes first.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The sentence for a condemned criminal, said as other countries say a grace. The pulled benches are the salt galleys, and the hands give out first, so that the seven years is a figure written for the benefit of the man who wrote it. We do not say it to a man being sentenced; he finds out in the ordinary way.}

\subsection*{What they sing at the Salt Walk}

\emph{Said by the young walking the pans barefoot at low tide, going out, not coming back. The name in the third line is the one nobody has seen. They write it in the salt and go home and it is gone by noon.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Out on the crust where the wind has been,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape barefoot, barefoot, and the pan holds;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I name you a tide that has not come,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and salt says yes and the sun says no.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Rake at the turn and rake at the fourth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull takes the coal and the clerk the mark;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what the pan keeps is what it keeps,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what’s in the mouth can’t enter the slate.\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — The fourth line is no contradiction. Salt says yes because the name is spoken there; the sun says no because it takes the writing. Both tell the truth and neither can be entered, which is the first thing a Vhaleni child learns of a contract: there are two parties to everything and one is weather.}

\subsection*{What the Council clerk did}

A Council clerk borrowed the leaves at Greybank on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the narrow upright counting-hand, with the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{there is no guest in Vhal}, he set \emph{the party is accommodated}, and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{what the rain takes, nobody can enter}, he wrote \emph{the instrument is void by weather}, a true thing in a language nobody at the pans speaks.

\item At \emph{name the tide you haven’t seen}, he put \emph{tide not entered} and a round nought in the space where the name would stand. A nought is a number. The tide was not a number and has not come back to be one.

\item At the wage-sayings he wrote \emph{two marks and one promise, current}, joining two unlike payments into one figure, which is the whole art of that hand.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a man barefoot on a pan wants to know who is doing the taking and whether he will get it back.

\subsection*{In the margin, in the leaning counting-house hand}

A Council tally-man wrote this below the song, in the sloped letters of tallies, never of decrees:

\begin{quote}\itshape They pay for the tide that’s entered, not the tide that’s seen.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have stopped telling them which is which.\end{quote}

I do not know his name and have not asked. It is the most honest line on these leaves, which is a poor recommendation for a line written by a Council man, but there it is.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom came up in a wet week at the pans and has eaten two letters of \emph{current}, which I have not written in again; a word about a current that the weather has taken is truer than one a clerk can still read. The tar thumb is mine; I turn the leaves with the hand I mend nets with. The peck-hole went through \emph{gull} and nobody has claimed the bird. The fish-hook nick is from a basket set down while a man paid for six herrings and was charged for five, or the other way, which he will not settle and I have not entered. The soft corner is the rain; two sayings went entirely and I do not know which two, which is the condition I described in sayings five and seven and have now been given in my own paper. The grey print nobody will own came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a pan. There is no Last Day at the pans and nothing gets swept.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The account is current until the weather says it is not. Everything else in Vhalen is entered.\end{quote}

I asked a dipper, a tally-man and a man come up from Greybank with road-mud on his boots, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back in the tin; tomorrow the dippers trail the nets at dawn, and I write what the water did, leave out what it meant, and am paid for the one and not asked for the other.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Six Under the Heel, Being the Treading Song of the Clay Yard at Sill, with the Rounds as They Are Trodden and What the Factor’s Clerk Made of the Count}
\CRsheetheading{Six Under the Heel, Being the Treading Song of the Clay Yard at Sill, with the Rounds as They Are Trodden and What the Factor’s Clerk Made of the Count}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A clay-yard’s treading song in the Low Kiln speech, called down into the slip pit and answered by the feet and not by voices; set down in charcoal by a rack-woman who treads slip in the mornings, with the rounds in the treaders’ own words, a correction in the margin by an old woman who has kept the racks thirty years, the factor’s clerk’s ruling in Ledgerhand above the seventh round, and a line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Written in Silt of Y.H. 813 in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln in Sill, in charcoal on the inside of a pot gone wrong that had split from lip to foot and been set by the wall of the wheel-shed for the sweeping; the charcoal went into the grain of the clay so that no scraping would take it out. Copied forward onto the back of a kiln-setting tally gone soft with damp, carried to Greybank in the pocket of a woman come to have a widow’s mark confirmed, and sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled paper. It survives with bone-pale slip rubbed into the head, a wet-clay thumb at the second corner, a green bead of lead-glaze in the gutter, a brown barley crust gone stiff in the fold, a tallow print, a tideline from the Slip Brook, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the old rack-woman’s correction standing in the margin, the clerk’s ruling standing above the seventh round, and the line at the back that has never been claimed.\par}\medskip
I tread the pit in the mornings before the wheel is warm, and I have done so eleven winters. There are four of us when the water stands high and two when it falls, and the work is the same: foot after bare foot into the slip until the lumps are gone and the clay closes over the instep the way water closes over a stone. You do not see the air go. You feel it come up between the toes and break, and the old women call it the pot’s breath and say that a pot which keeps its breath will burst in the firing. I do not know whether this is true. I have seen a pot go flat in a kiln that had been trodden by women who knew their work, and I have seen a pot come out singing from a pit any child might have trampled.

This is not a song for a fire. It is said to the clay. A caller stands at the lip of the pit and says the first line down into it; the treaders say the second with the foot, and the last line of each round is not said aloud but is the lifting of the foot, which is the rest. Say a line to a woman and it becomes an argument. Say it to the clay and the clay tells your foot when to come up.

Six rounds to a tread and the seventh held. The count is not ours. It is the count of a clay-bound year, six that the yard will speak of and one that the household enters into a slate; a man may serve six years in a pit and be in his eighth before the yard will say his name in the same sentence as his debt. We do not sing the seventh. We hold it the way the kiln holds one breath in four, which is to say we leave it where it is and go around it.

I set the words down on the inside of a pot that had gone wrong, because there is no slate in a yard that a pail of water will not spoil and no paper that will last a morning among the tubs. The charcoal went into the clay and stayed there. What follows is what the women said before the man from the counting house borrowed the leaf at Greybank, and what they said again after he had gone back over the north bridge.

\subsection*{The song, as it is trodden}

\emph{Called at the lip, low, into the pit. One line, one round of the foot. The last line of each part is said to the clay and not to a person.}

\subsection*{The wetting}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slip is cold and the pit is deep,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape put in the foot where the others keep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clay comes up over the ankle bone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape takes the print of the foot and keeps its own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The water lies where the water lay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and mud goes down to the mud by day;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pit has a lip and the pit has a floor,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the seventh stands at the lip and comes no more.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The six rounds}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the lump that the heel finds first,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the bubble that breaks and is not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the water that climbs and goes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the bone-coloured slip on the toes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five for the print of a thumb in the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the seam where the thumb let it fall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the seventh stands where the seventh has stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the cold of the pit and the print in the mud.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the wheel}

\emph{Not sung at the wheel itself. Said under the breath by the thrower while the pot goes up, with the thumb kept steady and the knuckle kept for afterwards.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wheel goes round and the seat is worn\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape on the left where a man leaned, and the lean stays on;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape put the pot where his thumb was put\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and listen to what the pot has got.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wall goes up and the thumb goes in\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape at the one place where the wall is thin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tap it once with the knuckle bone ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape full is a note that a house may own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tap it once and it answers flat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sweep it around where the potter sat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A crack once made is a crack kept true;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape leave the crack showing and the yard goes through.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the kiln}

\begin{quote}\itshape The kiln draws breath and the kiln lets go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the breath and a place in the row;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire takes what the fire will take\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leaves a brown edge on the loaf we bake.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The glaze runs sweet where the lead has been\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a girl at the cup has a pale at the gum;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape she sets the cup down on the bench and goes\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape out to the racks where the dry slip shows.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What the fire takes out of the clay\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house finds in the corner at dawn;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we leave it there and we leave the pot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the crack showing, and carry on.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they do not tread when a man from Slate Row is in the yard}

I have it from the caller, with the space left before it, which is the space the treaders leave in the singing. She would not say it to the clerk and would not say it within sight of his cuff. She said it to the pot I had set by the wall, with her back to the road.

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the years that the slate will name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the year that the household keeps;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes in and the man goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the grey in the corner goes up a thumb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the pot and one for the hand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that put the thumb in and could not command\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the place where it failed. The yard says weather.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The legs say nothing. The slate says never.\end{quote}

I asked her what the seventh was and she said a man who had never trodden would not know where the foot comes up, and went back to the pit. This is the answer the yard gives to everything it does not want entered, and I have set it down as she gave it, without mending the sense.

\subsection*{The old woman’s correction in the margin}

Against \emph{two for the bubble that breaks and is not}, a woman who has kept the racks thirty years wrote in a small hard hand: \emph{Not air. Water. My mother trod this pit forty years and it is water that comes up between the toes, not air, and water will not burst a pot in the firing. The pot that went flat in our kiln had been dried too fast against the east wall.}

Under it, in mine: \emph{Both stand. I have felt the bubble break and I have known the east wall. A song that has been corrected in the margin is a song that has been used, and a song nobody has argued with is a song nobody has trodden to.}

\subsection*{What the clerk wrote above the seventh round}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank, being a man who cannot leave paper lying. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He struck out \emph{the seventh held in} and wrote above it, \emph{one part in twelve withheld from the tread; the deduction is entered.} Against \emph{what goes out of the clay comes home to me} he set \emph{labour retained in the vessel; no residue arises.} At the foot of the last round he wrote \emph{six turns performed, rest nil,} and drew a line under it that went a finger’s breadth past the margin.

I have put the women’s words back underneath and left his standing above, as the floor keeps the ash and the foot that raised it. He has made a rest into a deduction and a deduction into a year. A rest is when the foot comes up; a year is what a clay-bound man does not get back. He has set one where the other stood, which is the whole art of that hand. The treaders stop when they see the soft cuff come into the yard. They take it up when he is past the bridge, and they never once sing the seventh.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The bone-pale slip at the head is off the hand that drew the line in the pit; it goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the yard uses it to mark a place and not to write a name. The wet-clay thumb at the second corner is mine. I signed in slip because I have no slate-name and the pot was mine before it was a leaf. The green bead came off a pot broken by the Glaze Room and rolled to the gutter while a woman held the tally down in the draught; I did not taste it and have not put it in my mouth, whatever the children say of that sweetness. The brown crust is a barley one with the edge burnt, given to a child who would not eat it and laid down here instead. The tallow print came off a lamp set too near the leaf at the Long Night. The tideline took two words off the back of the tally and I have not written them in again, because a song with two words gone is a song said slowly and all of ours are said slowly. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying in a yard; I have not swept it. The Last Day is for corners, and a folded leaf has none.

The tally goes back into its fold of oiled paper and into the pocket, and tomorrow the pit will be cold again and the four of us will be there or the two, according to the water. The caller will say six and the feet will answer six, and the seventh will stand at the lip where it stood this morning, and the clay will close over the instep the way it always does, and whatever goes out of it will come home to somebody.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The flaw is where the thumb was. The thumb was somebody’s.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six go into the pot. The seventh goes home in the leg.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the yard what it counts and it will tell you the weather.\end{quote}

I asked the caller, the old woman of the racks and a carter waiting on the road, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Apprentice Beam, Being the Standing Rules of the Kiln-Masters of Sill for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices, Read at the Cross and Nailed Beside the Moot-Post}
\CRsheetheading{The Apprentice Beam, Being the Standing Rules of the Kiln-Masters of Sill for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices, Read at the Cross and Nailed Beside the Moot-Post}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bench-copy of the guild’s standing rules in the hand of the clerk who keeps the kiln-masters’ bench at the Cross; the terms set in tables, the yard’s wheel-song pasted to the back, two corrections in the Thane’s narrow hand, one clause crossed in a potter’s charcoal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · First gathered at Sill in Y.H. 418, the year the Clay Road was made a Court road by the treaty of the Blue Cliff, and copied forward each generation from the bench rather than from a book; this leaf written at the Cross and in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried through the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives folded and soft at the nail-hole, with a thumb-worn centre where a hundred men have wiped their hands before reading, a green bead of lead glaze at the head off the Thane’s thumb, slip dried the colour of old bone down the gutter, a tallow spot at the wheel clause, a press of wet reed across the song from a day the bench stood in the rain, a grey print along the foot that is not mine and is not the Thane’s, two small corrections in his narrow upright hand, one line struck hard in charcoal by a potter who would not put his name to it, and one line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the guild’s bench at the Cross on market-days, between the pig beam and the Court table set at the Slate Row fringe. A house comes to take a child, or a child is brought to be tried, and I read what is below so that what is read in High Kiln is the same as what is read in the yard. The bench is worn smooth in the middle where thumbs have wiped it longer than any man can date, and this leaf has a nail-hole at the head and a green bead of glaze in the lower corner that came off the Thane’s thumb in the Thin Year and has not been swept since. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid in a corner where no cuff has business lying, and there is no Last Day for a bench-copy. I have set the rules down as they stand. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

They are not new rules. They were gathered in the year the Clay Road was made a Court road, when a man from the Cross could first reach Greybank in five days and the guild found it had neighbours it had not chosen. A rule with no thumb on it is a rule nobody has had to use. What follows has been used.

\subsection*{The standing rules, as read at the Cross}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A house takes an apprentice, not the guild. The house answers for the child’s food, his bed, his tools and the debt he makes; the guild answers only for the note. A man who takes a child and will not answer for him has taken nothing, and the child is sent back to the moot.

\item A child may be taken from his ninth year, and not before he can carry a board of wet pots the length of the yard without setting it down. A child bound by debt goes where the debt sends him, and his years count from the day the debt is entered, not from the day he could lift a board.

\item The taking is written in the house’s own roll, in a careful hand, and the roll is kept in the house. It is not taken to Slate Row and it is not shown to a man who comes down with a slate. A slate is for the measure; the roll is for the hand. The two are not the same book and must not be set side by side.

\item A foundling is named by whoever writes the slate, and has no house-name until a hearth claims him. Until then he is a coat any house may wear. See that the coat is mended where it tears, not worn till it thins.

\item A widow may hold her husband’s fire by the mark confirmed at the Cross and by the factor at Greybank. She touches the mark before she opens the kiln and at no other hour. A dusk is not an opening, and a bank is not an opening.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the first year}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The apprentice sweeps, carries, mixes slip and sets pots to dry. He does not touch the wheel, and he does not cut the glaze. A child set to the wheel too soon learns to humour the clay instead of hearing it, and a pot humoured is a pot that will not say what it is.

\item The apprentice is kept, not hired. He eats from the house’s dish and sleeps under the house’s roof. What he earns in the yard goes into the yard, and what the yard gives back comes back as bread, not as a figure in a man’s hand.

\item No child tastes glaze. Glaze is tasted by the master, with the side of the thumb and the back of the tongue, and spit out. A pale line at the gum is the glaze’s mark and not a mark of industry; a master who calls it a good sign is selling the child short by the ounce.

\item A wet pot is not set in the sun and a wet pot is not set near the door. You will pay for both in the thaw. Fire does not know a child is sorry; feed it and say nothing.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the wheel and the ear}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Knock with the knuckle, never the nail and never the flat of the hand. The hand says what it wants from the pot; the knuckle says what the pot has. This rule is the whole trade and the rest are its corners.

\item A sound pot under the knuckle gives its full note. A cracked pot answers flat, small and dead, and the sound stops at the surface and will not go through. A pot that answers flat is a pot gone wrong. It is broken at the door, not mended and sold, and the yard goes around the place where it stood.

\item A mended pot gives a note nearly full and never quite, and the yard calls it a pot that’ll do. Leave the crack showing. A repair that will not sing is a lie in clay, and a lie in clay is the only lie a kiln cannot burn clean.

\item The cupworm hides a flaw no knuckle will find. If a hand says a pot is wrong and the knuckle says it is right, set the pot aside another year. The yard has been wrong about pots and has never once been wrong about a hand that would not let a thing go.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Crossed hard in charcoal across rule 13 in the Thin Year, in a potter’s hand that did not sign:} Strike \emph{the knuckle says it is right}. Set above: \emph{the ear hears it before the hand gets there, and the hand gets there before the knuckle}. I have not swept the charcoal. I have not put the struck words back. Both readings stand, because the bench has held both and the bench is older than either of us.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the kiln and the breath}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No child sleeps in a closed kiln house. The kiln’s breath kills in sleep and is called a merciful death by those who have not had to carry the body out. A damper is a thing to be moved, not argued with.

\item Coals are banked under ash at dusk with the back of a broken pot, not with a shovel. Iron on iron wakes what should lie. The fire is left as it was found, so that the morning’s hand knows the night’s hand was there.

\item The master opens the kiln. The apprentice stands back from the lid, because a face over an open kiln learns nothing and loses its eyebrows. The kiln takes its breath in fours and a gap; a man who counts the gap aloud will be told to count the pots instead.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the term and the debt}

Condition — Term — What gathers\par

House child, taken at nine — seven years — The note of the pot; nothing written against the boy\par

Child bound by debt — seven years, or as entered — Grey Ash in the household account, by the year and by the loaf\par

Debt left uncalled — as long as the house holds it — The debt is not forgiven. It lies where it was put, and a man goes around it as around Ash in a corner\par

Kept hand — until returned thin — No measure in the house’s roll; the house keeps the body and not the name\par

Foundling with a slate-name only — until a hearth claims him — A coat anybody can wear, and a debt nobody has entered yet\par

Widow holding a fire — by the mark, confirmed — The fire must not go out; the mark is touched before openings only\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Seven years is the common term and not a short one. Interest gathers as grey Ash in the household accounts, which is why the house keeps its roll dry and why a debt left uncalled is worse than a debt called: a called debt has an end, and an uncalled one has only a place.

\item A clay-bound child sleeps in the loft and a taken child sleeps under the roof. This is a poor household’s sorting of its own members, and it is called kindness, and it is not entered anywhere. Ask the pot. The pot is more use.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Thane’s narrow upright hand, above rule 7:} The apprentice is kept. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that the apprentice is paid. He is not paid. He is fed, and the feeding goes into no figure, which is why it can be done. I have left my word standing under his, since a man should be able to see the thing he was told to change.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the levy and the First Firing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Two levies are called at the Cross, and the moot shouts at both. The levy of clay is worked out in barrow-loads and the levy of warmth in figures. The second is the heavier, and the notice says one in twelve. A household that has heard otherwise has heard wrong. The notice is what a man can be seen reading.
