I asked a man of Keld and he turned the slate face down and said he had not seen it.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The brown thumb at the head is mine; iron-gall will mark a man who keeps a quire open through a tend, and there is no washing it out of the creases. The slate dust in the gutter came off a surveyor who leaned over my table with the south-road dirt still on his cuffs, and he would not sit down. The tar along the fore-edge is from the quay, where I set the leaves while a barge unloaded salt and I counted a carter’s figures and let my own leaf take the weather. The reed between the second and third leaves was put there by the reeve who sang; he folded it the way a man folds a thing he means to come back for. The small square of bare paper is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. It is the only square in this quire that I made myself, and I made it deliberately, which is more than I can say for the others.

The leaves go back into the drawer at Greybank. At the Opening of the Slates I copied them again and put the squares in again with my own hand, because a square is the only figure the Court has never learned to read. The Cantons have no people and no smoke, but they have roads, and a road is a thing somebody meant to come back along. The annals go on. Next tend I copy the quay tallies, and after that the Weighing figures from the Hearthseat, and the squares will keep their places in the roll for as long as there is a hand to set them there.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Fifth Breath, Being the Firing Song of the Kilns of Low Kiln, Kept at the Damper with One Verse Held Back for the Watch}
\CRsheetheading{The Fifth Breath, Being the Firing Song of the Kilns of Low Kiln, Kept at the Damper with One Verse Held Back for the Watch}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A firing-woman’s watch song of the clay yards of Sill, pricked with a kiln-needle into soft clay and fired with the pots, so that the words are burnt into the body of a tile and cannot be struck out; the Grathic in the women’s own half-sung manner, said to the fire and not to a person, with a Court clerk’s copy on the back of a Greybank weigh-slip in Ledgerhand above it, and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Cut into a tile in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln by Wenna, a firing-woman of the third kiln, in Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and fired with a standing load, the words going into the throat green and coming out hard; the tile was set in a niche of the damper-shed where the watchers put their hands to warm them, and is kept there still. In Ilmen of Y.H. 813 a clerk of the factor at Greybank made a copy on the back of a spoiled weigh-slip, being a man who cannot leave a figure alone, and struck at the copy what he could not strike at the tile; the two lie folded together in a fold of oiled sacking. It survives coal-black in the gutter, with slip dried bone-pale in the letter-cuts, a thumb in slip at the head, a green bead of lead glaze melted into one corner in the firing and sweet to this day, a burn-pit where a coal fell, grey Ash along the base that comes off on a finger, and a hairline crack that goes around the word \emph{fifth} and does not cross it. The clerk’s hand stands above the copy and the women’s words under it, as the fire keeps above and below in one kiln.\par}\medskip
I keep the firing at the third kiln below the sill, and I have put this song into a tile before it went into the throat, so that a man with a pen could not take it out afterwards. That is the whole reason for the tile. A song written on paper belongs to whoever holds the paper; a song burnt into clay belongs to the kiln that fired it, and a clerk may copy it if he likes, but his copy is not the song.

We say it to the fire. Said to a woman it becomes an argument, and there is always a woman who will argue. Two keep the watch through a firing, one at the coals and one at the damper, and they take the lines turn about, the one at the damper saying the short lines because her hands are not free. Every fourth line is a rest. The rest is the fifth breath and it is not said aloud. A woman who says the fifth aloud has not kept a firing yet and will be told so, kindly, in the morning.

The tile was soft when I pricked it. Dessa set her thumb on the head to hold it and did not know she had marked it, which is how the slip thumb came there; the green in the corner was a bead off a girl’s lip who leaned over to see the writing, and it melted in the firing and stuck fast and is sweet if you put your tongue to it, which I do not advise. The crack around the word went there in the cooling. I did not mend it. A word a crack has gone around is a word that will not be lost in a straight line, which is more than can be said for most things in this yard.

\subsection*{The song, as it is kept at the damper}

\subsection*{The banking}

\begin{quote}\itshape Bank it blind and leave it low,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the coal keeps what the flame will spend;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape turn it with the back of a broken pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and don’t ask who paid to mend it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pit is cold before the sun,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the cold comes up when you tread, and not before.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The feeding}

\begin{quote}\itshape Feed it on the hour and not the eye,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire keeps its own account of the day;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a mouth that opens on the quarter goes shut on the half,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man who counts by his belly learns.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull goes off with a coal not cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and there’s one warmth less in the shed and none in the slate.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The damper}

\begin{quote}\itshape The damper bites and the damper holds,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the one iron keeps and the one iron takes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape put your finger to it, feel it take the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and be thankful for the hand it leaves you.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a room shut tight with the damper down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape is a room the breath gets out of, not the war.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The sweetness}

\begin{quote}\itshape Up the terrace the glaze breathes sweet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sweet enough to make a woman still;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a pale line at the gum is the first of it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and she sings on with the green at her mouth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sweet is the sickness and the sickness is dear,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the woman who tastes it has not stopped tasting it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The watch}

\begin{quote}\itshape Watch it, girl, and do not sleep,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the breath that kills comes soft as a mother’s hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four and four and a gap in the throat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the gap is where it comes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river keeps a note under the stone\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the town sets its clock by it and says nothing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the kiln keeps a count under the floor,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no man has made the two agree.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the river’s note comes through the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire’s count comes up through the boards,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and they were never the same sound.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The drawing}

\begin{quote}\itshape Let it cool. Let the pot speak first.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole one answers full under the knuckle;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a cracked one gives a little flat knock\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and will not be told what it should have said.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Leave the crack showing. Let the glaze go over\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the good part and the bad part alike;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a repair is a scar with a pot around it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot is the one that gets carried.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire has done what the fire was asked,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fifth was the breath it did not take.\end{quote}

I have set the lines as we keep them, with the rests standing where the rests stand. The fourth line of each part is not a line you hurry. A woman who hurries it comes up with a burned sleeve and a pot gone wrong, and the pot is the one that gets carried, as the song says, though nobody carries the sleeve.

\subsection*{The verse they do not sing while a man from Slate Row stands at the gate}

There is one more part. They take it up when the factor’s man has gone back over the north bridge with his satchel under his arm, and break off if he turns. I have it from the woman at the coals, with the space left before it, which is the space they leave in the singing:

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three of the four and one to the dish;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the number goes from a fist to a mouth\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and arrives at a shoulder and nobody’s ear.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The barrow goes out of the north gate\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the grey heaped a little above the sides,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody in the square looks at it twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the afternoon’s work and has always been.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tube comes cold and the hand comes grey,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mouth that reads is not the mouth that paid;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes into the pot is not what comes out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the account stands, and the bowl’s about.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and four and a place where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire keeps the count and the yard keeps the rest,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the eels run whether the priest has blessed them or not.\end{quote}

I asked her what the last line was worth. She said a song was not obliged to be worth a figure because a clerk had written it down, and then she put her coal thumb on the corner of the tile to keep it from the draught, as she had done when it was soft. I have left the space before the verse where they left it. It is the same space the kiln keeps.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

The clerk of the factor borrowed the copy on a morning when the weigh-slips were out drying. He writes with the cuff turned back twice and the ink on the first joint of two fingers and will not come out, the way a man writes who is paid by the line.

Where I pricked \emph{the coal keeps what the flame will spend}, he set above it, \emph{the measure is retained and the residue expended}. Against \emph{a room shut tight with the damper down is a room the breath gets out of, not the war}, he wrote \emph{decease by asphyxia; not attributable to hostilities}. At the count he put a round nought in the fifth place and wrote \emph{vacancy} in the margin, and at the foot of his copy he entered \emph{eight, fifth nil. Account stands.}

I have let his hand stand above the copy and put our words back underneath, as the fire keeps above and below in one kiln. A nought is a number. The fifth is a place where a woman lets the rope go and the fire draws breath. He has put a figure where a rest should be, which is the whole art of that hand. He could strike at the paper because the paper was his; he could not strike at the tile, which had gone through the throat with the words in it and come out harder than his pen. When he had done, Dessa looked at his \emph{vacancy} and asked whether a vacancy kept a pot warm, and he told her that a vacancy was not required to keep anything, and went off over the bridge. I have set her question here because it was asked and nobody answered it that was able.

\subsection*{In the margin, in the hand of a man with two fingers gone}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is no word in Grathic for the iron that keeps and the iron that takes. We say \emph{damper} and show the hand.\end{quote}

He wrote it of the third kiln and would not sign it, being a man who has kept his fingers in the damper since Y.H. 799 and has not got the two back. I have left it where he set it. It is true of every damper in the yard and of one or two other things the yard does not name.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip thumb at the head is Dessa’s; she holds the tile down with the hand she treads with and does not wash before the firing. The coal-black in the gutter came off the tile’s own corner where it lay nearest the coals and worked into the cuts of the letters, so that \emph{eighth} reads dark and \emph{fourth} has a notch gone that I have not written in again. The green bead melted into the corner in the throat and is part of the tile now and cannot be picked off; it is sweet and it is lead, and I have not put my tongue to it since the day it stuck and have told the girls not to either, which is a thing the glaze room does not tell them. The burn-pit is where a coal fell off the damper in the second firing and sat until it had eaten a small round place; a woman’s hand fits it exactly, which is how the watchers warm theirs. The grey along the base came off the ridge in the kiln-house where it turns the corner and has not been swept since a man died uncollected in the Long Cold; I touched it with the tile’s edge and it came away, and I have left it there. The crack around the word \emph{fifth} went there in the cooling and is not a break through. When the next firing comes I shall set the tile back in its niche and let the watchers warm their hands on it, and the word will still be whole inside its crack, and the clerk’s nought will still be where he put it, on the paper.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A pot is a breath the fire agreed to hold.\end{quote}

I asked the woman at the coals, the woman at the damper and a carter waiting under the sill, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was pricked. The tile goes back into its niche tomorrow and the firing goes on, and the watchers will take the short lines turn about and leave the fifth where it was left, and the river will go on keeping its own note under the stone and the kiln its own count under the floor, and nobody will make them one.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Flat Stone, Being What Was Said Over the Traps on Ilmen 15 of Y.H. 812, with the Old Words Left in Knots Because Fen Cant Will Not Write}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Flat Stone, Being What Was Said Over the Traps on Ilmen 15 of Y.H. 812, with the Old Words Left in Knots Because Fen Cant Will Not Write}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Weir preached at the blessing stone on the north bank at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill; the saying in Grathic, the three old lines held in the margin as knots of grey wool, with the tally-keeper’s corrections, a Court clerk’s in Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached at the Fish Blessing by an old woman of the Weir who had stood at the stone at thirty blessings, over the traps lifted and set on their sides on the plank walk, on Ilmen 15, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year; written that evening by a woman of the Weir who keeps the eel tally and has no slate-name, on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled by a wet figure out of Greybank, and sewn with eel-sinew into the folded reed wrapper that holds the knot-accounts in the Eel House. It survives with a salt crust at the head where a flat hand was set to brush the grit from the cut, a silt tideline along the gutter from a morning the plank walk stood under water, eel slime on the second leaf, a fish-hook nick nobody will own, a grey Ash print from a cuff at the stone, three knots left over right with the tail under against the three old lines, and a fourth knot tied through a hole in the first leaf for a word the preacher would not give out. Copied once at Greybank in Silt, Y.H. 812, and again in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the knots left as they were tied.\par}\medskip
I keep the eel tally at the Weir and nobody asked me for this. I write because the old woman’s words went into the water and the water kept them, and I wanted something on dry paper that a clerk could not carry away in a cuff. She stood on the flat stone with her sleeves salt to the elbow and spoke to the stone, the traps, the river, and last of all to us, which is the order the women of this place use when there is work to be done and somebody may be listening who wants a figure. I have set down what she said in Grathic. The three old lines are not Grathic and are not written anywhere; I have tied three knots in the margin against them, left over right with the tail under, which is how we keep a thing here that we cannot spell.

The salt crust at the head came off her hand when she flattened it on the stone to brush the grit from the cut. The silt tideline along the gutter is from the morning the plank walk stood under water and I carried the leaf under my apron. The eel slime is mine: I set the leaf down on the bench to count and a fish came out of the basket onto it, which the old woman called a blessing, and I did not argue. The fish-hook nick is not mine and I don’t know whose. The grey print came off a cuff at the stone and nobody will own it; I have not swept it. The knot through the hole in the first leaf is the fourth, and I tied it for the word she would not give out.

\subsection*{The order of the blessing, as the stone actually has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Brush the stone free of grit so the cut shows. Do not ask what the cut is. It was here before the tally and it will be here after.

\item Stand with your sleeves damp and salt in the creases of your hands. Salt on the stone and along the weir head, with a flat hand. Not on the traps. The traps have their own business.

\item Say the old words low, facing the water. A woman who says them looking at her neighbour is making an argument, and there is argument enough at the Cross without bringing it upriver.

\item Lift the traps and set them on their sides. Count them if you must, but do not say the number where a man with a slate is standing.

\item When the bell comes upriver from the Cross, stop. It is counting something that is not your river. Begin again after. Four, four and a gap, and the gap is not ours to fill.

\item The eels run whether anybody blesses them or not. This is the first thing she says every year and the last thing she will have written down, which is nothing at all.

\end{itemize}

I asked her why we bless them if they run without it. She gave me three answers: because they run; because a woman must do something with her hands on a cold morning; and because if we did not bless them, somebody from Greybank would come upriver and enter the blessing for us, and then we would owe for it. I asked for a fourth. She stood on the stone and looked at the water and did not give me one.

\subsection*{The sermon, as she said it}

\subsection*{Of the mouth}

She squatted by a trap on its side and put her finger into the mouth of it, the way you would show a child where a thing goes in.

“Look at it,” she said. “The mouth points upriver. That is the whole of the contrivance. An eel swims looking for the current and the current takes him in, and the basket narrows behind him, and there he is. He has not been bad. He has not been called. He followed the water, which is what eels do and what water does.

“Set it down among you now and tap it. It answers full when the wicker is sound and flat when it has a hole. That is all the preaching I have. A thing that holds, holds. A thing that leaks, leaks. We do not ask the pot why it cracked.

“Away up the river they read a figure over a basket and call the basket full because the figure says so. I have stood at the Cross and heard it done twice, once for the moot and once for them that came late. I do not know what figure goes with an eel. Nobody has ever told me, and I have never asked a man who was carrying a slate.”

Here she stopped and crossed two fingers at the cut in the stone and covered the act with a date, which is what the women here do.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} She gave me Y.H. 418, the year the Clay Road was made a Court road. I asked her again in a different way and she gave me the same year. I have set it down and left the question standing. Dates are safe. The Court likes a date and does not ask what it covers.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the blessing}

“Do not say I made the eels come,” she said. “I did not. Say the words with me, and then go and look at the traps. They came because they came.

“A priest come up from Greybank told us the blessing is a mercy of the Hearth and that the Hearth keeps what it is given. I have heard the same man read a whole return for a person not in the room. I believed him once. Then I tied a cord and counted what came back into this house, and the cord and the house did not agree with him.

“Here is what I know of keeping. The river keeps what falls in it. The mud keeps what the river puts down. A knot keeps what a woman tied and will not tell you. None of these three writes it down and none of them sends a collector.

“Say the old words. Put the salt on. Stand where your mother stood. That is the blessing. It does not make the eels run and it does not make them stay. It makes us stand in the same place on the same morning, which is more than most households in Sill can say for themselves.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk who came upriver on the fourth day and borrowed the leaf:} The rite is observed by long custom and is efficacious thereby. The measure is retained in the silt. Enter as nil.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have put \emph{keeps} and \emph{stand} back under his. A sentence with the verbs taken out travels well and arrives empty, which is what a man wants who has to carry it a league to a table. I have left his hand standing and my words below it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the figure}

“I will give you no number,” she said to me, when I asked what went into the cord. “Ask Orra. She will tell you which night the collector’s boat came and how many oars it had, and you may put that in your tally if you like.

“There is a number goes around this Weir from mouth to mouth and nobody gives it out. It gets into a fist and then a mouth and then a shoulder, and by the time it reaches the Eel House it has turned into weather. We say the river is up. We say the eels are running late. We say the book is lost. All true. None of them a figure.

“One in twelve is printed on the notice and read at the Cross and is not a lie. It is a true thing said to a room that is not this one. I have never seen the other figure and I have never wanted to see it. A figure is a thing a man can carry away in a cuff. A knot has to be looked at by the woman who tied it.”

\subsection*{Of the mark}

I asked her about the cut in the stone, which the chart draws and does not explain.

She put her thumb in it and said: “It was here before the stone was flat.”

“That is not a date,” I said.

“It is older than a date,” she said. “Your clerk will want a year. Give him Y.H. 418 and be shut of him.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the clerk’s hand at this place:} cut of uncertain antiquity; assign to the treaty-year, Y.H. 747. He wrote this above and underlined it twice, and set Y.H. 418 beneath it in a small stop. Both years stand, and the cut stands under both of them.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of them that come back}

“They tell us the dead come back warm,” she said. “I have stood at four returns in this district. Three came back as other people, with a hankering for a table they never sat at. One came back and said a word in a language I knew once and have forgot. The Court calls it a settling.

“I am not saying the Return is a lie. I am saying I have not seen the thing they say it is. There is a difference, and the difference has a place in the cord where nobody puts a figure.

“When my neighbour’s girl came back thin she went to the door and looked at the eel baskets and said she had been here before, which was true and no comfort to her mother. We gave her a crust. We did not read her a figure. If there is a mercy in this world it is in the crust and not in the reading.”

\subsection*{The old words}

\emph{Three lines said low, facing the water, in Fen Cant, which is not written. I have tied three knots in the margin against them, left over right, tail under, and set the sound of them here as well as I can hear it:}

\begin{quote}\itshape The eels run whether we bless them or not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the river keeps what the river got;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a way in is a way in and no way out —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the oars and one for the doubt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt on the flat and salt on the hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mouth points up and the basket stands;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we say the words and we say no more —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water does what the water bore.\end{quote}

I have put \emph{doubt} where I heard a word I cannot spell. It may be \emph{debt}. Orra says it is neither and will not say which. Two women have told me the last line means the same thing in Fen as it does in Grathic, which I do not believe, because a thing that means the same thing in two languages would have been written down by now.

\subsection*{The account of the morning}

\emph{Written as a tally, because that is the hand I keep.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Salt: a handful, from the Vhaleni jar in the Eel House. Berr Clay bought eels for the levy feast and paid two marks short; the trap-keeper has served him the same short measure ever since, and I keep the count of it. That is not a debt. It is an account no slate will take.

\item Rushes: a bundle cut above the plank walk. Nobody paid. They grow.

\item Words: three old lines and the Grathic saying after them. They cost the old woman her breath and cost me the afternoon. Not entered.

\item Eels: the traps came up full. I had the count in my mouth and put it in the water before anyone with a slate came round the bend. The second basket I did not count.

\item The stone: brushed, salted, stood upon, left as it was. It has never been entered and has never asked to be.

\end{itemize}

Nothing on this leaf was carried into the square. That is the only figure the Weir has ever agreed on.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came upriver on the fourth day with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers, borrowed the leaf at the Eel House, and gave it back with the verbs taken out. Where I wrote \emph{the river keeps what falls in it}, he set \emph{the measure is retained in the silt} above and left mine below. Where I wrote \emph{we say the river is up}, he wrote \emph{the figure is withheld pending the thaw}, which is the same sentence said by a man who has never stood in water. At the three knots he put a round nought and wrote \emph{nil} beside it, and when I asked him what a knot was worth he said nothing a clerk could enter, which was the first true thing he said all morning.

I have tied the verbs back in wool. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of them; I tie them in because a woman standing on a wet stone wants to know who is doing the keeping, and whether she will get it back.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the old woman’s and not the clerk’s, struck through once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape A way in is not a way out. The stone knows this and says nothing.\end{quote}

I asked the old woman, Orra, the girl who brings the salt, and a man come up from Greybank, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back in the wrapper with the knot-accounts. Next Ilmen the women will brush the stone and stand on it and say the three old lines into the water, and the eels will run as they always run. If the clerk comes again I shall let him take the verbs out; I shall tie them back as I did this time, and keep the fourth knot through the hole in the first leaf, which is the one I tied for the word she would not give out.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Fourth Name, Being a Letter from a Room with Good Light in Greybank to a Sister of the Ember House in the Bowl of Sere, with the Three Deaths Set Down, the Bowl-Song, a Factor’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and the Answer Left in the Margin}
\CRsheetheading{The Fourth Name, Being a Letter from a Room with Good Light in Greybank to a Sister of the Ember House in the Bowl of Sere, with the Three Deaths Set Down, the Bowl-Song, a Factor’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and the Answer Left in the Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A letter between two women of one great house, the one written in the open courtesy of Sere and the other answered in the same warm hand; a tally of three names against three deaths, the feast-song in verse, the correction of a factor’s clerk laid over both, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in a room with good light in the counting house at Greybank, eighteen leagues east downriver of Sill, by Solene Ember, returned whole in Y.H. 799, 804 and 809, to her sister of House Ember in the Bowl of Sere; written on the back of a spoiled grain docket from the Court’s granaries, the third-day hand unsteady and the wine of the public bowl gone cold on it. Carried south with the grain factor’s convoy in Smoke, answered in the margin at the Bowl in Ash, and brought north again with the glass in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. Kept since in a dry tin in the room with good light, under a fold of cloth that smells of myrrh. It survives with a ring of warm wine at the head, myrrh worked into the grain, a grey bead of Ash from a public bowl pressed into the fold, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a greenish mark where a ring lay on the leaf, a line that runs out toward the gutter and stops, the three deaths set down in a small table, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the factor’s office, the sister’s answer in a warm sloped hand in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
To my sister of the Ember house, who keeps the seventh name and will not say which of the seven she kept. From the north, from a room with good light that I am not permitted to enjoy, in the counting house of the man who brought me.

Sister, I have taken the first ring off before I began, and the second is off and lying by the ink, and the third I have left on because I have not yet decided whether what follows is true enough to cost it. You know the habit. You have watched me remove them one at a time since we were girls, and you have never once asked why, which is a kinder thing than asking and being told.

I write on the back of a grain docket from the factor’s granary, because there is no paper in this room that is mine, and a letter on a man’s paper is a thing a man may read if he has a mind to. The smell on it is myrrh. I have begun to smell of it myself, which in the Bowl would make you laugh and here makes the serving women put a hand to their mouths, the way these lowland folk cross themselves when a thing is said badly. I have not crossed myself. I am a woman of the Ten Bowls and I know what a bowl is for.

It is the third day after a feast and my hand is not steady. Look at the line that runs out toward the gutter and then stops. I have not straightened it, and I have not written the word again. The priests at home call the third-day tremor the price of beauty. Here they say nothing at all, because nobody in Greybank has ever seen a beautiful return and would not know a price if one were laid in their hand. The wine on the leaf came from the public bowl and went cold while I was finding the word I wanted, which is the whole history of warmth in the north in one small circle on a counting-house docket.

\subsection*{Why I am writing, which is not the ring on my finger}

There are three of me and there may be no fourth. A woman with three deaths ought to set them down in her own hand before a clerk sets them down in his, because a clerk will write them as \emph{returns entered: three} and leave the deaths standing out of the sentence where they cannot be read. I was returned in the year of the green bowl. No --- the third one. I was returned in the year of the green bowl and I have had two since. You were at the first feast. You stood where the fire in the court lit the whole bowl of us, and you clapped for the debt and not for the girl, which was correct, and which I have never quite forgiven you for being correct about.

The name I answer to — The year — The death that belonged to it — What the new walls let me keep\par

Solene, the one I chose out of seven — Y.H. 799, the green bowl — the Spending fire, in the open court — the taste of the wine, and the applause for the debt\par

Ilyra, which was our mother’s — Y.H. 804 — the fall from the balcony at the feast of Grain; nobody pushed, which is why it was entered as a kindness — the fall itself, and the noise the bowls made below me\par

Vey, the shortest of the three — Y.H. 809 — quiet ash, given by a woman who smiled the whole while and said it was a mercy — the smile, and nothing at all of the face above it\par

The third one is the one I remember least and therefore the one I fear. When Valen Openhand asked me whether I was grateful, I said yes three times, and on the third I took a ring off before I said it, and he saw me do it and did not mention it, which was the only mercy in that court that had nobody’s name on it.

When you write back, ask me which death I mean, the way you used to. If I do not say \emph{the third one} inside a year, I shall know that the part of me that knows the difference has gone, and you may have the room and the light and the rings and welcome to them, but you will not have me to write to.

\subsection*{The song, as we sang it at the end of the feast}

They burn the debt-slates of one household by lot when the eating is done, and then they make new ones. I have set the song down as it is sung, going out from the bowl rather than coming back from it. The ends of the lines fall away in the court; I have put them back where I could hear them and left them gone where I could not.

\begin{quote}\itshape We emptied the bowl and the fire said yes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we burned the slate and we made it again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the debt we carried went up with the smoke,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bowl stands full for the next of the house.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven names at the naming, one kept at the Bowl,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that we kept was the one we let go;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wine goes down and the fire goes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate goes where the slate is owed.\end{quote}

That is how we sang it. I used to think the last line was a courtesy. I have since seen a slate carried out of a room in this country with the same face on the man carrying it, and I no longer think it a courtesy.

\subsection*{What I ask you, which I ask everybody now}

What debt do you intend to carry? I ask it of everyone. In the north they think it is a question about money. It is not. When I asked it of a man who sits at a table in this house, he turned a slate face down before he answered me, so that I should understand I was not being entered, and then turned it face-up again when he had done, so that I should understand I had been. He has eleven words for a deduction and not one for \emph{sorry}. I have tried to teach him the word. He said it was the same absence wearing a different coat, and asked me to write the sentence again without the verb in it, which I did, and which is the most Sarnish thing that has ever been said in Sere.

There is a custom here of leaving the grey Ash in the corners on the last day of the year and burning it the next morning and calling it dealt with. In the Bowl we burn the slate and make a new one, and call that glory. I have stood between the two and cannot tell you which of us is the more honest. A woman here broke a pot at the door of a death-house so that the heat might get out. We would have poured a bowl. I have watched both and I have not decided which lets go the better.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did to this leaf}

A clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the narrow upright hand they teach in the College in the Hearthseat, with the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff. He set his hand on the top sheet before he looked at me, which is the manner of that table, and said that it was entered as it stood and there was nothing in it I need correct.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against the three names he wrote \emph{returns entered: three; fourth not entered}.

\item Against the deaths he set a figure for each, as though a fall from a balcony and a smiling woman with quiet ash were the same article at two prices.

\item Where I wrote that I am kept in a room with good light, he wrote \emph{the party is accommodated}, and underlined it twice.

\item Where I wrote that I have three deaths, he wrote \emph{measures current}.

\item Beside the name I left empty for the fourth he put a round nought. A nought is a number. The fourth has not come back to be one.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing, his hand above mine and mine under it, as a repaired pot keeps the old break under the new seam and does not pretend the first hand never touched the clay. He took the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman writing home wants to know who did what to her sister, and the answer is in the sentence if the sentence has someone in it.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, warm and sloped, the long vowels open}

You always did name the death before you named the guest. Do not tell me you are kept. Tell me which room has the light and whether the window opens, and I shall know whether you can bear to sit in it. We burned the green bowl’s slate at the feast of Smoke and made a new one, and I put your name in it, which is no loss, because a slate that burns is a slate that cannot be read aloud by a man who never met you.

I have asked Valen Openhand what debt I intend to carry and he said \emph{the house’s}, which was correct and not an answer. Ask me again when the bowl is empty and I will tell you something else. Ask me on the third day and I will lie to you in the warmest voice I have, which you will believe, because you always do.

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep the third ring. It was our mother’s before it was yours,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a thing that goes through a mother’s hands\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape does not stop being hers because a clerk has entered it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name the fourth when you have seen it. Not before.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A tide that has not come is still worth more\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape than a figure written in the rain.\end{quote}

The last of that is not mine; I copied it off a salt girl in a counting house and she charged me nothing and said so at once, so that I should know it was no favour. She is the only person I have met in the north who understands that a debt can be paid and still be owed.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wine ring at the head is mine; I set the cup down to find the word and left it standing until it went cold. The myrrh has come up out of the paper itself, or out of the cloth it was folded in, and I have not washed it. The grey bead in the fold is from the public bowl at Greybank, pressed there by a woman who leaned over to see what I was writing and said nothing; it is Ash, and in this country Ash is swept up and burned, and here it is in a letter going south. The green at the lower corner is not myrrh. A girl with the sweetness of the glaze still at one corner of her mouth touched the leaf with her thumb and went away, and I have kept the mark where she put it. The greenish print by the ink is where the third ring lay while I wrote the name Vey, and I have not lifted it or covered it. The line that runs toward the gutter is the third-day hand and I have left it running, because a letter written by a steady hand would be a letter from someone else.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three deaths entered, four names carried, and the bowl stands where it stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire under it is paid for by somebody who will not be named at the feast.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the fourth one when it comes what debt it intends to carry, and listen to what it says before you applaud.\end{quote}

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Gallery Leech, Being Remedies for the Sweating, the Stone-Cough, the Clamp-Bite, the Hand Gone Rope-Coloured and the Cold That Stays, Set Down Under Keld Keep}
\CRsheetheading{The Gallery Leech, Being Remedies for the Sweating, the Stone-Cough, the Clamp-Bite, the Hand Gone Rope-Coloured and the Cold That Stays, Set Down Under Keld Keep}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A mine-leech’s book of remedies in the Keldish measure-first manner, set down in Grathic letters with the counts notched into the board cover in iron; the cures in a gallery-leech’s hand, the objections of a clamp-master pressed in coal, the corrections of a Court survey-clerk in Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Keld Keep in the First Seam between Y.H. 808 and Y.H. 812, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Dren of the Ninth Gallery, a leech who tended the clamp-hands and the stone-cough of the deep workings and went up and down the shaft by the same rope for nineteen years; written on the back of a survey sheet spoiled by a sweating in the Ninth Gallery and on four strips of birch bark, sewn with iron wire into a board cover and carried in a coat pocket against a splinter of warm-stone. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded tally-roll. It survives with coal dust ground into the head, a clear stain of lamp-oil down the fold that has made two words transparent, iron filings caught in the gutter off the Duelling Floor, a scorch where a lamp-spark took the corner of the second leaf, the splinter of warm-stone sewn into the cover which keeps the whole book a little warm, a ring of frost on the third leaf from the climb over the Cold Pass, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one note in the blocky coal-pressed hand of a clamp-master, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I write on the back of a survey sheet that spoiled in a sweating in the Ninth Gallery. The surveyor had set it down near a seam giving off the smell of hot lead, and the heat took the figures off before anybody could read them, which is a mercy of a kind: a figure that cannot be read cannot be entered. I have cut the counts into the board cover with a file, because a notch is still there when the paper has gone soft, which is more than can be said for the Court’s figures. I am a leech of the deep. I tend the clamp-hands and the stone-cough and men who come up from the lower galleries older than they went down. I have set down what I do and what the men before me did, and where the two disagree I have set them side by side, as the survey office keeps two readings of one seam.

Nothing in this book is free. That is the only thing I will stand behind.

The coal at the head is mine. I sign in coal because it goes into the grain and will not come out, and a leech who signs his cures in a hand a clerk can read is a leech who will be asked to answer for them.

\subsection*{The number before the name}

In Keld a man gives his number before he gives his name. At the lamp-room door I ask it too. A man with no number is come down from the low countries, and I tend him last, for I do not know what is owed against him and will not ask. This is not cruelty. It is the order of the room: the man with the least number goes first, for he has the least held between him and the cold.

If a man cannot say his number, look at the forearm. If there is a smooth place where a number was cut out, do not ask how it went. I have asked twice in nineteen years and had the same answer both times, a shrug and a look toward the shaft. A place the size of a thumb is the whole of what a man will tell you about it.

A survey-clerk from Greybank asked why I number the dying. I told him so the iron would know who to take from. He wrote it down and went away pleased, which is how I know he did not hear me.

\subsection*{The order of the lamp-room}

\emph{Cut into the first leaf, in the coal hand, with one word gone over in lamp-oil.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the lamp in the niche, never on the bench. A lamp on the bench will be knocked into a man’s wound, and then the wound has two troubles where it had one.

\item Lay the warm-stone in wool and try it on your own wrist before it goes to a hand or a belly. The stone takes from the lamp’s account, and somebody down the shaft paid for the lamp.

\item Ask the number before the name, and write it first, so that if the man goes while you are writing, the figure is the part that stays.

\item Look at the hand before the iron. A hand you cannot save is still a hand you must not make worse.

\item When the sweat comes sweetish with the smell of hot lead, get the men up. A man who stays to argue with such a gallery will not argue with you again.

\item Do not tap a man to hear him. A body is not a cup. I have seen a man do it and have not forgotten the sound he said he heard.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who burns\par

The Sweating — Get the men up the shaft; cold iron to the wrists, never the chest — Heat comes up through the stone and takes a man by the head. Iron at the wrist gives it somewhere to go. Whether out of him or only lower down him, I have never been able to say. — The gallery, which gives back nothing.\par

Stone-cough — Steam of lamp-oil and hot water under a cloth; honey if the house has it — To the mouth, not the face. The dust of the Ninth gets into a man and he coughs it up in the morning in a colour he will not discuss. — The lamp and the man’s own morning.\par

A hand gone rope-coloured below a clamp — Take the clamp off — Leave it to the sixth day, which is what we have always done. If the colour has not come back by then, the hand is gone; do not set the clamp again higher up and call it a second chance. — The hand. This is the honest row.\par

The cold that stays — Walk it off; rub with warm-stone; set the man to work — See what I have written below. I have done these three things and I have not stopped doing them. — Nobody knows.\par

A cut from the Duelling Floor, or a first way gone bad — Tallow first, then a clean fold — The clamp-master says cold iron to draw the heat out, and that the iron takes as well as draws. I have set his words above mine and both stand. — The man who opened the way.\par

A greyed hand, from years at the iron — Nothing I know. Keep him from cold iron for a tend — It does not come back with rest and it does not come back with warm-stone. A collector’s hand is paid partly out of other people’s heat, and the debt shows at the fingertips. — The collector who paid him.\par

A fever that cooks a man from within — Cold iron to the temple; bleed at the elbow to let the head fall — A physician come up from Greybank says bleeding lets the measure out and not the head, and the man is weaker after. I have watched four such men and two were quieter by evening; quiet is not the same as better, and I have set that down. — The man, in the arm.\par

A boy at the Descent — A warm-stone in the pocket and a number across the forearm — Thirteen is early to have a number cut in a bone that is still growing, but the Warden’s roll wants it and the roll gets what it wants. Give the stone after the knife, not before. — The boy, at thirteen.\par

A man come up from beyond the pass — A stone, a place by the lamp, and no questions — He will give you a number if he still has one and a name if he still has that. Take whichever he offers and do not ask for the other. — Nobody. He has paid already, and not here.\par

\subsection*{On the full note, and why a man is not a cup}

Tap a sound warm-stone with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. The surveyors of the First Seam use it on the stone of the shaft, and it is the one thing in this country that costs nothing and is still allowed to be true.

I knew a man who tapped the chest of a clamp-hand gone thin and said the note came back flat, and said it as though the man had refused him. The man had not refused him. There was simply nothing there for the knuckle to find. I did not say so at the time, because there was a slate in the room and a man who was going to be entered on it. I have written it here, which is a different matter.

The ways run down the arm the way a river runs, with smaller ways coming off it, and this is what every leech in the Keep believes and what I was taught at the Descent. I have put no drawing of them in this book, because a drawing is a thing that can be carried into a Court room and read aloud there. Whatever runs in a man was put there before the slate was, and the slate has never had the better of it yet.

\subsection*{The cold that stays}

Below the sill, and in the lower galleries where a man stands in water to the calf through a shift, a foot or a hand will come up cold and stay cold after the water has gone and the wool has gone on. In the low countries they call it the cold and go home warm on the word. We know it by the feel under the thumb: the extremity goes first and the heart holds out, and there is an hour on the far side of the warming when a man gets worse before he gets better, or does not.

I have no name for that hour. I have left the place where the name would stand, which is the right length for a name of that kind.

We walk it off. We rub it with warm-stone. We set the man to work, because a moving man does not notice how cold he is going and can finish his shift. I have done all three and seen a man lose two toes on the fourth day, and I have gone on doing them. There is no honest remedy in this book for the cold that stays, and this is the row where I have been least honest, so I have set it in the middle where nobody can miss it.

\subsection*{A song for the Descent}

\emph{Sung going down, not coming up, by a boy of thirteen with the number newly cut in the forearm. The last line is said twice, the second time for the one who has had his number taken out.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the lamp and one for the rope,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the stone that has kept the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut me a number across the arm\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and let the name wait till the shift is higher.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the lead and two for the sweat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the hand that holds the light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Ninth Gallery takes and does not forget,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Warden counts us at night.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the going-down, three for the up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the place where the number was;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask me my measure, I’ll give you my name ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the measure goes down and the name stays above.\end{quote}

There is a space before the last line in the singing, the length of the smooth place on the arm. No clerk has yet put a figure in it, which is the only reason it is still a space.

\subsection*{What the Court clerk did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaves at Greybank, being a man who cannot let paper lie. The ink sits in two fingers of his cuff and will not come out. He struck out my column headed \emph{Who burns} and wrote \emph{No cost entered} above it, which is a true thing in a dishonest place. Where I set that the gallery gives back nothing, he wrote \emph{The measure is retained in the stone.} Against the smooth place on a man’s arm he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}, as though a place where a number had been were the same as zero.

I have filed the notches deeper in the cover. He can take a word off paper because paper is soft. He cannot file a notch out of a board without the board being the thinner for it, and then he has entered something of his own, which is the only kind of entering I have ever seen him avoid.

\subsection*{From the clamp-master}

\emph{At the foot of the remedies, in a blocky hand pressed in coal, the letters wide apart as though cut with a chisel.}

\begin{quote}\itshape On the fifth take the iron off. I have held it on the sixth and carried the hand away in a pail. What you have written is what we did. It is not what I do. --- H.\end{quote}

Hald Iron of the Duelling Floor borrowed the leaf before the clerk did and returned it with the fold changed. I have set his line above my row and mine under it, as the floor keeps the clamp and the hand that was in it. A man who has lost a hand to his own trade is allowed one sentence in a book of physic.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal at the head came off my own thumb setting down the sheet in the lamp-room and went into the grain before I knew I had touched it. The lamp-oil down the fold came from a lamp knocked over on the third night of a sweating, and has taken the ink clean off two words, which I have not written in again: a remedy with two words gone is a remedy said slowly, and everything down here is said slowly. The filings in the gutter are off the clamps on the Duelling Floor. The scorch on the second leaf is a spark that caught while I was writing and went out under my hand; the hand was mine and I have not entered the burn. The splinter sewn into the cover is warm-stone from the Ninth, and is why the book is a little warm in the morning, a kindness bought by somebody whose name is not in here. The frost on the third leaf came up out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass, and is the only thing in this book that entered itself. There is no Last Day under the Keep and nothing gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the heat and the iron keeps the number;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape neither of them asks who paid.\end{quote}

I asked a clamp-master, a survey-clerk, and a man with a smooth place on his arm, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back into the coat pocket against the splinter of warm-stone. Tomorrow a man will give his number before his name at the door, and I shall write the number down and cut another notch in the cover, and the notch outlasts the figure and the figure the man, which is the whole trade here.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Half Share, Being the Quay’s Drinking Song for a Man Come Aboard}
\CRsheetheading{The Half Share, Being the Quay’s Drinking Song for a Man Come Aboard}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A Vhaleni drinking song for the coming-aboard feast and the spring launching, taken down in Grathic letters from a mouth that has no word for guest; the verses on salt-paper squared at the edges, with three lines the damp has made void by the Council’s own law, a factor’s clerk’s correction in Ledgerhand, a dipper’s note in charcoal, and one verse in a hand nobody will own · Set down at Vhal on the Sallow coast in Ember of Y.H. 807 by Vessa of the Quay, a woman who held a boat-share from her mother, for the coming aboard of a man whose name she did not enter, because a name entered is a name held; carried up the Salt Road in Frost of Y.H. 810 in a dry tin and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled harbour tally; copied forward in Stone of Y.H. 812 with the damp-void lines left void. It survives with a white salt crust along the gutter, a ring of red wine that has eaten one word clean through, a fibre of wet rope pressed into the second fold, a green bead of Glaze glass, a fish-hook nick at the head, and a thumb printed in salt where the writer signed, because a boat on this coast is signed in salt and not in ink. One correction is in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk who borrowed the sheet at Greybank; one note is in charcoal and is a dipper’s; the verse at the foot is in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I have set this down in the letters of the clay country, because that is the hand of the account that comes down the Salt Road and the factor at Greybank reads nothing else. The song itself is Vhaleni and loses something in the writing, the way a net loses what it was made to hold. There is no word in my language for \emph{guest} and no word for \emph{please}. I cannot ask you to drink. I set the cup on the bench and go away, and the cup does the asking. This is the whole of our hospitality, and it is why people upriver call us cold. They are welcome to think it. A man who has been called cold by a Grathic household has at least been noticed by one.

The song is not for a quiet room. It is sung at the coming aboard, when a man marries a boat-owning house and is given the half of a share he did not bring with him, and at the launching in Ember when the new hull goes down the ways and everybody’s words are worth half of what they will be worth next year. The women sing the verses. The man come aboard answers the refrain at half voice, because his opinion on the boat counts at half and he has known it since the day he married; a man who cannot take a joke about his own share has no business aboard one. There is salt on the rim of every cup. A man who drinks the wine without the salt has drunk only wine, which is a Grathic habit and a poor one.

The tune goes like water going over water, low and without a rise, and it is sung through the nose. The last line is held until the ebb.

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The women. A cup set down. Salt on the rim.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The boat was laid before the daughter,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the share went down the mother’s line;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man may come aboard by marrying,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but he does not steer by right of mine.\end{quote}

\emph{The man come aboard answers, at half voice.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Half a share and a whole thirst;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat goes where the women go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tide goes where it will.\end{quote}

\emph{The women.}

\begin{quote}\itshape We count his word at half, not in spite,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but because half is what he brought:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a tongue, a debt, a pair of hands,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boat was here before his word.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not tell him it is kindness.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He will spend it. He will enter it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Give him the half and call it half,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and there is no argument in the room.\end{quote}

\emph{The refrain. The man at half voice. Nobody crosses himself; nobody in Vhal ever has.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Half a share and a whole thirst;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat goes where the women go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tide goes where it will.\end{quote}

\emph{The women. This verse is sung to the cup, not to the man.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Put salt in it. The Sallow’s in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who drinks without the salt\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape drinks only wine, and wine’s a clay-country habit;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we take the sea with everything.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea is the colour of skimmed milk\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it runs against the wind,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dippers say it follows the Warm\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and not the moon. Let the moon go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody has taxed the moon.\end{quote}

\emph{Here three lines stood, and are gone. Rain got into the tin in Grain of Y.H. 810, between the coast pass and Greybank. I have left the place the length of them and written nothing in it. By the Council’s own law a wet document is no document, so those lines are void, which is a virtue, says the Council, and I have not put them back. I remember two of them and have not written either. A verse remembered is not a verse kept, and I was not going to make the Council a present of one.}

\emph{The women.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Write it on salt-paper. Let it rain.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A contract that has rotted is no contract,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the virtue of it, and half the fortunes\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape of this port have turned on exactly that.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A thing that lasts too long stops earning.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A bench that will not rot has no business\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape in a room where men are buying boats.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wet paper, clean hands, and a good ebb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape That is the whole of our law and most of our religion.\end{quote}

\emph{The refrain.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Half a share and a whole thirst;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat goes where the women go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tide goes where it will.\end{quote}

\emph{The women. This verse is sung at the launching, with the rope in the singer’s hand.}

\begin{quote}\itshape At dawn the dippers trail the net\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and read the draw the Sallow makes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Warm goes seaward under the hull\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we go after it with salt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I walked the pans at fourteen barefoot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and named a tide I had not seen;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they gave me that name to keep\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape for a thing I could not write down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The gull will steal a coal out of your fire\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and carry it upriver warm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the salt-thing taps the hull at midnight\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the store of warmth lies thin.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A boat that’s warm at dusk and cold by morning\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape has no slate to answer to. That’s the trade.\end{quote}

\emph{The women. The last verse before the refrain is said low, to the boat, while the rope goes over.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Our glass comes green off the Cliffs\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the old lead sweetens in the heat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape drink from it and you will taste the colour\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape of a thing made beautiful by burning.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Fill to the half. Drink it whole.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cup is not a guest. The cup has no name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If you want a passage, name a tide\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we will say it has not happened yet.\end{quote}

\emph{The refrain. The man come aboard answers at half voice; the women answer him at full, and the difference is the point of the song.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Half a share and a whole thirst;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat goes where the women go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tide goes where it will.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come aboard. Come aboard.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Bring nothing. It is already counted.\end{quote}

\subsection*{How it is used}

\emph{Written small in the margin, in my own hand.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sung standing. A sitting singer is a singer who has been bought.

\item The man come aboard sings the refrain at half voice the first year. In the second year he may sing it at full if the women have voted it, which they never have while I have been singing.

\item The salt goes on the rim before the wine goes in the cup. Done the other way it is a Grathic cup with salt on it, which is a thing nobody in this port would drink.

\item At a launching the rope is held through the last verse and let go on \emph{Come aboard}. A man who lets go early has paid for a boat that will not hold him.

\item If a collector is in the room, sing the third verse and the law verse and skip the tide verse. He cannot enter the draw, and a verse he cannot enter makes him uneasy enough to drink. This is not a kindness. It is a manoeuvre.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank borrowed the sheet on a wet morning and gave it back dry in one corner and damnable everywhere else. I have left his hand standing and mine under it, the way a boat keeps both the water’s mark and the painter that holds it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the share went down the mother’s line} he wrote above, \emph{The share is entered to the female line, the male entrant taking a half interest.} Mine stands beneath. His is true in a language nobody on the Quay uses to describe a mother.

\item At \emph{we count his word at half} he set \emph{the vote of the come-aboard is rated at one half} and underlined it twice, as though I had discovered a figure and might be proud of it.

\item At \emph{Write it on salt-paper. Let it rain} he wrote \emph{Instrument voided by exposure to water} and added, in a smaller hand, \emph{no value attaches.} He was quite right. He has made a living out of being quite right in a room full of wet paper.

\item At \emph{the Warm goes seaward under the hull} he wrote \emph{The Sallow draw is a taxable current} and put a figure against it. The figure has not been paid by anybody in eleven years, which is the kind of figure the Court likes best.

\item Where the three lines are gone he wrote \emph{three lines lost, no entry} and then, underneath, \emph{no claim can lie against a lost line, which is fortunate for all parties.} I have left it. He has taken the verbs out of a song and called the result an account, and if he had ever sung one he would know why we keep them in.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{In the dipper’s hand}

At the foot of the second leaf, in thick charcoal that has rubbed onto the fold, in the hand of a dipper who borrowed the sheet in the Council room when it smelled of tar and wet rope:

\begin{quote}\itshape At dawn we trail the net and read what the Sallow is doing. We tell the Council the figure that buys salt. The draw itself we keep. A current that is measured honestly is a current that gets taxed, and there is no virtue in being taxed honestly.\end{quote}

He did not sign it and did not take the sheet away. When I asked him why he had written it on a song he said a song is the only paper in Vhal that nobody thinks to read. I have left the charcoal where he put it and not washed the fold.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt crust at the head and along the gutter came up out of the paper on the two nights the tin went damp, and has taken the ink off one word in the law verse; I have not written the word back, because a verse about rot with a word rotted out of it is in better order than I could have made it. The ring is red wine and has eaten through to the other side. The rope fibre in the second fold came off the launching rope in Ember and is wet when the weather is wet, which is a nuisance and a useful one, because it tells me when to keep the tin shut. The green bead is from a cup off the Cliffs and is not slip and not lead; it fell out of a girl’s hair when she leaned over to see the writing, and she did not ask for it back. The nick at the head came off a fish-hook set down in a hurry by a man who was paying me and did not apologize. The salt thumb is mine. A boat on this coast is signed in salt, because ink will not stay on a wet hand and a wet hand is the only kind we have.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A boat is a pot with its crack below the water.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea does not knock. The sea has no knuckle.\end{quote}

I asked the women, the dippers, a factor come up from Greybank and a man who had been come aboard for nine years, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The sheet goes back in the tin and the tin goes in the drawer where we keep the paper we mean to let rot. A slate is a thing that gets read in a clean voice; this is a thing that gets sung with salt on the rim and goes damp at the fold, and is the better for it. If the clerk borrows it again, let him take the verbs out. The next singer will put the salt back, as I did, and the cup will do the asking.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of Quiet Ash, the Licence to Buy, and the Greyed Hand, Being Title the Fifth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Factor’s House at Greybank with the Licence-Clerk’s Margin, the Scrape of a Phial-Cork, and a Correction in a Borrowed Hand}
\CRsheetheading{Of Quiet Ash, the Licence to Buy, and the Greyed Hand, Being Title the Fifth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Factor’s House at Greybank with the Licence-Clerk’s Margin, the Scrape of a Phial-Cork, and a Correction in a Borrowed Hand}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the counter of the factor’s house at Greybank, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the licence-book; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, a table of offences, a form of licence left blank, one line scored with a phial-cork, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at Greybank in Seed of Y.H. 813 from Title the Fifth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as first licensed in Y.H. 683, fifteen years after the Rising, and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept under the licence-book in the factor’s counting house: a grey Ash thumb at the head, salt bloom along the gutter from the Sallow wind off the quay, a tar thumb at the fold, iron-gall in the creases of two fingers, a scrape where a phial-cork crossed the lower margin, a green bead of cliff-glass, a damp tide-line along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the licence-book at this counter. A man comes up from the quay with a phial under his coat and a mark in his fist and wants the mark entered against the phial before the factor’s clerk comes down from the Hearthseat; a woman of a house of Sere gives a name that is not hers and asks that her previous life stop arriving in dreams. I write what the ordinance tells me, and I set the verbs back underneath the words it has taken out, because a medicine with nobody in it is a medicine nobody took, and that is the kind the Court has always liked best. What follows is Title the Fifth, copied out so that a person may know what is being entered against him before it is entered.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the first leaf, in the same hand, written very small:} Copied by the counter, and for it. The verbs were put back by me and struck out again by a man who does not keep a counter. Let both stand. A leaf with two hands on it is the only kind a buyer believes.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Fifth, as it stands in the factor’s book}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Fifth: Of the Sale and License of Quiet Ash, and of the Greyed Hand. First licensed in Y.H. 683, fifteen years after the Rising; added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the thing itself}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The grey that gathers in corners is not swept before the Last Day; it is gathered, bottled, sealed and licensed. In daylight it is not seen; by tallow-light it is plain. It is not dirt. What it is, is not entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sold only by licence of the factor, in a phial bearing the Court’s mark, at sixty marks the phial. No phial sold without a figure; no figure entered without a phial.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where the grey is gathered from a house in which a promise was left unkept, the gathering is entered to the house and not to the promise. The house is not asked.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I wrote what the grey is on this leaf and scraped the word away with the cork of a phial still wet at the mouth. The bare place is scored in the lower margin and the length of it is the length of the word. A clerk who supplies a definition has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied. I have left the place as it is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A man come up from the Fenmarch with a jar under his coat priced the same grey by the thimble at four bits and called it paste. I set his four bits beneath the sixty and left the two unjoined. A jar with a Fen name and a jar with the Court’s name stand on different shelves here, and I am the man who puts them there. I have not written the likeness in the book. It is a short sentence and it would cost me the counter.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the buyer}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A licence to buy is entered in the name of the household and not of the person. It is written in the hand of the buyer or his factor; the hand that writes is not the hand that drinks. It is renewed at the end of each tend. A licence that lasts longer than a tend is a licence that has stopped earning.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The buyer is not asked what the phial is for. No physician’s certificate is required where the buyer has a house and a mark. Dreams are not entered; the previous life is not entered; the wanting of quiet is not entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The woman of Sere gave a name that was not hers and paid in marks, which anyone can write down, and with a sentence at the counter, which is not a figure. I entered the name she gave. A name that is not the name of the woman who speaks it is common in this trade, and the ordinance has no word for it. She asked if the phial would keep her mother’s dreams from coming. I said it was sealed. She took that for an answer and went up the road with it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a second and narrower hand:} Article 4 was added in Y.H. 782, the year the maids were first paid. A licence renewed each tend is a law that earns its keep by ending, which the Council of Tides would call a virtue if it had thought of it first. The ordinance does not say so, and I have not put it in the article.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the unlicensed sale}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Quiet ash sold to any not licensed to buy it is punished by a greyed hand. The hand is greyed by the Court’s own iron and gives no warmth back. This grey is not the grey of a collector’s fingers, which comes with years at the tube and is a mark of the trade; the other is set deliberately and is called a correcting.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where a phial is sold without licence, the phial is broken and the figure is not returned. A phial broken is entered as broken; the grey is not entered as returned.
