\end{enumerate}

Offence — As entered — Correction\par

A phial sold to one not licensed — The hand greyed — The figure carried forward\par

A phial sold without a figure — The phial broken — Nothing returned\par

Quiet ash sold by the thimble, under a Fen name — Not entered here — The jar left on the other shelf\par

A licence lapsed in the tend — Carried forward — Not called ended\par

A definition supplied by the clerk — Scraped away — The bare place left standing\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have seen both greys. The one comes up under the nails by slow years and a man may carry it into any room and nobody ask him about it. The other comes all at once, like a hand dipped in skimmed milk gone off; the man keeps it in his pocket, in a glove, under a cuff gone soft from washing. I have never been asked which I have, and I have never told anybody, because I have neither. This is a fact about this counter and not a virtue.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The Court owns no slaves, which it calls civility, and greys a hand by iron, which it calls a correcting. Both go into the book in the same neat hand. That is the whole mercy the ordinance allows itself.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the keeping of the book}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The licence-book is kept under the counter and is not shown to a household. The keeping of it is not explained, only kept. Where a name is disputed, the figure stands and the name is not changed.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item An account is never closed; it is only carried forward. A licence lapsed is carried forward as a licence lapsed, and not as a licence ended.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The rolls of the dead are kept open, and so are the licences of the living. I have carried one name forward for eleven years after the household that gave it was empty of people. Nobody came to close it and I did not close it. A name carried forward is a different weight from a name bought, though the hand that writes them is the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The seal on the phial is the Court’s mark and not a priest’s. A dipper of Vhal would trail the jar in the sea at dawn and call that a licence; the factor calls it nothing at all. I have copied neither saying into this book.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As entered in Ledgerhand — What the clerk sets beneath\par

A verb in the roll — Page copied again, in the same hand — The verb restored, where it stood\par

A buyer’s name disputed — The name as given — No note made\par

Sixty marks written as a rate — The figure as the notice has it — The figure as the phial was sold\par

A licence called ended — Carried forward — Not called ended\par

A grey too dark to hide — A glove — Nothing, which is not an entry\par

\subsection*{The form of licence}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Fifth. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In eleven years nobody has filled one in the hand the factor requires.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the licence to buy one phial of quiet ash granted to ---------------------- of ----------------------, at ------- marks, to be renewed at the tend’s end and carried forward where not ended; the hand that writes not the hand that drinks; the phial sealed and the figure entered, and the name not changed where disputed. Granted by ----------------------, who is not the man who sold it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse the weighers say at the phial-draw}

\emph{Called under the breath at the beam when the phials come up off the boat, never while the factor’s clerk is in hearing. It is not a song for the quay and has never been sung there.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Grey in the corner, grey in the jar,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one has a name and one has a mark;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sixty marks for the sealed and licensed,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four bits for the same under a fen-name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Put the cork to the leaf and leave the word out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hand goes grey and a hand goes cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the account stands where the phial stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dream comes back where the figure went.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, against the fourth line:} One article entered. \emph{In mine:} There are two greys and I have set both. He has put no figure against the Fen jar, which is how I know he has looked at it. A man does not number what he has not looked at.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man came down from the Hearthseat with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers. He struck \emph{gathers} out of article one and set \emph{is gathered} above, as though a thing that gathers in a corner had nobody who left it there. I put \emph{gathers} back. He struck the verb out of the buyer’s sentence also, leaving a wanting with nobody to want it. Both stand.

The other hand is leaning, with a little gold in it, from a counting house of Sere. Against \emph{sixty marks} it wrote \emph{quiet ash, market rate}, and put a figure in the margin where I had put the price. I left both standing. A house of Sere can call a figure a rate, because a rate is a thing that can be emptied and refilled; a man who has held the phial and smelled the cork calls it a price.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is Ash, off my own thumb turning the leaf toward the light while the factor read a figure over it; it is the colour a corner leaves when it has been swept too late, and it does not wash out of the creases. The white in the gutter is salt bloom blown up from the Sallow under the counting house door; it comes and goes with the weather and is never entered. The tar at the fold came off a Vhaleni boatman’s coil, and the green bead in the corner is cliff-glass from that coast and not lead glaze from High Kiln, which has a sweeter look and a smell. The iron-gall is in two fingers and will not come out, which is how the factor knows I have copied a thing before he asks. The scrape in the lower margin is the cork, drawn across while I decided what word to leave out; the tide-line along the foot is a phial set down through a morning, the seal holding and the leaf taking the damp. There is no Last Day under a counter, and nothing here is swept and burnt and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody has claimed}

\begin{quote}\itshape The jar keeps the grey. The hand keeps the colour. The slate keeps the figure, and none of them says what it was for.\end{quote}

I asked the factor’s man, a man come down from the College, and a woman who stood here about a phial, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back under the counter. Tomorrow a man will come up with a phial under his coat and a mark in his fist, and a woman will give a name that is not hers, and I shall enter the figure and not the wanting, and put the verbs back where I can. The scrape in the margin is the length of a word. I have not written it back, and I have not forgotten it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany Before the Grating, Being the Prayer of the Keepers of the Hearth-Fire at the Weighing, with the Voice’s Corrections and a Junior Keeper’s Margin}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany Before the Grating, Being the Prayer of the Keepers of the Hearth-Fire at the Weighing, with the Voice’s Corrections and a Junior Keeper’s Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A litany of the Return said by the keepers of the Hearth-fire in the Weighing Hall, the Voice reading and the keepers answering through the bars; set down by a keeper of the third watch who signs with a coal-cross, with the rubrics of the grating, the eight stations and their answer, the Voice’s struck corrections, the second watch’s note, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written in the Weighing Hall in the Hearthseat on Weighing of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the junior keeper of the third watch, on the back of a spoiled slate-copy of the year’s first measure, and corrected by Hesta Clay, Voice of the Return, before the Remembering; carried through the Opening of the Slates and copied forward in Ash of Y.H. 813 into a quire kept in the iron box under the grating ledge. It survives soft along the fold and scorched at the upper edge, with coal-dust worked into the creases of the first leaf, a lamp-black thumb, iron filings caught in the gutter from the grating hinge, a spot of tallow off the watch lamp, a hair, a grey Ash print from a cuff that had been in the residue room, and a small coal in the fold that nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I am a keeper of the third watch at the grating and I write this where I stand, which is on the north side with my hands behind me. The Voice reads from the ledge in the clean voice, the one that takes her neatly out of her own sentences, and we answer through the bars. I have kept the answer as we say it and the rubrics as the room actually has them, because a rubric written in a clean hand is a rubric for a room with no fire in it. The Voice has borrowed the leaf and given it back with four of my lines struck through. I have left every struck line standing under her words, as a keeper leaves a repair showing.

The coal-dust at the head came off the grate when the hinge was worked on the morning of the Weighing; it goes into the grain and will not come out. The scorch along the upper edge is from a night when a draught came off the Keel and carried a spark against the leaf while I held it to the lamp. I have not cut the scorch away. A prayer with a burn on it has been used, which is more than can be said for a clean one. The filings in the gutter are off the hinge. The grey came off my cuff after I had been in the residue room, and I have not swept it off the leaf. The little coal in the fold is not mine and I have asked the second watch about it and had two answers, neither of which I have written down.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The grating is not opened. The fire is behind iron and no priest may touch it. We answer through the bars and keep our hands behind us.

\item Do not count the bars. There are nine on the north side and eight on the south; the ninth on the north is the one the fire leans against, and a keeper who counts from the wrong end will find eight and think he has lost one. He has not. Begin at the hinge.

\item The litany is read, not sung. A sung line travels up into the vault and comes back as something the keepers did not say, and the Voice does not answer to echoes.

\item When the Voice says the last line, lay the slate on the ledge face down. It has been read enough for one year.

\item The answer is said by every keeper present, including the one on the night stair who cannot see the ledge and says it a half-beat late. We do not correct him. He is counting a different thing.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{The Voice says. The keepers answer. The words between are mine where I have set them, and hers where she has struck them.}

\subsection*{I. Of the firing}

\begin{quote}\itshape Before the slate there was the clay.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Before the clay there was the fire in the dark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dark had not yet been given a name to be afraid of.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The world was set up and fired whole.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It answered when it was tapped. The tap was not a hand.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{II. Of the Breaking}

\begin{quote}\itshape One anger, and the lid was off the pot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Warm went out where no wall held it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and ran into the country that keeps nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The crack has a name. Say it once. Do not go looking for it in the floor.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What went out is going still, and the going is not finished.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{III. Of the Nine}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine hands went after what had run away.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They drove the repairs home the way a potter drives a staple,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the staple is the same iron in a small vessel and a large one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name them by their number and not by their houses.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ninth repair is in the Hearth’s hand and is not finished.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine went. One is still abroad.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{IV. Of the iron and the gate}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire is behind iron and no priest may touch it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The iron does not keep. It is a gate with a cold face.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire keeps. We stand where the grate lets us stand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and give our answer through the bars.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hands behind. A hand at the grate is a hand in the account.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{V. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count embers, not years. A year is a pot nobody weighs.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, as the notice says. Printed. Read twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The notice does not lean. It is the Hearth’s own hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate is a piece of stone with a clean figure on it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure does not sweat and the hand does not shake.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Write it small. A great thing written small still balances.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{VI. Of the pouring}

\begin{quote}\itshape One measure into one vessel: the shape comes back with its name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the price of bread and the handle of the cup.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many measures into many: the shape comes back as it can,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a hankering for a table it never sat at.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured. Both go into the same clean hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep the one that wants. It is the one that can be kept.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{VII. Of the Kept}

\begin{quote}\itshape Blessed are they that are Kept. No want can reach them.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They do not feel the cold and they do not ask for bread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There are fewer than twenty in the world.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand a moment at their place and do not ask them whether they are warm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they will say no, and you will have spent your only question.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{VIII. Of the year}

\begin{quote}\itshape The year’s measures are read while the fire behind the grate\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape burns as it burned before the counting began.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rich learn how whole they are. Low Kiln learns what it gives.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both learn it from the same slate, which does not know the difference.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say the name of each returned, once for the moot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and once for them that came up the road too late.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{The close}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The Voice:} Nothing is lost that we have kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The keepers:} The measure is banked. The account stands. Your return is recorded.\end{quote}

Here I lay the slate face down on the ledge and take my hands out from behind me. The third watch ends with the fire not touched and the account not argued with, which is the whole of a keeper’s trade.

\subsection*{What the Voice struck out}

She borrowed the leaf on the morning after the Weighing, with the ink still wet in two fingers, and gave it back with four lines of mine under her own.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At II, against \emph{the crack has a name. Say it once. Do not go looking for it in the floor}, she wrote: \emph{The First Breaking is a mystery of the faith and not a place in a room.} Under that, in mine: \emph{It is a place in a room. I have seen the seam in the Keel behind the cistern, and it has been mended more than once.} Both stand.

\item At IV, against \emph{a hand at the grate is a hand in the account}, she wrote: \emph{The grating is not to be approached.} Mine stands below. She would have the rule and not the reason for it; I keep the reason, because a keeper on the night stair wants to know why he has his hands behind him.

\item At VI, against \emph{keep the one that wants}, she wrote: \emph{All returned measures are entered alike.} Under mine: \emph{A keeper can tell which child wants. The slate cannot. Both are true, and the second is the one that gets read.}

\item At VIII, against \emph{Low Kiln learns what it gives}, she wrote: \emph{The deduction is one in twelve for every vessel of the Keeping.} Under mine: \emph{I have copied the figure from the notice in the lower court. I have not copied the other. A keeper of the grating has no business with figures that are not printed, and I have kept my hands behind me.}

\end{itemize}

I have left her hand above mine and my words below it, which is the order the Hearthseat uses when it wants a thing looked at and not answered.

\subsection*{What the second watch put in the margin}

At VII, in a hand that writes with the ends of the words shaken, a keeper who stood at the Remembering has written:

\begin{quote}\itshape In the Remembering a whole return was announced for a name nobody in this hall had seen. She read it twice. I have kept the twice.\end{quote}

At the close, against \emph{your return is recorded}, the same hand has set a small coal-cross where a name would go and written no name beside it. I have asked him whose it was and he gave me the hour of the watch instead. A coal-cross is a keeper’s way of signing a thing he has stood at and will not carry out of the hall.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lamp-black thumb is mine; I held the leaf with the hand I write with and did not know I had marked it. The tallow is off the watch lamp, which stands on the ledge where the draught comes off the Keel and gutters down one side. The hair is not mine and I have left it where it fell, because a hair in a fold means somebody leaned over to see what was being written, and at the grating the only person who may lean is the Voice. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff that had been in the residue room and nobody will own the cuff. The filings have worked into the scorch and stay there. The coal in the fold I have not identified, and I have put it back each time I have taken the leaf out.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the Voice’s and not the second watch’s, struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire keeps what is given. The account keeps what is entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire is not an account.\end{quote}

I have asked three keepers and had two answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the iron box under the ledge, and next Weighing the Voice will read the eight stations and we shall answer through the bars, and the ninth repair will still be in the Hearth’s hand. I have copied this once into Ash of Y.H. 813 with the scorch left scorch and the struck lines left struck. On the day the ninth repair is finished the litany will be read no more, which is the one line in it I have never been able to say with my hands behind me.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Mercy Telling at Mud End, Being Six Stories Spoken on the Long Night in the Peat Byre, the One Told to the Floor, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Dead}
\CRsheetheading{The Mercy Telling at Mud End, Being Six Stories Spoken on the Long Night in the Peat Byre, the One Told to the Floor, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Dead}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A byre-keeper’s record of a winter telling, set down for the settling of which death was called merciful and not for the comfort of the reader; the rules in the hand the byre keeps, the stories in the words they were spoken, a score in peat-blocks on the trodden floor, the figures of a factor’s clerk entered over them, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written on the Long Night of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the peat byre at Mud End three leagues downriver of Sill, by the woman who keeps the byre where the moot sits when the peat is too wet to stand on; copied out in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled winter-peat tally, folded into oiled sacking and kept in a wall-niche behind the peat-stack under a flat stone. It survives with a peat thumb at the head, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a small ale ring, a grey Ash print along the gutter, frost-crisp at one edge, one sheep’s-wool fibre off the Tallow road, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter peat, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the byre at Mud End where the moot sits in winter. There is a fire until dusk and none after, because this is the Long Night and the Keeping says a man may tell the Return in the dark and be heard the better for it. I have kept this byre eleven winters and I have never once seen anybody hear better in the dark. They hear the same. They hear it with nothing to look at, which is a different thing.

We hold the mercy-telling on this night. A person tells of a death the hamlet called merciful --- one that went quietly, where nobody had to be sent for and no collector came up from Greybank for it --- and the teller must give the dead one’s name. A story that keeps its name gets a peat-block set on the floor. A story that lets a figure into it gets nothing, and the teller owes a peat to the winter stack, which is the only fine this byre knows and the only one anybody pays without an argument. I do not say why a story served. A reason given is a story given away, and a person who has told one well can go home and sell it in Sill.

The moot meets here because the bog takes a man’s weight in Silt and his boots in Stone, and there is no dry room between us and the river but this one. Nine houses and their peat stacks, and one byre with a floor packed hard as old bread. On the Long Night the floor is the book. Nothing is written in it that a clerk can carry off, and in the morning I tread the blocks into the ash and there is no score left, which is the point of a byre and the difference between a byre and Slate Row.

\subsection*{The rules, as the byre keeps them}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Tell once. A story told twice is a different story and is not heard; the second telling is for the teller and he may pay for it himself.

\item Give a name. A figure is not a name. A figure travels; a name stays in the room where the person said it.

\item Four blocks lie in a row and a fifth lies by the wall. The fifth is not a prize and is not the best story’s block. It is for the one the year took and nobody in these nine houses could tell.

\item No fire after dusk. The last coal is banked before the first voice. A story told by firelight counts for nothing, being a story told twice --- once to the living and once to the coal.

\item Say it to the floor, the door, or the pot. Said looking at a person it becomes an argument, and there is enough argument in Mud End over the winter peat without bringing the dead into it.

\item The byre judges. I say whether a name was kept and I do not say which name I wanted.

\end{enumerate}

Before the first voice we sing the short song, standing, with our hands on the byre wall because it is the only warm thing in the room by then.

\begin{quote}\itshape Four blocks for the four that went quietly,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a fifth by the wall for the one not told;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the peat keeps warm what the peat has held,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name goes round while the figure goes cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tell it to the floor, tell it to the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tell it to the place where the fifth would stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clerk writes one and the house writes none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and both go down in the same dry hand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The four that were told}

\textbf{Vey}, said the widow who cuts peat on the west bank. She said it to the pot. Her man went out after the frost with a spade and sat down in the cut and did not stand up again, and the district called it merciful because nobody had to go looking and no slate went up to Sill over it. She said his name three times, once for the byre, once for the floor, and once for the cut he sat in, and would not let me set a figure against it. “He’s Vey,” she said. “That’s the whole of it. A number’s what you write when you’ve lost the person.” She took her peat-block and went and stood by the door until the next story, which is how a widow stands in this hamlet.

The second was put by a woman come over from Cold Acre, where the well never freezes. She told of a child returned thin in the year of the flower, come back to a house where three had gone into the measure and the house could not say which of the three had come home. The child was quiet and wanted nothing and grew no shape, and the house called it merciful because it asked for no warmth and so cost nobody. She did not give the child’s name. She gave the name of the woman who kept it, said low into the pot, and said the child’s name was not for a byre where a clerk had been known to lean in the door. I set a block for the keeper’s name and none for the child’s, and we left it so. A name kept in one house is still a name kept.

The cooper told the third. He is the man the hamlet means when it says a cooper’s seventh, though he has never explained the seventh to anybody and gives a different date for it every time he is asked, which is a way of answering that costs him nothing. He told of the man they called merciful who slept before a banked kiln with the damper shut and did not wake, and he told it to the floor with his cap in his hand. “Merciful is the word the district used,” he said. “His name was Ansel. You can have the one or the other, but not both, and I’ll have the name.” There was a silence after that, the kind that has four in it and a gap where the fifth would be, and the bell from Sill came across the frozen fields four, four and a gap, and nobody crossed himself. I set the block. Ansel’s name went round the byre and came back to the cooper, and the figure never arrived.

The fourth I put myself, because the room had grown too quiet and a story put by the byre is not scored against anybody. I told of the year’s fire that comes up in a clay dish before light, house to house, each hearth touching its own flame to it, and the last house keeping what is left. There was a woman in this row who took the dish in and did not pass it on, and her house was warm all that winter and she went cold in the spring, and the hamlet called her merciful because she went in her sleep and nobody had to tell her the fire was spent. I did not say where the coal came from. She did not say either. That is the part we call merciful, or the part next to it. I set no block for my own story, because a byre that scores itself will soon be a Court, and I have seen how those rooms go.

\subsection*{The fifth by the wall}

The fifth block lay by the wall all night and nobody moved it. A girl from the Tallow road, who had come in with wool on her sleeves and stayed silent, put her hand toward it twice and took it back, and I have not written which girl, because she would stop coming if I did. In the morning there was a small grey print of Ash where the block had lain, the colour of the ridge that gathers where a promise is not kept, and I trod it in with the rest of the floor and called it the thaw, as we call everything in this hamlet that we do not want to name. The fifth was not a story that failed. It was the year’s taking that nobody in nine houses could put a name to, and a thing left in place is still a thing kept.

\subsection*{The score, in peat-blocks on the floor}

Story — Told by — Name kept — Block\par

The cut in the bog — Vey’s widow — Vey, said three times — set, paid\par

The thin child — Cold Acre woman — the keeper’s name only — set, child’s name not given\par

The banked kiln — the cooper — Ansel — set, figure refused\par

The dish not passed on — the byre — none; byre does not score — not scored\par

The year’s taking — nobody — none — by the wall, not moved\par

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A factor’s clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter peat borrowed the leaf on a morning when the stacks were being measured and his cuff was soft at the edge from washing. He set the four tellings down as \emph{four merciful returns entered, nil deduction}, and put a figure of marks against each of the three names, which was more than the byre had scored, because the byre scores in whether a name comes back out of the room and he does not.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{he’s Vey, that’s the whole of it}, he wrote \emph{one life surrendered without claim}.

\item At the thin child he wrote \emph{third party unidentifiable; vacancy}, and put a round nought in the place where the child’s name would have stood.

\item Against \emph{his name was Ansel}, he struck the name and set above it \emph{the measure was voluntarily resigned}, and underlined it twice.

\item At the year’s fire he wrote \emph{the warmth was transferred by consent}, which is a true thing in a language nobody in this byre speaks. Consent of whom he did not write, and I have not asked him.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words under his and left his standing, the way the floor keeps a peat-block under a spilled quart. He has entered four and struck a name and numbered the empty place; I have kept three names and a place that is not a number. Both hands are on the leaf. Both will travel, his further than mine, which is the whole trouble with writing.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat thumb at the head is mine; I held the leaf down on the byre wall in the draught that comes under the door and did not know I had marked it. Peat goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the moot uses it to sign. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the girl from the Tallow road when she leaned over to see what the clerk had written; the sheep’s-wool fibre caught in the fold is off the same coat, and I have left it where it fell. The small ale ring is from a quart that stood from the first voice to the fifth and was drunk by nobody, which is how a quart usually goes in Mud End. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff that had no business in the corner where I keep the leaf, and I have not swept it. The frost-crisp at one edge is from the morning the leaf went out to be copied and was left under a stone too short for it; the writing there is thin and I have not gone over it, because a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The block by the wall was never set. The Ash came where it stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four names went home. The fifth stayed where the year put it.\end{quote}

I asked the widow, the cooper and the girl from the Tallow road, and had three answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the sacking and under the stone, and the blocks go into the floor with the heel of a boot, and the byre is swept for the next moot as if nothing had been told in it. If the clerk comes again with his pen I shall give him the verbs to take out and keep the names underneath, as I did this year. On the next Long Night the fire will go out at dusk and the dark will come in, and I shall set four blocks in a row and one by the wall, and let whoever has a name to keep come in out of the cold and say it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Moot Board at the Cross, Being the Prices Cried at Sill Market and the Dues of the Roads That Go Out of It, with the Counts That Go Round the Square Set Beside the Printed One}
\CRsheetheading{The Moot Board at the Cross, Being the Prices Cried at Sill Market and the Dues of the Roads That Go Out of It, with the Counts That Go Round the Square Set Beside the Printed One}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pig-weigher’s fair copy of the board at the moot-post, being the prices of the last market of Stone carried forward into Ilmen and the dues paid at this end of each road; corrected in a Court clerk’s soft-cuffed hand and a carter’s, with a third hand at the foot that nobody will own · Written and kept at the Cross in Sill by the man who weighs the pigs on Account-day, who has held the moot board since the year before the Long Cold; the figures taken at the last market of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and copied forward at the market mornings of Ilmen, Y.H. 813, as the levy was called for the thaw. Set on the back of a Court notice gone soft at one corner and kept under the moot-post’s nail in the finger’s width of shade, where a basket may be set beside it. It survives with pig-bristle in the head, a tallow thumb, barley grease from a crust laid down and not eaten, eel slime at the foot, a green bead of lead glaze from the Glaze Room rolled into the fold, marsh mud on the Reedholt corner, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first price to the last, a grey Ash print along the margin that nobody will own, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim.\par}\medskip
They put me at the block on Account-day because I can lift a pig by the ear and not be argued out of the weight in my hand. That is the whole of my authority. I keep the moot board because somebody must, and a figure cried where two hundred people stand has a better chance of being true than one written in a room with the door shut. What follows is what things fetched at this square between the last market of Stone and these mornings of Ilmen, and what a man pays to leave Sill by the roads, set down so a carter may know his charge before he loads. The clerk down at Greybank keeps the far end of the figure. I keep the end shouted here, where the pigs go over the board and the bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself.

Small coin is the bit, twelve to the silver mark; twenty marks make a Sere crown, which comes north because it must and cannot be spent here, so a man may be paid in one and go hungry all the same. The Court keeps its figures in embers and calls five marks an ember. I have left embers off the board. In six years of weighing I have never seen one change hands at the moot-post, and a column with nothing in it is a thing I will not put up on a wall in the rain.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk borrowed from Slate Row:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He set the figure down without the verbs, as though an ember were a thing a carter could put in his pocket. I have put \emph{called} back, because it is the Court that calls it five marks and not the coin that agrees.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The board as it stood at the post}

\subsection*{Things cried at the block}

\emph{Account-day, the tenth, twentieth and thirtieth. Read twice: once for the moot, and again for those who came late.}

Article — Price\par

Brown-edged barley loaf — 1 bit\par

Quart of small ale, watered — 1 bit\par

Sour milk, a quart — 1 bit\par

Turnips, two — 1 bit\par

Salt herring — 2 bits\par

Smoked eel, at the Fishstairs before the bridge shade goes off — 3 bits; salted, 2\par

Eel skin, dried — 1 mark\par

Pig, over the weighing board — 6 marks, and a bit to the weigher to have it cried twice\par

Coarse pot off the racks — 4 bits the score\par

Barley gruel at a house door — not sold; given, and not entered\par

A brown crust laid in a basket — not sold, not lifted, not named\par

Barrow of grey going out through the north gate — not weighed, and no figure reaches it\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in mine:} The Slate Row clerk took the last three lines off, saying a thing not sold has no price. I have put them back. A bowl given at a door is the greater part of what Low Kiln eats and the whole of what it does not discuss. The grey goes out every market-day over the wet boards, heaped a little above the sides where the load has shifted, and nobody looks at it twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a tall leaning hand, with eel slime at the tail:} At the stairs they will sell you six eels for five marks or five for six, and call both the same bargain. Do not ask which. \emph{In mine:} I asked. They said a bargain was a bargain and went back to the water.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The counts that go round the square}

\emph{Not prices. I set them beside the prices because the district sets them beside everything.}

Count — Where it is said\par

One in twelve, as the notice says — Read from the block in a clean voice; the crowd leans in and goes back to the pigs\par

Four, four and a gap — The bell, morning and afternoon; let it go on\par

Nineteen out and nineteen back — The slip pits; put into a thumb and not said\par

The number for the thaw — Fist, then mouth, then shoulder; thought better of giving\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Slate Row hand:} Only the first is a figure. \emph{In mine:} He is right, and the square would not know what he means. A man who has stood here through a Long Cold knows four ways of counting and three of them are ways of not giving a number.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The dues of the roads that go out of Sill}

Five ways leave the Cross. A man pays at four of them and at the fifth he pays the water. The quay clerk at Greybank keeps the far end; what is below is taken at this end, before the cart has begun to rut the clay.

\subsection*{The Clay Road, east to Greybank, eighteen leagues}

Packed clay over corduroy, a Court road since the treaty of Y.H. 418; five days by cart in Grain, six in Silt. An assessor may stop a cart on it without asking the thane, and does.

Due\par

Cart with a load, at this end — 2 bits\par

The same at the quay, by the factor’s man — 2 bits more\par

Beast on the hoof — 1 bit\par

Drove of pigs — 4 bits, and every pig weighed at the block besides\par

Foot passenger — 1 bit; nothing on Account-day, when a man may come to hear the figure\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The carters say they pay to travel one road and pay again for having travelled it. There is truth in it and I have not put it on the post.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The river road, to the Weir and Stonemouth}

One league upriver to the traps, four further to the quarry village at the meeting of the Ferr.

Due\par

Beast on the bank way — 1 bit\par

Foot passenger in Silt — nothing; the water has already charged him\par

Plank walk at the Weir — 1 bit; the boards are counted, but which will bear a man is not said\par

Basket of eels at the north bridge shade — nothing; the Fishstairs folk argued it and won\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand:} Paid two bits at the Weir in Silt and was told it was the walk. The clerk sets nought against it. \emph{In the Slate Row hand:} No such due. \emph{In mine:} Both rows stand. The boards move after rain, which is more than can be said for a clerk’s figure.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The north gate road, to the Bone Orchard and Cold Acre}

One league to the orchard, another to the ridge and its well that never freezes. On market-days the barrow goes out through this gate in the afternoon.

Due\par

Barrow of grey going out — not weighed, not entered, nothing asked\par

Pot broken for the dead, on a cart — 1 bit; in the arms, nothing\par

Pig driven north to the ridge — 2 bits\par

Man going up for the never-freezing well — 1 bit; he brings back a common stone, which is not a warm-stone and is not called one\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A man asked why the grey goes out unpaid when a broken pot pays a bit. I told him the pot had been bought and the grey had not. He went away with his question, which I have kept here rather than my answer, being the better kept of the two.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Nine Pots and marsh roads}

Eight leagues west to the kiln village in permanent feud with Sill over the road; four east to the reed-cutters’ huts at Reedholt, three downriver to the peat hamlet of Mud End.

Due\par

Nine Pots road — no toll, and none ever collected; it is ours and theirs both, which is why neither mends it\par

Cart using it in Silt — a pot from the shared pit, or a knuckle; the two villages have never agreed which\par

Reedholt, firm boards pointed out to a stranger — half a bit, and half again after rain, because the firm boards move\par

Barrow of peat out of Mud End in Stone — 5 bits; no figure in the Long Cold, when there was none to sell\par

\subsection*{The Rim Road, the long roads, the bridges}

West-north-west to Keld Keep, a hundred and twenty leagues and worsening weather; the Cold Pass ten leagues beyond. The Hearth Road runs a hundred and forty leagues south-east to the Court, and the Salt Road north-east to Vhal.

Due at this end\par

Surveyor’s mark upon a load for the Rim Road — 2 bits; the load is not weighed again in Grath\par

Man going west without a warm-stone — not lent one here\par

Man going farther into the Rim — no due, and no guarantee\par

Grain going down the Hearth Road — weighed here, and the figure read to him twice\par

South bridge, loaded cart — 1 bit\par

North bridge, the winter ford under ice — nothing: the Fishstairs argued the bridge and won, and no collector crosses the ice\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A carter from High Kiln asked what the last of these cost and was shown \emph{no due, and no guarantee}, which he called the dearest figure on the board. The Court takes nothing at the gate because it has taken it at home. I have not put that on the board; it would stop nobody from loading. In the Long Cold the Ilm bore ice for ninety-four days and no collector crossed, so the ford’s nought is the only figure here that has never been paid.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they tie to the board}

\emph{Sung at the block while the pigs go over, not while a man from Slate Row is within hearing. The crowd says the last line with the singer.}

\begin{quote}\itshape A loaf for the block and a crust for the fold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape an eel for the shade and a pig for the scale;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the roads and one for the ford,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fifth goes unpaid because it is water.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and four, and a place at the end\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the driver sets down what the clerk will not take;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell says come and the moot says paid,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the yard says come back as you can.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Slate Row hand:} Four roads entered. \emph{In mine:} There are five, and I have put nothing in the place. A nought is a number and the fifth is a way of going. A carter sang this with his back to the factor’s table and would not sing it facing it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The Slate Row clerk took the verbs out of everything, as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle through the north gate in his boot. Against the bowl given at a door he wrote \emph{nil}; against the grey, \emph{not weighed}; he put a nought in the place where the verse has a gap and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. He asked what the board was for, and I told him so a man might know his charge before he loaded. He wrote \emph{figures published for the information of carriers} above my words and went back over the bridge with his cuff wet at the edge and ink in two fingers that will not come out.

I have put my words back under his and left his standing above, as a floor keeps the ash and the foot that raised it. A sentence with its verbs taken out travels well and arrives empty, which is what a Court wants of a sentence and what a carter standing in the rain has no use for. The other hand is the carter’s, tall and leaning, with eel slime on it; he put his two bits at the Weir under the clerk’s nought, and I have not swept either away. A board with three hands on it is the only kind this square believes.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The bristle at the head is off a pig that went over with a driver holding one ear and me the other; it goes into the grain and will not come out. The tallow thumb is mine, from holding the notice down in the wind. The barley grease came from a crust laid on the leaf while a woman told a child to eat and the child would not; a crust put down and not eaten is a thing this square knows how to read. The slime at the foot came off a basket set down at the edge of the fish-trade, where no Court slate has ever reached. The green bead is lead glaze out of the Glaze Room; it rolled into the fold from a girl who leaned over to see the figures with sweetness at one corner of her mouth, and she said nothing and went back up the steep street. The marsh mud came off a man who stood too close with a bundle of wet reed. The grey along the margin is not mine and not the Court’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a moot-post.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board has a figure for a pig and none for the warmth carried in a basket. The yard knows which is dearer and does not say it in the square.\end{quote}

I asked the carters, the eel-women and the man from Slate Row, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back under the post’s nail and the board onto the wall; tomorrow the pigs go over and the figures are scraped off, and a man will ask the morning price, and by afternoon it will be a thing that was true.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Finding and the Naming of Vessels, Being Title the Second of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied for the Assessor’s House at Sill with the Margin Kept by the Clerk Who Writes the Names}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Finding and the Naming of Vessels, Being Title the Second of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied for the Assessor’s House at Sill with the Margin Kept by the Clerk Who Writes the Names}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the assessor’s house in Slate Row, Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps that house’s foundling slate, a hearth-maid’s crossed mark in charcoal, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the College, and one line struck through and left legible · Copied at Sill in Slate Row in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; two leaves folded into a board cover and kept in the assessor’s house built in Y.H. 776, taken down when a child with no house is brought to be named. It survives with slip dust in the gutter, a tallow thumb at the head, a brown grease spot where a crust was laid, a drop of sour milk, a grey Ash print worked into the outer fold of the board, and a narrow pale crease where the leaf was carried in a coat pocket against a wrist.\par}\medskip
I write the names in this house. A woman comes across from the low bank with a child in a fold of grey wool and asks me to write the child’s name, and I write the name the slate gives me, which is seldom the one she hoped to hear. She wants a house for the child. The ordinance provides a vessel, a finder, a claimant and a hand. It has no column for the woman who carried him up the yard.

I put the verbs back where the College took them out. A woman standing at my counter wants to know who did what, and the ordinance will not tell her, because in the Keeping a thing entered is a thing that has always been entered. I have had both my putting-back and the College’s striking copied forward. Let the two hands stand together, as they do on every slate in this district that anybody believes.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the first leaf, written very small, in mine:} Copied for the house, not for the College. If this is read in the Hearthseat, let it be seen that the verbs were mine and the absence of them was not. Let both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The extract, as it stands in the book}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Second: Of the Finding, the Naming and the Claiming of Vessels. Sent down to the factor at Greybank in Y.H. 418, entered in this house when it was built in Y.H. 776, amended in Y.H. 782 and again in the Thin Year.}

\subsection*{I. Of the finding}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A vessel found without a house entered within three days of the finding, as a birth is entered. Entry in Ledgerhand. Hand that writes not hand that carries. Finder not claimant.

\item Where entry made after the third day, the reason entered also. No reason entered for the third day itself.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in mine:} A child left at the meal mill in a fold of grey wool, with a stone warmed at another hearth under his belly, was entered on the second day. The finder brought the stone in with her and asked whether the stone was a name. I said no. She wrapped it back and carried it away, and I wrote a name that will do him until a hearth claims him, which in this district means until a house with a chimney and a roll of its own takes him in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Hand that writes not hand that carries. This is the only article I have ever had cause to be grateful for. A woman who has carried a child three doors up the yard in the cold should not have to hold the slate as well as the child.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the name}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Foundling named by the hand appointed to the slate. Birth-name not entered. House-name entered in the margin where a hearth claims him; the first name not struck out.

\item Where no hearth claims by the thirtieth day after finding, entered as unhoused, the slate-name standing alone.

\end{enumerate}

What is entered — Where it stands — What is not entered\par

Slate-name — the line — Birth-name\par

Day of finding — the head — Hour of finding\par

House-name, if claimed — the margin — The woman who carried him\par

Figure — the account — Who paid for the finding\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I drew the last column and left it empty. A man from the College borrowed the leaf and struck the column out, writing \emph{No such column} above it in a hand so upright that it hurts the eye. I have struck his striking out and left the column as I drew it. A place is not a debt. The College has never learned the difference, though it teaches the eleven words for a deduction to its own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have heard tell of a branching red flower written across a child’s ribs and have not entered it. There is no column. The hearth-maids cross two fingers over such a thing and cover the sign with a date, which is a kind of writing and not the kind that reaches this house.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the claim}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Claim entered before the tenth day after finding; after that only by leave of the assessor. Where two houses claim, the house of longer standing entered first and the other entered also and not struck.

\item Claim made for warmth already paid entered as a kindness and not as a debt. Kindness entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Longer standing means the house with the most pots. I write \emph{standing} because that is the word the ordinance uses, and a woman from the low bank who has no pots has no standing, which is the whole of it. In the Thin Year a house came for a child and wrote its own name above his and set a thumb to it. I put the house-name in the margin where the ordinance requires and kept the child’s name in the line. The woman who had carried him stood with her hands in her apron and asked whether the hearth was a good one. I told her I had no slate for the warmth of a hearth. This was true, and was not what she asked.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a second and narrower hand, the letters leaning, in charcoal:} A crossed sign, which the maids make at a birth-flower. It is not a word and I have not translated it. It was laid against article six, where the kindness is entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the house roll}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Claimed vessel entered upon the house roll in a careful hand. Roll kept in the house. No duplicate required.

\item Every vessel entered upon one line of the slate. Two vessels not entered upon one line.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} No duplicate required. I have asked to see a roll and been offered a cup instead. A house that keeps its own account does not need to explain the keeping, only to keep it. This is the article the houses of Low Kiln live by, and the Court has never thought to enforce it, which I take to be the Court’s one kindness that it does not enter.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} There is a boy in a kiln-house who says: \emph{He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.} I have written them on two lines of one slate, which is the only sentence a slate knows. A household sorts its own members and calls the sorting kindness, and the ordinance has no word to dispute it with.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the drawing and the space after it}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where no claim entered, the measure drawn at the next collection and the account opened in the name written at the finding. Consent entered by the hand of the officer where no household offers it. Refusal is an unclosed account; the vessel clip-held by the wrist until consent entered.

\item No article provides for a measure left undrawn where no officer was called.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} On Ilmen 9 of this year I was set at the Fishstairs with a slate to take a measure that nobody had called for. I sat from the turning of the tide-light until the light went, and wrote the hour at which I was set and the hour at which I was not dismissed, and left the space between them empty. There is a line in the account for a figure and no place in it for a figure that never came. A woman went into the clay-heavy water at the end of nineteen steps and came out on a board, and the yard lifted her with their hands, and I had no article to read to anybody. The clerk at the Cross says a nought is a number. I put nothing. I sent the slate back as it stood and it was entered as a kindness.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The clip leaves a pale ring that shows through the winter and is spoken of as nothing. I have seen a woman hold up her wrist and ask whether the ring would go, and I said it would in the thaw, which is what my mother said about everything, and is not in the ordinance.\end{quote}

\subsection*{VI. Schedule of the days of a foundling}

Day — Entry — Where it stands\par

First day — Finding — Head of the slate\par

Third day — Entry, or reason — The line\par

Tenth day — Claim, or leave sought — The margin\par

Thirtieth day — House-name, or unhoused — Margin, or the line\par

The Five — No market, no claim — Nothing entered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} No claim taken during the Five, and no market either. The clerk at the Cross counts the bell four, four and a place where the fifth should be; I count the empty column. We are each of us keeping a place open, and neither of us has a word for it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the College hand did, and what I did after it}

The College hand struck three of my verbs, struck the empty column, and wrote \emph{No market, no claim, no entry} against the last row of the schedule, which is true in the way a closed fist is true. I struck out \emph{no entry} and set \emph{nothing entered} above it. There is a difference between the entry of nothing and a place where a woman might have stood, and the difference is the whole of what I have to do in this house. I have left the College’s fist standing above my words, as I have left the striking of the verbs above the verbs themselves. A slate with two hands on it is the only kind the household believes.

The brown spot on the second leaf is from a crust laid there while a woman was telling me where the child had been found and would not say the name of the house. The sour milk is the child’s; there was no cup in the house that morning and I gave him mine. The grey came off the outer fold when I carried the leaf in my coat pocket down to the Fishstairs on Ilmen 9, pressed against the wrist where the clip had been, or against a wrist that had never known the clip; I do not now remember which arm I used, and have not tried to find out. The tallow thumb at the head is mine. I held the leaf down with my whole hand because the door stood open and the yard wind came through.

One line at the foot was struck through and written again in my hand, and I have left both readings standing:

\begin{quote}\itshape No article provides for the measure left undrawn. In the low houses they keep these also.\end{quote}

The leaf goes back into its board cover and hangs on its nail behind the counter. Tomorrow a woman will come up from the low bank with a child in a fold of wool and ask me for a name, and I shall write the name the slate gives me, and put nothing in the last column, and she will go away knowing that the nothing is where she stood. That is the whole of my trade: to write names and leave places, and not to say which of the two will keep him warmer.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Ninefold Coming Back, Called the Litany of the Long Night}
\CRsheetheading{The Ninefold Coming Back, Called the Litany of the Long Night}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A prayer of the Return, said in the dark on the Long Night, at the bedside of the dying, and over a birth-slate; with the household’s answer · Written in charcoal and tallow on a leaf of birch bark by a hearth-maid of Low Kiln in Sill in Y.H. 811, the Long Cold, and added to in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year; she set her mark in the corner in place of a name, being two fingers crossed. The leaf is kept folded in the fold of a grey wool birth-cloth that passes from hearth-maid to hearth-maid in the low houses, and is taken out only after dark. It bears a tallow thumb, a smear of bone-pale slip, a spot of green from a glaze-room mouth, a charcoal print shaped like a pot’s foot, and two corrections in different hands. It survives because the cloth is washed oftener than the leaf.\par}\medskip
I am the fourth hand to write on this leaf and the first to say whose it is, except that I shall not say it. The fold had gone soft and I have not mended it, because a fold that has been mended sits shut and a prayer needs to be got at in the dark. What follows is what is on the leaf, including the parts a clerk would take out. It is not a thing to read standing up.

The manner of it, written small at the head in the first hand:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Turn the slate face down. It has heard enough for one night.

\item Bank the fire but do not cover it. A prayer needs somewhere to go.

\item Warm the stone in the hand before you put it to the belly. This is not part of the prayer. It is the part before.

\item The answer is said by whoever is in the room, including the child, who cannot say it and says it anyway.

\item When the bell goes at the Cross, stop. It is counting something else. Begin again after.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The nine callings}

\emph{The voice is the hearth-maid’s. The answer belongs to the room.}

\textbf{I}

The light under the Keel was here before the counting. It did not begin in a house. It was found in the dark.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{II}

Nine hands went after what had run away. Nine repairs were driven home, and the ninth is not finished.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{III}

The world was whole in the telling and cracked in one anger. What fell out of it went a long way and is going still.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{IV}

The pot was set down and answered full. Set down again, it answered flat. It was carried anyway. It is carried anyway. Leave the crack showing. Glaze what you will.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{V}

Write him in the house roll. Write him in the other book. Write him small. The slate is clean and does not care.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{VI}

One in twelve, as the notice says, for the keeping of the fire. The fire was kept. The fire is always kept.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{VII}

The iron is cold before anybody asks it. Take what you are owed and leave the shape. The fingers go grey. Somebody’s fingers go grey.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{VIII}

Warm the stone first. A cold stone is a stone, not a kindness. He will get worse before he gets better. That is the rule. If he comes back wrong, keep him. Keep him anyway.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{IX}

Say the name. Say it twice: once for the moot, once for them that came late. If you have no name, leave the place where the name would stand. Do not sweep the corner. It is not dirt. It is somebody.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

Here the leaf leaves a space. It is not a line forgotten. It is four, four, and the place where the fifth should be, which the kiln keeps and the bell keeps and this house keeps. Nobody fills it.

Four for the corners. Four for the walls.

And one for the one that is not in the room.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm.

\subsection*{What stands in the margins}

At calling IV, a hand that writes with its verbs missing struck out \emph{Leave the crack showing} and set above it, \emph{A return is whole by definition; strike the line.} Under this, in a different hand, the thick round letters of the birth-slates: \emph{It is a proverb about pots, and pots are honest. Put it back.} Both lines stand. I have not chosen between them. It is a prayer, not a slate; it is allowed to disagree with itself.

The \emph{one in twelve} above was added by the same verbless hand, which borrowed the leaf one Long Night and underlined its own figure twice. We left it where it was. It is the figure they like to see. In this house we give the other one, and say it into the clay, where it goes soft in the winter and comes back in the thaw.

The line about the fingers was put in by a woman who had sat with a neighbour two doors down. She wrote \emph{somebody’s} and then scratched the word until the bark showed through, and wrote it again the same. I have left both.

The ninth calling was not on the leaf in the Long Cold. It was added in the Thin Year by a hand that had stood at a Drawing and watched a child grow worse on the third day. She wrote it, turned the leaf face down, and went home without the answer.

The green at the top right is not from our glaze room. A girl with lead at her mouth leaned over on the Long Night to see what the words were and touched the leaf with her thumb. She may not have known it was a prayer. She may have known and not cared. I have not washed it, and neither did the third hand, who washed everything else she came near.

At the foot, in the first hand, two fingers crossed and under them: \emph{Say it in the dark. It will not bear the light, and neither will we.}

The leaf is not for the Hearthseat. If it goes there it will be copied properly, with the verbs put back and the empty place filled, and then it will be a notice, and no use to anybody.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Book of the Open Bowl, Being the Seven Remedies of a House-Physician in the Bowl of Sere, with the Eighth Place Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Book of the Open Bowl, Being the Seven Remedies of a House-Physician in the Bowl of Sere, with the Eighth Place Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bowl-house physician’s book of remedies in the southern courtesy hand, written in the thin gold so that no clerk could mistake physic for a contract; the cures in a house-leech’s hand, the leaning entries of the tally-clerk above them, a northern bond-woman’s charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own; with one song for the third hour and an eighth place kept empty · Written in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in a house of the Ten Bowls in the Bowl of Sere, by Orylla Vanee, a house-physician who kept the sick-bowls and attended both the slave births and the exhibited returns; set down in thin gold on prepared paper, the back of the leaf carrying the thick gold of a contract that was never signed. Carried north with a consignment of oil and tallow-wasp resin and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with the thin gold worn from half the remedies so that the uncleared contract shows through, the yellow dust of the burning winds worked into the sewing rather than lying on the face, a thumb of olive oil, a resin smear that caught dust and will not come out, a wine-ring at the foot, a scorched corner where the leaf lay near a court fire, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a grain of southern wheat stuck fast in the resin, and a single pale hair in the fold that is not gold. The corrections stand above in the leaning hand of the house tally-clerk and underneath in the charcoal of a woman of the grain mills who would not give her name.\par}\medskip
I keep the sick-bowls of this house. That is my office: to set a bowl of barley water at the head of a bed, to carry it away when it has been drunk, and to know which of a girl’s seven names to say when the household asks for somebody who is not in the room. I have kept these bowls eleven years and nobody has ever asked me which of the seven I meant, which tells a person how much a name is worth here and how much a bowl.

I write in the thin gold because thick gold is for contracts, and a contract is a thing said to a man who is not in the room. A remedy is said to the bowl. If the bowl answers, that is between them. The tally-clerk writes above my lines and a northern woman writes underneath, and I have left both standing, because a house that keeps only one hand in a book of physic has stopped learning, which is the same as a bowl that has stopped pouring.

The thin gold has gone off half the remedies, and where it has gone the uncleared contract shows through: nine marks, a date, a house-name grander than the house. I have not written over it. A physician who covers her leaf will soon be covering a patient.

\subsection*{The order of a sick-room}

\emph{Written small in the thin gold, with one word gone over in resin.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the bowl at the head, never at the feet. A person takes from the top down, as a bowl empties from the lip.

\item Leave the court door open. A sick one who cannot hear the third hour will die of wondering what the bell said, which is the more expensive death.

\item Ask whose bowl it is before you fill it. A slave’s warmth is the house’s holding and a free servant’s is her own, and a physician who gives the same physic to both has made a gift of goods that were never hers.

\item Pour for the house, not for the person. The person belongs to the house and the house knows what it wants. I have set down what I was told, not what I would choose, which is a physician’s whole art here.

\item When the burning winds come off the east, wet a cloth and lay it over the lips. The wind takes what is loose, and a man’s lips are the loosest thing he has.

\item At the third hour, stop. The bowl is being emptied in every court in the city and our small room is not behindhand.

\item Do not tap a person to hear whether they hold. A bowl-surgeon taps the clay; a man who taps a person is asking a question whose answer belongs to the owner.

\end{itemize}

I have set down more bowls than I can count, which is why I count them in sevens and leave the eighth place standing. A girl here may have seven names by the time she is grown and keep whichever the household prefers, and a book of remedies ought to be at least as honest as a household.

\subsection*{The seven remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who is emptied\par

A fever that burns — Bleed at the elbow; a bowl of wine at the head — Take from the arm while the head is still clear, and give the wine after, to fill what was taken. A physician of the north would leave the blood in and give water. I have set her words underneath mine and both stand. — The patient, in the arm, by the house’s leave.\par

The thirst of the south — Water, and a wet cloth over the lips — Not wine. Wine is for the third hour and for the emptying, and a man who drinks it in a sick-room is being emptied without a slate. The water-carrier brings it up from the court well and is not thanked. — The water-carrier, who carries it and is not entered.\par

A hand taken by the grain mills — Tallow, a clean fold, resin if a graft must hold — A nest of tallow-wasp resin costs four marks and holds a patch until the vessel takes. The bowl-surgeon lifts the nest to the light and listens to it before he buys, the way a potter listens to a pot. In Grath they burn the nests. I have never asked why. — The mill. It takes no account and names no names.\par

The stone-cough of the dust — Steam of hot water under a cloth; honey if the house has it — To the mouth, not the face. The burning winds put a yellow grit in everything, and a man coughs it up in the morning in a colour he will not discuss. The woman of the mills writes that no steam will bring it up and that I am treating the symptom of a wind. Both stand. — The wind, which does not answer.\par

A wall that has given way within — A living patch, held under pressure with resin — Take the wall from a donor whose measure was shaped like the sick one’s. A patch from a donor shaped otherwise takes anyway and goes on wanting, and a person who wants a life that was not theirs is unsafe to exhibit. The bowl-surgeons know this and the buyers do not. — The donor, first, and the buyer afterward.\par

A child that will not take milk — A wet-nurse come up from the mills, for a season — She was returned thin and has milk enough for one; the house has bought her for two. Give the child barley water when she sleeps and do not tell the house how little there is. — The other child at the mill, who was not bought.\par

A wound that will not close — A pinch of quiet ash, then a clean fold — The house buys back its own funeral ash, a year’s grain burnt under one person and the remainder sold at the price they ask. I have set a pinch in a wound gone three days yellow and watched it go quiet by evening. The Court licenses such ash only to the rich; the penalty for selling it unlicensed is a greyed hand. I have never sold any. I have set it in wounds. — Nobody. This is the row I keep turned down.\par

There is an eighth place in this book where a remedy would stand for the trouble a person has when they remember who they were. I have left it the length of a name. The tally-clerk has put a figure in it; the figure stood and the place stood beside it and the two did not touch.

\subsection*{On the full note}

Tap a sound bowl with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. The bowl-surgeons listen to the clay before they pour a graft into it. A green-glazed bowl bought from a northern potter gave a flat knock in its first frost and went from lip to foot without anything falling out that I could see. In the Clay Yard they would call it a bowl gone wrong and sweep around it. Here the house calls northern clay inferior, and I have not corrected the house.

A northern potter tapped the ribs of an exhibited man at a feast and said the man had gone flat. He was a guest in that court and I did not correct him; in this country a guest who is corrected stops being a guest and becomes a witness. I have written his words without his name, which is the only mercy a physician here can practise without a slate.

\subsection*{Of the beautiful return}

This is the part of the book the house would have me leave out, so I have set it in the middle where nobody skipping to a remedy can miss it.

When a person has been emptied and brought back thin, the bowl-surgeons warm them and pour until the head rises. The memory goes first, then the appetite, then the sense of self; what comes back is calm and wants nothing. The house calls this a beautiful return and exhibits it at feasts as proof of generosity. A woman with seven names came back from one and kept the name the house preferred, saying she had always been that one, and the house was well pleased.

A physician of the north wrote that the calm is a burn. The copy that came down to me had the word taken clean away, as though a word could be taken off paper the way wine is taken off a bowl. I have written it back in the thin gold. I have not seen the burn. I have seen the calm, and a woman who said she had always been the name the house kept. I have set both sentences down, because a book that holds only one of them is a ledger, and I would sooner be wrong in a book than right in a ledger.

\subsection*{The song for the third hour}

\emph{Sung at the wine-press, not at the feast, with the vowels open and the ends thrown into the fire. The last line of the third part is said to the bowl and not to the company.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wind comes yellow and takes the lip,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mill turns under and takes the hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bowl goes round and a name goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that is kept is the one that stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Pour for the house and pour for the heat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pour for the ash that the house buys back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the calm comes first and the wanting goes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bowl goes dry and says no lack.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three at the board and a fourth on the shelf,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven on a girl and one on the slate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ash comes back and the wine comes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what went out . . . . . . . . . . .\end{quote}

There is a space before the last line where a name would stand. I have left it the length it is. The tally-clerk has tried twice to fill it; both times the space stood under the figure, which is the only argument this house has ever lost and never admitted.

\subsection*{What the tally-clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf after the third hour, being a man who cannot let paper lie, and writes in the leaning counting-hand with the gold gone thin.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a house-leech’s mercy} he struck out \emph{mercy} and set above it \emph{return completed, current}.

\item Against the quiet ash he wrote \emph{licensed residue, market rate}, and put a figure in the margin where I had put a pinch.

\item Against the eighth place he set a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} underneath, as though a place where a name had been were the same as nothing.

\item He took the verbs out of two lines. A sentence with no verb travels through a counting room without catching on anything, which is what a counting room wants of a sentence.

\end{itemize}

I have put the words back underneath his and left his standing above. He can enter the ash at the market rate, for the house paid it. What he cannot enter is the space at the end of the song, which tells a person he knows the difference between a figure and a place better than a physician has any right to.

\subsection*{What the woman of the mills wrote underneath}

She is a bond-woman come up from the grain mills, returned thin, and she writes in charcoal on the backs of barley ration tallies with a hand that shakes at the ends of words. She would not let me put her name.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the bleeding:} I have seen four bled. Two were quieter by evening. Quiet is not better.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the beautiful return:} The calm is not peace. It is a room with the door shut and nobody in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the eighth place:} That is where my name was. I have not forgotten it. I have only stopped saying it where a clerk can hear.\end{quote}

I have left her words without a name, which is the only kindness in this house that a clerk cannot enter. She took her charcoal away and did not ask for the leaf back, which is how I know she meant it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The olive thumb at the head is mine; I turn the leaves with the hand I carry the bowl with.
