The dust of the burning winds has worked into the sewing rather than lying on the face, which is how a person tells a book carried in a coat from one read in a court. The resin smear caught dust in the third year and will not come out, and I have stopped trying. The wine-ring at the foot belongs to the third hour and is small. The scorched corner is where the leaf lay too near a court fire and went brown without burning through, so the writing there is thin and I have not gone over it, because a word written thin is a word said quietly and most of ours are. The grey print along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a house of the Ten Bowls and nothing gets swept. The grain of wheat in the resin came from a loaf sent north and returned uneaten. The pale hair in the fold is not gold and is not mine.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire takes the grain and the house buys back the smoke;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bowl takes the wine and nobody buys that back.\end{quote}

I asked the bowl-keeper, the tally-clerk and a woman who would not give her name, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back under the fourth bowl, where I can find it in the dark. Tomorrow the third hour will come, and I shall set a bowl down at the head of a bed and carry it away when it has been drunk, and if a girl has seven names I shall say the one the house keeps and leave the other six standing.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Price Board at Greybank, Being the Rates for Goods, Carriage and the Tolls of the Four Roads, Copied from the Beam Beside the Quay}
\CRsheetheading{The Price Board at Greybank, Being the Rates for Goods, Carriage and the Tolls of the Four Roads, Copied from the Beam Beside the Quay}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A weigh-clerk’s fair copy of the public board, with the dues of the Clay, Salt, Rim and Hearth roads set after it, corrected in two borrowed hands and left standing in a third · Written and kept at Greybank, eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, by the clerk who tends the weighing beam on the quay; begun in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813. The board itself hung on the quay wall beside the grain doors and was scraped and rewritten each tend; this leaf was pinned inside the Vhaleni counting house for the factor’s use, and survives soft at the nail-hole, with a white salt bloom along the gutter, a tar thumb at the head, a dark streak of eel slime at the foot, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a spot of barley grease, a grey Ash print along the margin, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the beam on the quay. A man brings a barrow of peat and wants a figure, and I give him the figure of that morning; by afternoon a barge has tied up and it is not the figure any more. The factor wants a number that will stand still. I have told him that a number which stands still is a lie told by a man with a roof over his goods, and he has told me to copy the board again in a better hand. I have copied it in the same hand. What follows is not what things are worth but what they fetched at the beam between the last market of Stone and the Opening of the Slates, set down so a carter may know his charge before he has unloaded.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark. Twenty silver marks to a gold crown, which is a Sere coin and does not stay in Grath. The Court books in embers and will tell a man an ember is worth five marks; no man has ever exchanged one for the other, and I have not left a space for them on the board.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Court’s factor’s clerk:} Coin and reckoning entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} An ember is a word the Court uses for warmth it has already counted. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them; I put them back because a carter standing in the rain does not know he is hearing something always true.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The board, as it stood on the quay wall}

\subsection*{Bread and the pot}

\emph{Copied from the Cross at Sill, where the same figures are cried on Account-day. These do not move with the barges.}

Article — Price\par

Coarse barley loaf, brown-edged — 1 bit\par

Quart of small ale, watered — 1 bit\par

Sour milk, a quart — 1 bit\par

Salt herring — 2 bits\par

Smoked eel — 3 bits\par

Turnips, two — 1 bit\par

Barley gruel, a bowl at a house door — not sold; given, and not entered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} The factor’s clerk took the last line off the board, saying a thing not sold has no price. I have put it back. In Low Kiln a bowl given at a door is the greater part of what the district eats and the whole of what it does not discuss.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Goods that go downriver and goods that come back}

\emph{Weighed at the beam on the north bank. Eels and coarse pots go down to Greybank; salt and iron come up. The figure is for the load at the beam, before the road takes its share.}

Article — Price\par

Coarse pots, the score — 4 bits\par

Tile, the hundred — 9 bits\par

Peat, a barrow — 2 bits in Grain; 5 bits in Stone\par

Eels, a basket at the Fishstairs — 3 bits the eel smoked; 2 bits salted\par

Eel skin, dried, at this quay — 1 mark\par

Salt, a sack from the pans — 3 marks\par

Iron, a bar, Keldish — 2 marks in the lowlands; half a mark in Keld\par

Glass from the Glaze Cliffs, a sheet — 2 marks\par

Rope, a coil — 1 mark\par

Tallow, a stone — 2 marks\par

Lead, a pig, from the western workings — 6 marks; the seller does not say which workings\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The peat row stood blank through the Long Cold of Y.H. 811; fuel doubled in Stone, then stopped being quoted, because there was none to sell. I have set two figures above it for the Thin Year and struck neither out. A man who buys in Grain and pays the Stone figure does not complain, which is how I know this is not a list of what things are worth.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Wages, hire and beasts}

Article — Price\par

A kiln hand, the day — 1 mark\par

A journeyman, the day — 2 marks\par

A child sweeping the yard, the day — 6 bits\par

A collector’s clerk, the day — 4 marks\par

A carter and cart, the day — 2 marks and the beast’s feed\par

Rent, two rooms in Low Kiln, the month — 8 marks\par

Fuel, the month — 4 marks\par

Food, the month — 12 marks\par

Sheepskin coat — 3 marks\par

Good axe — 2 marks\par

Pig — 6 marks\par

Cow — 24 marks\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a tall upright hand, the letters leaning, the ink gone brown at the edges:} A sailor’s share is two marks a month and keep; a salt-worker gets one mark and a binding promise. The Council has instructed me to enter these beside the wages of the clay towns, so that a man may see which country feeds him. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I asked the gentleman whether a binding promise could be spent at this beam. He said it could not, and went on writing.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Articles a man asks for after he has paid}

\emph{Not on the board. I keep the list behind the beam.}

Article — Price\par

Leeches, dried, by the dozen, Fishstairs — 3 bits; no questions\par

Ice-mouse skin — 1 bit in Sill; 1 mark in Keld\par

Brine-gull feathers, a bundle, at Vhal — 1 bit\par

Reed-wolf tooth, for a clamp-handle, Stonemouth — 2 marks\par

Ash-mite paste, a thimble, in Mud End — 4 bits\par

The same, in the Hearthseat — 60 marks, taxed\par

Tallow-wasp resin, a nest — 4 marks to a bowl-surgeon of Sere; burnt in Grath\par

Quiet ash, a phial, by the Court’s licence — 60 marks\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The paste and the licensed medicine are the same grey in two jars, one with a Fen name and one with a Court name. I have not put that on the board. A clerk who writes it down does not last a tend at this quay.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Court’s figures, copied from the notice and not traded here}

Entry — Figure\par

Deduction, as printed on the Weighing notice — one in twelve\par

Thin return, paid by the district — 30 marks, in labour\par

Whole return, booked by the Court — 1,200 marks and forty unspent measures\par

Ember, as booked — 5 marks\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The factor keeps a damp leaf of these in his drawer and desires that the board agree. One in twelve is printed and unchallenged and I have put no other figure beside it. I have heard other figures spoken upriver and have not entered them, not being figures I can weigh.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The tolls of the roads}

Four roads leave Greybank, and a fifth, which is the river. The dues below are what the beam collects or what the factors at the far end collect, and the difference between the two is the whole art of travelling.

\subsection*{The Clay Road}

From the Cross at Sill to this quay, eighteen leagues, packed clay over corduroy, a Court road since the treaty of the Blue Cliff in Y.H. 418. Five days by cart in Grain, six in Silt; rutted and then clay again. Because the treaty made it a Court road, an assessor may stop a cart on it without asking the thane, and does.

Due\par

Cart with a load, at the Sill end — 2 bits\par

The same at this end, by the factor’s man — 2 bits\par

Beast on the hoof — 1 bit\par

Drove of pigs — 4 bits, and the pigs weighed at the Cross besides\par

Foot passenger — nothing on Account-day; 1 bit any other day\par

Barrow of grey going out through a north gate — not weighed, and not entered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The cartmen say they pay twice to travel one road, once to the moot and once to the Court, and that the road is in a better state before the payment than after. I have put the last row on my copy and not on the board. What goes out of Sill in a barrow is the afternoon’s work, and no figure reaches it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Salt Road}

From this quay north-east to Vhal, sixty-two leagues beyond the eighteen, eighty in all, by the coast pass. Salt, glass, rope and dried fish go out; coin and contracts on salt-paper come back, and the damp gets into both.

Due\par

Sack of salt, at the coast pass — a mark to the Council of Tides\par

Coil of rope, or a sheet of glass — 1 bit\par

Boat-share passing inland — paid in kind, by the lot and not the league\par

Contract written on salt-paper — no fee; it will not survive the journey, which the Council calls a virtue\par

Man going up with the glass at the turn of the month — 3 bits, returned if he comes back with the answer\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand:} \emph{toll} is struck and \emph{contribution freely entered} written over it. \emph{In mine:} He has left the figures standing. A Council that cannot charge a toll has found a finer name for one, and a man pays it all the same.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Rim Road}

West-north-west from Sill to Keld Keep, a hundred and twenty leagues of improving road and worsening weather; the Cold Pass ten leagues beyond, at a hundred and thirty. Karric VII shut it in Y.H. 741 and the agreement of Y.H. 747 fixed it as the border. Keldish surveyors keep the record and state a man’s measure before his name.

Due\par

Cart, at the pass — 1 mark, or iron to the value\par

Beast on the hoof — half a mark\par

A man without a warm-stone — the stone off the next man who has one\par

Surveyor’s mark upon a load — 2 bits; the load is not weighed again in Grath\par

Traveller going farther into the Rim — no due, and no guarantee\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Only fools and factors travel it without a warm-stone, and the factors charge the stone to the account. I have kept the last row: the Warden’s surveyors do not promise to bring a man back.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Hearth Road}

South-east from this quay to the Hearthseat, a hundred and forty leagues, the merchants’ road to the Court, spoken of in Grath as if it were a fever. There is no barrier on it and no figure at any gate.

Due\par

Toll at the barrier — none; there is no barrier\par

Grain going south, weighed here — by the deduction, entered at this end\par

The same again at the Hearthseat — booked in embers\par

A man who asks what he has paid — the figure is read to him twice, once for the moot and once for those who came late\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A carter from High Kiln asked what the Hearth Road cost and I showed him the empty column. He said it was the most honest figure on the board and the dearest. The Court takes nothing at the gate because it has already taken it at home. I have not put that on the board; it would stop nobody from loading.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Bridges, ford and river road}

Due\par

South bridge at Sill, loaded cart — 1 bit\par

North bridge at Sill — nothing; the Fishstairs folk argued it and won\par

River road to the Weir and Stonemouth — 1 bit a beast; passable on foot in Silt when the low way is under water\par

Winter ford at this quay — 1 bit, when there is water to cross\par

The ford when the Ilm bears ice — nothing, because no collector can cross\par

Plank walk at the Weir — 1 bit; the boards are counted and nobody says which will bear a man\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} In the Long Cold the Ilm bore ice for ninety-four days and no collector crossed from this quay. I have left the figure standing because the factor wishes the board to be complete. It is the only figure on it that has never been paid.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse the carters tie to the board}

Four roads out of Greybank and one road down, Clay to the bank and Salt to the sea; Rim to the stone and Hearth to the fire, and the four pay twice and the fifth pays free.

Four and four and a place where the fifth should be, the beam keeps the weight and the river the rest; a man goes up with a mark in his coat and comes back with a figure he cannot digest.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow Court hand, against the fifth line:} Four roads entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There are five, and I have put nothing in the place. A carter sang this on the quay and would not sing it while the factor’s clerk was in hearing, which is how I know the fifth line matters.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The factor’s clerk struck \emph{brown-edged} before \emph{loaf}, saying a board has no use for a description. I put it back: no household in Low Kiln has seen a loaf without an edge. The Council clerk numbered the roads as three, leaving the river and bridges out; I wrote four above his three and left both standing. Where he put a nought against the fifth line I set nothing; a nought is a number, and that line is a place.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road to the Hearth is paid at home. The road to the river is paid by the river.\end{quote}

I asked porters, carters and the clerk, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the counting house and the board onto the quay wall; tomorrow the barge comes in with salt from Vhal and the peat row wants copying again. A man will ask for the morning’s figure and I shall give it, and by afternoon it will be a thing that was true.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Reading of the Slate, Being Certain Articles of the Ordinance of the Keeping for the Drawing, Banking and Returning of Measures}
\CRsheetheading{The Reading of the Slate, Being Certain Articles of the Ordinance of the Keeping for the Drawing, Banking and Returning of Measures}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, copied out for the use of the open-air table at the Cross in Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps that table · Copied in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the unnamed clerk of the Court’s table at the Cross in Sill, and carried into Y.H. 813 at the Opening of the Slates; a quire of four leaves sewn with wire into a board cover, kept in the drawer of the table and taken out at market mornings. The cover is warped from a winter against the outside wall of Slate Row. The lower corner of the second leaf carries a tallow thumb, the inner margin a grey streak, the top edge a candle-singe, and there are three corrections in the clerk’s own hand and one in a hand he did not own.\par}\medskip
I keep the table at the Cross. On market mornings I lay my hand on the top slate before I look at the woman waiting, and say that it is entered as it stands and there is nothing in it the household need correct. My cuff is gone soft from washing and the ink sits in the creases of two fingers and will not come out. What follows is copied out of the ordinance for the use of this table, so that a man standing in the square may know what he is being told before he is told it. I have put the verbs back where I could. The ordinance has no need of them, being always true; I have. A thing that is always true is a thing a woman cannot argue with, and I have had to stand here and argue with a great many women.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the first leaf, in the same hand, written very small:} Copied by the table, not for the table. If this is read in the Hearthseat, let it be seen that the verbs were put back by me and struck out again by another. Let both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The extract, as it stands in the book}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Third: Of the Drawing, Banking and Returning of Measures. As confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, and added to in Y.H. 782 and Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the entry of vessels}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Every vessel born within the Keeping entered upon a slate within three days of the first breath. Entry in Ledgerhand, without verbs. Birth-name not entered. Slate-name entered in its place where the vessel enters the service. Slate kept face up upon the bench. The hand that writes not the hand that holds.

\item Where entry made after three days, the reason entered also. No reason entered for the third day itself.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The third day is a bad day to choose. A child that has taken a chill will grow worse on the third day and be entered anyway, and the entry will stand as a birth and not as a worsening. I have seen this and I have not put it in the article. There is no article for it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a second and narrower hand:} This article was added in Y.H. 782, which is the year the maids began to be paid, and the two things are not unrelated, though the ordinance does not say so. A hearth-maid lays the slate on the bench before she goes to the child. I have watched them do it. They do not say why, and I have not asked.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the drawing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Measure drawn by an officer appointed thereunto, a cold iron tube set against a way. Walls giving way; drain entered to the account. The draw witnessed by a slate. Where consent withheld, the account unclosed; the vessel clip-held by the wrist until consent entered. Consent entered in the hand of the officer.

\item Theft of warmth, being a draw without a slate, punished by a cold iron brand upon the wrist and a deduction from the thief’s own measure. Quiet ash sold to any not licensed to buy it punished by a greyed hand.

\item Drawing from the Hearth without a keeper’s key forbidden. The Nine Wells sealed; keys kept. A keeper who drew without authorisation was hanged in Y.H. 618.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have seen the wrist. The clip leaves a pale ring that shows through the winter and is spoken of as nothing. The woman asked me if the ring would go, and I said it would in the thaw, which is what my mother said about everything, and is not in the ordinance.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The officer who came on Stone 12 had fingers the colour of skimmed milk gone off, under a cuff softer than my own. I wrote him down on a slate of my own. I did not say what the fingers meant, because I do not know, and I did not join him to anybody.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the figure and the reading}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item One part in twelve of every measure kept back for the Hearth, as the notice says. Figure printed upon the Weighing notice and read aloud at the Cross. Read twice: once for the moot, and again for those that came late. Account-day the tenth, twentieth and thirtieth of every tend. No market held during the Five.

\item Correction of a slate by one hand only. Lawful deduction entered only by the College of Assessors. A house roll kept close and not shown; the keeping of it not explained, only kept.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The figure is one in twelve and I have never known a household in Low Kiln that paid it. I do not say what it pays. I have no slate for that and will not invent one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The bell at the Cross goes longer than a church bell and nobody crosses himself at it. I have counted it four, four, and a place where the fifth should be. I have put no count of it in the ordinance, because the ordinance has no place for a thing that is not a debt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} There is a small stop in the neat upper line of the top slate, between two clusters, in a hand I do not know. I have seen it five times and joined none of them. When I say \emph{there’s nothing in it the household need correct}, I am not lying. There is nothing in it that I can correct.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the five days outside the months}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Five days outside the months, named and not numbered, outside the tend. On Ilmen 1 the count begins again at Firstday.

\end{enumerate}

Day — As the ordinance stands — In the margin\par

\textbf{Kindling} — Every hearth lit from the Hearth-flame. Collectors take the year’s first measure. — Here the first hand wrote \emph{Weighing}. I have struck it and set \emph{Kindling} above it. The measure was taken before first light in Y.H. 812. No figure reached the roof, which is another way of saying I did not see it.\par

\textbf{Weighing} — The year’s measures read aloud. The rich learn how whole they are. — An officer read them in a clean voice and the district learned its figure from him. Berr Clay passed a finger over his own slate and wiped his thumb. Neither of them said the figure twice.\par

\textbf{the Long Night} — No fire after dusk. Stories of the Return told in the dark. — The stories are not entered. I sat in one room where the bell was told as four, four and a gap. I kept the told bell in my head away from the heard bell. They are not the same bell and I will not make them one.\par

\textbf{the Remembering} — Names of the dead spoken. Whole returns announced in a clean voice. — A whole return was read for one not in the room at the Weighing in Y.H. 812, and the household did not repeat the name. Under another roof a name was not spoken at all. I entered the return and not the name.\par

\textbf{the Last Day} — Bread baked. The grey Ash in the corners not swept away; burnt the next morning and called dealt with. — Two ridges were measured with one thumb. I put my cuff into a corner I had no business in and the grey came off on it. The streak in this book’s margin came from the same hand. I washed the cuff. The ink is still in the two fingers.\par

\subsection*{V. Of the keeping and the returning}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Measure banked. Account stands. Nothing lost that has been kept. Embers booked. Rolls of the dead kept open. Where one measure poured into one vessel, the return whole, with memory; where many pooled and divided among many, the return thin. Return announced in a clean voice. The Kept held in the Weighing Hall, fewer than twenty, spoken of with pity.

\item No article provides for the coming back wrong. In the low houses they keep these also.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have seen one of the Kept go through the Hall. It was courteous and asked after the weather. There are fewer than twenty and they are spoken of with pity. I do not know what the pity is for, and I have never asked.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The rolls of the dead are kept open. I have entered a name twice, once in the house roll and once upon the Court’s slate, and the two entries did not agree, and neither was corrected. A dead man with two figures is worth more than one with none. That is not in the ordinance either, and yet I have done it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, at the foot, struck through and written again in the same hand:} No article provides for the coming back wrong. In the low houses they keep these also. \emph{Written again because I struck it the first time, and then thought better of striking it. Let it stand. A clerk who takes a line out of a law because it frightens him has no business at a table where women stand.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{What I corrected, and why}

In article one the first hand wrote \emph{entry made}. I set \emph{is} above it. A man come down from Slate Row in a clean coat passed the table, looked at my \emph{is}, and struck it out again, saying that an ordinance has no need of a verb, being always true. I have left both stand. A slate with two hands on it is the only kind the household believes.

Where the book said \emph{Weighing} for the year’s first measure, I struck it and wrote \emph{Kindling}. A collector drew before light on Kindling in the Thin Year and the draw went into the account without a figure anyone in the yard could spend. I know the day because I set my hand on the slate that morning. I do not know the figure and have not asked for it.

In the schedule of the Five the first hand allowed four days. I have set five above it. There are five, and no market in any of them, and the count begins again on the first day of Ilmen. I cannot think how a man came to write four unless he left one out on purpose, and I have no mind to find out which.

The candle-singe at the top is mine. I set the book too near the lamp in the Waiting Room, where the collected are kept overnight before banking, and held it there longer than I should, because a woman in the room was telling me something and I wanted the end of it. She did not tell me the end. She looked at the book burning and stopped, and went back to sitting. I have left the singe as it is. It is the only entry in this quire that nobody has corrected.

The book goes with the table. On Ilmen 1 the slates opened and I copied it again, and struck the same word out again. A woman will come and set her hand on the top slate, and I shall say it is entered as it stands. It is. That is the trouble with it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Riddle Bench at the Cross, Being Five Cold-Night Questions, the One That Was Not Answered, and the Tally Left in Charcoal on the Bench Top}
\CRsheetheading{The Riddle Bench at the Cross, Being Five Cold-Night Questions, the One That Was Not Answered, and the Tally Left in Charcoal on the Bench Top}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A tapster’s record of a winter contest, set down for the settling of arguments and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand the house keeps, the riddles in the words they were spoken, a charcoal tally of one night, the figures of a Court clerk entered over them, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Banked Coal at the Cross in Sill, by the woman who keeps the bench and the fire behind it; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled tally leaf from the Court’s table, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled paper and kept in the jar by the hearth. It survives soft at the fold and stained at the head, with a tallow thumb, a ring where a quart stood all night, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a spot of barley grease, a grey Ash print along the gutter, the charcoal rubbed thin where a sleeve has gone over it, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the bench at the Cross and the fire behind it, which is a different work from keeping an account, though both begin with the hand on the board before the eye goes to the person standing there. In the cold months the road shuts, the Ilm goes under its skin, and there is nothing to do of an evening but count what is left and ask one another questions we already know the answer to. That is a riddle. A question whose answer you do not know is a gamble, and there is enough gambling in Sill without ale in it.

The bench is black ash with the grain standing up where four thousand sleeves have gone over it. I score the night in charcoal on the end away from the fire, where the charcoal shows, and I rub it out in the morning with the heel of my hand. Nothing is carried away from this bench in a slate. A man who wants a thing entered can go up the street to Slate Row and sit with people warmer than himself, and he will not get a riddle there.

\subsection*{The rules, as they are kept}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A riddle is put once. Ask for it a second time and you owe a quart, because the second asking is for your own pleasure and not for the bench.

\item Answer in one breath. A second answer is a different riddle and is not heard. A man who gives two has not understood the first.

\item Four questions are scored. A fifth may be put and is not scored, being a thing said from a door and not from a stool.

\item The judge is the bench. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a riddle given away for nothing, and the giver can go home and sell it.

\item No slate lies on the bench. The score goes off with the morning, as the ale does, and neither is carried into an account.

\item A cup is set down before the first question and no one lifts it until the fourth. If it answers flat when it is set down, the night’s answering will go badly. I have never known this to fail and I would not say so before a kiln-master.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The four that were scored}

The first was put to the eel-woman from the Fishstairs, who smells of silt and answers a question with a question. She had given hers before the verse was finished, which is why she never wins anything and is always first.

\begin{quote}\itshape Mouth and no lip to speak with,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape belly that gives nothing back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a door you cannot find from inside:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes in head-first stays?\end{quote}

“An eel basket,” she said, and laid a bit toward the pot though nobody had asked her to pay. The carter said a basket has no door. She told him to ask the eel, which is the whole of the answer and the proper way to give it.

The second was put to a girl who sweeps the yard for six bits a day.

\begin{quote}\itshape Carried in a clay dish before the light,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape given once and never twice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape every house has it by morning\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no house will say where it was lit.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What is it?\end{quote}

“The year’s fire,” she said, and I gave her a quart of small ale watered until it barely counted, which she drank standing with her sleeve over the rim because she had been told not to spill. Nobody asked her where she had learned it. A child of eight in this town knows which dish the coal comes in and which houses will not tell you who paid for it.

The third went to the man from the kiln, who had slip dried on both forearms to the colour of old bone.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am not a warm-stone and nobody calls me one;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am borrowed from a neighbour’s fire and carried in wool;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am put under a head that cannot turn\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and by morning I am a stone again.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A river stone,” he said, and there was an argument about whether a thing borrowed is the same thing when it is given back. I stopped it by setting the cup down. There is no winning an argument about a stone; there is only the stone, and it is cold by morning whichever way you decide it.

The fourth I put myself, because the room had got noisy and wanted quieting, and a riddle put by the bench is not scored against anybody.

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing at noon and plain by tallow;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I gather where a promise was not kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they leave me lying on the Last Day,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape burn me in the morning and call it dealt with.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name me.\end{quote}

No one answered for a while. Then a clay-hand from the pits, with the grey worked into his knuckles that no scrubbing lifted, said the grey in the corner, and said it to the bench and not to the room. I passed him the pot. He set it down again without drinking and said it was a thing his mother said to the skirting board, and that he had said it to his own daughter the week before and had not known he was going to. That is the best answer I have heard in eleven winters and the only one that cost the man something.

\subsection*{The fifth, which was put from the door}

It was the middle of Stone, when the ice had set for good and the bit for a quart had gone up two and come down again. A man stood at the door and did not come in. He was dry, which a man cannot be in that weather without having come a long way or else not having come from the weather at all. He asked whether anybody here was warm. Nobody answered him, which is an answer in this town. Then he put the fifth:

\begin{quote}\itshape I go back to a house that knows my face and not my name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape my mother is glad of me and does not know me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I want a thing I never wanted\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and cannot say what it is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

The eel-woman said, “A thin return.” He said, “That is what the slate calls it,” and asked what it was to the house. The room went the way a room goes when everybody has the answer in their mouth and nobody will be the one to say it. He waited a little, and said, “Then you have not lost it,” and turned back into the cold. He did not come in and I did not ask him. Where he stood the boards were wet with the melt off every coat in the room, and in the morning there was a round dry place on the bench where no cup had stood. I rubbed the charcoal over it and it came back. I have stopped looking for the hand that did that.

\subsection*{The tally, in charcoal}

Question — Put by — Answer given — Score\par

The basket — the bench — an eel basket — one, paid\par

The dish — the bench — the year’s fire — one, drunk\par

The stone — the bench — a river stone — one, argued and allowed\par

The grey — the bench — the grey in the corner — one, not drunk\par

The face and the name — a man at the door — none served — not scored\par

The figure read at the Cross that morning was one in twelve, as the notice says, and it went over the bench with the ale and no one looked at it twice. There is a pause in that figure the length of a held breath, which the clerk reads past and I do not, but that is not a thing for a riddle night.

\subsection*{What the narrow hand did}

A clerk of the Court’s table borrowed the leaf on a market morning when the square was full and his cuff was soft at the edge from washing. He set the riddles down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses entered}, and put a figure of marks against each of the four, which was more than I had scored, because the bench scores in whether a man sits down again and he does not. Against the fifth he wrote \emph{no answer tendered; struck}. He asked who had put it. I told him a man at the door. He asked for the man’s name, and I said the man had given none, which is a true thing and not the thing he wanted, and he wrote \emph{party unidentified}.

I have put my words under his and left his standing, the way a bench keeps a charcoal score under a spilled quart. He has entered four answers and struck the fifth, and the fifth was not struck: it stands where a man stood and did not sit down. I asked him what a figure was for and he said a figure was for carrying away. He has carried away four and left the one that would not go.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The tallow thumb at the head is mine; I held the leaf down in the draught that comes under the door and did not know I had marked it. The ring came off a quart that stood from the first question to the fifth and was drunk by nobody; three men have claimed it and one woman has denied it and I have not given it to any of them. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the man who held the door while the stranger spoke, and I have not written down which man, because he would stop holding doors if I did. The barley grease is from a crust the sweeping girl set down on the leaf and took away again uneaten, which is how a crust is usually taken in this town. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff that had no business in the corner where I keep the leaf, and I have not swept it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four went home warm. The fifth went home with them.\end{quote}

I have asked the carter, the eel-woman and the clay-hand, and had three silences and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the jar and the charcoal goes off the bench with the heel of my hand. The road will open at the thaw and there will be more to do of an evening than ask one another what we already know, and the bench will be wanted for cups again. I will set the fifth where it was and let the next man stand in it. If he asks whether anyone here is warm, I shall tell him to ask the pot.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Salt Wife’s Book, Being Remedies for the Glass-Sickness, the Chill, the Bite and the Third Night, Set Down at the Quay in Vhal}
\CRsheetheading{The Salt Wife’s Book, Being Remedies for the Glass-Sickness, the Chill, the Bite and the Third Night, Set Down at the Quay in Vhal}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A boat-midwife’s and healer’s book of remedies in the Vhaleni tide-words, written in Grathic letters so a girl of the Quay could read it; the cures in a salt-wife’s hand, a lowland physician’s objections in the margin, and the corrections of a Council clerk set down on salt-paper that has since gone soft, with one song for the third night and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the Quay in Vhal in Ember and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Eda of the Quay, a midwife who went aboard with the eel-boats and kept the households of the glass-workers; begun on the back of a Council tide-table spoiled by rain and sewn with eel-sinew into an oiled sailcloth wrapper, carried up the Salt Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a discarded weigh-slip. It survives in a dry tin among a boat’s things, soft at the fold and sweet at the edges, with a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the head, a thumb of tar, a white bloom of salt along the gutter, a ring of brine, a fish-hook nick, one correction the damp has eaten down to a figure with no verb, and a line struck through and written again underneath in the writer’s own hand.\par}\medskip
I write on the back of a tide-table the Council left out in the rain. The figures have gone where the Council’s figures go, which is nowhere a man can put his hand on, and what is left is paper enough for a book nobody has asked to see. I am a salt-wife of the Quay. I go aboard when a birth will not wait for the quay, and I keep the households of the glass women, who are the only people in Vhal who sweat sweetness. I have set down what we do and what the lowland physician at Greybank told me to do, and where the two disagree I have left both standing. A remedy is a thing the sea has been paid for already. A woman who takes a line out of a book of physic is answerable for the next body that takes it.

My hand is not a clerk’s. I put the verbs in because a direction without a verb is a thing a Council clerk can read aloud at a table and a woman cannot use at three in the morning with a boat coming up under her. The green at the head is not tar. It is a bead of cliff-glass a girl pressed into the leaf with her thumb while I was writing, and she had sweetness at her mouth and said nothing. The tar is mine, off the oar I held down in the wind. The salt along the gutter came up out of the paper itself. I have not washed any of it.

\subsection*{The order of a sick-room aboard}

\emph{Written small in the margin, with one word gone over in brine.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Get the brazier under the lee of the hold, not in the wind. A fire in a draught is a fire that has been taking warmth from somebody and giving it to the air. Nobody in this port will agree to pay for the air.

\item Set the sick one’s feet toward the ebb if the trouble is a chill, toward the flood if the trouble is a swelling. This is what we do. A lowland physician told me it should be toward the fire in either case, and both stand here.

\item Turn the slate face down before you go to the child, as the hearth-maids do in Grath. I have no slate-name and never shall; a salt-paper contract is a thing that rots in the damp, which is a virtue in this country and a folly in every other.

\item Salt the water before you wash a wound. The sea does it for nothing and we charge for it, which is the whole of our trade.

\item When the quay-crier calls the turn of the tide, stop and begin again after. He is counting something that is not in your room.

\end{itemize}

I have done three hundred births and I still look at the door before I look at the child. It is a trick the room plays on a woman. After the first hundred you stop calling it a habit and call it the order of things.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who pays\par

Glass-sickness (the sweetness) — A draught of seawater, and cliff-glass scraped into it — The glass women rub their gums with it and say the sweetness answers sweetness. A lowland physician says it is the lead in the glaze and that the draught makes it worse. I have seen the pale line at the gum and the hand that cannot hold a cup. I have not seen the lead. — The glass furnace, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

A chill off the water — A common stone warmed at the brazier, in a fold of wool; the feet to the ebb — To the belly, never the feet. Change it when it goes cold in your own hand, not when the child stops crying. A Grathic hearth-maid says a stone is a stone and not a kindness, and I have let her words stand. — The brazier, and whoever paid for the coal.\par

A hot wound, or a fever that burns — A cold-iron knife blade laid across it — We say the iron draws the heat out. A Keldish man at the quay told me cold iron draws and gives nothing back, and that a blade on a wound takes the measure as well as the heat. I have set his words beneath mine. — The wound. There is no other answer.\par

A bone set wrong — Two hands, a splint of straight reed, a fold of wet cloth — Set it while the vessel is quiet, before the swelling takes; leave the reed on till the third day. A bone-setter from Nine Pots says leave it a tend and a half. Both stand. — The patient, in the holding still.\par

A birth-flower — Salt, rubbed in — We call it the tide-mark and rub it with salt, believing the sea set it there. A Grathic woman crossed two fingers at the corner of one and gave me a date instead of an answer. I have put the date in the margin. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

Milk that will not come — Another woman to hold the child while the mother sleeps — The favour is paid out of the other woman’s own house, and I say so before I ask it. — The other woman’s child.\par

A cut from glass — Tallow first, then a clean fold — Do not salt a glass cut if you can help it. The glass women salt everything, and their hands are mapped in white lines. — Whoever opened the furnace.\par

The bite of a salt-thing — Nothing I know — Keep her from the water at the turn. Salt does not hold that bite, and a brine-gull will take a coal off a brazier but will not take this. — Nobody. This is the honest column.\par

A child emptied by leeches — Nothing. Do not set them. — They draw through a small wound and leave the body thin; a collector would call it a draw and ask for a slate, and I have never seen one ask. If you find them on a child, take them off and count them, and do not put them back. — Whoever put them there.\par

The third-night chill — Warmth, quiet, and a watch kept till the fourth day — Keep her against a living body under the quilt and give barley water by the spoon. Do not leave her to sleep it off, and do not call a collector for the worsening; it is the night’s own work and goes off by the fourth morning. — The household, one night’s sleep and a loaf.\par

A lowland physician came up the Salt Road in Y.H. 798 with a book that said the sweetness came from the lead in the glaze. He left a page of it in the glass-house and went off with a purse. The page came back to me with the word taken clean away, as though a word could be taken off paper the way salt is taken off a net. I have written the word here in my own hand, which is a thing a salt-wife is not supposed to do. I have also left the draught of seawater standing under it, because it is what I have seen done for thirty years and I have not yet seen what it does to a person beyond the month.

\subsection*{The full note}

Tap a sound cup with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. The glass women know it in their cups and I have borrowed it from them. A girl of the furnace told me her mother used to tap the ribs of a sick man and say he had gone flat. I do not do it. A body is not a cup, and a cup’s answer is none of a person’s business.

The dippers say the Sallow gives back a note like a cup three-quarters full, and that the Council enters it as full because the difference is not worth a figure. I have left the three-quarters where I heard it. A figure a clerk can carry away in a cuff; a note is not.

\subsection*{The tide and the draw}

We say the draw runs seaward and a body empties into it. The dippers bless the nets at dawn so the eels will not notice, which is a kindness spent on eels. If the warm goes from the full to the empty, as the lowland books say, then a sick body turned to the ebb should lose what ails it. That is what I used to think. I have watched nine such bodies and eight of them went colder before the turn; the ninth did not, and she had been carried in the other direction by her daughter, who did not tell me. I have left the old line standing and set the nine beside it. When a thing has been done wrong nine times I want the ninth to keep her place.

There is a shape of salt and cold water in the Sallow that taps the hull and takes a boat’s store away. We call it the salt-thing. A healer who cannot tell a tide from a taking will set a sick man facing the water at the turn and wonder why he goes thin. I have done it. I do not say I was right.

\subsection*{The song for the third night}

\emph{Sung low, to the child, while the watch is kept. The room says the last line with her.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ebb takes and the ebb keeps,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the glass gives back what the furnace grieves;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a body is a boat with a seam\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the seam is where the warmth leaves.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the brazier, two for the bite,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the hand that holds the light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the twelfth goes down and the twelfth comes in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one goes out on a wind not seen.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three nights, three watches, a hand kept true;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the child, sing to the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and come back on the flood. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

The twelfth is left where the twelfth should be. The Council would put a figure in it. A figure is a thing that can be written and then rained on and then entered again in a dry hand; a tide is not.

\subsection*{What the Council hand did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a market morning in Ember. He writes on salt-paper, and the salt-paper has taken the damp and let his hand go, so that of his three corrections only one figure and half a verb survive. Where I wrote \emph{the draught of seawater}, he set \emph{the measure is restored} above it, and the damp has eaten \emph{restored} so that only \emph{the measure is} stands. He put a round nought in the place of the unnamed tide and wrote \emph{vacancy} under it, and the vacancy has outlasted the nought, which is the Council’s own art in a small space.

I have put my words back under what is left of his. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them in because a woman on a boat at three in the morning does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to hold the child with.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The green bead at the head was pressed in with a thumb and has left a sweet smear that will not dry. The tar is off the oar, and came off when I held the sheet down on deck in a wind that was taking everything else. The bloom along the gutter is salt out of the paper and not out of the sea, which is a thing only a person who has kept salt-paper knows the difference of. The ring of brine came from a cup set down while I was telling a girl to eat and she would not; the hook nick came off a man paying me with his hook still in his hand, and he did not apologize. The grey print at the foot is not mine and not the Council’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a tin.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea keeps what it takes. It has no slate and no clerk, and it does not call it a debt.\end{quote}

I asked the dippers, the glass women and a factor come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tin goes back among the boat’s things and the leaf goes aboard when the ebb comes. A girl will press another bead into it and say nothing, and I shall put the verbs back where the damp has taken them.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Broken Pot, Being What Was Said at the Bone Orchard on the Remembering of Y.H. 812}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Broken Pot, Being What Was Said at the Bone Orchard on the Remembering of Y.H. 812}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pot-break sermon preached at the shrine of broken pots outside Sill’s north gate, over the year’s pots and the one pot nobody brought; the manner of the breaking in the niche-keeper’s hand, the sayings in Grathic, the breaking-song in verse, the row of pots in a tally, a factor’s clerk’s correction in Ledgerhand set above the keeper’s verbs, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached by an old woman of Sill who had broken pots at the Bone Orchard for one and thirty years, on the Remembering of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, over the pots set in the niche a league north of the Cross; written that evening by the woman who keeps the niche, in charcoal and with the point of a broken nail on the inner face of a grave-tile that came away whole when it should have broken, and kept under the flat stone among the sherds. It survives with grey Ash ground into the slip along the gutter, a salt bloom in a hairline at the head, a tallow thumb where the tile was held down on a man’s knee, a green bead of lead glaze caught in a chip of the rim, a morsel of dry clay in the fold, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come out from Greybank that takes the verbs out and numbers the nameless pot as nil, and one line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand nobody will own. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the empty place left the length it is.\par}\medskip
I keep the niche of broken pots at the Bone Orchard. It is my work to set the year’s pots in a row and lift the flat stone on the Remembering and put the sherds back. What follows is written on the back of a grave-tile that came away whole from the row and would not break, so I kept it, the way this ground keeps everything that fails at the work it was made for.

The old woman stood with her back to the north gate and spoke first to the pots, as potters do, and to the clay under them, and to the fire that had made them, and only at the end to the people standing in the row. She had broken pots here for one and thirty years and had never once broken one at the foot. She said the same things every year. I have written them as she said them, with the verbs where she put them, because a sermon said over a pot is a thing a household has to use.

The grey in the gutter came off my cuff when I measured the ridge two doors down in Low Kiln and came back to write, and I have not swept it. The salt at the head is from a woman’s hand laid flat on the tile to hold it still in the wind off the ridge. The tallow is mine. The green bead is not slip; a girl with sweetness still at her mouth leaned over to see what I was writing and touched the rim with her thumb. The tile has a chip at the upper right where somebody tapped it with a knuckle and did not say what answer it gave.

\subsection*{The manner of the breaking, as the niche keeps it}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the pots in a row on the flat stone with their lips to the north. Feet toward water is for the body; lips toward the Hearth is for the pot. Do not mix the two.

\item Tap each pot with the knuckle before you lift it. Listen for what it answers. Do not say what you heard where a man with a slate is standing.

\item Break at the lip with one blow. A blow at the foot sends the heat into the clay and the clay will keep it, which is a kind of burying twice.

\item Break it whole. A pot broken into dust has let the heat out through a hundred little doors and cannot say which way it went.

\item If a pot answers flat, break it gently. It has given already and asks no help from you.

\item When the bell comes up the north road from the Cross, stop. It has counted something that is not your pot. Begin again after. Four, four and a gap, and the gap is not ours to fill.

\item Break the nameless pot last. Do not let anybody bring it. It comes out of the niche by itself.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The sermon, as she said it}

\subsection*{Of the lip and the foot}

She put her thumb in the chip at the rim of a milk pot and turned it so the row could see where the star was.

“You bring me a pot and you say, break this, it is my mother’s. I ask you nothing. I break it at the lip, because the lip is the mouth and the heat goes out of a mouth the way breath goes out of a person. Break it at the foot and you have put your mother’s warmth into the ground twice: once in the grave and once under the grave, where the clay keeps it and will not let it go.”

She struck the pot with the heel of her hand and it opened clean across, two pieces and a third small one that fell among the sherds.

“A whole pot keeps. A broken pot gives. That is the whole of my preaching and I have had one and thirty years to find another sentence and could not.”

\subsection*{Of the note}

“Before I break, I tap. You have all heard a pot tapped at the wheel. A sound one answers full and a cracked one answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. You bring me a pot that answered flat three days before the person went and you say nothing about it, and I say nothing either. We are not fools in this district. We know what a pot was doing while we were looking at the person.”

She tapped the cup with the cupworm in it. It gave nothing that I could hear from where I sat, and she put it down on its side.

“This one I break gently. It has been giving since it came off the wheel and there is no heat in it to let out. Do not break a pot that has given already as though it had held. That is a cruelty to the pot and a lie about the household.”

One of the women in the row said that a pot was only a pot. The old woman turned her head a degree toward her and said: “A body is only a body, too, and we wash it and put its feet to the water and send for a man with a tube. Do not tell me what a pot is. I have made them.”

\subsection*{Of the one nobody brought}

There is one pot in the niche that no household brings. It is a plain clay pot, smaller than a milk pot, with no mark on it and a lip worn smooth by hands that have lifted it every Remembering since I can remember. The old woman took it out from under the flat stone and held it a moment against her apron before she set it on the row.

“This is for them that have no house to break for them,” she said. “The little graves lie over there beyond the broken stake, shallow, because the clay was frozen when they were put in. You can walk past them and not see them, and people do, and I do not blame them, because a person can only look at so much in a winter.”

She struck it at the lip. It opened with a dry sound, smaller than the milk pot’s, and the three pieces lay where they fell.

“The Court reads a whole return at the Weighing in a clean voice for a person not in the room. I have heard it done. I have stood outside the door and heard it done, and come up here and broken this. Somebody has to break for the ones the clean voice does not name. That is not an argument with the Court. It is a pot with a name left out of it.”

She would not say how many graves lay beyond the broken stake, and when the clerk asked her she said the clay was frozen and she had not counted that year. A woman beside me wrote something in the margin of her tally and covered it with her thumb. I have not read it and it is not on this tile.

\subsection*{Of the keeping}

A factor’s clerk had come out from Greybank with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers, and stood at the end of the row with a slate held to his forearm. He asked the old woman what became of the heat once the pot was broken.

“It goes up,” she said. “That is what I know of it. It goes up out of the mouth and into the air and the air is bigger than the house. I have stood at more breakings than I could set a figure to, and never once seen it come back to the pot.”

“It is banked,” the clerk said.

“It is gone from the pot,” she said. “I have not said where from. Those are two sentences and I will not have one put over the other.”

“Nothing is lost that we have kept,” he said, in the voice that takes the speaker out of his sentence.

“I have never kept one,” she said. “I have let go of a great many. If the Hearth wants what went up, let the Hearth come out of its iron and fetch it. It has not come yet, and I have been waiting one and thirty years.”

After that she gave the mark on the niche the same answer she gives every year. The clerk asked what it was, the crossed thing cut in the stone above the pots, which the surveyor draws in the chart and does not explain. She said it was cut in Y.H. 668. He asked her again in a different way and she gave him the same year.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the margin, in my hand:} A date is safe. The factor’s clerk says so himself, and he is right, because a date is the only answer that cannot be argued with. I have set down her year and left the question standing.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The breaking-song}

\emph{Sung low, standing, while the nameless pot is lifted out of the niche. The row says the last line with her. There is a gap before the last line, the one the bell leaves, and I have left it here as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Break at the lip and not at the foot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the heat goes up and not into the root;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a whole pot holds and a cracked pot gives,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clay keeps only what the clay receives.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the corners, four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the place where a name should fall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell comes four and four and a gap,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot gives back what the pot had.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask the fire where the fire has gone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape do not ask the ground what it stands upon;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say the name, or leave the place it had,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and come back warm, as the Keeping said.\end{quote}

A girl from High Kiln asked what the space before the last line was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it later, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The row, as the niche counts it}

Pot — Brought by — Broken — What was said over it\par

Milk pot, lip starred — a woman of High Kiln — at the lip, one blow — her mother’s name, said three times\par

Cup with a cupworm in it — a man of the Clay Yard — at the foot, by mistake — nothing; the heat went into the clay\par

The nameless pot — the niche — at the lip — no name; a place left the length of one\par

A grave-tile, came away whole — nobody — not broken — kept, and written on\par

There were two and twenty pots in the row besides these, and I have not set them down, because a tally of pots is a thing a clerk can carry away and a name is not. The two and twenty went into the barrow with the grey the next market-day and nobody in the square looked at it twice.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He borrowed the tile on the morning after and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where she said \emph{a whole pot keeps, a broken pot gives}, he wrote \emph{retention and leakage are lawful conditions of a vessel} above and left hers below.

\item Where she said \emph{the heat goes up}, he wrote \emph{the measure is released to the keeping} and underlined it twice.

\item At the nameless pot he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it, and when I asked him what a pot was worth that nobody had brought, he said nothing a clerk could enter, which was the first true thing he said all morning.

\item At the line about the Hearth coming to fetch its heat he wrote \emph{claim not established}, and drew a small stop between two clusters of his neat dark hand.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath where she put them and left his hand standing above, as the flat stone leaves the sherds and the sherd leaves the clay. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman standing in the cold wants to know who did the letting go, and whether it was her own hand.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not the old woman’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole pot is a lie told by a sound vessel.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole pot is a vessel that has not yet been asked.\end{quote}

I asked the old woman, the woman of High Kiln, the man who brought the cupworm cup, the girl who asked about the gap, and the clerk, and had five answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The tile goes back under the flat stone with the flat side down, so the writing is kept from the wet. Next Remembering I shall lift the stone and set the row out, and the nameless pot will come out of the niche and be broken at the lip as it is every year. If the clerk comes again I shall let him take the verbs out. I shall put them back.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sixth Repair, Being a Letter from the First Seam to Nine Pots, Answered in the Margin and Entered Over by the Court}
\CRsheetheading{The Sixth Repair, Being a Letter from the First Seam to Nine Pots, Answered in the Margin and Entered Over by the Court}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A letter between brothers, the one hand Keldish and number-first, the other Grathic and given to proverbs; a tally of repairs set down in a small table, the sentence of the Vorr kept as it was spoken, the answers of the man addressed written in the margins, the corrections of a Court survey-clerk laid in Ledgerhand over both hands, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, in the survey room off the Duelling Floor beneath Keld Keep, by Varek of the First Seam, a clerk of the rim-seam tally, to Ollen of Nine Pots, a thrower, his brother by a mother who came down from the clay country and never learned to say a number before a noun. Set first on the back of a survey sheet spoiled by wet slate and carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road in Seed of Y.H. 813 with a survey party bound for Greybank; answered in the margins at Nine Pots and corrected at Greybank by a clerk of the factor’s office who borrowed the leaf on a market morning and would not give it back until the verbs were out of it. Kept since in a clay tube stoppered with wool on the shelf of the thrower’s shed in Nine Pots. It survives with coal dust at the head, a smear of hot lead at the fold where the leaf lay against a surveyor’s cuff, bone-coloured slip dust worked into the gutter, a thumb of tallow, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first question to the last, the figure for the sixth repair struck through and written again underneath in the writer’s own hand, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own.\par}\medskip
To Ollen, thrower, of Nine Pots, from Varek of the First Seam, his brother. Six repairs counted this week. One letter. No answer looked for.

I write from the room off the floor where the survey sheets are kept, which is warm in a way a room should not be warm. The stone sweats here in Bone and the smell comes up before anything shows, hot lead and a mineral sweetness like a glaze pot left too near the fire. Two men went out of this shaft in my first season and came back with their fingers the colour of a skimmed milk skin. I have counted the repairs in the wall behind the tally desk six times and got six each time, which is a small thing to be glad of. A number that comes back the same is the only honest company down here.

We had the same mother, who came down from Nine Pots with clay under her nails and a way of addressing the pot before she addressed the room. She taught you the wheel and taught me to hold a slate. I have kept the slate. You got the wheel, which is the better inheritance and I have never once said so in a letter until now, so you may put this down to the lead smell.

\subsection*{The tally, as I keep it}

The wall behind the desk is not the oldest in the seam. It is only the one I can see from my stool. I have entered what I can see and left the rest where it is, which is a rule the Order is not so strict about as it used to be.

Repair — What it is made of, by the Keldish translation — What the factor’s copy at Greybank calls it — How many times repaired\par

One — Stone, dressed and keyed — Stone — Twice\par

Two — Stone and iron pins — Stone, iron not entered — Once\par

Three — Stone — Stone — Three times; the third over the second\par

Four — Warm-stone dust in a clay bed — Material not entered — Once\par

Five — Stone — Stone — Once\par

Six — Not stone — Language — Once; crossed out and written again\par

Five of the six are stone and are no trouble. The fourth wants a word I will not use of a wall, because warm-stone is a thing a man carries against a child’s belly and not a thing he puts in a hole in the world. I have entered it as dust in a clay bed and let the translation stand beside it.

The sixth is the one I am writing to you about. The Keldish translation calls it Ash. The factor’s copy calls it language. I have copied both words into the margin and chosen neither, because a surveyor who chooses between two guesses has made a fact of one of them and will have to answer for it at the Weighing. The Vorr were asked. One of them sat against a stone for a season and came back with three sentences, all the same sentence, which was that the numbers were correct. I have written that down too. It is a complete answer if you are a Vorr and a very thin one if you are a man trying to sleep above a seam that sweats.

\subsection*{The entry of Y.H. 588}

There is an entry in the old survey of a man with a branching red mark on his forearm and ribs. The entry is crossed out. It was crossed out before I came down the shaft and I do not know whose hand did it, which is a thing I have said to myself often enough that it now sounds like an answer.

I have copied the shape of the mark onto the back of this sheet so that you can look at it and tell me whether clay ever makes it. I do not want an opinion. I want to know whether you have seen it under a glaze or in the bottom of a jar, and if so, on what day and out of which pit. Give me the day and the pit and leave the rest where you found it.

There is a paper in a tin lined with warm-stone in the room off the floor. The men who keep the floor read it once a year and do not act on it, which I am told is a great skill and is certainly an old one. I have read it twice. The second time I found a line about a vessel that holds without leaking and went back to counting the wall, which was easier and paid the same.

\subsection*{What I want to know from you}

This is the question I cannot put to any man in Keld without being told to state my measure first and ask afterwards:

A pot that has cracked all the way through and been mended, does it hold the same as a pot that never cracked? I do not mean whether it holds water. I mean whether the holding is the same holding. Tap a sound pot with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface. I know the two sounds as well as I know my own number, which was thirty-three when I went down and thirty-nine when they changed it, and has been cut out and written again twice since, so that my forearm reads like this letter does. But nobody has ever tapped a repaired pot for me and asked it the question twice, once before the mending and once after, and told me what changed.

You will say a pot is a pot. You will say this with slip on both forearms and the little finger bent where the splinter went in at eleven, and you will be right in the way that potters are always right, which is from the wrist and not from the mouth. Answer me from the wrist.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, the letters round and pressed hard, with slip in the strokes}

You always did ask the wrong question first. A pot that never cracked is a pot that has not been mended, and there is no holding to compare with it. Tap mine and it answers full because I set the seam myself and it sang when it went home. If it had not sung I would have sold it for a flower pot and said nothing. A crack that is mended keeps the crack. Ask it to be a pot it was not and you are asking a lie of the clay, which is a thing the clay charges for in the thaw.

On the red mark: third firing of Y.H. 806, a jar from the Old Kiln clay that would not take a glaze and went grey in the firing. The mark was on the bottom, branching like frost on a pane. A girl from the terrace crossed two fingers at it and said it was a flower. I asked her which flower. She gave me a date. I have kept the jar under the bench and I have never turned it up in company.

On the road: it is ours and Sill’s both, which is why neither of us mends it. Come down in Seed when the clay has set and bring the warm-stone if you are still carrying one. Six repairs in a wall is enough for a man to carry without a stone as well.

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the wheel and one for the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the crack that the glaze won’t hide;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tap it at noon, it answers at night,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the seam keeps the word the potter denied.\end{quote}

I have never written a verse in my life and I would not begin now if there were not a man above me in a shaft who needs one. Put it under the numbers where it belongs.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did, at Greybank, in the second tend of Seed}

A clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf on a market morning; his cuff was gone soft at the edge from washing and he had ink in the creases of two fingers. He laid his hand on the top sheet before he looked at either of us, which is the manner of that table. He took the verbs out of both hands as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff, and set a figure against each repair, and struck the question about the mended pot and wrote \emph{No such comparison} above it. Against the red shape he put a round nought and wrote \emph{mark, not entered}. Where my brother wrote that the seam keeps the word, the clerk wrote \emph{repair retained; material not entered} and left mine underneath, which is more than he usually leaves.

In my hand — In the Court hand\par

Six repairs counted this week — Repairs entered: six\par

The sixth is not stone — Material not entered\par

The Vorr said the numbers were correct — Figures confirmed\par

Does a mended pot hold the same? — No such comparison\par

A mark on the bottom of a jar — Mark, not entered\par

The seam keeps the word — Repair retained\par

He asked me what a verse was worth and I said nothing a clerk could enter, which was the first true thing he said all morning. I have left both hands standing, mine under his and my brother’s under both, as a repaired wall keeps the old break under the new keying and does not pretend the first hand never touched it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal dust at the head is mine; I held the sheet down with my whole hand because the draught in the survey room comes along the floor and takes paper before it takes a man. The hot lead at the fold came off a cuff on the day a passing was measured two hours early and we all went up faster than we had any right to. The slip in the gutter is my brother’s and has gone bone-coloured with dry, which is the colour of his forearms by noon and of mine by never. The tallow thumb is mine. The ring came off a cup that stood from the first question to the verse and was drunk by neither of us, which is how small ale is drunk in Keld when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in the First Seam.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six repairs in the wall and one with no name. The Court has entered the five it can spell. The wall keeps all six and has never once been asked to explain itself.\end{quote}

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Slack Tide, Being a Winter Riddle Night on the Quay at Vhal, Five Questions Scored in Chalk on the Tarred Post, the One Put from the Door, and the Tide That Was Named and Has Not Come}
\CRsheetheading{The Slack Tide, Being a Winter Riddle Night on the Quay at Vhal, Five Questions Scored in Chalk on the Tarred Post, the One Put from the Door, and the Tide That Was Named and Has Not Come}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A tavern-keeper’s record of a cold-month contest, set down for the settling of arguments and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand the house keeps, the riddles in the words they were spoken, a score in chalk on the tarred door-post, the figures of a Council clerk entered over them, a boat-master’s note in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Slack Tide on the Quay at Vhal, by the woman who keeps the house and the lamp over the door; set first on the back of a spoiled tide-tally from the house beside the Council room and on two strips of salt-paper that would not hold ink, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled sailcloth and kept in a dry tin under the till, where nothing else in this house is kept dry. It survives with a thumb of tar at the head, a white salt bloom along the gutter, a press of frozen rope across the first leaf, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a fish-hook nick, a coal-smudge near the fifth question, the chalk rubbed thin where a sleeve has gone over the post, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Council of Tides, one note in the blunt hand of a boat-master, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the Slack Tide on the Quay. It is a different work from keeping a tally, though both begin with the hand on the board and end with a figure somebody wants to carry away. In the cold months the east wind holds, the Sallow skins over at the edges, and the galleys lie up on the pulled benches with their oars in, and there is nothing to do of an evening but ask one another what we already know and call the asking a riddle. A question with an answer nobody knows is a bet, and there are men on this Quay who would bet on which way the wind will sit by morning.

The door-post is tarred and the chalk shows on it. I score the night there and take the score off in the morning with a wet rope-end, which is the only erasure this house has ever needed. Nothing is carried away from the Slack Tide on a slate.
