A man who wants a thing entered can go up to the Council room and sit with people warmer than himself, and the paper there will rot before he gets home, which the Council calls a virtue.

\subsection*{The rules, as the house keeps them}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A riddle is put once. Ask for it again and you owe a quart, because the second asking is for your own pleasure and not for the post.

\item Answer in one breath. A second answer is a different riddle and is not heard.

\item Five are chalked. A sixth may be put and is not scored, being a thing said from the door and not from a stool.

\item The house judges. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a riddle given away for nothing, and the giver can go home and sell it.

\item No paper lies on the board. A contract left here overnight is a debt the weather has settled, and this house does not settle debts for the Council.

\item A quart of small ale is set down before the first question and no one lifts it until the fifth. If a white bloom comes up on the board before then, the night’s answering will go badly. I have never known this to fail and I would not say so before a dipper.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The five that were chalked}

The first went to a woman who holds a twelfth of a boat through her mother and will not say the fraction before company. She had her answer before the verse was fairly out, which is why she never takes the quart and is always asked first.

\begin{quote}\itshape I go from mother to daughter and never by buying;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man may come aboard and hold me in his hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and still his word upon the boat is counted half;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am not the hull, and I am not the sea.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A share,” she said. “And the half is his opinion, not mine.” I gave her the quart and she drank standing with her sleeve over the rim, because she had been told not to spill. Nobody asked her how many twelfths she held, which is the proper way to ask nothing in this house.

The second went to Kett of the Quay, who reads the draws at the tide-tally house and keeps his cuffs dry by not touching anything.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am set down to be kept and I keep by going;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wetter the room, the less I owe;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council has made a virtue of my dying\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and hired a man in a clean coat to write it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“Salt-paper,” he said, without looking up from his tally, which is how he answers everybody. The house allowed it. A man who reads the draws all day does not need to look at a person to know what that person has brought in.

The third was put to a dipper come in off the pans with salt dried white in the creases of her neck.

\begin{quote}\itshape I run against the wind and am blessed before light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council is surprised by me every year;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they tax me in a figure I never carried.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What runs seaward and is counted by men who never saw it?\end{quote}

“The draw,” she said, and said it to the pot and not to Kett, because a dipper does not argue with the tide-tally house before company. She took no quart. Dippers are paid by the pan-master, who pays in the weather and never in ale.

The fourth went to a boat-master who had lost a store below the waterline and had come back to sit down again, which not every man does after such a loss.

\begin{quote}\itshape I knock where no hand can reach, below the waterline;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I take the store and leave the rope behind;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the nets are blessed at dawn and I come all the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What taps a hull and takes what the hull was holding?\end{quote}

“A salt-thing,” he said, and set the quart down again without drinking, which in this house is how a man says he has already paid for the answer. There was an argument about whether a blessing that does not keep a store is a blessing at all. I stopped it by touching the post, because there is no winning an argument about a blessing and there is only the thing that came in the night and the store that is not in the boat.

The fifth I put myself, because the room had grown noisy and wanted quieting, and a riddle put by the house is not scored against anybody.

\begin{quote}\itshape I steal the warm and do not eat it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I go up the wind with a coal under my crop;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no tally in this town stands one mark the poorer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What carries the fire out of the account?\end{quote}

An old woman who mends nets said “a brine-gull” and said it low, the way people say things they have said to the fire at home. I passed her the pot. She set it down again and told me a gull had taken a coal off her brazier the week before and she had not gone after it, because a thing that goes up the wind with your coal has already been paid and there is nobody to charge. That is the best answer I have heard in nine winters and the only one that cost the teller nothing by telling it.

\subsection*{The sixth, which was put from the door}

Toward the end of the night a girl came to the door and did not step over it. There was salt dried white on her shins and at the hem of her coat, as if she had come up off the pans and walked the Salt Road without putting her shoes back on, which nobody does who owns a pair of shoes. She asked whether anybody in the house had seen the tide she named at the Salt Walk. Nobody said yes, which is a way of saying no that costs nobody anything. Then she put the sixth:

\begin{quote}\itshape I was named at fourteen with my feet in the pan\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and written in salt where the dippers could read;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape by noon there was no word, and the pan kept nothing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have carried the shape of it all winter, not the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

Kett said, “A tide not yet seen.” The girl said that was what the dippers wrote in the salt and asked what the house called it. The room went the way a room goes when everybody has the answer in their mouths and nobody will be the one to say it, which is the same in Vhal as in any town with a Council. She waited a little. “Then leave it where it is,” she said, and went back into the wind. Where she stood there was a small drift of salt on the boards. In the morning it was gone, and I have not swept the place where it lay, because the wind does the sweeping on this Quay and always has.

\subsection*{The score, in chalk on the tarred post}

Question — Put by — Answer given — Score\par

The share — the woman with the twelfth — a share — one, drunk\par

The paper — Kett of the Quay — salt-paper — one, allowed\par

The draw — a dipper — the draw — one, to the pot\par

The tap — the boat-master — a salt-thing — one, not drunk\par

The coal — the house — a brine-gull — one, given low\par

The named tide — a girl at the door — none served — not scored\par

The Council’s figure for the draw went up on the tally board that morning and came down by noon, which is what the Council’s figures do. It went over the post with the ale and nobody looked at it twice, which is how figures go in this house.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a morning when the till was being counted and his cuff was soft at the edge from the damp, which is the only way a Council cuff ever gets soft. He set the riddles down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses entered}, and put a figure of marks against each of the five, which was more than I had scored, because the house scores in whether a person sits down again and he does not. Against the sixth he wrote \emph{no answer tendered; struck.} He asked who had put it. I told him a girl at the door. He asked for the girl’s name, and I said she had given none, which is a true thing and not the thing he wanted, and he wrote \emph{party unidentified; interest in a tide not entered.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{a share, and the half is his opinion, not mine}, he wrote \emph{one-half interest, contingent}.

\item At the salt-paper he wrote \emph{instrument voided by damp}, and underlined it twice, which is what the Council does when it wants a thing to look like a mercy.

\item Against the draw he wrote \emph{current taxed at source}, which is true in a language nobody on this Quay speaks unless they are being paid to.

\item At the salt-thing he wrote \emph{loss not entered}, and put a round nought in the place where the store had stood.

\item Against the brine-gull he wrote \emph{no value transferred}, which is the only one of his answers I have ever wanted to keep.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words under his and left his standing, the way a tarred post keeps the chalk under the salt. He has entered five and struck the sixth, and the sixth was not struck: it went out on the wind with the girl and is still going.

\subsection*{From the boat-master}

At the foot of the scored leaves, in the blunt hand of the man who had lost his store and sat down again:

\begin{quote}\itshape A man’s word on a boat is counted at half. His loss is entered whole.\end{quote}

He says he wrote it about the salt-thing and not about his wife, and I have let him say so. A man who has married aboard is allowed one sentence in a book he did not write, which is more than the Council allows him anywhere else.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The tar thumb at the head is mine. I held the leaf down on the Quay in the wind and did not know I had marked it; tar goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the Council room uses it for a seal and this house uses it for nothing. The salt bloom along the gutter came up out of the paper on the third night, when I carried the leaf inside my coat and the coat crusted white at the fold. I have not brushed it off. A bloom written by the weather is the only writing in Vhal that a clerk cannot strike. The press of frozen rope across the first leaf came off the man who held the door while the girl spoke, and I have not written which man, because he would stop holding doors if I did. The green bead in the lower corner came off a string of cliff-glass a carrier left on the till; it has the colour of the Glaze Cliffs after rain and I have kept it where it fell. The fish-hook nick is from a hook set in the edge by a man paying for his quart, and he did not apologize, which is how hooks are paid for here. The coal-smudge near the fifth question is from the brazier, where the leaf lay too close while the net-mender was telling us about her gull; the coal was ours and the answer was not. The grey print along the outer fold is not mine and nobody has claimed it. Nothing on this Quay is swept until the wind does it, so the print is still there.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pan keeps the shape and the sea keeps the name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape neither gives back what was made in it.\end{quote}

I asked the woman with the twelfth, Kett and the boat-master, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back in the tin and the chalk goes off the post with a wet rope-end, and in the morning the Council clerk will come for the till and find nothing in it that rots. Next winter the galleys will lie up again and the east wind will hold, and I shall set five questions on the post and leave the sixth standing at the door, for whoever it is to come in out of the wind or not, as they please.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Smoke-Side Dog, Being a Soldier’s Field Notes on the Kiln-Hound at the Old Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{The Smoke-Side Dog, Being a Soldier’s Field Notes on the Kiln-Hound at the Old Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A soldier’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch and not natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on a spoiled levy-roll, a watch-song as it is sung, a kiln-master’s correction in slip-white, a clerk’s ruling in Ledgerhand · Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Hobb of Sill, one of the Thane’s men watching the Old Kiln road, in the watch-shed with a tallow end; set down on three levy-rolls spoiled by rain, then on the back of a granary docket, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with soot ground into the head, a brown spot on the second leaf, a wet boot-print from the Slip Brook, a singe from the fire-pot, the charcoal rubbed thin, two corrections from the factor’s clerk, one line in slip-white from the kiln-master, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the road to the Old Kiln for the Thane. It is no post a man writes home about. The ruin stands one league south of Sill where the clay has gone grey and will not take a glaze, and the ash in its throat is deeper than a man is tall. I am set there to see that no one digs the grey in the dark and that no one lies down in it and stays there. I carry a short spear with the head gone blue on the quay stone and a fire-pot of coals under ash, and I write these lines at the end of a watch with the tallow down to a knuckle and the cold coming up through the soles.

The rolls I wrote on first were spoiled in a rain that took the figures clean off, which was a mercy of a kind: a figure the rain has eaten cannot be entered. I write in charcoal now, because charcoal goes into the grain and a clerk cannot take it off with a cuff. The soot at the head is my own thumb setting the sheet down on the watch-shed bench. I have not knocked it off.

\subsection*{The road and the river}

The hound keeps to the smoke side. That is the first thing a new man must learn and the thing that costs him a night’s sleep. It will lie all watch on the side of the ruin where the warm comes up through the clay and the air moves, and it will not come round to the cold side though a man stand there with his coat open and his pot hanging. The folk of High Kiln say the river is a wall. I thought it was a saying until the night I watched one stand in the mud at the Slip Brook with its nose across the water and a man lying three paces beyond on the other bank. It stood. It did not go over. The man was not saved by it, but he was not eaten either, and in this trade a man takes what the night gives.

It comes off the smoke side in the second watch, when the tallow is low and the kiln-yards down at Sill have stopped their shouting. It does not bark. The sound it makes is low in the throat, like a man clearing himself in his sleep, and you hear it in your boots before you hear it in the air. I have set the watch-song down below with the hearths’ words standing where the watchmen put them, which is not where I would have put them.

\subsection*{What it is}

It is a dog. I will set that down before anything else, because the hearths will not. It has a dog’s teeth and a dog’s neck and a dog’s way of putting its head on one side when it listens. It is bigger than the yard hounds at the Tallow Works and thinner, with a coat the colour of wet clay and no grey on the outside. The grey is in the mouth and under the nails. Behind the ears it is hot to the back of the hand, hotter than a beast that has merely been near a fire should be. It smells of smoke and hot clay, and when it has been lying in the throat a man smells of it too, for a day after.

I have opened three. Two were brought down on the road and one was found dead at the mouth of the old flue, where it had gone in after the warmth and not come out. In all three I found a dog altered by the place it lived in, the way a potter’s hands are altered by the wheel. I found no more than that and I have not put a cause beside it. A man who writes a cause into a book he keeps in his pocket is a man who will be asked for it by somebody with a slate.

\subsection*{The breath}

The danger is the air. The dog is the thing that brings a man to where the air is.

I have stood on both sides of it. A man who stays in the throat with his head low will come out with a headache and a thirst that outlasts the watch, and his lips are a little too red, which is all the evidence there is. There was a potter of Low Kiln came up in Ash to look at the grey and went down on the second morning in his own house with the window shut, and the physician said it was a merciful death, which is a thing physicians say when they have not had to lay the body out. He had never seen a hound in his life. The potters leave a window open in a firing though the draft spoils the glaze. A spoiled glaze is a loss a man can count. A man is not.

I have written the air where the watchmen write the dog, and I have left both standing.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the blocky hand of the kiln-master of Low Kiln, written in slip-white with a potter’s stylus, down the margin of this leaf:} It is the air. I have buried two who never saw a dog. Leave the window. The glaze can bear it. --- K.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The bite}

It does not bite a man on his feet. I have stood within two paces with the spear down and it went on with its own work. But let a man go down and it comes for the face, and it does not shake him or drag him. It puts its mouth to him and waits, the way a collector sets a tube and waits, and the waiting is the part I cannot write about without my hand going still.

The boy they set with me in the second watch went in at Ash 5 after a man we had heard in the grey. We found him face down with the hound at the cheek. I struck it across the back with the spear-shaft and it went three paces off and stood, which is what it does; it does not run and it does not come back at a man who has hit it. The boy’s cheek was two small holes and not much blood, and his lip was red on the side next the ground. I washed with water and bound it. At the end of the tend the holes were closed and the lip was still red and he was asking for water at every watch. He has never said what he saw down there and I have not asked him. Salt does not hold that bite and there is no physic for it that I know. Keep the man out of the close air and let him ask for water. That is the whole of what I have.

The tongue, dried, is bought by Fenfolk to test a close room, for it discolours where the breath is. Two bits a tongue and no questions. The hide is too smoky to sell, so we burn it. A man who tells you he has found a use for a kiln-hound hide is a man who wants another one, and you should keep your coals between you and him.

\subsection*{The watch-song}

\emph{Sung going in at the first watch, not coming back. The fourth line is the hearths’ line and every watchman sings it wrong on purpose. I have set it down as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the clay and one for the smoke,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dog keeps the side where the fire has been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it does not bark at a man on his feet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is the kiln’s own breath that comes to him.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep the window. Let the glaze go bad.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A draft is a thing a man can pay.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The lips go red where the head lay down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the next day’s water is never enough.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the watch and one for the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the man who did not come back to it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not name him at the singing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we leave his place where the gap should be.\end{quote}

The gap is the fifth breath the old kiln does not take. The watchmen know it and sing it and have never once said what it is a gap in. There is a man at Sill who sings the last line twice and will not say why, and I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the nights I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine.

Night — Place — Hounds — Overcome — Tongues — Entered\par

Bone 6 — South road at the broken flue — one — one — one — 2\par

Bone 12 — The throat, east side — two — none — none — 0\par

Bone 19 — Smoke side below the ash-heap — one — one — one — 2\par

Bone 28 — Old damper, not gone in — three — none — none — 0\par

Ash 5 — The throat, where the boy went down — one — one — one — nil\par

Ash 14 — North bank of the Slip Brook — one — none — none — 0\par

Ash 26 — The road, after the rain — two — one — two — 4\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, struck through the “Overcome” column:} Persons overcome: not entered. Air not a vessel. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. A clerk’s hand has its use: it keeps a man from arguing with what he cannot change. But the boy asked for water through the whole of Ash and the clerk has put \emph{nil} against him with a neat instrument and no name on it. I have written the thirst in the margin below, where his column cannot reach, and I have put my own mark beside it in charcoal.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

They say it is the kiln’s breath given legs, a thing that got up and went walking because the fire was put out unkindly. There are songs in the Fenmarch with a man’s name in them and a wrong done at a flue. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. I have opened three of these and found a dog, and a dog is the least of what is wrong with that place. If the breath has legs, then it is the room that does the work and the legs only carry a man into it. I have written that last sentence out once and crossed it out twice, because it is the kind of sentence that gets a man called a natural philosopher, and natural philosophers are not set to watch roads in Bone.

I do not know what the hound wants in the throat. I know the order it goes in: the ash-heap first, then the broken flue, then the old damper if the watch is long and the tallow is low. I have set the order down and no cause. The complexion of the place is not mine to explain and I have never been paid to explain it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The soot at the head is mine. The brown spot on the second leaf fell there from the boy’s cheek when he sat down to have the rag changed, and I have not scraped it, because it is the only entry on this leaf that cost anybody anything. The boot-print across the foot came off the morning I crossed the Slip Brook after the rain and came up to the calf in grey silt; it has dried into the grain and will not rub out. The singe on the lower corner is where the leaf caught when I held it over the fire-pot to read, and the hand that pulled it back was mine and is not entered. The charcoal is rubbed thin where I carried the roll against my thigh. The clerk’s line I have not touched. The slip-white line is the kiln-master’s and will fade before the charcoal does, which is a small kindness in the ordering of things. The song is as they sang it, with the hearths’ lie left standing in the fourth line.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape What kills in the room was there before the dog came in.\end{quote}

There is a place down in the throat where the ash stands deeper than my spear and the air comes up warm on the stillest day of Ash. I have not gone in. Next Bone I will take a fire-pot and a coil of cord and go down to where the old damper was, and if the breath comes up in a place where no kiln has burned in a hundred years I will set that down too, in charcoal, and let the clerk take what figure he can out of it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Articles of the Tenth Clamp, Being the Standing Rules of the Order of the Tenth Clamp Beneath Keld Keep for the Taking, Cutting and Trying of Apprentices at the First Way, with the Table of Hands, the Iron-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, and the Master’s Corrections}
\CRsheetheading{The Articles of the Tenth Clamp, Being the Standing Rules of the Order of the Tenth Clamp Beneath Keld Keep for the Taking, Cutting and Trying of Apprentices at the First Way, with the Table of Hands, the Iron-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, and the Master’s Corrections}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A board-copy of the Order’s standing rules in the hand of the under-master who keeps the irons and the roll of hands at the mouth of the Duelling Floor; the articles cut in short Keldish clauses, the tables in number-first order, the iron-song in the hard Rim speech pasted inside the cover, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one line struck in coal by the master of the floor, one objection in the leaning hand of a leech come up from the Ninth Gallery, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · First gathered beneath Keld Keep in Y.H. 747, the year the Cold Pass was shut and the border fixed by men who had never walked it, and copied forward each generation from the iron board beside the clamps rather than from paper, which is why the rule about the rope-coloured hand is worn through at the corner and the rule about the nail is as sharp as the day it was cut; this leaf written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Vek of the Tenth Clamp, the under-master who keeps the irons, and carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party bound for Greybank, where it was copied onto the back of a spoiled tally-roll. It survives with coal dust ground into the head off the master’s sleeve, a smear of hot lead at the fold where a passing was measured two hours early, iron filings caught in the gutter from the clamps on the floor, a scorch where a lamp-spark took the corner of the second leaf, a thumb of tallow, a ring of frost raised out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass, a splinter of warm-stone sewn into the board cover which keeps the whole leaf a little warm, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the Court, one line struck hard in coal by the master, one objection written twice and struck twice by a leech from the Ninth Gallery, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the irons. Nine clamps lie on the board at the mouth of the floor and the tenth hangs on its nail behind me, and has hung there since before I came down. A boy asks which is the tenth and is told: the one that goes to the stone. He asks what it does there. Nobody answers him twice, because the answer is a number and he will have it soon enough.

These articles were first gathered beneath the Keep in Y.H. 747, and have been copied forward from the board and not from paper. An article nobody has had to use is an article nobody believes. These have been used. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings, because a floor with one hand on it is a floor with one man in it.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand on the board}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Order takes a boy at thirteen, on the day of the Descent, and not before and not after. A house gives him up for a day and has him back by dusk with a number, which may be the number it sent and often is not. The house does not ask for the old one back. The floor has never given one back.

\item Number first, then the name. The clerk writes the figure before he has heard who the boy is, and if the boy gives his name first he is asked again. This is not pride. A name is a thing a man can change at a moot; a number is cut into the bone and stays when the skin is corrected around it.

\item No boy is asked whether he wants the way. He is asked whether he understands what is bought: a cut across a surface way in the forearm, held open while it scars, a fortnight in which the arm is of no use, and a mark that will not close while he lives. The master cuts. The wanting comes after, or it does not come; the Order has never claimed to teach that part and has never stopped charging for it.

\item A lowlander may be taken if he states a measure before a name and keeps his face while it is checked. No master now living has taken one, and no master’s master either, which is three generations and not a rule. The article stands because a rule forbidding a thing has to be read aloud every time the thing arrives, and the floor has better uses for a morning.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the coal-pressed hand of the master of the floor, against article 2:} Number first. Then the name. Everyone in Keld knows this. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that the figure goes first so that a boy cannot change it with a smile. The master has struck the smile. There is no smile in this room after the first cut, so the rule is for the morning before, when a boy still thinks a face will do instead of a figure. I have left both.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the cut}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The way is opened across a surface way in the forearm and kept open while it scars. The master cuts it. No boy cuts his own and no boy cuts another’s; a way made by a friend is a way two men must answer for, and this floor has room for one answer.

\item The arm is useless for a fortnight. On the fifteenth day the boy is given a clamp to hold. A boy who cannot hold it is given the keys instead, which is the kindness the Keep shows to men who cannot descend, and is not a kindness. He will keep the keys all his days and will know what they open and will never open it.

\item Cold iron is set to draw the heat out of a cut that will not settle. The iron takes as well as it draws. A master who tells a boy the iron only draws is selling him the fortnight twice, and the boy finds it out in the sixth week when his fingers go the colour of skimmed milk gone off and he cannot feel the clamp he is holding.

\item A way once cut is never closed. Men have closed them with grafts and with salt and with the long cold beyond the Pass, and the way comes back in the season when the stone sweats, and aches before the thaw and after it. A boy who says his arm aches is told the weather will have the last word. A boy who says it twice is given a warm-stone out of somebody’s fire, which is theft from an account the boy did not open and is entered nowhere.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand of a leech come up from the Ninth Gallery, against article 7:} The hand comes back on the sixth day or not at all. Do not set the clamp again higher up and call it a second chance. \emph{In mine, underneath:} I have set his line above the rule where the master can see it. He struck it out twice in the winter and wrote it again both times, which is how a leech argues with a floor.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the floor}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Nine clamps go to the floor and one goes to the stone. The tenth hangs behind the board and is not taken down. A master who takes it down must answer to the Warden’s roll for the answer, and the Warden’s roll asks its questions in a voice nobody down here has learned.

\item A clamp is set across a way, never across a bone. A man who clamps a bone has stopped nothing and broken something, and the something does not grow back.

\item The first man to open a way usually wins, because the other is busy bleeding. This is not a trick and is not taught as one. It is the whole of what the floor is for, and a boy who learns it as a trick will use it on a man who has already lost, and will not know why he won.

\item A hand that goes the colour of old rope below a clamp is left alone. The clamp comes off; the hand is wrapped; nobody sets the iron again above the place where it failed. A man who has lost the use of a hand is still a man with a number, and the number stands whether the hand lifts a cup or not.

\item Hot iron is put to the palm when the roll wants to know whether a man is honest. The honest come back with a hand gone dead. We have had a great many honest men under this Keep and not one of them lied, and nine in ten of them cannot lift a cup. No man is put to the iron for a question the roll has already answered.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of hands}

\emph{Kept by the clerk at the mouth of the floor. A number is written before a name, and where the number has been changed the second is set beside the first without a mark, which is the only honest thing a clerk can do.}

Condition — What is entered — What gathers — Discharged\par

Boy at the Descent — the number, before the name — a mark in the forearm — on the fifteenth day, if the arm answers\par

Boy whose number changes — the second number, no mark beside it — nothing entered — never; both numbers stand\par

Boy who cannot hold a clamp — the keys — a hand that does not close — never\par

Man gone cold in a season — the number in the floor’s roll — grey at the fingertips — not discharged\par

Lowlander taken — measure, then name — the master’s answer — as for a Keldish boy\par

The tenth clamp — the nail — nothing — never\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The roll is kept under the board and a Court clerk may read it but may not change the order of the two entries. Last winter one of them set a name above a number and wrote \emph{the vessel was re-entered} in the margin, which is a true sentence in a language nobody on this floor speaks. I have put the number back above it. A name can be entered in a second column; a number cannot, because it is already in the arm.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected on the floor\par

Name before number — Asked again; the number set above\par

A verb in the roll — Struck by the Court’s hand; set back underneath by mine\par

A clamp set on bone — Taken off; the boy set to counting irons for a tend\par

A way opened by a second boy — Left to heal as it can; both boys lose the fortnight\par

A hand gone rope-coloured — The clamp removed; no second chance above it\par

The tenth clamp taken down — The master’s own number entered against it\par

A question about what comes up through the stone — Answered once: the numbers are correct\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The last row is not a punishment and is not a rule about clamps. It is the only answer the floor has for the stone, and a boy who asks a second time is told to ask the Vorr, who will say it once in a voice like a man using a tool he has no use for, and will say it twice: the numbers are correct.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The iron-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Sung on the fifteenth day, in the room off the floor, with the clamp laid on the table and not in the hand. Nobody sings it on the stone and nobody sings it at the Descent. The boy whose fortnight is out says the middle verse, and nobody says his name.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine on the board and one on the nail,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tenth is kept for the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count the irons, count the head,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and give the number, then the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One cut across the living way,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a mark to keep and a fortnight’s cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the iron takes what the iron draws,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boy pays before the floor.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four to the arm and a fifth gone wrong,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand goes rope and the rope stays put;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape do not set it higher and call it a chance,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape for a number stands and a hand does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine on the board and one on the nail,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tenth is kept for the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the master cleans what the master cut,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boy says his number, then his name.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaf when the survey table sat at the Keep, ink settled in two fingers of his soft cuff. He struck \emph{the arm is useless for a fortnight} and set above it \emph{the vessel was clamped}, which is a thing always true and therefore true of every boy who ever came down. Against the nail he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. I have put the nail back. A nail is a place and a place is not a number; he has spent his whole trade putting figures where places stood, and has never once been thanked for it.

The master of the floor struck the word \emph{taught} out of article 3 and wrote above it \emph{that will hold. Don’t make me say it twice.} I have left \emph{taught} underneath, because a boy should be able to see the word the master would not let stand. He cleaned his clamp while he did it and did not look at me.

The leech’s objection has been struck twice and written twice; I have set the second above the first. A nail, a nought, a hand, a number: four things on one leaf, and no man has joined them.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal at the head came off the master’s sleeve when he leaned to read the third verse standing and would not sit down; he said a song that had never been in a mine was not worth the paper. The hot lead at the fold came off a cuff on the day a passing was measured two hours early and we all went up faster than we had any right to; it has burnt one word of the fifth article clean through and I have not written the word back in. The filings in the gutter are off the clamps on the floor. The scorch on the second leaf is a spark that caught while I was writing and went out under my hand; the hand was mine and I have not entered the burn. The tallow thumb is mine, from holding the sheet down in the draught that comes up the shaft. The frost on the third leaf came up out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass and is the only thing in this book that entered itself. The splinter sewn into the cover is warm-stone from the Ninth, and is why the leaf is a little warm in the morning; somebody paid for that warmth and his name is not in here. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s, and I have not swept it. In the clay country they leave the ash in the corners on the Last Day, burn it in the morning and call it dealt with. Under the Keep the dust has nowhere to go.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The floor keeps the number. The stone keeps the hand. Nobody keeps the boy who gave both.\end{quote}

I have asked the master, the clerk who keeps the numbers and the leech come up from the Ninth Gallery, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back under the iron board and the tenth clamp goes back on its nail. Tomorrow a boy will be brought down at thirteen and will give his number before his name, and the master will clean the clamp while he asks the second question, and whatever he answers will be entered in the same neat hand as the boys who stayed warm. The nine will go out on the board and the tenth will stay where it has hung every morning since before I came down.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Untaken Turn, Being the Well-Game of Cold Acre, with the Passing, the Bringing Back, and What a Clerk of the Factor Made of the Warm That Is Not Counted}
\CRsheetheading{The Untaken Turn, Being the Well-Game of Cold Acre, with the Passing, the Bringing Back, and What a Clerk of the Factor Made of the Warm That Is Not Counted}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A well-woman’s setting-down of a children’s passing-game in the Cold Acre speech, written with a charred stick on the back of a meal-mill tally gone soft at one corner; the verses in the children’s own half-sung words, the manner of the play in the writer’s hand, a correction in the margin by the woman who winds the well-rope, the factor’s clerk’s ruling in Ledgerhand above the eighth line, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Set down in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at Cold Acre on the ridge two leagues north of Sill, by the woman who keeps the well-rope there, on the back of a barley tally from the meal mill that had given up its figures at one corner; carried down the ridge road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank, where a clerk of the factor’s house borrowed the leaf for a morning and gave it back with the verbs taken out. Kept since under the loose stone of the well-curb, in the nick where the rope is coiled, which the children do not lift. It survives with a thumb of well-clay at the head, a grey Ash print nobody will own along the gutter, a white frost-ring that has eaten two words off the fourth line, a barley awn stiff in the fold, a nick from a turnip knife at the fore-edge, a thread of sacking caught in the second leaf, the rope-woman’s correction standing in the margin, the clerk’s ruling standing above the eighth line, and the line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the well-rope at Cold Acre and have drawn at this curb for thirty-one winters. I set this down because a man come up from Slate Row stood on the ridge in Stone and asked what the children said when they passed the stone round the well. He wanted a figure for the warmth. I told him there was a turn in it and no figure, which is the truth of the thing, and he went away and sent a clerk, which is what a man does when he has been given an answer he cannot carry back.

The leaf is the back of a mill tally whose figures had gone soft at one corner, and I wrote with a charred stick out of the barley kiln, because ink will not stay on a paper that goes into a bucket. The children’s words I have set as they came, half-sung and with nothing mended in them. What they do not say before a man with a clean cuff I have put at the end, where such things belong. I have left the clerk’s hand standing where he set it and the children’s words under it, as the curb keeps both the rope’s mark and the water’s.

\subsection*{Where it is played}

In Stone and Frost, on the bare ring of ground that goes around the well, where the frost will not hold. The river lies ice at the Sill and the Singing Sill keeps its note under the ice, but the ground at our well stays dark and a little soft to the boot, and the children say it is because the well is breathing. I have heard men say it is a current under the ridge. Nobody has asked it with a slate in his hand, and I have not asked either.

They do not play in the Five, because in the Five a child stands and listens and there is no round for it. They do not play on a market-day while the barrow goes out of the north gate and along the ridge on its way to the Bone Orchard, heaped a finger above the sides where the load has shifted. The children stand and let it pass and say nothing, and take up the stone when the road is empty again. This is not a rule anybody taught them.

\subsection*{The choosing, said before the stone is taken up}

\emph{The children stand in a ring with their hands behind their backs. One among them, facing the well, passes the stone from fist to fist behind the ring and says the words. She does not look at the faces. On the last word the child who has the stone takes the first turn. Said to the well. Said looking at a child, it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six houses and a well,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a well and six houses;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape stone in the fist and thumb on the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one it stops with starts the round.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The passing, as it is played}

\emph{Eight lines, one line to each passing of the stone from hand to hand round the ring. The words go low and are mostly sung. A child who passes late has let the turn go and is cold at once; a child who passes early has taken a turn that was not hers, and must give the stone back and breathe on it herself before the round can go on. At the eighth line the passing stops, whoever holds the stone. That hand is the untaken turn. The child shuts her fist on the stone, sets the fist on the curb, and does not open it. She is the turn that stands.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the north road where the barrow goes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the gate that lets it through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the turnips under the snow,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the stubble the frost holds to;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five for the rope too stiff to bend,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the breath that warms it again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the curb where the bare ground is,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a turn for the water that comes without a hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well gives. It does not ask.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Let the stone go. Let the turn stand.\end{quote}

The eighth is not a number. I have asked them why and they say it is the turn, and if I ask what the turn is they ask me why a woman wants to know what a well does when nobody is at it. There is always a child who will say the water comes up because somebody let the rope go, and there is always another child who will say no, the water came up first and the rope went after it. The argument never settles and the game goes on all the same.

\subsection*{The bringing back}

A child who stands on the curb with a shut fist is brought back in one way only. Another child takes the stone out of her hand — she does not give it, it is taken — breathes on it twice, and puts it into her hand again. Nobody says who gave the warmth and the child who was cold says nothing when she comes in. If the stone is breathed on three times and still nobody takes it, the standing child stays where she is until the well-rope is let down and drawn up again, which the children call the ebb, and the ebb takes a while.

I have seen a child go to the curb on purpose on a morning when there was no fire in her house and the bare ring held more warmth than the hearth did. I have set that down and have not mended the sense of it. A gift on this ridge is not a thing that gets entered, and a child who has never been given a figure knows where to stand in a game about giving.

\subsection*{The verse they do not say while a man from Slate Row is on the ridge}

\emph{From the child who keeps the curb, with her back to the road. She would not say it to the clerk and would not say it within sight of his cuff. She said it to the well.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The barrow goes out and the well stays in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate says six and the ridge says none;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a breath is a gift and a gift’s a debt\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape in the hand that writes in the town.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The turn stands where the fingers let go;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody took it, nobody owes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water comes up when the river is ice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Court has never asked its price.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Pass it behind and pass it back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and warm the one you left in the cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone says nothing, the well says less,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the well gives still, and asks no more.\end{quote}

\subsection*{In the margin, in the hand of the woman who winds the rope}

Against \emph{a turn for the water that comes without a hand}, in a small hard hand pressed close to the gutter:

\begin{quote}\itshape Not without a hand. I have let go at this curb and the bucket has come up all the same, full, with nobody standing to it. There is a hand somewhere, only it is not mine.\end{quote}

Underneath, in mine: \emph{She has put a hand back into a line where I put none, and both stand. A well that gives when nobody winds is a thing a woman will argue about, and a thing a woman will not let a clerk enter.}

\subsection*{What the clerk wrote above the eighth line}

A clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank borrowed the leaf on a morning in Ilmen, being a man who cannot let paper lie. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits on the first joint of two fingers and will not come out. He wrote above \emph{and a turn for the water that comes without a hand}: \emph{one turn unperformed; unmeasured yield; presumed to accrue to the Keeping}. Against \emph{The well gives. It does not ask} he set \emph{source unentered; no deduction arises}. At \emph{six for the breath that warms it again} he wrote \emph{warmth passed between vessels without slate; no value attaches}. At the foot, where the child is brought back with a breath, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{one restored, nil}.

I have put the children’s words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child with a shut fist on a cold curb does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know whose hand will warm the stone. He has made a giving into a yield and a turn into a nought, and the nought belongs to the Keeping while the turn belongs to nobody. That is the whole art of that hand. He said the game was an account of the Return taught before a child could read a slate, and he entered it. The children stop when the soft cuff comes along the ridge. They take it up when he is back down the road, and they never once change the eighth.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The thumb of well-clay at the head is mine. I sign in clay because a wet hand will not take ink and because this curb is the only thing in Cold Acre that keeps a print the whole winter through. The grey along the gutter came off the barrow road, where I laid the leaf down while the Ash went past on its way to the north gate; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day on a ridge. The white ring took two words off the fourth line one night when the leaf lay outside the door on the frost; I have not written them back, because a rhyme with two words gone is a rhyme said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The barley awn in the fold came off a sack by the door and has gone stiff as a splinter. The nick at the fore-edge is the turnip knife’s, and the thread in the second leaf is sacking, which is the only sort of clothing this hamlet has ever had. Frost is the only clerk Cold Acre ever had, and it takes two words where the factor’s clerk takes the verbs.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well kept its own account before there was a slate. It has never entered it, and it has never once run short.\end{quote}

I asked the rope-woman, the children, a man come up from Greybank and a neighbour who carries turnips to the north gate, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back under the loose stone in the nick where the rope is coiled. Tomorrow the children will draw their ring on the bare ground and pass the stone and leave the turn standing where it stands now, and the bucket will come up with nobody at the rope, and the Court’s figure will stay where the Court put it, which is not at the well.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Want in the Count, Being the Hopping Game of the Drying Racks in Low Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{The Want in the Count, Being the Hopping Game of the Drying Racks in Low Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A children’s counting game, set out with its words, the scored ground, the forfeits, and the two hands that disagree over the empty place · Set down by an old woman of the drying racks in the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, having no slate-name and signing with a thumb pressed into slip; written in charcoal on the back of a spoiled drying tally and kept folded in the band of a cast-off apron. It survives with the score of a knuckle in slate dust, a tallow thumb, a drop of barley grease, a green bead of lead glaze from a girl who leaned over to see the writing, a grey print of Ash, and one correction in the narrow hand of a clerk borrowed from Slate Row. The game is held to be older than the bell at the Cross.\par}\medskip
I have no slate-name. The rack has one, and the kiln has one, and a pot has a number chalked on its foot where the thrower puts her thumb, but I have never been entered in anything that I can read. So I have set my thumb in slip at the foot of this leaf, which is how we sign a pot in this yard, and if a man come down from Slate Row wants a name for the hand, let him write \emph{the racks} and be done.

I write it because the little ones have begun to leave the want out. They hop the eight and stop, and say the count is finished, and stand looking at the bare clay where the ninth score should be, waiting for somebody to tell them it is finished. It is not finished. A count that closes is a Court count. I have taught them the words before they had the legs, and now I set the words down, because a thing carried only in the legs goes out with the legs.

\subsection*{The words}

\emph{Said while hopping. The row says the refrain; the hopper says the lines. No one says the want alone.}

One for the stone that was warmed at the fire, two for the pot that answers full, three for the grey that turns the corner, four for the loaves that go on the levy. Four and no more before the want.

Five is the bell that is longer than a church bell, six is the step that is not at the landing, seven the eels in the bridge’s shade, eight the pots on the rack, bone-pale. Four and four, and a place where the fifth should be.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Refrain, all together, stamping:} Hop it, hop it, call it out — four and four and a want. Put your foot where the foot should be and the whole count comes to nought. Hop the want and come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

If you set down in the want you are gone wrong, a flat note under the heel; go stand in the grey where it turns the corner and do not answer when they say your name. Bide till the bell goes. Then come back warm. Come back as you can.

The big ones carry nineteen out and nineteen back from the pit to the rack and again; we carry eight and the place where a step should be, which is as much as our legs can hold. When your legs are long enough the want becomes a step and you go on.

One in twelve, as the notice says, four and four as the kiln breathes, nineteen as the women tread — three counts and never one agreement. The Court has a figure for every place. We have a place with no figure in it. That is the one we keep.

\emph{The calling at the end, which is not a verse but the way they end:}

\begin{quote}\itshape Who is not in the row? — One that was not in the room.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What do we call her? — Kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What do we say to her? — Come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The ground, and how it is scored}

Eight places are scored in the trodden ash beside the racks, a hand’s breadth apart, with the end of a broken pot or a bit of slate. The ninth is not scored. On the Last Day the ash is not swept, and there is no need to score anything, because the grey shows the places of its own accord; after it is burned the game is played on the bare clay and the want is marked with a chip of pot set on its edge, so that it can be moved aside and put back.

Where there is a cord, two of the bigger ones turn it and the hopper runs in on the first line. At the word \emph{want} the cord is lifted over her head and comes down empty; she must call the word while no rope is under her foot, and come in again on the next line. Where there is no cord — and there is seldom a cord — the children stand in the eight places and say their lines each from her own ground, and the hopper goes from mouth to mouth. The want is then said by nobody and by the whole row at once, which is the only way it can be said.

They play it behind the racks on Account-day, when the square is full and the mothers have sent them out of it. They play it in the dark on the Long Night without any scores at all, going by memory, which is the hardest way, because a want you cannot see is a want you are likely to stand in. No one plays it on the Last Day after the bread is baked. I do not know why, and I have not asked the little ones, and they could not tell me if I did.

\subsection*{The forfeits}

To set a foot down in the want is to be \emph{gone wrong}, which is what the yard calls a pot cracked from lip to foot. The hopper says nothing; the row says \emph{flat}; she goes and stands in the grey against the skirting board, where it turns the corner without a break, and she does not answer if one of the others says her name. This is the whole of the punishment and the reason for it, which the children know as well as I do: a place with no name in it cannot hear itself called.

If she stays there till the bell goes she is fetched in and made warm, and the game begins again. If the game ends before she is fetched, she is \emph{kept} — she stands in the middle while the others go in for bread, and is not warmed and is not called. I have put that in the words because it is in the game. I did not put it there for a reason.

I have seen a child stand in the want on purpose, to be gone wrong, because the house she goes home to is colder than the skirting. I have not struck that out either.

There is a second game played at the edge of this one, with a nail of cold iron out of the smithy sweepings and a chip of slate. One of them is the collector, and goes among the ones standing in the grey, sets the nail to a wrist and asks the figure. The one in the grey gives a number — six, or eleven, or none at all — and the collector writes it on the chip with chalk and says the account stands. I have told them not to set cold iron against a living wrist. They say it is only a game, the way their mothers say the cough is the pits, and I have let it be.

\subsection*{What the narrow hand did}

A clerk borrowed the leaf one account morning and struck out the word \emph{want} wherever it stood, setting a round nought above it in the Court’s small upright hand. He wrote \emph{vacancy} beside the ninth place. He asked me what the count was for, and I told him it was for keeping the little ones from standing where they should not, and he wrote that down too. Then he asked how many stood in the row, and I told him eight and a want, and he wrote eight.

I have put the words back under his noughts and left his noughts standing. A nought is a number, and a want is a place; he has put a number where a place should be, which is what the Court does with everything it comes near. The children prefer my reading. When they come a second time they jump the nought as well, which I did not teach them and will not discourage.

He also numbered the five days outside the months as four, having left one out without appearing to notice, and wrote a figure against Kindling where there should be no figure at all. I have not corrected that one. It is not my leaf to correct a man’s counting on, and besides, the five are not ours to give away.

\subsection*{In the margins}

The green bead at the top right is not slip. A girl with sweetness at her mouth leaned over on a morning when the glaze room had been open and the whole terrace smelled sweet enough to make a body careless; she touched the leaf and said nothing, and went back to the rack. I have not washed it, and I would not if I knew how.

The tallow thumb is the little one’s who says the refrain loudest; she holds the leaf down with her whole hand when the wind comes up the yard, and does not know she marks it. The grey print at the foot came off my own thumb when I pressed it into the slip to sign, and is the only mark on the leaf that is mine. The barley grease is from a crust laid on the leaf while a child was being told to eat and would not; I left it, because a crust put down and not eaten is a thing this yard knows how to read.

In a hand I do not know, written very small between the fifth and sixth lines, there is one sentence, unfinished:

\begin{quote}\itshape Senn put her foot in the want and we left her till the bell went and she\end{quote}

The hand stops there. It is a child’s hand; the letters lean and the last word is written smaller than the rest. I have asked which Senn it was, and been told three different names, and have stopped asking. It may be that no child of that name ever stood in this yard. I have left the space as it is, because it is the right length for a want.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The leaf goes back in the apron band after the little ones have gone in. It is soft now at the fold and the charcoal has come off on my fingers, the way charcoal will. I have not copied it onto a slate and will not. A slate is a thing that gets read aloud at a market by a man in a clean voice, and this is not a thing to be read aloud.

They are hopping it behind the racks now as I write, and getting the refrain wrong in the same place every time: they say \emph{come back as you can} too fast, so that it sounds like \emph{come back as you was}. I have not corrected them. There is a difference, and they will learn it soon enough without me.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Warm Within, Being a Book of Remedies Gathered in Low Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{The Warm Within, Being a Book of Remedies Gathered in Low Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hearth-maid’s book of household physic for births, chills, burns, coughs, bites and the second chill; the remedies in Grathic, with a Court clerk’s corrections in Ledgerhand and one song for the third night · Set down in Low Kiln in Sill between Y.H. 809 and Y.H. 812, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by a hearth-maid of the district who attended births and put no name to a book an officer might read; written in charcoal and tallow on the backs of spoiled birth-slates and on a quire of sauce-stained paper from the factor’s house at Greybank, sewn with wire into a board cover. It survives behind the meal bin of a house east of the Clay Yard, soft at the fold: a bone-pale slip thumb at the head, a tallow print where a mother held it down in a draught, a green bead of glaze from a girl with sweetness at her mouth, a grey Ash print along the gutter, a streak of barley grease, one correction in the narrow hand of a Court clerk who borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, and one line struck out and written again in the writer’s own hand. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs left where she put them.\par}\medskip
I write on the backs of birth-slates spoiled by a late entry, which is paper enough for a book that nobody has asked to see. I am a hearth-maid of this district. I have set down what I do and what the women before me did, and where the two disagree I have left both standing. A remedy is a thing a body has already paid for. A woman who strikes a line out of a book of physic is answerable for the next body that takes it.

My hand is not a clerk’s. I put verbs where a clerk would take them out, and I have not corrected this, because a direction without a verb is a thing a man can read aloud at a table and a woman cannot use at a birth. The tallow print at the top came from a mother who held the sheet down in a draught and did not know she marked it. The slip thumb is mine. I signed in slip because I have no slate-name, and a thumb in slip is how this yard signs a pot.

\subsection*{The order of a birth room}

\emph{Written small at the head in charcoal, with one word gone over in tallow.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Warm the stone first. A common river stone out of the neighbour’s fire, in a fold of wool, tested on your own wrist before it goes to a belly. It is not a warm-stone and I will not put that word on it; the Keldish stone is another thing and no house here owns one. A cold stone is a stone, not a kindness.

\item Bank the fire but do not cover it. A birth needs somewhere for the heat to go.

\item Set the slate face down on the bench before you go to the child. The hand that writes is not the hand that holds. If there is nobody else to write, write after, and enter within three days as the ordinance says. Do not ask why the third day is a bad day to choose. It is a bad day to choose and that is the whole of it.

\item Wash in this order: face, neck, groin, knees, cord. Do not hurry the cord. It knows its own hour better than you do.

\item At the red flower, cross two fingers at the corner of it and say nothing. If someone asks, give a date. Dates are safe. The Court likes a date and does not ask what it covers.

\item Leave the grey in the corner. Sweeping it into a pail does not make it gone, and the Court has a word for gone that I have never seen happen.

\item When the bell goes at the Cross, stop and start again after. It is counting something that is not your room.

\end{itemize}

I have done four hundred births and I still lay my hand on the slate first. I have tried to stop doing it. It is a trick the room plays on a maid, and after the first hundred you stop calling it a habit and start calling it the order of things.

\subsection*{The second chill}

The third day is a bad day. A child that has taken a chill will grow worse on it, and if the entry was made on that day the worsening goes down as a birth and stands as a birth for the rest of the child’s life. This is entered nowhere in the ordinance and the ordinance has no place for it. We call it the second chill. The physician at Greybank calls it a settling of the graft, which is a kinder phrase and costs less.

In Y.H. 651 a physician at Greybank struck a word out of his own report and paid the hearth-maid who had written it for her trouble. The word has not come down to us. I have asked three older women and had three dates and no word. I have left the place where the word would stand, which is the right length for a word of that kind.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The narrow hand of the Court clerk wrote above this paragraph:} The worsening is a settling of the graft. No chill is entered. Entered as a birth, not a worsening.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Under it, in mine:} Worse before dusk. Warm and breathing was all I set down. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who pays\par

A newborn gone cold — A river stone warmed at a neighbour’s fire, in wool — To the belly, never the feet. Change it when it goes cold in your own hand, not when the child stops crying. — The neighbour’s fire. Repay with a crust, and do not call the crust a gift.\par

The second chill — Warmth, quiet, and a slate turned face down — Skin to skin under the shawl, barley water by the spoon, watch kept till the fourth day. Do not send for the collector because the child has got worse; that is what the day does. — The household, one night’s sleep and a loaf.\par

Cough off the pits — Barley water steamed under a cloth — Steam to the mouth, not the face. A hand over the mouth when it comes up, so the wall does not get it. — The pot and the fuel under it.\par

A burn from the kiln — Tallow first, then a clean fold — Cool it with tallow and keep the air from it. The old women lay wet slip on a burn: the slip cools while it is wet and cooks when it dries. I have left their line standing under mine. — Whoever opened the kiln, if the house can bear to ask.\par

A wound the salt will hold — Salt from the herring barrel on a feather — A brine-gull’s feather is better if you live near the coast and can bear to take it. In Low Kiln we use what the barrel gives. It is a brute method and it often works. — The barrel.\par

A bite from a bone-hound — Nothing I know — Keep him from the orchard. Salt does not hold that bite and neither does tallow. A dog that has eaten the little graves puts the grey into a wound and the wound will not close. — Nobody. This is the honest column.\par

The sweet sickness — A cup set down and not taken up — There is no physic for it. The glaze is sweet and the sweetness is the sickness. Stop the cup, if the house can afford to stop the cup. Most cannot. — The glaze room, which cannot pay and does not ask.\par

Kiln’s breath in a closed room — An open window — It spoils the glaze. The potters leave the window shut and call a death in sleep a merciful one, which is a phrase for people who have not had to identify the body. — The man who sleeps.\par

A child emptied by leeches — Nothing. Do not set them. — A silt-leach out of the shallows draws as the collector draws and without a slate. A child can be emptied by a handful in an hour. If you find them on a child, take them off and count them, and do not put them back. — Whoever put them there.\par

Milk that will not come — A warm stone and another woman to hold the child — Let the mother sleep while the child is held. The other woman’s own child goes a little colder for it. Say so. A kindness that has no payer is a kindness somebody else has paid for already. — The other woman’s child.\par

A physician from the College wrote in Y.H. 641 that the sweetness came from the lead in the glaze, and the copy that came back to us had the word taken out. I have seen the pale line at the gum. I have seen the hand that cannot hold a cup. I have not seen the lead, and I do not set down what I have not seen; but I have set down that a man wrote it and that it was taken away, because a thing taken away twice is a thing worth leaving a place for.

\subsection*{The full note}

Tap a sound pot with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. This is a thing the kiln-masters keep and the rest of us borrow when a pot is set down on a bench.

Once, in a birth room, a cup across the room gave the flat note while nobody touched it. I did not say what it was. There was a woman in labour and a slate on the bench and no advantage in adding a third thing to the room. I have written it here because a thing heard in a birth room and never mentioned is still a thing heard.

Do not knock a person to try it. A body is not a pot and the note of it is not ours to take. I knew a woman who tapped the chest of a child gone thin and said she had heard nothing back, and she said it as though the child had refused her. The child had not refused her. There was simply nothing there for her to hear.

A woman of the drying racks told me of a pot set down that answered nearly full --- a note between the two, almost the full one and never quite. I have not heard it and I have written it down because she was not a woman who made things up, and because a note that is almost full may be a thing a household could live with, if it came to that.

\subsection*{The song for the third night}

\emph{Sung low, to the child, while the watch is kept. The room says the last line with her.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone goes cold before the milk,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the milk goes cold before the bread;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a body is a pot with a flaw\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the flaw is where the heat has fled.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Warm the flaw and warm the pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape warm the place where the heat is not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the corners, four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one that does not answer when you call.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three days, three nights, a watch kept true;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the child, sing to the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

There is a space before the last line in the singing. I have left it on the page. It is the same space the kiln keeps and the bell keeps, and I have never filled it and never will.

\subsection*{What the narrow hand did}

A clerk borrowed the leaf on an Account-day and struck out my verbs. Where I wrote \emph{the heat went out of him}, he set \emph{the measure was drawn} above and left mine under it, saying that a book of physic is not a slate and need not be true in the same way. He wrote \emph{deduction} against the warmed stone and \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} against the night’s watch. He put a round nought in the space before the last line of the song and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. I have put the words back under his and left his standing. He has a figure for everything and a place for nothing.

There is a line at the foot in a hand I do not know, struck through and written again underneath: \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept.} It is not a remedy. It has no business in a book of physic. It is in the book now, and when I copy the leaf in Ilmen I shall copy it again, in that hand and not my own, as it stands.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The grey along the gutter came off my own cuff when I measured the ridge in a room two doors down and came back to write. The barley grease is from a crust laid on the leaf while a child was being told to eat and would not. The green bead is not slip. A girl with sweetness still at her mouth leaned over to see the writing and touched the paper and said nothing and went back to her work. I have not washed any of it.

The book goes back behind the meal bin. A slate is a thing that gets carried into the square and read in a clean voice; this is a thing that gets carried under an apron and taken out when the room is quiet. If an officer ever finds it, let him strike out what he will. The next woman will put the verbs back, as I did, and warm the stone before she reads.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The White Hands, Being the Drinking Song of the Stonemouth Quarry, Set Down in the Ale-Room Beside the Lime Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{The White Hands, Being the Drinking Song of the Stonemouth Quarry, Set Down in the Ale-Room Beside the Lime Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A quarrymen’s drinking song in Grathic, called over small ale after the lime draw and never at the quarry face; the words in a housekeeper’s small hand, the count as the men keep it, the lift said by the whole room, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk come up from Greybank, a face-man’s note in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Set down in Bone of Y.H. 811, the Long Cold, at Stonemouth where the Ferr comes into the Ilm, by the woman who keeps the ale-room beside the lime kiln and takes the men’s names for their ale; written in charcoal and lime-dust on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled by wet slate, and copied forward in Bone of Y.H. 812 into a quire of three leaves sewn with eel-sinew. It survives in a cracked pot on the shelf behind the room door: white lime ground into the grain at the head and worked into the creases of the first leaf, a blue-grey streak where a sleeve wet from the Ferr touched the fold, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first question to the last, a thumb of tallow, a lap of sandstone grit in the gutter, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, the clerk’s correction standing above the words, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the room where the men drink after the lime draw. I take their names for their ale and give the names back at the end of the tend when the factor’s man comes up from Greybank, which is a way of keeping accounts without owning them. I do not sing. I write down what is sung, which is quieter work and needs a better ear than singing does, though no man has ever said so.

The white at the head of this leaf is lime, not Ash. There is Ash enough in this room without bringing it into a book, and I have not swept either. A woman who sweeps before she writes will write a different song, and it will be a true one and no use to anybody.

\subsection*{The manner of it}

\emph{Written small at the head, in charcoal, with one word gone over in tallow.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item It is not sung at the face. A man who sings at the face has not yet learned where to put his feet, and the bank-man will send him home.

\item It is called after the lime draw, when the kiln has given up and the men have washed as far as their wrists. It is not a song for the kiln month. In Ember the kiln is working and a man’s heat is already spoken for.

\item The bank-man says the first line of a part and the room says the line after it. The lift belongs to everybody and is said into the cup, not across the table. A man who calls a lift loudly has to mean it, and there is not one man in this room who wants to be meant.

\item If a man in a clean coat comes up the road from Greybank, stop at the end of the part. Begin again when he has gone back down it. Nobody in Stonemouth will say why we stop, and the man in the clean coat never asks, which is how we have kept the habit for thirty years.

\end{itemize}

The lift, which ends every part:

\begin{quote}\itshape Lift to the stone; it outlasts the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape White hands, full cup, and the rest goes round.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the face}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven to the hole and the powder in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape stand where the bank-man tells you to stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone gives a note that is not a note\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dust comes up white on the land.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rope burns true and the cart goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sandstone answers dull when the wedge is set;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lift to the stone; it outlasts the name.\end{quote}
