The Court’s private answer is in the sealed file. Their real enemy is want itself, which they mean to abolish. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} They did not make the blizzard and they did not put the minivan on the ice. They wanted a vessel that gave at the moment of breaking, and found one in a country they could not have named. They paid to have the memories left in, which is the most expensive single purchase a banker in Sarn can make. Rusk taught Corin to make him the instrument. Marra has been paying for it ever since.

\section*{The Deep Hand}

\textbf{Kind.} Secret society of scholars; a reading of the oldest slates. \textbf{Seat.} A back table in the Keld survey shaft, and one room in the Hearthseat whose key is held by an assessor. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Ludo of the Old Kiln}, a Grathic scholar who found a slate in the ash throat; \textbf{Derren the Younger}, an officer’s son with access to the sealed file. \textbf{Goals.} To read the Deep Hand and learn what the oldest repairs were made of. \textbf{Methods.} Copying slates that are not meant to leave the shaft; comparing the Keld translation \emph{Ash} with the Court’s translation \emph{language}; asking the Vorr the wrong question and recording that the numbers are correct. \textbf{Resources.} One slate from the Old Kiln, a crossed-out page from Y.H. 588, and the observation that a pot mended many times is not the pot it was. \textbf{Enemies.} The College of Assessors. The Court, which removed a surveyor from the shaft in Y.H. 717 for writing \emph{words that hold}. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} They believe the oldest repairs are made of promises that were never kept, made solid. If this is true then the world is being held together by the very thing the Court’s economy produces, and the Keeping cannot be abolished without finding out what holds the walls up.

\CRrule

\section*{IV. Foreign powers at the border}

\section*{Keld — the Warden of the Rim}

\textbf{Kind.} Foreign power; mountain kingdom of iron, lead, coal and warm-stone. \textbf{Seat.} Keld Keep, with the First Seam beneath it and the Cold Pass ten leagues beyond. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Karric VII, Warden of the Rim}, who shut the Cold Pass in Y.H. 741; the mine-reeves beneath him. \textbf{Goals.} To hold the passes, keep the true Hearth claim alive, and sell iron and warm-stone to whoever pays without becoming anyone’s subject. \textbf{Methods.} Mercenaries, the Descent at thirteen, a measure stated before a name, and a treaty enforced at the point of a surveyor’s slate. \textbf{Resources.} Iron, lead, coal, warm-stone, the survey shaft, and a population that can hold a hot clamp against its palm without flinching. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court, which has never accepted the Hearth claim and has never bothered to argue it. The Sweating. Grathish clay-men levied into a war they did not choose. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The Warden knows the true Hearth is not under his mountain. He keeps the claim because it keeps the Court out of the shafts, and because a kingdom that believes it owns the source can charge more for its stone.

\section*{Sere — the Sun-Emperor}

\textbf{Kind.} Foreign power; hot empire of grain, wine, bowls and open slavery. \textbf{Seat.} The Bowl of Sere, three hundred leagues south of Sill. \textbf{Named leaders.} The \textbf{Sun-Emperor}, whose acts are announced by the emptying of a public bowl of wine; the Council of Bowls beneath him. \textbf{Goals.} To grow north by purchase rather than conquest, to buy measures cheaply, and to keep the Peat Line from becoming a border it has to defend. \textbf{Methods.} Agents with credit, the Bowl feast, a public burning of debt-slates followed by the making of new ones, and a phrase \emph{measure for measure} that means whatever the emperor has already decided. \textbf{Resources.} Gold crowns, grain, oil, wine, fine glazed ware, and the largest slave population in the world. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s deduction on grain. The Fenmarch. The northern habit of calling Sere spendthrifts. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The empire does not want territory in Grath. It wants the poor. A northern district that has been bought is more useful than a northern district that has been conquered, because nobody in a conquered district signs a contract.

\section*{Vhalen — the Council of Tides (as foreign power)}

\textbf{Kind.} Foreign power and trading republic; the gate between Grath and the Sallow Sea. \textbf{Seat.} Vhal, eighty leagues north-east of Sill by the Salt Road. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Avis Wake}, \textbf{Mav Hull}, \textbf{Dolf Brine}, rotating yearly. \textbf{Goals.} To keep the Salt Road open, to tax nothing that can be avoided, and to make the Court’s assessors feel poor in a room full of salt-paper. \textbf{Methods.} Contracts that rot in damp, a welcome for any traveller who pays, and the pulled benches for those who do not. \textbf{Resources.} Ships, salt, glass, rope, dried fish, and a legal system in which a wet document is no document at all. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s lists. The salt-thing. A hard winter that closes the coast pass. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} Half the port’s fortunes have turned on a contract going damp at the right moment. The Council’s real doctrine is not the Sallow Hearth but the convenient disappearance of evidence, which it has elevated into an art and a foreign policy.

\section*{Glossary of Sarn}

\emph{Entries for the reader. Every coined name set down in the Compendium so far is gathered here, in alphabetical order. Where a thing is known by different names in different countries, the common Grathic name is given first. A term whose deeper meaning is will be found in its own place in the Compendium; this glossary gives only what a traveller may hear in a market or a hearth.}

\CRrule

\section*{A}

\textbf{Account-day.} The tenth, twentieth and thirtieth day of every tend, when the slate is read aloud. In Grath these are also market-days.

\textbf{The Afterdrop.} The worsening before recovery in a rekindled or rewarmed vessel. The ordinary cause is a graft settling; midwives call it the second chill.

\textbf{The Ash.} Grey silt that gathers where promises are unkept, in corners and under beds, invisible in daylight and plain by tallow-light. The poor leave it on the Last Day and burn it next morning. On Stone 29, Y.H. 812 a woman at the tubs told a girl beside her that the grey would be left where it lay until the Last Day and burned the morning afterward and called dealt with.

\textbf{Ash-mite.} A small grey mite that lives in the Ash and drinks the thin edge of a sleeper’s measure. Invisible by day; troublesome in poor rooms.

\textbf{Ash-runners.} Criminal smugglers of the Fenmarch who move Warm and sell quiet ash without a Court licence.

\textbf{Ash Rising.} The rising in Low Kiln in Y.H. 668 after ninety children’s warmth was taken for a private account; put down by Assessor-Marshal Pell Varr.

\textbf{Ash-sickness.} The condition of dreaming in another person’s voice after long exposure to an Ash-wraith.

\textbf{Ash-wraith.} A grey shape seen by tallow-light where many have been spent; it follows the Ash ridge from room to room.

\textbf{Assessor.} An officer of the Warm Court who decides what a life was worth and how much of its measure may be kept back.

\section*{B}

\textbf{The bell at the Cross.} A bell struck at market morning and afternoon, longer than a church bell; nobody crosses himself at it. The boy counts four strokes, four, and a place where the fifth should be. No one in Sill explains what it is for. On Seed 10, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of Seed, it went four, four and a gap over the market while Berr Clay read one in twelve twice over the basket, and nobody crossed himself; the heard bell stayed in its own place beside the told bell of the Long Night. The phrase \emph{the bell’s fourth stroke had been missing} in one paragraph of that day is a slip: the missing stroke is the fifth.

\textbf{Birth-flower.} The branching red mark some infants are born with, shaped like frost on a pane or a burn gone into the skin. Hearth-maids call it a flower, cross two fingers over it and say nothing about the sign. Alda Reed crossed herself over Corin’s on Stone 7, Y.H. 812, and covered the act with the word.

\textbf{Birth-slate.} The flat slate a hearth-maid keeps within reach at a birth, on which the child and the day are entered. In Low Kiln it lies on the bench, and a midwife’s hand goes to it before it goes to the child. A second hand may have written on it before anyone looked at the face.

\textbf{The Bowl.} The Sere coming-of-age feast at sixteen, where a young person empties a bowl of warm wine and names a debt they intend to carry.

\textbf{Bought breath.} A person sold for a term, usually a season or a year, to repay a debt. The common form of slavery in the Fenmarch.

\textbf{The Breaking.} The spring flood, when the Ilm comes up over the Fishstairs and takes the low houses; also the Silt thaw itself. The year’s flood of Silt 9–15, Y.H. 813 came up in a thin brown sheet, stood on the Fishstairs and went around both the Vail corner and the burned ridge two doors down, then went off into mud; the district called it weather and then the thaw that was. It is not the great Breaking of later years, when the low houses are taken and the town’s thin place is named.

\textbf{Brine-gull.} A Sallow-coast gull that steals anything warm: a loaf, a warmed stone, a coal not yet out. On Ilmen 16, Y.H. 813 one went off upriver below the north bridge with a coal from somebody’s banked fire that was not yet cold, carrying the warmth out of the fire’s account; no slate in Sill stood one mark the poorer for it.

\textbf{Broken Slates.} A rebel network of Low Kiln, descended from survivors of the Ash Rising, which seeks to destroy the slates and end the levy.

\textbf{C}

\textbf{The carried fire (the year’s fire).} The new fire taken into every house on Kindling: a coal under ash comes up the yard in a clay dish, each hearth touches its own flame to it and passes it on, and the last house keeps what is left. In Low Kiln nobody says where the flame was first lit or what it cost, and the Vail house keeps it banked under ash and never answers a question about its payer. On Ilmen 16, Y.H. 813 a brine-gull carried off one of its coals, not yet cold, upriver; one warmth less went out of the house’s account and was missed in no account, and the fire went on taking its breath in fours and a gap. Through Ilmen 19–25, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four; the coal the gull took was entered in no slate and missed in no account.

Through Silt 2–8, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed; the coal a brine-gull took on Ilmen 16 was twenty-two days gone and entered in no slate. Through Silt 9–15 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed; the coal the gull took was twenty-nine days gone and entered in no slate. Through Silt 16–18 it still lay at four, four and a gap under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed; the door stood a finger’s width open and the river’s note came through the gap, kept apart from the fire’s four-four-and-a-gap as it had been for seventy-seven days. Through Silt 19–25, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed; the mud of the lean week went around the two lines in the corner and the fire’s gap came up through the floor while the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door, the two sounds kept in two places. Through Silt 26–30 and Seed 1 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees; its payer had gone unnamed for ninety days and the coal the brine-gull took upriver was entered in no slate and missed in none. Through Seed 2–4 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed for ninety-three days; Sella told it the thaw each day and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot. Through Seed 5–11 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, missing one breath in every four and warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and touched no widow’s mark, because a shelf, a strip, a basket, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings. The river’s low note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the fire’s gap came up through the floor, in two separate places as for a hundred days. Through Seed 2–4 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed for ninety-three days; through Seed 5–11 it was unnamed for a hundred days; and through Seed 12–14, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed for a hundred and three days. Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, and touched no widow’s mark, because a shelf, a strip, a basket and a bed are not openings. Through Seed 15–17, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred and six days; Sella told it the thaw each day and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, and the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. Through Seed 18–20 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nine days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and stood a moment at the fire counting something under her breath, joined to no opening. Through Seed 21–23, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred and twelve days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and fed them, and the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. Through Seed 24–26 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed for a hundred and fifteen days; Sella told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and the fire gave back four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been while the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the two counts did not meet.

\textbf{Clay-bound.} A debt-servant working off a term, commonly seven years, with interest gathering as grey Ash in the household accounts.

\textbf{Clay-name.} The name a slave is given by the household that owns them; the old name is forbidden.

\textbf{Clay Road.} The packed-clay road from the Cross at Sill to Greybank, eighteen leagues; a Court road since the treaty of Y.H. 418.

\textbf{Clay Yard.} The slip pits, wheel shed, drying racks and kiln in Low Kiln; the whole world of a clay child.

\textbf{The clinical ear.} The ability to hear a faulty vessel before touching it. Dan possesses it to an unnatural degree; the Kiln-Masters of Sill have quietly noted it.

\textbf{Closed counting room (the Greybank saying).} A counting room shut during the last war with the damper closed, in which the men inside died of the breath rather than of the war’s hand. On Ilmen 26, Y.H. 813 a man come downriver from Greybank told it at the Low Kiln well as a curiosity with a date, eighteen leagues east; the yard took it for history and nobody joined it to any kiln in the district. In houses that keep their breath in fours and a gap the saying is heard differently, though no one says so aloud. On Silt 25, Y.H. 813 a second man come downriver from Greybank repeated it at the same well as a curiosity with a date, and the yard took it as history again; the boy filed the second telling on the same tray as the first without letting the two touch, keeping the likeness and the difference --- breath through the nose against breath in the throat, both saying \emph{not the war’s hand} --- and joined neither to any kiln. No third telling came in the last five days of Silt or on Seed 1, and the two stayed on their own tray beside the told bell, the heard bell, the early Sill note and the kiln’s gap, likeness and difference kept and joined to no kiln. Sella, who lost a husband to that danger, heard both and told the fire it was the thaw, and never once described it that way herself. On Seed 13, Y.H. 813 a neighbour at the bucket-round only mentioned a counting room shut in the war with the men inside dead of the breath — a mention with a date in it and none of the weight, not a telling — and no third telling came. The two earlier tellings stayed on their tray joined to no kiln, likeness and difference kept; Sella, who lost a husband to that danger, told the fire it was the thaw and never once described it that way herself.

\textbf{The Cold.} The absence of Warm; a material substance in Sarn, with a place to put what is taken.

\textbf{Cold Acre.} A barley-and-turnip hamlet two leagues north of Sill on the ridge, with one well that never freezes.

\textbf{Cold iron.} Iron that draws Warm out of a vessel and gives none back; used in the collector’s tube and in clamps.

\textbf{Cold Pass.} The mountain pass beyond Keld Keep, closed in Y.H. 741 and fixed as Grath’s northern border by the agreement of Y.H. 747.

\textbf{The cold that stays.} A foot or hand that remains cold after the water around it has gone down and the person has been wrapped in wool and carried inside. On Silt 12, Y.H. 813 a child wading below the sill at Sill came up with a foot that stayed cold after the water fell; a woman wrapped it and called it the cold, while the yard called the water weather, so the two names never met. Nobody in the yard gave the staying cold a cause or a treatment, and it was entered in no account. A surgeon’s eye would read the extremity going before the core and the worse hour waiting on the far side of a warming. Through Silt 19–25, Y.H. 813 the foot stayed the cold to the woman who wrapped it and weather to the yard through the whole lean week, with no hand placed, no cause and no treatment; the boy read the extremity going before the core and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, and the reading bought nothing. Through Silt 26–30 and onto Seed 1 it was still the cold to that woman and weather to the yard, carried across the turn of the month uncured, uncaused and unnamed; the surgeon’s reading of the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform worked perfectly and bought nothing. Through Seed 2–4 it was still the cold to one woman and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed, while the first seed went into the strips; the boy’s reading had the usefulness of an instrument held behind glass. On Seed 9 the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool, the woman wound it round and called it the cold and a neighbour at the tubs called the water weather, so the two facts went past each other and never met; the boy read the extremity going before the core and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, and had no hand two paces long. Through Seed 12–14, Y.H. 813 the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool below the sill; the woman wound it round and called it the cold while a neighbour at the tubs called the water weather, so the two facts still went past each other and never met. The boy read the extremity going before the core and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, and the reading bought nothing. Through Seed 18–20 the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, the cold to one woman and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed, and no silt-leach, cause or cure was spoken. Through Seed 21–23, Y.H. 813 it was still the cold inside three turns of wool below the sill, uncured, uncaused and unnamed, the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform; the boy’s reading of the extremity going before the core worked perfectly and bought nothing, and no silt-leach, cause or cure was spoken. Through Seed 24–26 it was still the cold inside three turns of wool below the sill, cold to one woman and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed; the afterdrop waited past a warming nobody would perform and the reading bought nothing.

\textbf{Cold work.} Work done in cold rooms, especially the greyed-finger labour of a collector; the Court’s phrase for a punishment that damages the hand.

\textbf{Cold-eater.} A Wasteling shape that stands close to a vessel and draws its Warm away; it takes, and does not give.

\textbf{Collector.} An officer of the Warm Court who draws the measure from the dying with a cold iron tube and records it on a slate.

\textbf{College of Assessors.} The academy in the Hearthseat that teaches Ledgerhand and the valuation of lives, and holds the only right to write a lawful deduction.

\textbf{Council of Tides.} The elected government of Vhalen, composed of ship-owners and salt-masters, whose decrees are written on salt-paper that rots in damp.

\textbf{Court’s room.} The room in Slate Row where the slate is read aloud on market-day and the district’s measure is spoken for; in the Keeping, bank and church are one room. A neighbour come back from it on Stone 19, Y.H. 812 described a bench by the door, a pot on the bench, a draught under it going along the floor to the corner, and a place in the figures where a line should stand and does not --- the same furniture as a birth room, a kiln-house and a death-house, which the boy keeps in four separate places rather than call them one room.

\textbf{Crown.} A gold coin worth twenty silver marks, common in Sere and rarely seen in Grath.

\textbf{Cup-bank.} A procedure for storing Warm outside the body in clay or iron, to be spent later or by another.

\textbf{Cupworm.} A blind worm that bores clay from the inside, so that a pot looks sound and breaks at first pouring.

\textbf{D}

\textbf{Damper.} The iron gate across a kiln’s throat that stops the heat running and lets it out by degrees. The Grathic word carries only the holding; on Seed 3, Y.H. 813 Jorra Vail put his bent finger into it ahead of an unfinished sentence, and the boy read it as the same bite that keeps a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man --- mercy and mutilation in one piece of iron, with no word in Grathic that holds both. It is the iron of the Greybank saying about a counting room shut with the damper closed, which the yard takes as history eighteen leagues east and the Vail house keeps under its own roof. On Seed 7, Y.H. 813, Jorra Vail put his bent finger into the damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, the cold iron taking the cold out of his fingertip, and the household straightened around his silence as cloth straightens when a weight is lifted; the boy read the same bite that keeps a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man, with no word in Grathic that holds both mercies, and filed the reading as an object worth nothing. On Seed 13, Y.H. 813 Jorra Vail again put his bent finger into the damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, the cold iron taking the cold out of his fingertip, so the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted; he read the iron as the bite that holds a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man, with no word in Grathic that holds both mercies, and filed the reading as an object worth nothing. On Seed 16 he put the bent finger into the cold iron ahead of her sentence again, the iron taking the cold out of his fingertip while the household straightened around his silence; the reading of the double bite was filed as an object, exact and worth nothing, joined to no kiln and still with no Grathic word for both mercies. On Seed 19 he did the same before first grey with men unnamed in the back room; the iron took the cold out of his fingertip, the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted, and the boy read the bite that holds a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man and filed it as an object joined to no kiln. On Seed 22, Y.H. 813 he put the bent finger into the cold iron ahead of her unfinished sentence once more, the iron taking the cold out of his fingertip and giving a little back in reverse of the core; the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence. \textbf{For the first time} Tarn’s broom checked half a beat behind the finger standing in the iron and then went on toward the road without a word or a turn of the head: the two silences stood in one room unjoined, the loan that can hear was not called, and the boy filed the half-check beside the bent finger on one tray without laying a finger across them.

\textbf{Debt left lying.} A debt nobody has picked up, which is not the same as a debt forgiven; a saying kept in the Vail kiln-house in Silt, Y.H. 813, where Garl’s tile debt lay where it lay through seven days of higher water.

\textbf{Debt Loft.} The narrow sleeping loft above a potter’s wheel-shed in Low Kiln where a household’s clay-bound hands sleep. In a poor house a foundling may be given a bed under the roof while a debt is given the loft, and the difference is not argued about.

\textbf{Deep Hand.} The unread script of the oldest slates and seam records; the Vorr recognise its numbers but will not translate it in full.

\textbf{Deduction.} The portion of a banked measure kept back for the Hearth. Taught as one part in twelve and printed on the Weighing notices.

\textbf{Descent.} The Keldish coming-of-age at thirteen: one day down the mine, after which some have their number changed.

\textbf{Dippers.} The salt priests of Vhalen, who bless nets by trailing them in the sea at dawn and read the Sallow draw.

\textbf{E}

\textbf{Eel-bones.} The small bones a Fishstairs seller flicks against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, one put away when the deciding is done. Mira Silt’s are a tell the boy watches without anybody knowing he watches; the movement is entered nowhere.

\textbf{Ember.} The Court’s unit of booked warmth, said to be worth five marks; a newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen embers.

\textbf{Empty Cantons.} A province sixty leagues south of Grath with roads, wells and doorways but no people after Y.H. 40.

\textbf{F}

\textbf{The Fenmarch.} The reed and peat confederacy south-west of Grath, governed by reeves chosen for standing longest in a bog.

\textbf{Fen-leech (bog-cow).} A large horned beast of the peat bogs that stands half-submerged and pushes a man down into the mud.

\textbf{The Ferr.} A cold tributary of the Ilm, about forty leagues long, carrying lead dust from the western workings.

\textbf{The Final Banking.} The Unbanked’s design for making every vessel perfectly retentive, so that nothing leaks, nothing is owed, and nothing can be given away.

\textbf{The First Breaking.} The temple’s name for the single moment of anger in which the world was cracked.

\textbf{The First Firing.} The Grathic coming-of-age at twelve: a child makes a pot, fires it, and knocks it with a knuckle. A clear note means a feast; a flat note means another year in the yard.

\textbf{The First Seam.} The deep survey shaft beneath Keld Keep, where the oldest repairs are recorded and a crossed-out entry of Y.H. 588 is kept.

\textbf{The first way.} The procedure of opening a channel in the forearm by cutting across a surface way and keeping it open while it scars.

\textbf{The Five (Five Cold Days).} The five days outside the months at the year’s end: Kindling, Weighing, the Long Night, the Remembering and the Last Day.

\textbf{Fish Blessing.} The rite held at the Weir one league upriver of Sill on Ilmen 15 (in Y.H. 813 it fell on Day 44), when the hearth-maids stand on the flat stone with its crossed mark and bless the weir and the eel traps. The traps have their mouths upriver so an eel goes in and cannot find the way out; the eels run whether anybody blesses them or not. A saying of the Weir: \emph{the brook takes what no slate will enter; the knot keeps what no clerk can spell; the eels run whether anybody blesses them or not.}

\textbf{Flat note.} The small dead sound a cracked vessel gives when it is set down or tapped --- the shadow of the full note, a sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. Dan hears it before anyone touches the vessel and has no Grathic word for it. By Stone 12, Y.H. 812 he has heard it five times from four sources --- a cup across a birth room, a pot in the Vail house, the district’s own reading slate twice, and a dying man at the Hearth Drawing, the fifth and the first from a person --- and nobody has tapped any of them for him. On Stone 13 a pot was turned toward before it was set down and gave nothing --- an interval with the shape of a sound, not a sixth hearing, which the boy kept as an object. On Stone 17 a second pot was turned toward under the Vail roof and gave nothing; the two intervals lie on a separate tray from the hearings, On Stone 22 a vessel carried past the Vail door gave it too far and too muffled to confirm, and on Stone 25 a pot cracked all the way through two paces from the basket and was called a pot gone wrong; both went on the separate tray of intervals, and through Stone 30 the count stands at five from four sources with no sixth. On Ilmen 6, Y.H. 813 a pot set down out of a woman’s shadow answered \emph{nearly full} --- a third sound, neither the flat answer nor a silence --- and was filed as the first earthly answer to the interval first kept on Stone 13; it is not a sixth hearing and there is no Grathic word for nearly. On Ilmen 9, Y.H. 813 the small flat knock came out of a woman lifted from the clay-heavy Slip Brook --- the sixth hearing, and the second that had ever come from a person --- and lay beside the five from four sources without being among them; no seventh came. Through Ilmen 16–18 the count stood at six, five from four sources and one from a person; the clerk’s open slate at the Fishstairs gave nothing and no seventh hearing came. On Ilmen 21, Y.H. 813 a vessel carried past the Vail yard door gave its note too far and too muffled to place and Tarn’s head did not turn, and on Ilmen 23 a second pot set down in the Clay Yard answered \emph{nearly full} with air under the note and a want in it; the boy filed the second answer beside the first as an answer to the interval kept since Stone 13, advanced and not paid. The count still stood at six with no seventh, no hand to tap either pot and no Grathic word for nearly.

Through Days 61–67 the count stood at six hearings --- five from four sources and the sixth out of a person --- beside and never among, with no seventh; a third pot answered \emph{nearly full} on Silt 6 and was filed advanced and not paid beside the answers of Ilmen 6 and Ilmen 23, while three intervals stayed objects and water-over-water was a fifth low thing that was not a hearing at all. Through Silt 9–15 the count stood at six beside and never among, with no seventh; a vessel gave its note past the yard door on the afternoon of Silt 15 and Tarn’s head did not turn, and the boy did not call it a hearing. In the flood the note of the whole district went on underneath the four low sounds as a fifth thing with no word in Grathic. Through Silt 16–18 the count still stood at six beside and never among, with no seventh; a vessel gave its note past the yard door on Silt 16 and a whole vessel did so on Silt 18, and neither Tarn’s head nor the boy’s turned toward either. At the well a foundling turned his head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy’s --- after the knuckle and after the note --- and the boy filed that turning with the intervals as a thing that came after the knock and was not a hearing. Through Silt 26–30 and Seed 1 the count held at six hearings --- five from vessels and the sixth out of a person --- beside and never among with no seventh; a vessel gave its note past the door on Silt 27 and again on Seed 1 and neither Tarn nor the boy turned toward it or named the sound, and the foundling’s head turned a half-beat late at the market’s edge on Silt 30, which was not a hearing either. Through Seed 2–4 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among; a vessel gave its note past the yard door on Days 91 and 92, Tarn’s head did not turn and neither he nor the boy named the sound or called it a seventh hearing. Through Seed 5–11 they stayed six beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with no seventh; vessels gave their notes past the door on Seed 7 and Seed 9 and neither head turned nor was the sound named. At the market’s edge on Seed 9 a foundling turned his head toward a pot half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, and stopped and rubbed the green sliver at his throat; the boy filed that delay as a thing that comes after the knock, not a hearing and not a seventh, and kept his own turning beside it without letting the two touch. Three near-full answers stood advanced and not paid, three intervals on another tray, and the river’s note of water going over water was a fifth low thing and not a hearing. Through Seed 2–4 and Seed 5–11 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with no seventh, while vessels gave their notes past the door and neither Tarn nor the boy turned toward them or named them. Through Seed 12–14, Y.H. 813 the count still stood at six beside and never among; no seventh came. A woman moving a pot on Seed 12 lifted it a hand’s breadth too high and something came up to the rim of a note and went back down, a near thing kept on the interval tray and added to no seventh, because a thing that comes up to the edge of a sound is not the sound. Through Seed 15–17 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among with no seventh; three near-full answers advanced and not paid, three intervals on another tray, four low things in four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut counting room joined to no kiln; no Grathic word for the flat note and no hand to tap any of them. Through Seed 18–20 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among with no seventh, three near-full answers advanced and not paid, three intervals, the word forty unspoken with the readable double turn and the weight of a thumb apart, four low things in four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut room joined to no kiln; the heard bell stayed beside the told bell and no seventh hearing came. Through Seed 21–23 the count still stood at six beside and never among with no seventh; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, and Tarn’s broom checking half a beat behind Jorra’s bent finger standing in the damper on Seed 22 was filed on the interval tray as another place where a stroke should have gone on and did not --- not a hearing, not a seventh, and joined to no cause. The word forty stayed unspoken, four low things kept their four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut room stayed joined to no kiln. Through Seed 24–26 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among with no seventh; three near-full answers stood advanced and not paid, and the unchecking stroke of Seed 25 — Tarn’s broom going on over the flagstones without the half-check it had made the day before, the stones keeping the place where it had stopped — was filed beside the earlier half-beat on the interval tray as another place where a stroke should have gone on and did not, held and not repeated, not a hearing, not a seventh and joined to no cause. The word forty stayed unspoken with the readable double turn and the weight of a thumb apart, four low things kept their four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut room stayed joined to no kiln.

\textbf{The full note.} The full sound a sound vessel gives under the knuckle; a cracked vessel answers flat. The first tool of the clinical ear.

\textbf{Forty.} The number the hearth-maids and the people of the Weir give to the children of Low Kiln taken in the levy in Y.H. 812, kept in knots on grey wool rather than on any slate. It is spoken of as a count and is not explained in the market. Orra Weir tied forty knots in the year of the flower and then a forty-first she could not account for; on Ilmen 15, Y.H. 813 she said the word low into a basket and watched what the child in it would do, and the child could not answer. On Ilmen 16 the boy read the shape of the extra knot without a name for it, and the word was not spoken a second time.

\textbf{Frost-bloom.} An ice flower that grows where Warm has recently left; a map of the leak that made it. On Ilmen 18, Y.H. 813 it stood up in white fronds on the stone lip of the Low Kiln yard well where the Warm had lately gone out of the stone; the bucket knocked the heads off it and the sun took the rest by noon, and the yard called it weather. On Ilmen 19 and again on Ilmen 25, Y.H. 813 it wrote itself back onto the same lip in white fronds after the argument over the ice had ended; the rope went over the lip without touching it, and the yard called it weather both times, so that a woman could go home warm without owning the morning.

\textbf{G}

\textbf{Glass eel.} An eel of the Ilm and Ferr that stores a little Warm in a sac behind the head and can stop a wader’s ways in the water.

\textbf{The Glaze Cliffs.} Blue-green cliffs on the Vhaleni coast stained by old lead workings, sweet-smelling in the heat.

\textbf{Grath.} The clay country of river towns, kilns and peat in the north-west of the bowl; Corin’s birth country.

\textbf{Grathic.} The common tongue of the bowl: short vowels, hard \emph{k} and \emph{thr}, little inflection, written on slate with chalk.

\textbf{Greybank.} The Court’s granary and factor’s house eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, where the Clay Road ends and the Hearth Road begins.

\textbf{Grey fingers.} The discoloration of a collector’s fingertips after years of drawing Warm; a mark of the trade and, in extreme cases, of exhaustion. On Stone 22, Y.H. 812 a collector fetched for a neighbour two doors down had them the colour of skimmed milk gone off under a cuff soft from washing; the boy filed him on a tray of his own, not joined to the woman at the flare or to the clerk at the Cross.

\textbf{H}

\textbf{Half-beat.} A head turned a breath after the knock rather than before it. On Silt 16, Y.H. 813, at the Low Kiln well, a small foundling in cast-off clothes turned his head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy in the basket did --- after the knuckle came down on the wet stone and after the pot gave its note --- then stopped, rubbed the green lead-glaze sliver at his neck and could not say why he had turned. The boy, who turns toward a pot before anyone taps it, filed the delay as an object on a place of its own: a thing that comes after the knock is a different thing from one that comes before it, and this was neither a hearing nor a seventh. He kept his own turning beside the child’s without letting the two touch. The half-beat is the physical tell held for the day the foundling’s small sales land as a betrayal; the yard took it for a child’s quickness and the warm loaf he took from a man from Slate Row for a kindness, with no slate standing between giver and receiver. On Silt 19, Y.H. 813 the same small foundling was glimpsed once more at the well in cast-offs with the green sliver at his throat: when a pot was set down his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s and he rubbed the sliver and could not say why, and no loaf passed and no slate was seen. The delay stayed a thing that comes after the knock, neither a hearing nor a seventh. On Silt 30, Y.H. 813 at the last market of Silt he was glimpsed a second time at the market’s edge, unnamed in the narration, cast-offs worn like a uniform and a gap in his grin; when a pot was set down his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped, and he rubbed the green sliver and could not say why. No loaf passed, no slate was seen and no secret was sold; the boy kept the second delay on a place of its own beside the first and wrote no cause across either. On Seed 9, Y.H. 813, he was glimpsed a third time at the edge of the Fishstairs market, unnamed in the narration, with silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap in his grin and the green sliver at his throat; when a pot was set down his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, then stopped, and he rubbed the sliver, opened his mouth on the tail of a kiln-hand’s sentence and let nothing out that a slate could take down. No loaf passed, no slate was opened within reach of the basket and no sale was paid. The delay is held for the day the watcher’s small sales land as betrayal. On Seed 19, Y.H. 813, he was glimpsed an unnamed fourth time at the dawn market below the north bridge, cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap in his grin and a green sliver at his throat; when a kiln-hand set a pot down near the eel shade his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped, and he rubbed the sliver and opened his mouth on the tail of a sentence without letting anything out that a clerk could take down. No loaf passed, no slate was seen and no sale was paid; the boy set the delay after the knock, not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh, and set the watcher’s turning beside the two tellings of the shelf as a third shape, joining none of them.

\textbf{The hands go in by the look.} A planting saying of Low Kiln: \emph{The seed goes in by the fist and the hands go in by the look. Ask either what it cost and it will tell you the weather.} On Seed 15, Y.H. 813 the hands the strips had been said to want went into the worked ground east of Low Kiln, counted in glances and handfuls and never in a figure; a woman let seed out of her fist and would not say what it held, and a man with a barrow shaped the number of hands and thought better of it, so that the district’s withholding was done in the planting itself. The season’s figure went from the strip to a man’s teeth and back to the strip and was given to nobody. See \textbf{Seed}.

\textbf{Hearth.} The great source of the Warm, a chamber of stone beneath the Keel, said to hold what the world had when it was made.

\textbf{The Hearth Drawing.} The first collection of the year, on Stone 12; a collector may draw from the dying and the newly born on the same day. In Y.H. 812 the year’s first measure was taken in a Low Kiln death-house and entered on a slate in the same figure the Cross had read aloud on Account-day; before the day was out a newly born child in the same room grew worse on the third day of a return.

\textbf{Hearth-fire (Hearth-flame).} The flame kept behind a grating of cold iron in the Weighing Hall; it has never gone out and no priest may touch it.

\textbf{Hearth-maids.} The midwives, collectors’ assistants and keepers of the birth-slates in Grathic villages.

\textbf{Hearth Road.} The merchants’ road from Greybank south-east to the Hearthseat, a hundred and forty leagues.

\textbf{Hearth-tongue.} The Hearth-fire drawn up through the Keel; a procedure by which the Hearthward draw, and the name of the fire in the Weighing Hall.

\textbf{Hearth-wisp.} A small light that gathers where a banked fire has been left and draws warmth from a sleeper.

\textbf{Hearthseat.} The Court’s city on the Keel, built over the Hearth, where the Weighing Hall, the sealed files and fewer than twenty Kept vessels are kept.

\textbf{Hearthward.} The rank of a vessel that can draw from the Hearth itself and is therefore never cold.

\textbf{Held.} The rank of a vessel that can carry more than its natural measure.

\textbf{High Kiln.} The master potters’ quarter on the terrace above Low Kiln, where the glaze is mixed and the lead smell hangs.

\textbf{The Hollow.} A vessel whose head has fallen so low it can no longer draw warmth from food; also a thin-return child with almost no shape in it.

\textbf{Honeyed ice.} The low country’s word for ice going soft from underneath while the top still looks sound; on Ilmen 2, Y.H. 813 a man come up from the Ilm told the yard the ice was honeyed under the mud, and a woman at the well said the water tasted different. The district passes the word around and will not say the word for the thaw itself, which lets a person go home without owning the day. On Ilmen 19 and Ilmen 25, Y.H. 813 the man who had said \emph{honeyed} kept his counsel and the woman who had said the ice would hold said nothing at all, so that the old argument ended with nobody left to carry it.

On Silt 8, Y.H. 813 a man come back from looking said the ice was \emph{honeyed all through, not just at the edge; you could cut it and find it yellow in the middle}, and the dark current showed through the skin of the Ilm in veins; the boy set the saying and the sight on places that did not touch. On Silt 15 the ice that had been honeyed all through was spoken of past tense as the thaw that was.

\textbf{Hot trace.} Warmth that leaves a vessel in an act of giving and stays hot, tangled with an unpaid promise, instead of cooling into the bank.

\textbf{House roll.} A household’s own slate of names and entries, kept close and not shown to the Court’s assessor. In Low Kiln a house that keeps its own account does not need to explain the keeping, only to keep it.

\textbf{House Vail.} The kiln-house of Low Kiln held by the Vail family for four generations; Sella Vail keeps the fire.

\textbf{I}

\textbf{Ice-mouse.} A field mouse of frozen fields whose bite leaves a spreading numb patch, frostbite by another road.

\textbf{The Ilm.} The great silty river of Grath, frozen from Stone into Ilmen, breaking in the Silt flood; it rises in the Rim and drains into the Sallow Sea.

\textbf{K}

\textbf{Keld.} The mountain kingdom of the Rim, living on iron, lead, coal and warm-stone and ruled by the Warden of the Rim.

\textbf{Keld Keep.} The Warden’s fortress city where a man states his measure before his name and the deep survey shaft begins.

\textbf{Kept.} The highest rank in Sarn: a vessel the Court has made effectively unbreakable. Fewer than twenty exist; they are spoken of with pity and no longer feel the cold. Also a term for chattel slaves in Grath.

\textbf{Kiln’s breath.} The invisible poison of a closed kiln house or cellar; it kills in sleep and is called a merciful death by those who have not identified the body. On Ilmen 26, Y.H. 813 a man come downriver from Greybank described at the well a counting room shut in the last war with the damper closed and the men inside dead of the breath; he said it as something that happened eighteen leagues east, and nobody in the yard connected it to the kiln’s own missing fifth breath under their roofs.

Through Silt 2–8, Y.H. 813 the carried fire under the Vail roof still took its breath in fours and a gap, keeping the missing fourth as carefully as the breaths that came. On Silt 25 a second man come downriver from Greybank repeated at the well the saying of a counting room shut during the last war with the damper closed and the men inside dead of the breath, eighteen leagues east; Sella told the fire it was the thaw and nobody joined the story to any kiln in Low Kiln, though the boy filed the second telling beside the first with no cause written across either. On Seed 13, Y.H. 813 a voice at the bucket-round only mentioned a room shut in the war with the damper closed and the men inside dead of the breath, eighteen leagues east; it was a mention, not a third telling, and nobody in Low Kiln joined it to any kiln in the district, though the Vail fire under its own roof still took its breath in fours and a gap and Sella told it the thaw.

\textbf{Kiln-hound.} A feral dog of old kilns whose hot breath carries the kiln’s own poison.

\textbf{Kiln-Masters of Sill.} The craft guild that holds the kilns, the First Firing and the knowledge of the full note in Grath.

\textbf{Knot-string.} A length of grey wool in which a woman keeps her accounts by tying knots instead of writing names, so that an officer cannot read it and a fire cannot take a name from it. Orra Weir of the Weir keeps forty knots and a forty-first she cannot account for; Mira Silt of the Fishstairs keeps two cords, one twisted twice beneath the other, and has never counted the knots on either. A knot in wool has to be looked at by the woman who tied it, and stays where she left it. On Ilmen 16, Y.H. 813 the boy could read the \textbf{shape} of Orra’s forty-first knot --- a double turn with the tail tucked, tied left over right, the small extra weight of a thumb setting it --- but not its name; the word was not spoken again and the cord went back upriver to the Eel House unread. On Ilmen 24, Y.H. 813 Mira Silt showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey at the Fishstairs, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted, and her board stood beside Orra’s without touching it; the shape of the extra knot was legible to the boy without its name and the word was not spoken.

On Silt 2, Y.H. 813 Mira again showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey when a figure was spoken at the Fishstairs, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. On Silt 13 Mira again showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey when a buyer named a figure, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots uncounted; Orra stood at the flood’s edge with her board and her cord and got no answer, and the word was not spoken. On Silt 17 she showed it again when a buyer said \emph{two marks the pair and two short}, with neither knot counted and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it, and the word was not spoken. On Silt 20 and Silt 24, Y.H. 813 she again showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey when a figure was named at the Fishstairs, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the thin child’s knot untouched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. On Silt 29 she showed it again when a buyer named a figure, answering a question about the run with her own answer and moving eel-bones while deciding whether to lie; the second cord was never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot was counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver was not touched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. On Seed 8, Y.H. 813, she showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey when a buyer named a figure, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. Orra watched from where she watched and got no answer, and the word forty was not spoken. On Seed 14, Y.H. 813 Mira Silt shifted a creel at the Fishstairs and showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched; her board lay beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and did not touch it, and Orra watched from where she watched and got no answer. On Seed 17 she answered a question about the run with her own answer, moved eel-bones while deciding whether to lie, and when a buyer named a figure put her thumb under her apron to the grey cord and showed the second twisted twice beneath it with neither knot counted, her board beside Orra’s and not touching, the thin child’s knot untouched; Orra watched and got no answer. On Seed 19, Y.H. 813, at the end of the fish-trade shade she answered a question about the run with her own answer, moved eel-bones while deciding whether to lie, and when a buyer in a coat with the river in its hem named a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed longer than the figure required, showing the second twisted twice beneath it, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the thin child’s knot untouched; her board lay beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and did not touch it, and Orra stood where she stood and got no answer and the word forty was unspoken. On Seed 23, Y.H. 813 she worked at the very end of the fish-trade shade with pale slime dried in long grey strokes on her sleeves, silt dried pale in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where her left ear had been; asked whether the run would be thin she answered \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river}, moved eel-bones while deciding whether to lie and put one away, and when a buyer in a coat with the river in its hem named a figure her thumb went under her apron and stayed longer than the figure required, showing the second cord twisted twice beneath it with neither knot counted and the thin child’s knot untouched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it, and Orra was upriver and present only as the board.

On Seed 26, Y.H. 813 Mira Silt worked the eels at the outer boards of the fish-trade shade with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt dried pale in the hollow of her neck and her head held a little to the right where the top of her left ear had been; asked whether the run would be thin now that the planting had gone into its last tend she answered her own answer, \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river}, moved eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and put one away, and said something low about the boat that came up on the flood and nothing about the hands in the strips. When a buyer named a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed longer than the figure required; shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lay beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and did not touch it; Orra was upriver and present only as the board, the cord lying where a cord lies when a woman has gone away from it and left it where it was.

\textbf{Kindling.} The first of the Five, when every hearth in Sarn is lit from the Hearth-flame and collectors take the year’s first measure.

\textbf{L}

\textbf{Last Day.} The fifth and last of the Five Cold Days. Bread is baked, and the grey Ash in the corners is left where it lies to be burned the next morning and called dealt with.

\textbf{The last market.} The Account-day at the end of Stone, when the year’s stores are counted into the last tend and the Five are spoken of as three days off by a district that has already decided what it will pay. Sill’s last market of Y.H. 812 fell on Stone 30; no market is held during the Five that follow.

\textbf{Ledgerhand.} The Court’s script: Grathic grammar with the verbs removed, in a neat upright hand, all in the passive voice.

\textbf{Levy.} The share a Grathic household owes to the account, spoken of in loaves and bits rather than named outright: three of the four loaves baked in Grain go on the levy. People speak around the word, not at the thing it counts.

\textbf{The Listening Stones.} Standing stones in the high Rim against which the Vorr sit for days and come away with numbers.

\textbf{The living patch.} A graft of wall taken from a donor and set over a break, held until the vessel takes.

\textbf{The loaf shelf.} The shelf in a Grathic kiln-house on which a household keeps its days badly: loaves are pushed along the board, a glance goes to the clay jar on the wall, and a space at the end of the row is left with no figure because nobody calls it a number. A saying of the loaf-shelves of Low Kiln: \emph{Two gaps on a shelf are two gaps till a finger lays them together. After that they are an account, and an account wants a name. Keep your finger off the shelf.} On Seed 6, Y.H. 813, another loaf’s worth went off the Vail shelf between dusk and light with no scrape, crumb, print or word, leaving two empty places where one had stood; the boy set them beside the empty place in the fold in two rooms that do not touch and wrote no cause across the space. A further saying of the clay-bound of Low Kiln runs: \emph{A figure kept in a fist costs nothing; a place kept on a shelf costs a loaf a day and nobody counts it.} On Seed 24, Y.H. 813, a man brought a number up out of a fist toward the yard well, looked at it and put it back in his sleeve so the figure arrived nowhere, while a neighbour at this shelf laid the old space at the row’s end and the empty place at the child’s ear under one cause in a single breath; the boy kept the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s one crust and its empty place, and the neighbour’s saying on three places that do not touch and wrote no cause across any of them. Another saying is heard at the loaf-shelves of Low Kiln: \emph{Two gaps named in one breath become one hunger. Keep your breath for the pot, and keep the bread where it was put.} On Seed 12, Y.H. 813 a neighbour at the Vail shelf reached past the bare board and named the old space at the row’s end as a thing the planting brought in and the empty place at the boy’s ear as a child’s appetite in one breath, her hand going to the board before her eyes went to the boy; she took her loaf and went with her pot and never saw the two were one absence. The boy filed two tellings on two places and wrote no cause across the space (T097, planted). On Seed 15 a neighbour again said the old place at the end came in with the planting and went off with her pot, never seeing the empty place at his ear; the witness was advanced toward the far-off finger, not paid, and no third gap came. On Seed 18 a second neighbour reached past the bare board for a loaf, her hand going to the old empty place first and opening for the half-beat it takes to find what is not there, and said the gap came in with the planting with a short row to finish it; she went off with her pot without seeing the empty place at the boy’s ear. Two tellings of one absence were held on two places and kept from touching the one crust and its unnamed empty place in the fold; they were advanced, not paid, and no third gap came and no finger in Low Kiln laid them together. On Seed 21, Y.H. 813 a neighbour with a pot again reached past the palm’s breadth of bare board, opened for the half-beat it takes to find what was not there, closed on the hard heel of a loaf beyond and said in one breath that the old space at the row’s end came in with the planting and that this one was the price of a wet thing set down wrong, without seeing the two were one absence or seeing the empty place at the boy’s ear; her hand went to the board before her eyes found him. A \textbf{third} shaping of the held thing now stood beside the two tellings and the watcher’s late turn, advanced and not paid, with no joining, no name and no third gap.

\textbf{Loan that can hear.} A debt whose borrower has an ear for vessels. A loan that can hear is worth more than the debt that holds the borrower and can therefore be called; in the Vail house on Stone 22, Y.H. 812 such a loan was exercised when a flat note passed the door and Tarn’s head turned a degree, and it bought nobody anything.

\textbf{The Long Night.} The third of the Five; no fire after dusk, and stories of the Return are told in the dark.

\textbf{The Long Sitting.} The Vorr coming-of-age at forty: a season sitting still against a stone, listening.

\textbf{Low Kiln.} The poor quarter of Sill on the south bank below the sill, where the kilns stand and the Ash ridge lies thick.

\textbf{M}

\textbf{The Marsh Mother.} The peat cult of the Fenmarch, which keeps warmth in the mud and gives it back to whoever can reach it.

\textbf{Measure.} The amount of Warm a vessel holds, booked in embers; also the shape of that warmth, which is the self.

\textbf{Mender’s failure.} The name given in the deep accounts to a vessel recalled in an earlier age to solve the same problem, who failed in a particular way.

\textbf{Mire-fever.} A blight of the Fenmarch water that burns and then leaves the victim colder after each cycle.

\textbf{Mud End.} A peat hamlet three leagues downriver of Sill, whose winter peat decides whether anyone stays warm.

\textbf{N}

\textbf{Nine Pots.} A pottery hamlet eight leagues west of Sill with four kilns, a shared clay pit and a permanent feud with Sill over the road.

\textbf{The Nine Wells.} Hot springs in the Keel where the ground gives back more than it takes; five are sealed by the Court and the keys are kept.

\textbf{The Nine Who Kept.} The temple’s figures who came after the First Breaking, drove the first repairs and left the rite of the Return behind.

\textbf{O}

\textbf{One in twelve.} The figure printed on the Weighing notices and read aloud at Account-day: one part in twelve of a household’s measure is kept back for the Hearth. It is spoken as \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, in a voice that makes a market lean in. It was read again at the year’s last market on Stone 30, Y.H. 812, as the levy was called for the feast and said not to be called by the man who read it. What Low Kiln actually gives is another matter; see \textbf{Deduction}. On Silt 20, Y.H. 813, Account-day after the flood, it was read over a thinner crowd than had stood at the flood’s Account-day, the water and the lean week having taken bodies out of the market; the printed figure stood unchallenged over fewer people while the true subtraction went over the basket unspoken, so that a figure read aloud was not the figure paid. On Seed 10, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of Seed, Berr Clay read it twice over the basket at the Cross, called the levy for Seed and said it was not called by him; the number for the planting went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrived nowhere, the true subtraction stayed in the locked box, and the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself. On Seed 13, Y.H. 813 Berr Clay came up the clay road from the Cross with the cord of his office folded under his coat, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, called the levy and took himself out of his own sentence with \emph{There’ll be a slate at the watch}; the true subtraction stayed in the locked box and the number for the planting went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrived nowhere. On Seed 15 he came down off the north road at midday to the worked strips and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the hands, saying a number goes into a slate and not into a strip; the levy was called and not by him, the true subtraction stayed in the locked box, and a figure read aloud was not the figure paid. On Seed 20, Account-day, he read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the worked strips where the hands had gone in on Seed 15, called the levy and said it was not called by him; a number goes into a slate, not into a strip, and the true subtraction sat in the locked box in his house up the road. A figure read aloud was not the figure paid and nothing in the ground changed its figure because a man had looked at it, and the sentence went around the square like a bucket passed from hand to hand with nobody asking who was carrying it. On Seed 22, Y.H. 813 he came up short off the north road to the yard well, wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, passed a finger over a narrow slate held unopened against his forearm and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, saying a number goes into a slate and not into a strip and that there would be a slate at the watch; a man brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it, put the fist in his sleeve and went off, so the figure arrived nowhere, and the true subtraction stayed in the locked box in his house up the road.

\textbf{Opened.} The rank of a vessel that has cut a way and can move Warm deliberately within the self.

\textbf{The Opening of the Slates.} Ilmen 1, when the Court opens the new year’s accounts.

\textbf{The outward way.} A procedure by which a Drawn practitioner pushes a flow of Warm out of the body at short range.

\textbf{Overfilling.} Pouring more Warm into a vessel than its walls can hold; the head rises and the vessel cooks its own contents.

\textbf{P}

\textbf{The Peat Line.} The wet frontier where Sere’s northern advance stopped in Y.H. 634 and where the two powers trade, raid and buy measures.

\textbf{Pot gone wrong.} A Grathic household’s name for a vessel cracked from lip to foot. The phrase names the vessel, not the sound it made, and a pot gone wrong is swept around and gone past rather than decided about. On Stone 25, Y.H. 812 one cracked two paces from the boy in the Clay Yard and nobody called the knock a sound.

\textbf{Quiet ash.} The Court’s licensed medicine, sold to the rich who want their previous life to stop arriving in dreams.

\textbf{The quiet seal.} The forbidden procedure of closing a vessel so that nothing leaks in or out.

\textbf{R}

\textbf{Reed Cut.} The Fenfolk coming-of-age at twelve: cutting a bundle of reed alone in the dark and bringing it back without speaking.

\textbf{Reed-wolf.} A wolf of the lower Ilm reedbeds that hunts in packs and goes for the throat and the inside of the elbow.

\textbf{The Remembering.} The fourth of the Five, when names of the dead are spoken and whole returns announced in a clean voice.

\textbf{The Return.} The rite by which the dead are held to come back in new bodies through the mercy of the Hearth; the first thing a child learns and the last thing a dying person hears.

\textbf{The Rim.} The chain of cold mountains that rings Sarn, broken by a few passes, beyond which lies the Waste.

\textbf{Rim current.} The slow current of Warm draining toward the Waste, which makes the Keldish mines sweat.

\textbf{Rim Road.} The road from Sill west-north-west to Keld Keep, a hundred and twenty leagues of improving road and worsening weather.

\textbf{Rim-seam.} The seam at the horizon where sky and clay meet, riveted with stars; it carries many repairs laid one over another.

\textbf{S}

\textbf{The Salt Road.} The trade route from Sill through Greybank to the Vhaleni ports, eighty leagues.

\textbf{Salt Walk.} The Vhaleni coming-of-age at fourteen: walking the pans barefoot at low tide and naming a tide never seen.

\textbf{Salt-thing.} A shape of salt and cold water in the Sallow that taps the hull of a boat and draws its store away.

\textbf{The Sallow draw.} The current of Warm running seaward into the Sallow, blessed by the dippers and taxed by the Court.

\textbf{The Sallow Sea.} A cold inland sea the colour of skimmed milk whose tides run against the wind and are said to follow the Warm rather than the moon.

\textbf{Seam-blight.} A blight that travels along an old repair and widens it by a hair’s breadth each season.

\textbf{Seam-serpent.} A long thing that moves along the under-seam and draws Warm out through the stone.

\textbf{Seam-tide.} The rising and falling of the Warm in the seams of the world, read by the Vorr from the Listening Stones.

\textbf{The Second.} A person in whom a graft from a differently shaped donor has produced a want for a life that was not theirs.

\textbf{Second Want.} The Court’s struck-from-the-record name for the Warm trying to resume the shape of a former owner; the common name is the second chill.

\textbf{Seed.} The month of planting, third in the Sarnish year. In Grath the first work of Seed is not planting but sweeping: the yard goes around what the last flood left with a broom and a glance and no figure spoken, and the planting strips east of Low Kiln are spoken of as a direction that will want hands, not as a number. On Seed 1, Y.H. 813 the mud of Silt had set into a brown skin holding a boot’s print, and the new finer grey in the Vail corner was still unswept and still called the thaw. On Seed 2–4 the first planting work went into those strips east of Low Kiln: seed came out of a fist in handfuls nobody counted, brooms went around what the sweep had left, and a man who said the strips wanted hands was told the weather would have the last word, so that neither the hands nor the strips ever had a figure put to them. A saying of the seed-grounds: \emph{Sow with the hand and count with the hand; the slate lies in the sun and takes no seed.} Another planting saying of Low Kiln is \emph{the hands go in by the look}: \emph{The seed goes in by the fist and the hands go in by the look. Ask either what it cost and it will tell you the weather.} On Seed 15, Y.H. 813 the hands at last went into the worked strips east of Low Kiln --- stooped backs along turned ground, seed out of fists in handfuls nobody counted, brooms around what the sweep left --- still counted in glances and never in a figure; see \textbf{The hands go in by the look}. Through Seed 21–23 the last tend of the planting stood in those strips with the hands still counted in glances and handfuls and never in a figure; a woman shut her fist rather than say how many hands the work would want and a man with a barrow shaped a number and thought better of giving it, so the direction carried for a month had still no figure at its foot. Through Seed 24–26 the last tend held with the seed up and nobody giving a figure for the hands that set it; a man brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it and put it back in his sleeve so it arrived nowhere, and the figure for the hands still went nowhere at the close of the tend.

\textbf{Sere.} The hot southern empire of grain, wine, bowls and open chattel slavery, ruled by the Sun-Emperor.

\textbf{Sere factors.} The empire’s agents in the north, who buy poor measures with credit and ship them south.

\textbf{The shape of the measure.} The pattern of a vessel’s Warm, which is the self; it is fragile and thins with every pouring.

\textbf{The Singing Sill.} The ledge of hard stone under the falls at Sill, which gives a low note when the Warm rises in Ilmen. On Ilmen 25, Y.H. 813 it gave that note earlier than it should and the yard called it weather; the boy kept the early note beside the told bell, the heard bell and the kiln’s own missing breath in four places that did not touch.

On Silt 7, Y.H. 813 it gave its low note a week ahead of its hour, felt in the roots of the teeth before the ear placed it out in the water, and the yard said the water ran fast under the ice and then said weather; the boy kept the early note beside the told bell, the heard bell and the kiln’s gap in four places, joined by nobody. On Silt 15 it was spoken of past tense as the thaw that was, along with the honeyed ice and the hairlines that had stopped short of the edge.

\textbf{Sill.} The town of just over four thousand souls where the Ilm drops four feet over a ledge; Corin’s birthplace.

\textbf{Slate-name.} The only name an officer of the Keeping has, entered on the rolls in Ledgerhand on entering the service.

\textbf{Slate Row.} The Court quarter east of the Cross at Sill, holding the collector’s table, the assessor’s house and the Waiting Room.

\textbf{Slip.} The wet clay worked in the pits of Low Kiln and poured into moulds on the wheel; it dries the colour of old bone on a thrower’s forearms. Work in the slip is commonly paid for in the thaw.

\textbf{Slip pits.} The clay pits of the Clay Yard in Low Kiln, counted as nineteen steps to the drying rack and nineteen back; Dessa Silt has walked the count every day for six years. The cough that comes off them in cold weather is called weather, as if the pits owned it.

\textbf{The Slip Brook.} A narrow clay-coloured stream through the Clay Yard whose colour the children of Low Kiln read as weather. On Ilmen 9, Y.H. 813 its clay-heavy rise came up behind the drying racks in the night and took Dessa Silt from the end of nineteen steps; the yard lifted her out with their hands and no collector was called.

Through Days 61–67, Y.H. 813 it ran clay-heavy and higher behind the drying racks, going over itself with a low note the district had no word for, and the yard called it the thaw.

\textbf{The Spending.} The Sere doctrine that a vessel was made to be emptied gloriously and that a life hoarded is a life wasted.

\textbf{The Standing Post.} The raised boardwalk in the Fenmarch where reeves settle fines and feuds and which is the only Fen place outsiders are shown.

\textbf{Star-rivet.} A rivet of the rim-seam, one of the stars; one is said to have fallen in the Ash Times.

\textbf{Steward.} The head of the Warm Court; Steward Derren holds the office in the present year.

\textbf{Stone.} The month of deep winter, river ice and counted fuel; the year begins in it.

\textbf{The Sweating.} A Keldish calamity in which Warm comes up through the stone of the deep mines in a lethal flood, heralded by the smell of hot lead.

\textbf{T}

\textbf{Tallow Works.} A rendering house for sheep fat two leagues north-east of Sill, whose smell carries into town on a north wind.

\textbf{Tempering.} The practice of repeated small strains so that a vessel’s walls learn to yield without opening.

\textbf{Temple of the Return.} The public church of the Keeping, which teaches that the world was made whole and cracked once.

\textbf{Tend.} A week of ten days; every month holds three whole tends, and the tenth day of each is Account-day. A saying of the clay-bound of Low Kiln: \emph{A tend is counted by what is left on the board, not by what went into the ground. A hand reaches for the empty place and closes on the loaf beyond it and goes on; the shelf keeps its own account and gives nobody a figure.} In the last tend of Seed, Y.H. 813 the hands went on in the strips and the loaf shelf kept two gaps nobody called a number; through Seed 24–26 the last tend held with the seed up and the hands still counted in glances and handfuls and never in a figure, and the shelf kept its two gaps in a room that did not touch the fold’s one crust and its empty place.

\textbf{Thane of Clay.} Grath’s ruler, chosen by the kiln-masters of Sill and confirmed by the Court’s factor at Greybank.

\textbf{The thaw.} The spring working season, when the brook comes up and the clay goes soft. Debts in Low Kiln are often put off until then, in the phrase \emph{you’ll pay for it in the thaw}. Through Ilmen 19–25, Y.H. 813 the thaw came on in frost-bloom written back on the well-lip, oiled paper hanging slack in its frame, a silence where an argument used to stand, more hairlines stopping short of the edge of the Ilm, an early low note from the Singing Sill and a high clay-heavy brook, and the district had one word for all of it: weather. On Ilmen 25 a weak board in the plank walk at the Weir was said plainly to be still there and trodden by nobody. On Silt 1 a new hairline of grey gathered in the corner of the Vail kiln-house beside the clean dark line where the old Ash ridge had turned; Sella stood over it with a broom, called it the thaw and did not sweep it.

On Silt 2–8, Y.H. 813 the higher clay-heavy brook going over itself behind the drying racks, the early Singing Sill note, the weak board trodden by nobody, the widening hairlines, the honeyed-all-through ice and a new fine grey in the Vail corner were all called the thaw or weather, and the year’s flood stood four days off. On Silt 15, after the water had come and gone, the honeyed ice, the hairlines that had stopped short of the edge and the early Singing Sill note were renamed all at once as \emph{the thaw that was}, as though a thing said after the fact were the same as a thing said before it. Sella told the fire it was the thaw and went on not sweeping the new grey beside the clean dark line; the yard went back to its steps and its mud on the one word. Through Silt 16–18 the yard went around that mud with a broom and a glance and no figure spoken, and the new finer grey beside the old clean dark line lay unswept because the house called it the thaw and said it would go when it goes. Through Silt 19–25 the lean week went around the mud in a brown skin that kept a boot’s print, and the honeyed ice, the hairlines that had stopped short of the edge, the early Singing Sill note, the gone board at the Weir and the out-of-line landing were spoken of only past tense as \emph{the thaw that was} --- a thing said after the fact treated as if it had been said before it. Through Silt 26–30 and onto Seed 1 the finer grey in the Vail corner lay unswept beside the old clean dark line, still called the thaw that would go when it goes; on Seed 1 the first work of the planting month was sweeping rather than planting, and a man said the strips east of town would want hands by the morrow without putting a figure to them. Through Seed 5–11 the planting has become waiting: seed stands in the strips and the yard goes around the brown skin holding a boot-print, the clean dark line, the new finer grey beside it and the space under the lowest rack with a broom and a glance and no figure spoken. Sella tells the fire it is the thaw each day and leaves the new grey unswept; the two lines stay in two places and neither becomes the other. Through Seed 5–11 the planting became waiting: seed stood in the strips east of Low Kiln and the yard went around the boot-print, the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack with a broom and a glance and no figure. Through Seed 12–14, Y.H. 813 the new finer grey lay unswept beside the old clean dark line and was still called the thaw that would go when it went; the yard argued it early against late and Tarn agreed with both while wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went. Through Seed 15–17 the brown skin of the worked strips held the boot-print and the stone the flood left, the brooms went around both lines, and the new finer grey beside the clean dark line in the Vail corner stayed unswept because the house said it was the thaw and would go when it goes; Sella told the fire it was the thaw on all three days and Tarn agreed with the early and the late while wanting the late because it puts off the paying.

\textbf{Thin.} A vessel that leaks faster than it takes in; the common condition of the poor, the spent and the returned poor. Also the bottom rank of a vessel.

\textbf{Thin return.} A return in which many measures are pooled and divided among many infants; what comes back is a stranger with a faint interest in a life it cannot name.

\textbf{Thin-child.} \emph{See} The Hollow.

\textbf{Tide-lore.} The Vhaleni discipline of reading the Sallow draw, taught by the dippers.
