\textbf{Triage.} The old-life word for the surgeon’s act of sorting the wounded; Dan’s gift and his heresy in Sarn.

\textbf{Two tellings of one absence.} A neighbour’s saying at the loaf shelf of Low Kiln, from the morning of Seed 12, Y.H. 813: \emph{Two gaps named in one breath become one hunger. Keep your breath for the pot, and keep the bread where it was put.} It is spoken over the old space at the end of the loaf row and the empty place at a child’s ear, which the speaker takes for two things and never sees as one absence. The boy who hears it files the two sayings on two places and writes no cause across the space between them, having learned what likeness laid on likeness will do to a man who wants an answer; the witness is planted for a far-off day when a finger will lay the two places together and an account will want a name (T097). On Seed 18 a second neighbour named the old gap as a thing the planting brought in and went off with her pot without seeing the empty place at the boy’s ear; the two tellings were kept on two places with no finger laid across them, advanced and still unpaid. On Seed 21, Y.H. 813 a neighbour made a cause of two bare boards in one breath, calling the old space a thing the planting brought in and the new gap the price of a wet thing set down wrong, and went off with her pot without seeing that the two were one absence or seeing the empty place at the boy’s ear; this was a \textbf{third} shaping of the held thing, filed beside the two tellings and the watcher’s late turn, advanced and still not paid, with no joining, no name and no third gap. On Seed 24, Y.H. 813 a neighbour at the shelf again named the old space a thing the planting brought in and the empty place at the boy’s ear a child’s appetite in one breath, laying two rooms under one cause without seeing they were one absence; a \textbf{fourth} shaping stood beside the two tellings, the watcher’s late turn and the Seed 21 cause, advanced and still \textbf{not paid}, with no joining, no name, no fourth likeness and no third gap. See \textbf{The loaf shelf}.

\textbf{U}

\textbf{The Unbanked.} The Court’s name for a secret faction of persons of the sealed opinion, descended from the Ash Rising and dedicated to the Final Banking.

\textbf{Unclosed account.} The crime of refusing a lawful collection; the offender is clip-held by the wrist until consent.

\textbf{The Uncollected.} A dead vessel whose Warm has not been drawn and which walks until it leaks into the Waste.

\textbf{Under-seam.} The seam beneath the ground, below which lies the dark where nothing is kept.

\textbf{V}

\textbf{The Vail kiln-house.} The kiln-house in the Clay Yard held by the Vail family for four generations, where Corin is taken in as a foundling.

\textbf{Vhal.} The principal Vhaleni port on the Sallow shore, seat of the Council of Tides, with salt pans and glass furnaces.

\textbf{Vhalen.} The salt republic of port towns on the Sallow, governed by the Council of Tides.

\textbf{Vorr.} A people apart, tall, long-lived, who hold their measure in the bone, keep the Listening Stones and do not undergo the Return.

\textbf{W}

\textbf{Walking thin.} People with the measures of the returned poor who keep moving because stopping is the same as cooling.

\textbf{Warm.} The living, stored heat of which Sarn is made; the poor call it \emph{the warm} and the learned call it \emph{the kept heat}. It has pressure, currents, sources and sinks.

\textbf{Warm Court.} The institution that owns the Hearth, the banks and the Returns and calls itself the Keeping.

\textbf{Warm-stone.} A Keldish stone that holds heat longer than any other substance in Sarn. In Low Kiln a common river stone, warmed at a neighbour’s fire and wrapped in wool, does the same work for a newborn for a few hours; it is not a warm-stone and nobody calls it one.

\textbf{Warm-stone grub.} A beetle larva of the deep mines that eats warm-stone from within and is a sign that a sweating may follow.

\textbf{Warden of the Rim.} The hereditary ruler of Keld; Karric VII closed the Cold Pass in Y.H. 741.

\textbf{The Waste.} The cold country beyond the cracks at the edge of all things, where everything unheld goes.

\textbf{Wastelings.} The bands beyond the Rim who take what the world loses; they have no banks, no Returns and no word for a debt.

\textbf{Water over water (the river’s own note).} The low continual turning a stream makes when it has more of itself than its channel will carry; water going over its own rise. Heard behind the drying racks on Silt 2, Y.H. 813, it is not a vessel’s note and is not counted among the hearings; the district has no word for it and calls it the thaw. The boy files it on a place of its own beside the told bell, the heard bell, the early Sill note and the kiln’s gap, and writes no cause across any of them. In the year’s flood of Silt 9–15, Y.H. 813 it became the note of a whole district under strain --- a low turning of many small failures inside one slow, certain one, a vessel of such capacity that no hand in it could have got around it, with a thin place nobody would name. The boy filed it beside the told bell, the heard bell, the early Sill note and the kiln’s gap and wrote no cause across any of them; no one in the district had a word for it or a hand to point at the thin place. At the going of the light on Day 100, Seed 11, Y.H. 813, the river’s low muttered note of water going over water came through the door standing a finger’s width open while the fire’s four, four and a gap came up through the floor, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred days; the boy’s hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water and came down. At the going of the light on Day 103, Seed 14, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note of water going over water came through the door standing a finger’s width open, nearer at the going of the water than at its coming, while the fire’s four, four and a gap came up through the floor under blind ash, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and three days; the boards above kept four nails and four and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, and the two counts did not meet. At the going of the light on Day 106, Seed 17, Y.H. 813 the two sounds came in the same two separate places as for a hundred and six days, under the Vail roof where one brown-edged crust lay stiff in the fold and the fire’s payer was still unnamed; his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down, and the dark under the roof kept the count of one hundred and six without a figure. At the going of the light on Day 109, Seed 20, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note came through the door standing a finger’s width open, nearer at the going of the water than at its coming, and the kiln’s four, four and a gap came through the floor under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and nine days; the boards overhead kept four nails and four and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, the two counts did not meet, and his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down with the count standing at one hundred and nine, unspent. At the going of the light on Day 112, Seed 23, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the kiln’s four, four and a gap came through the floor under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and twelve days; the boards overhead kept four nails, four, and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, the two counts did not meet, and his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down with the count standing at one hundred and twelve, unspent.

\textbf{Weather.} The district’s one word for whatever a person can go home warm on. It does not name the thing it is said over; it grants permission to stop looking at it. On Silt 7, Y.H. 813 a washwoman said the water ran fast under the ice and then said weather and went home warm on the word, and a man come back from looking at the honeyed ice was answered with the same word and nodded as though it settled him.

\textbf{Weighing.} The second of the Five, when the year’s measures are read aloud and the rich learn how whole they are. In Sill the reading is given in a clean voice that wears a temple’s clothes and takes the speaker neatly out of his own sentences, in the same grammar heard at the Cross; a whole return may be announced for a person who is not in the room.

\textbf{Weighing Hall.} The hall in the Hearthseat where the measures are read at the Weighing and the Hearth-fire burns behind cold iron.

\textbf{The Weir.} The eel traps and plank walk one league upriver of Sill, where the Fish Blessing is held and Rusk walks at dusk.

\textbf{Welled.} The rank of a vessel that can draw on stores held in the world itself — wells, seams or another’s bank — without owning them.

\textbf{Well-draw.} The procedure by which a Welled practitioner draws on a store the world already holds; the level drops for everyone.

\textbf{Whole.} A vessel that holds without leaking; also the rank of such a vessel.

\textbf{Whole return.} A return in which one person’s warmth is kept intact and the person comes back as themselves, with memory.

\textbf{Widow’s mark.} The Grathic institution by which a widow holds a kiln in her own right; the only Grathic institution nobody argues with. A thumb-length of lead-glazed clay with the kiln scratched into it, worn at the throat and touched only before the kiln is opened. The Court’s factor at Greybank confirms the mark; the confirmation is spoken of as a kindness, and kindness is entered.
